REPORT 
The Action Taken Report (ATR) of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Science and Technology, Environment, Forests and Climate Change deals with 
the action taken by the Government on the recommendations/observations of the contained in its 
‘Three Hundred Sixty Third Report ’ on ‘Demands for Grants (2022 -23) of the Ministry of 
Environment, Forest & Climate Change ’. The Report was presented to Rajya Sabha and la id on 
the Table of Lok Sabha on the 15th March, 2022.  
2. Action Taken Notes (ATN s) have been received from the Ministry of Environment, 
Forest and Climate Change in respect of all the sixteen recommendations/observations contained 
in the ‘Three Hundred Sixty Third Report’. The replies of the Ministry of Environment, Forest & 
Climate Change have been categorized as follows:-  
Chapter I:  Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the 
Government:  
  Para Nos. 4.3, 4.6, 5.2, 6.5, 7.4, 7.6, 8.2, 9.5, 10.2, 11.2, 11.3, 12.3,    
13.2 and 13.3

 The Committee is pleased to note that the Ministry has accepted its 
fourteen recommendations/observations as mentioned in Chapter -I of the 
Report.  
Chapter II:   Recommendations/Observations which the Committee does not desire 
to pursue in view of the Government’s replies:  
Para Nos. 7.8  
Total recommendation – 01. Not to be pursued further. 
The Committee is convinced with the explanation furnished by the 
Ministry and, therefore, does not want to pursue the recommendation  
further. 
Chapter III:   Recommendations/Observations in respect of w hich replies of the 
Government have not been accepted by the Committee: ‘NIL’ 
Chapter IV: Recommendations/Observations in respect of which final replies of the 
Government are still awaited:  
Para Nos. 6.3  
Total recommendation – 01. To be pursued further 
 The Committee desires that the Ministry should furnish pointed and detailed 
Action Taken Notes i n respect of the recommendation/observation  made in 
Chapter IV of the Report. 
2. The details of the ATNs have been analyzed in the succeeding Chapters.  
 
 
 

2  
CHAPTER-I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED 
BY THE GOVERNMENT 
BUDGETARY DETAILS FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2021-22 AND ALLOCATION 
FOR 2022-23 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.1 The Committee notes the adverse effect of COVID -19 pandemic on the budgetary 
allocation of the Ministry due to which the  BE allocation of the Ministry for 2021 -22 was 
substantially reduced by Rs. 349.93 crore, a decrease of  12.9% at RE stage, thus resulting in 
non-release of funds for all proposed activities mentioned in the Annual Plan of Operations 
(APOs) of various schemes.  The Ministry has been able to spend 71% of the RE allocation up to 
31st January, 2022.  The Committee is satisfied with the utilisation of funds and recommends the 
Ministry to ensure its full utilisation by the end of the financial year.  
                                                                                                             (Para 4.3 of the363rd Report)   
Action Taken 
1.2 As on 31.03.2022, the Actual Expen diture (A.E) was Rs. 2444.62 crore  against R.E of 
Rs. 2520.00 crore  which is 97.01% with respect to R.E. Major non -utilization of funds i.e.       
Rs. 75.38 crore  is mainly due to non -utilization of funds (Rs. 70.00 crore ) under the National 
Coastal Mission (NCM) Scheme as the proposed activities of the Scheme could not b e 
undertaken due to delay in approval of the ENCORE Project. 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.3 The Committee notes that the reduction in funds of the Ministry at RE 2021 -22 was 
mainly due to the situation caused by the COVID -19 pandemic.  However, the BE 20 22-23 of 
the Ministry is still less than the BE 2020-21 (Rs.3100 crore). The Committee is of the view that 
the programmes for which the Ministry has sought additional funding are of utmost importance 
in the present day context, and must be given the topmos t priority. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry must be provided the requisite allocation for timely and efficient 
implementation of the programmes. At the same time, the Ministry should also review the 
capital requirement of the programmes/schemes and explore internal budgetary reallocations to 
ensure availability of funds for the projects. The Committee also recommends that the Ministry 
should make proactive efforts to ensure that the physical targets of the Ministry in respect of its 
various schemes/programmes are on schedule and the allocation made at BE is utilised 
optimally so that it is on a firm ground to seek additional funds at the Supplementary/ RE stage 
to achieve its physical and financial objectives during the financial year.          (Para 4.6 ibid)           
Action Taken 
1.4 The suggestions of the Committee have been noted for due compliance.  Apart from 
ensuring sufficient allocation towards various schemes of the Ministry, achievement of physical 
targets is ensured through various monitoring and evaluation mechanisms.   Key Performance 
Indicators are also being devised to achieve physical and financial objectives. 
 
 
 

3  
BUDGETARY ALLOCATION AND ACTUAL UTILISATION DURING THE LAST 
THREE YEARS 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.5 The Committee notes the pattern of utilisation of allocated amount by the Ministry during 
the last three financial years and finds the same satisfactory.  The Committee acknowledges the 
fact that there was drastic reduction of 35% at RE Stage for the year 2020 -21 due to the adverse 
effect of COVID-19 pandemic which resulted in non -release of funds for its proposed activities,  
even then the Ministry was able to utilise the allocation to the maximum during that year.  The 
Committee also notes that the Ministry has been able to utilise 71% of the RE 2021-22 allocation 
up to 31 st January 2022. The Committee recommends that the Minis try should take necessary 
measures to ensure proper utilisation of these funds by end of the financial year so that the 
targeted outcomes linked to the initiatives of the Ministry are not adversely impacted.  The 
Committee would like to be apprised about th e comprehensive details of the utilisation made 
during the last two months of Financial Year 2021-22.                                            (Para 5.2 ibid)                                                                                             
Action Taken

1.8 Major non-utilization of funds i.e. Rs. 75.38 crore is mainly due to non-utilization of funds 
(Rs. 70.00 crore) under the National Coastal Mission (NCM) Scheme as the proposed activities of 
the Scheme could not be undertaken due to delay in approval of the ENCORE Project.  
Recommendations/Observations 
1.9 The Committee notes with concern the poor utilisation of funds under the ‘National 
Coastal Mission’ (NCM). The Committee while acknowledging the impact of COVID -19 
pandemic which led to delay in activities envisaged under the programme during the financial  
year 2021-22, however urges upon the Ministry to streamline the activities/ projects which are to 
be undertaken in the current Financial Year 2022 -23 and also to impress upon the coastal States, 
which are involved in the Mission about the urgency of imple mentation of the Mission. In this 
regard, the Committee recommends that the Ministry should monitor the status of Project 
Monitoring Units set  up by the State Governments/UTs on regular basis and defaulters may be 
dealt with firmly.                                                                                                        (Para 6.5 ibid)

Action Taken 
1.10 Ministry of Environment, Forest &  Climate Change will closely monitor the 
projects/activities with State /Union Territories Governments and other executing agencies on 
regular basis.        
NATIONAL CLEAN AIR PROGRAMME 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.11 The Committee no tes that the Ministry has not categorically mentioned the actual 
utilisation made under the sub - component National Clean Air Programme (NCAP) during the 
year 2021 -22.  The Committee recommends that the Ministry should invariably furnish the 
information to the Committee to facilitate a more detailed analysis of Demand for Grants. Funds 
allocated to NCAP and its utilisation thereof in future, needs a transparent elucidation.  The 
Committee feels that the Ministry should make more efforts to get increased budgetary allocation 
for the NCAP considering the impact of increase in air pollution on climate change. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that concerted efforts should be made by the Ministry for 
optimum utilisation of funds under NCAP.  The Committee exp resses its satisfaction over the 
initiatives of the Ministry in extending incentives and motivating the agencies at municipal level 
towards the target of city-wise reduction of PM 10 concentration.                         (Para 7.4 ibid)                                                                                             
 
Action Taken 
1.12 It is submitted that an amount of Rs.290 cr ore was allocated for 82 cities in F.Y. 2021 -22 
from budget allocation of Control of Pollution Scheme. The same allocation has been made for 
F.Y. 2022 -23. However, the release of funds in a given financial year is totally based on the 
utilisation of funds released in the previous financial years. Following the guidelines of 
expenditure con trol in the General Financial Rules, 2017,   Rs. 98.75 cr ore has been released 
under the sub-component-"National Clean Air Programme" of the Control of Pollution Scheme in 
the FY 2021 -22 (covering 46 non -attainment cities). The Committee's remarks regarding  
transparent elucidation of funds allocated to NCAP and utilization thereof in the future have been 
noted. It may please be noted that under NCAP, Rs 497.94 crore have been released under the 
sub-component-"National Clean Air Programme" of the Control of P ollution Scheme up to 
31st March, 2022. 
 
1.13 With regard to Committee's concern on efforts to get the budgetary allocation for NCAP 
increased, Ministry has provisioned the same in the Expenditure Finance Committee ( EFC) 
Memo of the Control of Pollution Scheme for appraisal by the competent forum 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.14 On the basis of information furnis hed above, the Committee observes that the details 
furnished by the Ministry in respect of physical targets set and actually achieved during 2021 -22 
appear to be incomplete and incoherent. Further, it can be inferred from the above table that the 
Ministry has failed to provide quantifiable details of physical and financial targets and their 
achievements under NCAP during 2021 -22.  The Committee is constrained to note this casual 
approach of the Ministry in furnishing the data and strongly recommends the Ministry to en sure 
that such data is maintained in a proper format, updated regularly and provided to the 
Committee in a manner which is convenient and insightful for the Committee to examine so as to 
get a clear picture of the actual physical and financial targets achieved.                (Para 7.6 ibid) 

5  
Action Taken 
1.15 Committee's observations have been duly noted. Ministry is pleased to inform Committee 
that Ministry has launched PRANA  (Portal for Regulation of Air -pollution in Non -Attainment 
cities), a portal for monitoring implementation of NCAP on 7 th September 2021. In this portal, 
action plans of cities, States and line ministries will be reflected and monitored pertaining to 
implementation status thereon. 
CONSERVATION OF NATURAL RESOURCES AND ECOSYSTEMS 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.16 The Committee is concerned about the impact of the reduction in budgetary allocation on 
the outcomes and physical targets of this Central Sector Scheme. The Committee notes with 
concern the poor utilisation of funds and attitude  of the State Governments/Union  Territories in 
non-submission of Utilisation Certificates and Project Progress Reports. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends the Ministry to optimally utilise the funds and urges upon the State 
Governments/UTs to adhere to the guidelines of the Department of Expenditure for timely release 
of funds under the Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS). At the same time the Ministry should also 
develop a mechanaism for regular monitoring of the progress of the projects as well as utilisation 
of funds by the States/UTs so as to ensure timely achievements of set targets, both physical and 
financial.                                                                                                                     (Para 8.2 ibid)                                                                                                   
Action Taken 
(i) Biosphere Reserves are located in extremely hostile and interior places and the Management 
Action Plans (MAP) are received in variably at a very late stage, which hinders timely 
disbursement of funds. 
2.18 In addition, due to COVID -19 situation, there has been inordinate delay by the State 
Governments in taking timely action for implementation of the MAP. There has been also a de lay 
on the part of the B iosphere Reserves in subsequent submission for request for financial 
assistance in the form of MAP. 
1.19 From FY 2022 -2023 onwards, it has been decided with the approval of competent 
authority that financial assistance will be provi ded to the Biosphere Reserves only on submission 
of Five Year Integrated Management Action Plan, which shall have an in -built monitoring 
mechanism for set targets. This exercise is based on recommendation by NITI Aayog. 
1.20 Ministry is in the process of o btaining approval of the competent authority on draft Five 
Year Integrated Management Plan for Biosphere Reserve, which will be shared with all State 
Governments for implementation shortly. The process of fund disbursement under the scheme 
will also be initiated once duly filled in proposals are received from the States. 
 1.21  All the State Governments are requested from time to time for compliance of the 
guidelines of Department of Expenditure for timely submission of Utilisation Certificate/ 
Expenditure Statements and Progress Report for timely release of funds. 
(ii) The following is the monitoring framework for wetlands supported under National Plan for 
Conservation of Aquatic Ecosystems (NPCA): 
1.22 The Guidelines for NPCA Scheme of April, 2019 includes Guidelines for Preparation of 
Integrated Management Plans (IMPs) and also developing a monitoring and evaluation plan. This 
is appraised by the Ministry through its independent Appraisal Institutes bef ore sanctioning the 

6  
IMP. This monitoring and evaluation plan  is the basis of monitoring the IMP during and post 
implementation.  
1.23 A tripartite MoU between Government of India, State Government/ UT Administration 
and agency identified for implementation of IMP is also signed containing agreements on sharing 
of costs, timely implementation of IMPs, post project sustainability etc.  
Further, the following Monitoring Committees have also been set up  
 
 Inter-Departmental Monitoring Committee at the State/UT and Divisional/District levels.  
State level Committee is chaired by Principal Secretary of the Department concerned and 
a balanced and representative composition of representatives of all Departments and 
agencies concerned for ensuring time limits and qualitative sound execution of activities. 
 City Level Monitoring Committee (CLMC) is constituted under the chairmanship of 
District Collector to enhance accountability, transparency and to ensure effective 
implementation and timely completion of the IMP. 
 
GREEN INDIA MISSION- NATIONAL AFFORESTATION PROGRAMME 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.24  The Committee expresses dismay on the drastic reduction in budgetary allocation for the 
year 2022-23 vis-à-vis the demand made by the Ministry.  The Committee is concerne d about the 
impact of this reduction in budgetary allocation on the outcomes and physical targets of the 
Central Sector Scheme. The Committee is also concerned about the impact of reduction of 
budgetary allocation on wage employment in rural areas under Gr een India Mission – National 
Afforestation Programme (GIM -NAP), for which budgetary support is a must. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Ministry should prioritise the available resources and ensure full 
utilisation of funds. The Committee, fur ther, recommends that the Ministry must be provided the 
requisite allocation with respect to Green India Mission at RE Stage.                  (Para 9.5 ibid)                                                                                                                                                                                         
 
Action Taken 
 
1.25 Regarding the recommendation on ensuring full utilization of funds, it may be noted that 
under Green India Mission (GIM), 99.53% was utilised against R.E. during 2021 -22. 
Afforestation is critical for Ecological restoration of the degraded areas and also to meet various 
national and international commitments. Recognizing the fact that around 60% percent of the 
allocation under GIM -NAP goes for wage employment in rural sector, the budgetary support is 
essential to implement these schemes. BE 2022 -23 for GIM has increased from RE 2021 -22 i.e., 
Rs. 220 crore to Rs. 317.50 crore  However, the Ministry will also take up appropriate measures 
in addition to the demand for increase in the budgetary allocation. Further, suitable policy 
measures will be initiated to leverage private investments in afforestation and tree planting 
activities. Besides that, GIM will seek convergence with CAMPA to meet the shortfall in budget 
allocation and physical targets for implementing the various activities under various Missions. 
FOREST COVER IN THE COUNTRY 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.26 The Committee expresses satisfaction over the efforts of the Ministry towa rds expansion 
of forest cover area in the country and generation of employment through various forest 
activities. The Committee, however, recommends that the Ministry should take proactive steps to 
further strengthen the existing mechanism through new and effective innovations and strive 
towards further expansion of forest cover with a holistic approach towards maintaining a 

7  
balanced ecosystem. The Committee urges the Ministry to have better coordination with State 
Governments/UTs in implementation of forest activities and for expansion of forest cover. 
                   (Para 10.2 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.28 India’s National Forest Policy, 1988 aims at bringing one -third of geographical area of 
the country under forest or tree cover, and two -third in hills and  mountainous areas. Increasing 
sustainability in the forest/tree cover in the country through massive afforestation and social 
forestry programmes, especially on all denuded, degraded and unproductive lands is one of the 
basic objectives of the National Forest Policy (NFB), 1988.  The policy also encourages planting 
of trees on private lands under State/Corporate, institutional or private ownership along with 
raising of green belts in urban/ industrial areas including plantation of trees alongside roads, 
railway lines, rivers, streams, canals etc. under social forestry. Currently country’s 24.62% area 
is under forest and tree cover. 
1.29  Afforestation and tree plantation activities in the country are undertaken as a cross -
sectoral and multi departmental act ivity in the country under various centrally sponsored 
schemes of different ministries such as National Afforestation Programme (NAP), Green India 
Mission (GIM) of the Ministry of Environment, Forest  and Climate Change     (MoEF&CC);  
National Bamboo Mi ssion, Ministry of Agriculture;  Integrated Watershed Management 
Programme and Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee  Scheme of the 
Ministry of Rural Development , etc. Besides, such activities are also undertaken through a 
number of State Plan and Non Plan Schemes. 
1.30 The collective targets of afforestation for the State(s) are fixed under 20 Point 
Programme and achievement there -under is monitored. The average annual afforestation targets 
and achievements during the last five years have been abou t 1.8 million hectares.   
 
FOREST FIRE PREVENTION AND MANAGEMENT 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
1.31 While the Committee acknowledges the use of satellite technology for detecting forest 
fires, the Committee feels that there is need to strengthen the ground mechanism and develop a 
well equipped and trained workforce to fight forest fires. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
strengthening post -fire assessments, inter -state knowledge sharing and research to understand 
the longer-term impacts of forest fire whi ch will enable to identify gaps in implementation of the 
existing management system and finding solutions thereon.                                  (Para 11.2 ibid)                                                                                                                                                                       
 
Action Taken 
 
1.32 The number of incidences of forest fire in the country varies from year to year and occurs 
during fire season from November to May every year due to various natural and anthropogenic 
reasons including accumulation of inflammable materials such as dry leaves, twigs, pine needles 
etc. Most of the forest fires in the country are ground fires in which ground vegetation, etc. get 
burnt. 
 
1.33 Ministry prepared a National Action Plan on Forest  Fire in April 2018  after several 
rounds of consultations with all the States and Union Territories. The objective of this Plan is to 
minimize forest fires by informing, enabling and empowering forest fring e communities and 
incentivizing them to work in tandem with the State Forest Departments. The Plan also intends to 
substantially reduce the vulnerability of forests across the diverse forest ecosystems in the 

8  
country against  fire hazards, enhance the capab ilities of forest personnel and institutions in 
fighting fires and speed up recovery after a fire event. 
 
1.34 The Ministry issues advisories to all State and UT Governments before the start 
of fire season for adequate preparedness for effective prevention and management of forest fire. 
 
1.35 Forest Survey of India (FSI), Dehradun, an organization under the Ministry disseminates 
the satellite-based forest fire alerts to the State Forest Departments and other registered mobile 
users whenever forest fires are detected. Till date, around 1.30 lakh users have been registered to 
receive the fire alerts from FSI. 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.36 Tackling  forest fires is important for improving the sustainability of the country’s forests. 
The Committee is happy a t the increased allocation of Rs. 44.19 crore, for the Financial Year 
2022-23 for efficient utilisation and sufficient funding to the Ministry for implementation of its 
initiatives/ programmes for forest fire prevention and management at the central and St ate level. 
The Committee also urges upon the Ministry to promote awareness programmes in regions 
around forest areas for sensitising the concerned stakeholders to prevent accidental cases of 
forest fires. Proper fencing of forest areas,  real time monitorin g of illegal activities in forest 
areas and punitive action against the miscreants would further help the agencies in preventing 
forest fires. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should take into 
consideration national and international best practices for forest fire management.  
          (Para 11.3 ibid)                                                                                            
Action Taken 
 
1.38 FSI is currently working on a system similar to Canadian Forest Fire Danger  Rating 
System (CFFDRS), based on Fire Weather Index (FWI) for fire danger rating in India. 
Additionally, Forest Type Layer information and Forest Fire Archival information are also being 
used to generate Forest Fire Danger Rating. The parameters are quant ified and overlaid on grids 
of 5 km x 5 km. 
1.39 FWI consists of six components that account for the effects of fuel, moisture and weather 
conditions on fire behaviour. The first three components are fuel moisture codes, which are 
numeric ratings of the mo isture content of the forest floor and other dead organic matter. Their 
values rise as the moisture content decreases. The remaining three components are fire behaviour 
indices, which represent the rate of fire spread, the fuel available for combustion, an d the frontal 
fire intensity; these three values rise as the fire danger increases.  
1.40 All information regarding FWI is downloadable from GEOS-5 (Goddard Earth Observing 
System Model, Version -5) daily data from NASA’s GFWED database  (Global Fire Weather  
Database), which is satellite calibrated weather data. The FWI values from GEOS -5  daily 
database from NASA’s GFWED database are downloaded and thresholds are customized for 
different physiographic zones of the country using past archive data on a weekly basis. The Fire 
Danger Rating is categorized into five classes, which are Extreme Risk, Very High Risk, High 
Risk, Moderate Risk and Low Risk and uploaded as Web Map Service (WMS) in the Van Agni 
Geo-portal of FSI. 
1.41 During Fire season, the Extreme Risk  and Very High Risk categories of Forest Fire 
Danger Rating based on FWI values are disseminated as Pre -Fire Alerts (PFA) on every 
Thursday of the week to State Forest Departments ( SFDs). PFA’s are disseminated through e -
mail as KML (Keyhole Markup Languag e) file, which is Google Earth compatible file, to 

9  
Principal Chief Conservator of Forests (Head of Forest Force) and Forest Fire Nodal Officer of 
the State Forest Departments. 
1.42 The Ministry supports the efforts of State Governments/Union Territory Admi nistration 
in prevention and control of forest  fire by providing financial assistance for various 
forest fire prevention and management measures such as creation and maintenance of fire lines in 
forest areas, engagement of  fire watchers, creation of water storage structures in forest areas, 
strengthening of forest infrastructure, procurement of firefighting equipment, soil and moisture 
conservation works in high risk areas, awareness creation, incentivizing villages/communities for 
protection against forest  fire etc. During the curr ent financial year Rs. 44.19 crore  has been 
allocated to all the States /UTs under Forest  Fire Prevention and Management Scheme.    A sum 
of about Rs.113.1322 cr ore have been released to the States in last year (2019 -20 to 2021 -22) 
under this scheme. 
MAN-ANIMAL CONFLICT 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.43 The Committee is of the view that the cases of man -animal conflict are on the rise and it 
still remains an area of concern.  As such, there is an urgent need to minimize the instances of 
man-animal conflict that was resulting in both human and animal killi ngs. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Ministry should take proactive steps to sustainably manage and 
minimise man-animal conflict in a balanced manner, whereby the wildlife habitat is improved. 
The Committee urges upon the Ministry to evolve a  mechanism at the national level for uniform 
compensation, early settlement of compensation and rehabilitation of the victims of man -animal 
conflict. The Committee recommends that efforts should be made by the Ministry at local level 
and especially among the communities living in peripheral forest areas to sensitise them towards 
ecological balance through co -existence with wild life. The Committee urges for creation of 
grasslands for grazing of cattle outside the forest area to minimise man-animal conflict. Further, 
State Forest Departments should also be advised to improve availability of fodder and adequate 
water sources in the forests, especially during summers, which would reduce the chances of the 
wildlife venturing out of their habitat in search of these basic needs.                  (Para 12.3 ibid)                                                                      
Action Taken 
 
1.44 To minimize the instances of man -animal conflict, following procedure/advisory/SOPs 
are followed by the Ministry: 
 
I   Project Tiger 
 
1.45 The Government of India, through the National Tiger Conservation Authority, has 
advocated a three pronged strategy to manage human-tiger negative interactions as follows: 
 
(i)  Material and logistical support:  Funding support through the ongoing Centrally Sponsored 
Scheme of Project Tiger, is provided to tiger reserves for acquiring capacity in terms of 
infrastructure and material, to deal with tigers dispersing out of source areas. These are solicited 
by tiger reserves through an Annual Plan of Operation (APO) every year which stems out from an 
overarching Tiger Conservation Plan (TCP), mandated under Section 38 V of the Wildlife 
(Protection) Act, 1972.  Inter alia,  activities such as payment of ex -gratia and compensation, 
periodic awareness campaigns to sensitize, guide and advise the general populace on man -animal 
conflict, dissemination of information through various forms of media, procurement of 
immobilization equipment, drugs, training and capacity building of forest staff to deal with 
conflict events are generally solicited. 

10  
 (ii) Restricting habitat interventions:  Based on the carrying capacity of tigers in a tiger 
reserve, habitat interventions are restricted through an overarching TCP. In case tiger numbers are 
at carrying capacity levels, it is advised that habitat interventions should be limited so that there is 
no excessive spill over of wildlife including tigers thereby minimizing man -animal conflict. 
Further, in buffer areas around tiger reserves, habitat interventions are r estricted such that they 
are sub -optimal vis -à-vis the core/critical tiger habitat areas, judicious enough to facilitate 
dispersal to other rich habitat areas only. 
 
 (iii)  Standard Operating Procedure (SOPs):  The National Tiger Conservation Authority has  
also issued three SOPs to deal with human -animal conflict which are available in public domain. 
These are as under: 
 
i        To deal with emergency arising due to straying of tigers in human dominated landscapes 
ii       To deal with tiger depredation on livestock 
iii     For active management towards rehabilitation of tigers from source areas at the landscape  
level 
 
II Project Elephant 
 
(i) To address issue of human elephant conflict, the states have resorted to capture of 
problematic elephants and the  funds needs to be augmented for the establishment of 
rescue/rehabilitation centres for permanent or temporary housing of wild elephants. 
 
(ii)  Critical elephant habitats are notified as ‘Elephant Reserve’ (ER) for focus and synergy in 
elephant conservation and to reduce conflict. The notification is carried out with the approval of 
Steering Committee formed in the Ministry. So far 31 ERs have been established in 14 major 
elephant States in which 10 ER's are from North Eastern States such as Assa m, Arunachal 
Pradesh, Meghalaya and Nagaland. 
 
 (iii)  A guideline for Management of Human Elephant Conflict has been issued by the 
Ministry on 6.10.2017 and elephant range States have been requested for implementation of the 
same. 
 
III Development of Wildlife Habitats 
 
1.46 The Ministry is implementing CSS -Development of Wildlife Habitats under which 
financial assistance is provided to State/UTs for the protection and conservation of Wildlife 
including implementation of mitigation measures to avoid human -wildlife conflict. The funds are 
also provided under the scheme for making fodder and adequate water sources available in the 
protected areas, awareness programme and development of grasslands and payment of ex-gratia 
relief for loss of life or property caused by wild animals.  The Ministry has revised the rates of ex-
gratia payment vide letter dated 09.02.2018, which is as follows:  
 
Nature of damage caused by wild animals Amount of ex-gratia relief 
a) Death or permanent incapacitation to human 
beings  
Rs.5 lakh 
(b) Grievous injury  Rs 2 lakh 
(c) Minor injury Cost of treatment up to  Rs 25000/- 
(d) Loss of property/crops  States /UTs may adhere to the cost 
norms prescribed by them 
State Governments also provide ex -gratia relief for depredation by wild animals from their own 

11  
funds. The rate of ex- gratia payment varies from State to State. 
 
 (ii) Guidelines on eco-friendly measures to mitigate the impact of linear infrastructure have  been 
published by the Wildlife Institute of India to assist project agencies in designing linear 
infrastructure. 
 (iii) An advisory on dealing with human -wildlife conflict has been issued by the Ministry in 
February 2021, which also envisages that a suita ble portion of ex -gratia relief should be paid 
within 24 hours to the affected persons in the case of death and injury to persons.  
 The recommendation of the Committee, with respect to man -animal conflict, is noted and 
appropriate action will be taken by Ministry of Environment Forest & Climate Change. 
PLASTIC WASTE MANAGEMENT 
Recommendation/Observations 
1.47 The Committee recognizes the importance of plastic waste management and elimination 
of single -use plastics. Single -use plastics being a bio hazard no t only impact wild life and 
ecosystems but also pollute the environment. The Committee, therefore, recommends the 
Ministry to run awareness programmes on regular basis, to educate the people about the ill 
effects of single-use plastics and encourage them to use other sources as a replacement to plastic 
products in day to day usage. The Committee also recommends bringing  stricter norms and 
regulations to discourage the use of single -use plastics and also lay down clear allocation of 
roles and responsibilities.                                                                                      (Para 13.2 ibid) 
Action Taken 
(i) The Plastic Waste Management (PWMR) Rules, 2016, provides the statutory 
framework for plastic waste management in an environmentally sound  manner 
throughout the country. Thirty Four States/UTs have issued notifications/orders 
introducing regulations pertaining to complete or partial ban on plastic carry bags 
and/or identified single -use plastic items, over and above the Plastic Waste 
Management (PWM) Rules, 2016, as amended. 
(ii)    As per the Plastic Waste Management (PWM) Rules, 2016, there is complete ban on   
sachets using plastic material used for storing, packing or selling gutkha, tobacco and 
pan masala. 
(iii) Based on high littering p otential and low utility, the MoEFCC notified the Plastic 
Waste Management Amendment Rules, 2021, on 12th August 2021, 
prohibiting manufacture, import, stocking, distribution, sale and use of 
the following identified single use plastic items, which have lo w utility and high 
littering potential with effect from the 1st July, 2022: 
(a)    ear buds with plastic sticks, plastic sticks for balloons, plastic flags, candy 
sticks,  ice-cream sticks, polystyrene [Thermocol] for decoration; 
(b)    plates, cups, glass es, cutlery such as forks, spoons, knives, straw, trays, 
wrapping or packing films around sweet boxes, invitation cards,   and 
cigarette packets, plastic or PVC banners less than 100 micron, stirrers. 
(iv) The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Cha nge has notified the Guidelines 
on the Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) for plastic packaging vide Plastic 
Waste Management Amendment Rules, 2022, on 16th February, 2022. 
(v) The enforceable prescription of minimum level of recycling of plastic packaging waste 
collected under EPR by producer, importers & brand -owners will strengthen circular 

12  
economy of plastic packaging waste. 
(vi) The guidelines on EPR mandate use of recycled plastic content in plastic packaging by 
the industry. This step will generate demand for recycled plastic material. 
(vii) Food Safety and Standards Authority of India has laid down guidelines for use of 
recycled plastic content in food contact applications, after the notification of Plastic 
Waste Management Second Amendment Rules, 2021 on 17th September 2021. 
(viii) The EPR guidelines will strengthen circular economy of plastic packaging waste, and 
promote development of new alternatives to plastics and move towards sustainable 
plastic packaging. 
(ix) Steps have been taken for undertaking large scale awareness generation activities at 
national level, State and UT level and local authority/district level with respect to the 
upcoming ban and alternatives available. 
Recommendation/Observations 
1.48 The Committee yet again expresses  its deep concern on the issue of non -cooperative and 
unresponsive behavior of the officials dealing with environmental matters towards the public 
representatives.  The Committee reiterates its previous recommendation in this matter that the 
Ministry of En vironment, Forest and Climate Change, being the nodal central Ministry dealing 
with these matters, must impress upon the State Governments as well as their own officers to 
sensitize all the concerned authorities to accord due courtesy to the public represe ntatives, 
attend to their grievances, respond to their communications and make available the information 
sought by them.                                                                                                      (Para 13.3 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
(i) States/UTs have been requested to constitute a Special Task Force under Chairpersonship 
of Chief Secretary/Administrator for elimination of single use plastics and effective 
implementation of PWMR, 2016.  Thirty four States/UTs have constituted the Special 
Task Force till date. 
(ii) A National Level Taskforce has been constituted by the Ministry for monitoring and 
reviewing action plans of States/UTs and Union Ministries for elimination of single use 
plastic. 
(iii) The State /UT Governments and concerned Central Ministries/Departments have been 
requested to develop a comprehensive action plan and implement it in a time bound 
manner. 
(iv) Committees have been established at the National, State and District/City level. These 
Committees are requested to consider the publi c representations and address the 
issues/concerns raised by them. 
 
 
 

 
 
CHAPTER – II 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT 
DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE GOVERNMENT'S REPLIES 
 
BUDGETARY DETAILS FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2021-22 AND ALLOCATION 
FOR 2022-23 
Recommendations/Observations 
2.1 The Committee acknowledges the steps taken by the Ministry towards improvement in 
Air Quality Index and urges upon the Ministry to take proactive steps in coordination with the 
state machinery towards controlling air pollution. The Committee recommends tha t there 
should be transparency in the funding mechanism of the Ministry with the States/UTs, 
Municipalities, State Pollution Control Boards ( SPCBs) for better coordination and 
implementation of varied schemes under the Head ‘Control of Pollution’. 
               (Para 7.8 of the 363rd Report)                                                                                                                                                                     
Action Taken

under the  Public Financial Management System  (PFMS) after taking due concurrence of  
Integrated Finance Division  (IFD) of the Ministry on each and every proposal of release of 
funds to any entity i.e. CPCB/S PCBs/PCCs on the basis of utilization of funds by the 
concerned SPCBs/PCCs as indicated in the Utilization Certificate furnished by them in the 
prescribed format (i.e. GFR -12A). Regular Expenditure Review meetings are also being 
envisaged. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
13

THE GOVERNMENT HAVE NOT BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE 
 
 
 
NIL 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
14

REPLIES OF THE GOVERNMENT ARE STILL AWAITED 
NATIONAL COASTAL MISSION 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
3.1 The Committee understands under this programme, annual Management Action Plan 
(MAP) for conservation and management of mangroves are formulated and implemented in 
all the coastal States and Union Territories. In view of the same the Committee recommends  
that the approval of Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs ( CCEA) may be sought at the 
earliest to avoid further delay in activities to be taken up under the ENCORE Project.  
               (Para 6.3 of the 363rd Report)                                                                                                                
Action Taken 
3.2 Comment is noted.  
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
3.3 The Committee observes that due to climate change coastal belt is now highly 
vulnerable to frequent super cyclones and mangroves provide protection to a great 
extent against the same.  Apart from it, mangroves also stabilize the soil and save coastal 
region from rapid erosion. In view of the same, the Committee feels that activities taken 
up under EN CORE Project are vital for the conservation and management of 
mangroves in all Coastal States/Union Territories and given its critical importance it 
should be taken up on priority.  Therefore, the Committee recommends that the matter 
must be placed before the CCEA at the earliest and follow up steps taken by the 
Ministry thereon be intimated to the Committee.

REPORT 
The Action Taken Report (ATR) of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Science and Technology, Environment, Forests and Climate Change  deals with the 
action taken by the Government on the recommendations/observations of the contained in its 
„Three Hundred Sixty Fourth Report‟ on “Demands for Grants (2022-23) of the Ministry of Earth 
Sciences”.  The Report was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of Lok Sabha on the 
15th March, 2022. 
2. Action Taken Notes (ATNs) have been received from Ministry of Earth Sciences  (MoES) 
in respect of all the thirteen recommendations/observations contained in the „Three Hundred Sixty 
Fourth Report‟. The replies of the Ministry of Earth Sciences have been categorized as follows:- 
Chapter I: Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the 
Government: Para Nos.:- 2.3, 2.4, 2.7, 3.4, 3.5, 3.6, 3.8, and 5.2  
 Total recommendations – 08 accepted 
The Committee is pleased to note that the Ministry has accepted its eight 
recommendations/observations as mentioned in Chapter-I of the Report. 
Chapter II: Recommendations/Observations which the Committee does not desire to 
pursue in view of the Government’s replies: Para Nos.:-3.7 and 6.4  
  Total recommendations – 02 Not to be pursued further.  
 The Committee is convinced with the explanations furnished by the Ministry and 
therefore, does not want to pursue the recommendations further. 
Chapter III:  Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the 
Government have not been accepted by the Committee: Nil 
Chapter IV:  Recommendations/Observations in respect of which final replies of the 
Government are still  awaited: Para  Nos.:- 4.2, 5.4 an d 5.5  To be pursued 
further 
 Total recommendations – 03 
The Committee desires that the Ministry should furnish pointed and detailed 
Action Taken Notes in respect of recommendations/observations made in 
Chapter IV of the Report. 
3. The details of the ATNs have been analyzed in the succeeding Chapters.  
  

2 
 
 
CHAPTER-I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
GOVERNMENT 
OVERALL BUDGETARY DETAILS FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2021 -22 (BE, RE & 
ACTUAL EXPENDITURE) AND ALLOCATION FOR THE FIANANCIAL YEAR      
2022-23 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.1 The Committee finds that against the total budg etary support of Rs.2369.54 crore for the 
year 2021 -22, the Ministry could utilise Rs.1379.98 crore only which is just 58.23 per cent 
utilisation of the funds made available.  The Committee, thus, summarises that despite having 
higher allocation in certain components at RE stage, the overall utilisation of the same by the 
Ministry has not b een very encouraging.  The Committee observes that had the increased funds 
allocated to the Ministry at RE stage been given at  BE stage itself then the utilisation by the 
Ministry could have been better.                                                              (Para 2.3 of the 364th Report) 
 
Action Taken 
1.2 Allocation of the Ministry was enhanced at RE stage to Rs.2369.54 crore against BE of            
Rs.1897.13 crore.  Enhanced allocation included allocation of Rs.671.01  crore for new services/ 
instruments (DOM & Satellite rent lease payment. The approval for 2nd and 3rd supplementary was 
received only in last week of February and 3 rd week of March respectively.  Expenditure incurred 
as on 31 st March, 2022 was Rs.2190.42 crore against the allocation of Rs.2369.54 crore which is 
92.44% of RE.  Agreed with the observation of the Committee. 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.3 The Committee  further finds that the utilisation of the funds has been significantly low 
under the Head „Establishment Expenditure of the Centre‟ where the Ministry could manage to 
spend 43.64 per cent only of the total funds made available.  Further, utilisation under „Central 
Sector Schemes‟ has been to the tune of 66.99 per cent.  Given the budgetary allocation utilisation 
capacity of the Ministry, the Committee hopes that the Ministry would increase its absorption 
capacity in order to utilise the total budgetary allocation made for the year 2021 -22 optimally.  
The Committe e, therefore, desires that the details of the action taken for the purpose may be 
intimated for the consideration of the Committee along with the detailed reasons for unutilised 
funds, if any.                                                                                                                 (Para 2.4 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
1.4 Allocation for establishment expenditure was enhanced at RE stage to Rs.1064.96 crore 
from Rs.517.96 crore at BE stage.  The enhanced allocation included Satellite lease rent payment 
of    Rs.521.01 crore for which necessary approval could be obtained only by 22nd March 2022.   
1.5 As on 31 st March 2022, utilization under the Head “Establishment Expenditure of the 
Centre” was Rs.1030.41 crore which is 98.94 % of RE 2021-22. 
Details of Action taken: 
1.6 Ministry expedited re-appropriation proposal for 2 nd & 3rd supplementary.  For payment of 
lease rent for Oceansat -II Satellite to ISRO, Ministry of Earth Sciences pursued with M inistry of 
Finance for necessary approval which enabled utilization of funds.   
1.7 For procurement of High Performance Computing System ( HPC), the complex Request 
for Proposal (RFP) in terms of technical specification was finalized and vetted by a committee 
constituted by the Ministry which facilitated timely concurrence by Integrated Finance Division  

3 
 
 
(IFD) and Ministry of Earth Sciences for floating of RFP in Central Public Procurement ( CPP) 
portal.  
1.8 For acquisition of land from ONGC under Deep Ocean Mission, necessary negotiation 
with ONGC was done by the Ministry/NIOT.  
Detailed reasons for unutilized funds: 
1.9 Under Establishment expenditure, IMD could not util ize Rs.30 crore due to resignation of 
newly recruited official in the cadre of SA/Admin and recruitment of Scientists could be finalized 
by IMD for which budget was projected by IMD. 
1.10 Under Deep Ocean Mission, Rs.30 crore under Capital Section could no t be utilized as 
MoU with ONGC for acquisition of Land could not be finalized. 
1.11 Last date for submission of technical & financial bids was extended by 5 days as requested 
by the bidders and due to complexity of the tender, evaluation reports (Technical & Financial) 
was submitted only by 30 th March 2022.  Therefore , Rs.90 crore earmarked for payment of 
advance could not be utilized.  
Recommendation/Observation 
1.12 The Committee notes the roadmap shared by the Ministry for the year 2022 -23 and also 
the fact that against the projected demand of Rs.3144.56  crore only Rs.2653.51 crore has been 
allocated to the Ministry in BE 2022 -23 registering a total reduction of Rs.491.05 crore.                      
The Committee feels that the budgetary allocation of Rs.2653.51 crore at BE 2022-23 stage would 
be sufficient initially  to take care of the financial requirement of the Ministry under its various 
schemes/ projects/ programmes and if required, the Ministry  would seek higher allocation at RE 
stage specifically under the Deep Ocean  Mission (DOM) and Polar and Cryosphere Resea rch 
(PACER) components so that the objectives envisaged for the year 2022 -23 could be realised.     
The Committee, therefore, desires the Department to take necessary action in order to optimise 
the allocation made in BE 2022-23.                                                                            (Para 2.7 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
1.13 Noted for compliance.  BE of Rs.2653.51 crore allocated during Financial Year 2022-23 
will be sufficient. 
Details of Action taken: 
1.14 Ministry is ensuring on -time concurrence of approval of proposals for timely release of 
funds.

recommendation as contained in Para 2.4 of the 364th the Report (Para 1.4 of this Report).

REPORT 
INTRODUCTION 
 The Department of Atomic Energy (DAE), came into being on August 3, 1954, and has been 
engaged in the development of nuclear power technology, application of radiation technologies in the 
fields of agriculture, health care, industry and basic research. 
1.2  The Atomic Energy Commission (AEC) is the apex body for formulation of policies and 
direction of the programmes. The Commission implements its policies and programmes through the 
Department of Atomic Energy (DAE). The programmes of  DAE have been divided into four sectors 
viz. Research and Development, Industries, Minerals and Power Sector. 
1.3  The programmes being followed by DAE, can be briefly summed up as follows: 
 Increasing the share of nuclear power through deployment of indig enous and other proven 
technologies and also developing fast breeder reactors and thorium reactors with associated fuel 
cycle facilities; 
 Building and operation of research reactors for production of radioisotopes; developing 
radiation technology applications in the field of health care, agriculture and industry, cancer 
care, water related technology, waste management etc.; 
 Designing and developing advanced technologies such as accelerators, lasers, supercomputers, 
advanced materials and instrumentation and encouraging transfer of technology to industry; 
 Providing support to basic research in nuclear energy and related frontier areas of science; 
interaction with universities and academic institutions; supporting academic programmes 
having a bearing on DAE’s activities; and International co -operation in related advanced areas 
of research and contribution to national security. 
1.4 DAE’s programmes are multidisciplinary in nature. For their execution, DAE has evolved 
abroad based organizational structur e comprising research centres, industrial units, public sector 
undertakings and fully aided institutions, along with service organizations. These organizations are 
engaged in research, technology development and commercial operations in the areas of nuclea r power 
and associated technologies, radiation technologies and their applications, basic research and academic 
programmes. 
1.5 The Department is also engaged in the development of radiation technologies and their 
applications for better crop varieties, te chniques for crops protection, radiation based post -harvest 
technologies, techniques for radio -diagnosis and radiotherapy of diseases particularly cancer, 
technologies for safe drinking water, better environment and industrial growth. 
1.6 Over the years, t he Department has been able to establish a network of institutions engaged in 
R&D as well as industrial activities and acquired expertise in all aspects of the nuclear fuel cycle. The 
first stage of the nuclear power programme is in commercial domain and t he second stage has been 
launched with the ongoing construction of 500 MWe Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR). 
1.7 Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL) formed in 1987, is a Public Sector 
Enterprise under the administrative control of DAE. NPCIL is responsible for siting, design, 

2 
 
construction, commissioning and operation of nuclear power reactors. Safety is given overriding 
priority in all facets of nuclear power reactors. At presents, NPCIL is operating 22 nuclear power 
reactors with an installed capacity of 6780 MW. 
1.8 DAE has under its aegis – 
1. Six Research Centers: - 
 
i) Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) – Mumbai 
ii) Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research (IGCAR) – Kalpakkam 
iii) Raja Ramanna Centre for Advanced Technology (RRCAT) – Indore 
iv) Variable Energy Cyclotron Centre (VECC) – Kolkata 
v) Atomic Minerals Directorate for Exploration and Research (AMD) – Hyderabad 
  vi) Global Centre for Nuclear Energy Partnership (GCNEP) 
 2.  Three Industrial Organisations: 
 
  i) Heavy Water Board (HWB) – Mumbai, 
  ii) Nuclear Fuel Complex (NFC) – Hyderabad 
  iii) Board of Radiation and Isotope Technology (BRIT) – Mumbai. 
 3. Three Service Organisations 
 4. Five Public Sector Undertakings: 
  i) Nuclear Power Corporation of India Ltd. (NPCIL) – Mumbai, 
  ii) BharatiyaNabhikiyaVidyut Nigam Ltd. (BHAVINI), Kalpakkam, 
  iii) Uranium Corporation of India Ltd. (UCIL) – Jaduguda, 
  iv) Indian Rare Earths Ltd. (IREL) – Mumbai 
  v) Electronics Corporation of India Ltd. (ECIL) – Hyderabad. 
 5. Eleven Aided Institutions: 
 
  i) Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR) – Mumbai 
  ii) Tata Memorial Centre (TMC) – Mumbai 
  iii) Saha Institute of Nuclear Physics (SINP) – Kolkata 
  iv) Institute of Physics (IOP) – Bhubaneswar 
  v) Institute for Plasma Research (IPR) – Gandhinagar

terms of electricity generation from nuclear power plants.  As a percent of share in  total energy matrix

2.25  The Committee is of the view that even though an increase of 40 percent, i.e. from 4780 
MW to 6780 MW is substantial, it is not commensurate with the need of the country for more 
clean energy. With nuclear energy having a share of only about 3 percent in the total energy 
matrix of the country, it is high time that the contribution from nuclear power is increased 
substantially. This is not just crucial from a point of view of environment but also to ensure the 
country's energy security in times of ever increasing power consumption.  
2.26 The Committee, while being optimistic that the Department shall seek it's above stated 
objectives in increasing nuclear power production through commissioning of more nuclear power 
plants, hopes that these projects will be implemented on war footing and are not delayed or fall 
short of their objectives in any way. 
2.27 The Committee observes and highlights the fact that even though India's rank is 6th in 
terms of numbers of nuclear power reactors being operated, we are still at number 11 and 14 
when it comes to nuclear power produced and installed capacity respectively. This is indicative of 
the fact that the production capacity per power plan t is low. The Committee therefore 
recommends the Department to study the reasons for thi s anamoly and also apprise the 
Committee of its findings. Further, the Committee recommends that the Department devices a 
strategy to install higher production capacity power units so that the unit cost comes down and 
nuclear power becomes more affordable.

Recognizing the importance of electronics components design and development in such 
technologically intense s ector, the Committee sought information about the functioning of Electronics 
Corporation of India Limited (ECIL), its mandate, its achievement and its future goals. The Department 
replied that ECIL is engaged in the design, development, manufacture, supply , installation and 
commissioning of a wide variety of electronic equipment for the Atomic Energy, Defence, Aerospace, 
Security, Information Technology and e-Governance verticals. 
4.2  The Committee was further informed that the Company seeks to achieve pro duct realisation 
through in -house R &D, partnership with research laboratories, academic institutions and industry to 
create value for customers and stakeholders. The company is a key player in the strategic electronics 
space in the country and has unique m ulti-disciplinary competencies. ECIL has been consistently 
registering growth in its turnover over the past few years and is poised to leverage the large growth in  
strategic electronics. 
4.3  As regards the past achievements of ECIL, the following was brought to the attention ofthe 
Committee, through a written reply: 
 18 Mtr DSN antennae for Aditya Mission. 
A fully indigenous 18 Mtrmonopulse earth station antenna operating in S/X band has been 
commissioned by ECIL at Byalalu for Aditya Mission of ISRO. This earth station antenna is 
an integral part of Deep Space Network of ISRO. 
 Product Launch-Indigenous Programmable Logic Controller (PLC). 
ECIL in association with BARC has developed ‘Safe and Secure’ Programmable Logic 
Controller (PLC) (NUCON PLC). The p roduct was launched along with ECSCADA on 18 
May 2022.The product has been deployed for strategic applications in space and nuclear 
sector. The product makes the country fully Aatmanirbhar with complete safety and security 
feature for applications in strategic sector. 
 Commissioning of strategic communication network for SPIC. 
ECIL has successfully completed the strategic communication network project 
(PUSHPAK). The project was formally inaugurated by Chairman, DRDO on 25 Jun 22. 
 SMF 2.0 for Strategic Electronic Products. 
ECIL under guidance of Technical Expert Committee (TEC) of Election Commission of 
India (ECI) has undertaken development and deployment of Secure Manufacturing Facility 
(SMF 2.0). The facility ensures security, traceability and 4Sigma qualit y for manufacture of 
Strategic Electronic Products. 
 Hydrogen Steam Concentration Monitoring System (HSCMS).

ECIL has developed and qualified Hydrogen and Steam Concentration Monitoring System 
(HSCMS) based on Quadruple Mass Spectroscope designed by BARC. T he system has 
been commissioned at NPCIL, KAPP-3.

7. TATA MEMORIAL CENTRE  – IN NATION’S SERVICE AS A PRIMER CANCER 
CARE INSTITUTE IN THE COUNTRY 
The Committee, with  a view of highlighting the activities and impact of the Tata Memorial 
Centre, sought a note on the same from the Department. The information received from the Department 
is as below: 
The Tata Memorial Centre, a grant -in-aid organization under the Departme nt of Atomic 
Energy (DAE) is the oldest and largest cancer centre in the country. Registering close to 80,000 new 
patients and over 650,000 follow ups annually at Mumbai alone, it provides high quality cancer care to 
patients from across the country regard less of socio economic status and their ability to pay; more 
than 60% of patients are treated almost free of cost. The centre runs an active Bone Marrow 
Transplant (BMT) program with a 6 bedded BMT unit performing 60 to 70 transplants every year. 
Twenty-five percent of all transplants are funded by the institute so that patients who otherwise would 
not have been transplanted undergo this expensive but life saving treatment. 
7.2 TMC is the largest centre for cancer education in the country and trains close t o 200 students 
every year in various aspects of cancer including surgical, medical and radiation oncology, pathology, 
radiology and anesthesiology amongst others. TMC’s educational activities are affiliated to the Homi  
Bhabha National Institute (HBNI) Mumb ai – a deemed university of the DAE. Besides academic 
courses such as MCh, DM, MS, MD, PhD, MSc, etc. the center organizes various training programs, 
fellowships, and short courses for continuing education.  Some innovative courses started at TMC in 
the pa st 5 years include Masters in clinical research, patient navigation (Kevat) and physician 
assistants. These courses have had major impact on the conduct of cancer research and the holistic 
approach to patient care. 
7.3 The focus of TMC’s research remains t he identification of gaps in cancer management, 
addressing them by conducting high quality clinical trials, and finding cost effective solutions to cancer 
problems relevant to the region. While the Tata Memorial Hospital remains at the forefront of clinica l 
cancer research, ACTREC, the research wing of TMC houses several basic and translational scientists 
working towards unravelling the biology of cancer. The Centre for Cancer Epidemiology conducts field 
studies on various aspects of causation of cancer in addition to organizing regular cancer awareness 
and prevention programmes. 
7.4 Responding to the national need for more centres of excellence for cancer treatment like TMH 
and ACTREC in Mumbai, TMC embarked on a major expansion plan that will quadruple its  patient 
care capabilities as well as broaden its geographic presence in the country. TMC has now expanded to 
six other hospitals located in Varanasi (2), Guwahati, Sangrur, Vishakapatnam, Chandigarh and 
Muzaffarpur. ACTREC, which had 100 beds till 2020, i s now a 500-bedded facility, and will expand to 
900 beds by end -2023, offering cutting -edge treatment with dedicated facilities for solid tumor 
chemotherapy, hematolymphoid cancers management, treatment with radionuclide isotopes, and the 
first Proton Beam therapy unit in the government sector.  
7.5 Starting from 840 beds in 2017, TMC has grown to 2200 beds (in 2022) and will further 
increase its capacity to 2800 beds by the end of 2023, and 3400 beds by the end of 2026. Currently, 
TMC treats about 125,000 new patients with cancer annually (approximately 10% of all of India’s 

19 
 
cancer burden). The hub and spoke model of cancer care has been successfully implemented in Punjab 
and in Uttar Pradesh. In addition, a proposal is being considered for a cancer hospita l in Odisha 
(NISER campus of DAE), which is at a fairly advanced stage of discussion with joint funding from DAE 
and the Tata Trusts. TMC is also planning an Integrated Centre for Treatment, Research and 
Education in cancer at Khopoli, Maharashtra which wi ll house a medicinal plant facility, and include 
infrastructure and resources for cancer research involving traditional Indian systems of medicine 
(AYUSH). 
7.6 With the expansion envisioned with the creation of these new hospitals, it is expected that TMC 
will soon treat close to 200,000 new patients with cancer annually, which will account for 
approximately 12 -15% of all patients with cancer diagnosed in the country every year. TMC also 
provides technical support to several state governments with their can cer treatment facilities including 
Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, West Bengal, Andhra Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir amongst others. 
TMC’s increasing capacity to train individuals in all branches of oncology will ensure that there are 
adequate human resources to run these centres.  
7.7 The following chart shows the number of patients covered under affordable cancer care during 
F.Y. 2021-22 and F.Y. 2022-23 (till Dec. 2022) in 6 regional cancer care hospitals under DAE: 
 
7.8 The National Cancer Grid, an initiative of the Tata Memorial Centre, was created in 2012 with 
the broad vision of creating uniform standards of cancer care across India. Ten years later, it has 
grown into the world’s largest cancer network with 289 members , comprising cancer centres, research 
institutes, patient advocacy groups, charitable organizations and professional societies. The mandate 
of the NCG is establishing uniform standards of patient care for prevention, diagnosis, and treatment 
of cancer, cre ating adequate trained human resources, and facilitating collaborative basic, 
translational and clinical research in cancer. Between the member organizations of the NCG, the 
network treats over 750,000 new patients with cancer annually, which is over 60% o f all of India’s 
cancer burden.

7.9 Some of the activities of the NCG include: uniform standards of care – resource stratified 
guidelines for cancer management, External Quality Assurance Schemes (EQAS), training in Quality 
Improvement through the EQuIP program, institutional peer review, online second opinion service for 
patients, multidisciplinary Virtual Tumor Boards, Price Discovery Cell / Group negotiation for 
equipment, drugs and consumables, National Cancer Library resources, unique educational ini tiatives 
– “Traveling Schools of Pathology and Oncology Nursing”, training in cancer research methods – the 
International Collaboration on Research methods Development in Oncology – CreDO workshop and 
NCG funded multicentric collaborative research. With th e creation of NCG “Vishwam”, the 
international component of the NCG, the network is rapidly being acknowledged as one of the most 
influential organizations in global cancer care. 
7.10 During the meeting of the Committee, the Department informed that TMC ha s conducted three 
trials that can be implemented immediately: 
 The first on Yoga in breast cancer tested , adding Yoga to standard surgery, radiotherapy and 
chemotherapy show ed improvement in quality of life, compliance to treatment and a 15% 
reduction in deaths due to breast cancer.  
 The other two trials tried two low cost interventions in the form of injections that saved 29% 
and 26% lives in breast cancer. Both these injectio ns are available across India as part of 
arogya shree as well as state insurance schemes. The cost of these injections is Rs25 and Rs 
2000/- only.  
7.11 In summary, the Tata Memorial Centre has spearheaded major advances in patient care, 
training, research , public health and policy in cancer over the past decade in India. TMC has 
expanded its scope, presence and influence across the length and breadth of the country through its 
own expansion and the development of the National Cancer Grid. Over the next dec ade, TMC will 
remain at the forefront of all aspects of cancer management - provision of high-quality evidence-based 
cancer care to all strata of the population, creating human resource adequate to tackle the growing 
burden of cancer in the country, conduct meaningful, cost effective, contextually relevant research, and 
help frame and advance India’s cancer policy. 
7.12 The Committee lauds with a full heart, the efforts of Tata Memorial Centre as well as the 
Department for anchoring the various aspects of cancer diagnosis, treatment, management and 
cutting edge research. It also highlights the stellar service that TMC has provided to this country 
in terms of serving the needy by delivering  high impact low cost cancer care. TMC’ s hub a nd 
spoke model is exemplary in terms of the geographical expanse it covers, number of patients it 
treats and the quality & standards of care it maintains. The Committee would like to 
congratulate TMC and the Department along with a request to identify more  underserved 
regions and reach out.  The Committee would like to extend its full support to TMC for all its 
future endeavours.

1. INTRODUCTION 
 
1.1  The Department of Biotechnology was set up as an independent Board in 1982, and thereafter 
became a full -fledged Department under Ministry of Science & Technology in 1986. The mandate of 
the Department is given below: 
 
- To evolv e policies and integrated programmes in biotechnology and ensure their 
implementation and monitoring. 
- To identify specific programmes of Research and Development and manufacturing in 
biologicals and biotechnology and oversee the initiation and pursuit of r elated research and 
manufacturing activities. 
- To identify, set up and support Centers of Excellence for Research and Development in 
biotechnology and ensure proper dovetailing of their activities as per national priorities and 
objectives. 
- To act as a scree ning, advising and approving agent of the Government with regard to import 
and transfer of new technologies for the manufacture of biologicals, biotechnological products 
and their intermediates. 
- Evolve safety guidelines for Biotechnology Research and Devel opment and manufacturing in 
India. 
- To act as the central agency for the import of genetically manipulated materials, culture, cells, 
specimens, tissues and biotech products including DNA and RNA of any type or size and for 
promoting their production in the country. 
- Serve as the inter -ministerial and interagency nodal point for all specific international bilateral 
and multilateral Research and Development collaborations and agreements in the area of 
Biotechnology, act as the nodal point for all technology tr ansfers in the area of biotechnology. 
Manufacture and ensure application of recombinant, cell -based and DNA vaccines, diagnostics 
and other biotechnological products. 
- To evolve programmes for Human Resource Development in the area of biotechnology. 
- Serve a s an administrative and implementing Department of agencies, commissions, boards, 
etc. specifically formed by the Government for fulfilling the national objectives in 
biotechnology and also to serve as the nodal point for Bio -informatics including training  and 
creation of infrastructure, collection, dissemination and exchange of information relating to 
biotechnology.

3. BIOTECHNOLOGY RESEARCH & DEVELOPMENT – MAJOR INITIATIVES 
3.1 The Committee sought to know from the Department the major initiatives during the year in the 
field of research and development.   In response, the Department informed that the major  thrust areas 
for the year 2022 -23 and 2023 -24 include agriculture, affordable healthcare and  medical technology, 
food and nutritional security, animal biotechnology, environmental safety,  clean energy a nd bio-fuel, 
and bio-manufacturing. The research projects related to basic, discovery and translational research in 
the areas of agriculture and allied areas including Animal Biotechnology and Aquaculture, Healthcare 
including vaccine, drugs, medical devic es and implants, Bio -engineering, Food and  Nutrition, 
Environment and Clean Energy and Industrial Biotechnology have been considered for support.  
3.2 On the basis of the information provided by the Department, some of the major 
programmes/initiatives and the achievements under them are: 
- The Department in partnership with DARE/ICAR is implementing three Mission programmes, 
namely Mission programme on minor pulses, Mission programme on oilseeds of Indian  origin 
(sesame, niger, safflower and linseed) and Miss ion programme on characterization of  genetic 
resources (rice, wheat, chickpea). These programmes are aimed at screening genetic resources 
for abiotic and biotic stresses and finding new genes which can be utilized for developing 
climate and pathogen resilient varieties for future. In addition, the Department is implementing 
network projects in ICAR institution/SAU‟S in rice which have led to development of varieties 
in rice tolerant to submergence, salinity and drought. Researches supported by the Departmen t 
have led to development of varieties by various institutions, which have  been released to  small 
and marginal farmers through extension network of ICAR/SAU‟s as well as Biotech -Kisan 
programme of the Department. A programme on plant biotechnology catering to engineering of 
smart plant types for enhanced  productivity under a range of environmental conditions as 
well as R&D projects to improve stress resilience in cereals, vegetables, pulses, etc., have been 
supported. 
- Plant genome editing being amongs t one of the most promising technologies with a huge 
economic potentia l in a wide range of sectors, D BT proactively initiated the development of 
draft „Guidelines for the safety assessment of Genome Edited Plants’, which were notified in May, 
2022. The Departme nt ha s notified the Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for regulatory 
review of Genome Edited Plants under Site Directed Nuclease -1 (SDN -1) and SDN -2 
categories for enabling regulatory streamlining of genome edited plants and resilient crop s for 
future. These SOPs shall be applicable to all organizations involved in R&D and handling of 
the Genome Edited Plants under these categories. 
- India‟s first  indigenously developed quadrivalent Human Papilloma Virus (qHPV) vaccine,  
CERVAVAC, against cervical cancer s upported by the Department and BIRAC through the 
pioneering partnership  programme „Grand Challenges India‟, received market authorization  
from DCGI in 12th July, 2022. The affordable vaccine is effective against HPV serotypes 6, 11, 
16, and 18, which are responsible for most of the invasive cervical cancer cases. This is fitting 
example of the Government‟s focus on „Preventive Healthcare‟. 
- Through Translational  Research Platform for Veterinary Biologicals (TRPVB), which was  
established to develop cutting ed ge technologies such as next generation  diagnostics, vectored 

10 
 
vaccines etc., a vaccine candidate for Lumpy Skin Disease (LSD) virus in cattle has been 
identified. The virus isolates have been transferred to M/s  Biovet Pvt Ltd, Bangalore for 
developing a live attenuated vaccine. The live attenuated Theileria annulata vaccine technology 
which is at TRL-6 level has been transferred to M/s Hester Biosciences Pvt Ltd., Ahmedabad. 
- Study of a large  cohort of patients with Covid-19 was undertaken through the Transl ational 
Research in Health Science and Technology Institute (THSTI), Faridabad, for understanding the 
durability of immunity and risk of re -infection and long  COVID. The study establishes how 
inactivated vaccine BBV152/Covaxin induces robust immune memory to SARS -CoV-2 and 
variants of concern (VOCs) by novel mechanisms involving follicular T -helper cells having B 
cell help potential. The study revealed that majority of the participants have persistent 
antibodies for more than 8 months after vaccination/infe ction; majority of them have increased 
antibody titres post omicron which neutralize all subvariants of omicron; and T -cell responses 
persist in most even though antibody is negative.  
- Genome India, a pan India multi -institutional project, was first implemented by the Department 
in 2020 to build an exhaustive catalogue of genetic variations (common, low frequency, rare, 
SNPs and structural variations) and construct a reference genome and haplotype structure, by 
performing whole-genome sequencing (WGS) of 10,000 individuals representing the Indian 
population diversity. The project spanning across 20 institutions envisages the creation of 
national resource of  genetic information and also caters to build capacity in the country in the 
areas of whole genome  sequencing, data analysis, and methods development for high 
throughput genomic studies and  analysis. The whole genome sequencing for 6305 individuals 
has been completed and 8065  genome wide genotyping accomplished. Analyses of joint 
genetic variants calling in these genomes have been carried out for 3966 sequences. 1297 
sequences have been analyzed after joint calling using DRAGEN analysis pipeline. 
- Human Microbiome Initiative, implemented in 2020, is aimed to map the reference microbiome 
of 3400  healthy indivi duals across 11 non-tribal and 6 tribal communities spread across the 
country. Considering the geographic, ethnic and dietary diversity of Indian population, the 
study envisages  the association of „Genetics, biogeography and diet with Microbiome‟. The 
project also looks at the microbiome various with respect to Ayruvedik Prakriti. Complete 
microbiome profiling of 2181 individuals and  partial microbiome profiling of 789 subjects has 
been completed. Diet showed highest influence on microbiome followed by ethn icity and 
geography. Ayurvedic prakriti assessment of  993 subjects by  Ayurvedic physicians has also 
shown high correlation with human microbiome.  
- A network Mission Program on Pediatric Rare Genetic Disorders has been initiated to study  
disease-associated novel genetic variations and development of new genomics-based 
diagnostic tests for pediatric  rare genetic disorders  that are relatively more prevalent in  India. 
The Mission aims to analyze a total of 6000 individuals (2000 patient-parent trios) over 5 years, 
to identify the cause  of undiagnosed genetic  diseases, and to reduce the burden of genetic 
diseases in India by the joint efforts of doctors, scientists and citizens. 
- Under the programme on Energy Biosciences/Biofuels & Waste  to Value, a facility of 1,00,000 
L scale for cultivation of marine algae has been created at Mumbai coast, using a  custom-made 
sunlight-distributed algal growth system for improved algal biomass and lipid  productivity. A 

11 
 
microalgae-based sewage treatment plant (photobioreactor facility) has also been commissioned 
at BPCL Campus, Mumbai to clean sewage at 2,00,000 liter/day scale. 
 
3.3 The Committee was informed that the Department has so far sanctioned a total of 1146 new 
proposals and supported 7,056 ongoing proposals for undertaking innovative research and development 
activities in the areas of Biotechnology. This  support has resulted in about 8343 publications and 
development/commercialization of 567 technologies.  
3.4  The Committee appreciates the achievements of the Department under the various 
programmes/schemes towards Biotechnology Research and Development––especially 
development of the qHPV vaccine CERVAVAC, and hopes that the Department would be able to 
achieve its targets for 2023 -24, through judicious and efficie nt use of  the budget allocation for 
this period.  
3.5  The Committee is of the considered view that setting of realistic and achievable targets, 
both short term and long term, as well as existence of a robust monitoring mechanism to monitor 
and review the  progress of ongoing schemes and programmes, are extremely crucial. The 
Committee recommends that the Department of  Biotechnology should ensure an  effective 
monitoring and periodic review of all its schemes and programmes and take corrective measures, 
wherever required, so that they proceed as per schedule. 
3.6 The Committee recommends more collaboration with DARE/ICAR to accelerate the R&D 
in agriculture, especially plant genomes, so that more productive, drought and flood resistant 
varieties of various important crops can be developed in the next 3-5 years. 
4.  HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT AND CAPACITY BUILDING 
4.1 The Committee asked the Department about its initiatives towards development of human 
resources and capacity building. The Department informed that capacit y building, competence building 
and skill development in broad areas of biotechnology are the key verticals defining the mandate of
