7.   HUMAN GENETICS & GENOME ANALYSIS 
7.1. Considering the importance and scope of genetic res earch, the Committee, in its endeavour to 
know about the initiatives  taken by the Department in this direction and the progress  
made by the Department, has been given to understand that the  Department is making efforts in this 
field. The Committee was info rmed that an important programme of the Department, viz., Human  
Genetics & Genome Analysis program supports basic, translational and clinical research, to generate 
knowledge about how to use genomic information to advance medical care.  This  program, which  

19 
 
primarily addresses issues  related to inherited diseases, supports research and development activities 
across the spectrum: basic, translational and clinical research to establish how to use genomic 
information to advance medical care. The diseases which have been studied through ongoing and new 
projects under this programme include: pediatric rare genetic disorders, lysosomal storage disorders, 
Covid – 19, beta thalassaemia, schizophrenia and Parkinson‟s disease, hemophilia, congenital 
nonsyndromic deafne ss, primary cardiomyopathies, monogenic diabetes, movement disorders, celiac 
disease, etc. 
7.2 The Department submitted that, a bout 25 research publications emanated from the R&D 
activities supported under this programme, and more than 150 human resources have been trained in 
this area. It has also established research platform and National Genomics Core, to facilitate pursuit of 
biomedical genomics at the national level by opening up its core facilities of genome sequencing and 
analysis to universities and  other national labs. The Department also informed the Committee that, for 
the first time, a novel gene therapy using cutting -edge biotechnology for hemophilia A, a rare blood 
disorder, has  been developed by the team of researchers from the Centre for Stem  Cell Research 
(CSCR), Christian Medical College, Vellore. Regulatory approval for conducting Phase -I clinical trial 
of gene therapy has been given by the Central Drugs Standard Control  Organization (CDSCO), and the 
clinical trial has been initiated at CMC, Vellore with the first subject recruited in May, 2022.  
7.3 During the financial year 2023-24, the Department plans to provide continued  support to R&D 
projects under the human genetics and  genome analysis program; support cross -disciplinary proposals 
having near-term translational potential; initiate  R&D activities  and support  projects/activities in 
thematic areas and facilitate creation of biorepositories/biobank, for various human genetic disorders. 
7.4 The Committee recognizes the immense potential that genetic research and gene therapy 
hold for altering the treatment paradigm of many genetic diseases, including those that are 
currently incurable. However, as it is a relatively new field of medical science, the many 
challenges still associated with it are not lost on the Committee. Despite the existing challenges, 
such as issues regarding delivery methods, safety and effectiveness concerns, potential long -term 
effects of genetic modification, high costs of developing and administering the therapy making  it 
inaccessible to masses, etc., the potential benefits are far too significant to ignore and, therefore, 
it is highly essential to prioritize research in the area.  
7.5 The Committee appreciates the ongoing efforts of scient ists and researchers in this f ield. 
The Committee recommends the Department to undertake deeper research in collaboration with 
other institutes under the government and private sector, explore avenues for using latest 
emerging technologies including Artificial Intelligence (AI), in ord er to  fully explore the 
untapped potential of genetic research. The Committee also recommends that adequate funds be 
earmarked for the purpose, so that financial constrain ts do not hinder the much-needed R&D. 
The Committee would also like  to be kept informed about the progress made by the Department 
in this regard.

that this target will be met within the remaining quarter of the current financial year.   (Para 6.2) 
 The Committee commends the work being done by BIRAC towards promoting 
entrepreneurship by empowering start-ups and SMEs in the country.                             (Para 6.6) 
 The Committee is of the firm belief that the development of an entrepreneurial ecosystem 
is critical for any country's economic growth and prosperity, for which support to start-ups and 
SMEs is a must. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should make 
concerted efforts towards fostering a thriving ecosystem of entrepreneurship in the country.  The 
Department should strive towards better c ollaboration wi th other stakeholders to create a 
supportive policy environment, build a culture of innovation, provide access to funding, develop 
infrastructure to support new ventures/ startups/SMEs, collaborate with other incubation  and 
mentorship programmes of the gove rnment etc., all of which will go a long way in achieving the 
objective of fostering a thriving ecosystem of entrepreneurship in the country.      (Para 6.7) 
 The Committee especially recommends that the Department should ensure equitable 
distribution of r esources/initiatives across the country, so that the benefits  of its programmes 
aimed at supporting start -ups and SMEs can reach the under -served regions of the country as 
well.                                                                                                                                        (Para 6.8) 
 The Committee recommends that the Department must carry out a detailed analysis on 
the investment in R&D over the last 10 years, the financial value created by the products, the 
potential revenue generated and the multiplier effect in the market.      (Para 6.9) 
 

23 
 
HUMAN GENETICS & GENOME ANALYSIS 
 The Committee recognizes the immense potential that genetic research and gene therapy 
hold for altering the treatment paradigm of many genetic di seases, including those that are 
currently incurable. However, as it is a relatively new field of medical science, the many 
challenges still associated with it are not lost on the Committee. Despite the existing challenges, 
such as issues regarding deliver y methods, safety and effectiveness concerns, potential long -term 
effects of genetic modification, high costs of developing and administering the therapy making it 
inaccessible to masses, etc., the potential benefits are far too significant to ignore and, therefore, 
it is highly essential to prioritize research in the area.                                                           (Para 7.4) 
 The Committee appreciates the ongoing efforts of scientists and researchers in this field. 
The Committee recommends the Department to undertake deeper research in collaboration with 
other institutes under the government and private sector, explore avenues for using latest 
emerging technologies including Artificial Intelligence (AI), in order to fully explore the 
untapped potential of genetic research. The Committee also recommends that adequate funds be 
earmarked for the purpose, so that financial constraints do not hinder the much -needed R&D. 
The Committee would also like to be kept informed about the progress made by t he Department 
in this regard.                (Para 7.5)

INTRODUCTION 
1.1 The Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (DSIR) is one of the three Departments of 
the Ministry of Science and Technology. It was established on 4 th January, 1985, for the promotion of 
industrial research through indigenous technology promotion, develop ment, utilization and transfer. 
The allocation of business shown under this Department in the Notification is as under: 
(i) All matters concerning the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR). 
(ii) All matters relating to National Research Development Corporation (NRDC). 
(iii) All matters relating to Central Electronics Limited (CEL). 
(iv) Registration and Recognition of R&D Units. 
(v) Matters relating to UNCTAD and WIPO. 
(vi) National Register for Foreign Collaborations. 
(vii) Matters relating to creation of pool for temporary placement of Indian Scientists and 
Technologists. 
1.2. The primary endeavor of DSIR is to foster development of state -of-the-art technologies and 
products through research and development (R&D), encourage industry to increase their share in the 
country‟s R&D expenditure, support industrial units in developing competitive technologies of high 
commercial potential, catalyze faster commercialization of labor atory-scale R&D, and strengthen 
consultancy and technology management capabilities. 
1.3. The DSIR has two autonomous institutions, viz., CSIR and Consultancy Development Centre 
(CDC) and two public sector undertakings, viz., NRDC and CEL, under its administrative control. The 
Department also provides institutional host facilities to Asian & Pacific Centre for Transfer of 
Technology (APCTT). 
1.4. The Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology, 
Environment, Forests an d Climate Change considered the Demands for Grants (2023 -24) of the 
Department of Scientific and Industrial Research in its meeting held on 22nd February, 2023.

is far from satisfactory . The Department has been able to spend an abysmal 40.6 % of its revised

in respect of the Central Sector Schemes/Projects, as over 50 per cent of the funds allocated 
under this r emain to be utilized within the remaining quarter of the current financial year . The 
Committee, therefore, urges the Department to ensure optimal utilization of funds during th e 
course of the financial year. In future, periodic monitoring preferably on qua rterly basis may be 
undertaken to facilitate the same. 
2.4 The Committee inquired about the budgetary allocation proposed by the Department vis-à-vis 
the amount actually allocated to it for t he year 2023 -24. The Department  informed that against a 
proposal of Rs. 6871.77 crore, an amount of Rs. 5746.51 has been allocated, which is about 16 per cent 
lesser than its budgetary demand. There is an overall shortfall of Rs. 1125.26 crore in actual allocation 
to the Department.

proposed budget and the strategy of the Department for dealing with the challenges arising thereof, the

3.3 The Committee wa s also informed that, under the umbrella scheme „Assistance to PSEs‟, the

technologies developed by all the  research laboratories and institutes of CSIR and other public fun ded 
research institutes,  universities including autonomous research institutions. It undertakes 
programmes/activities under two promotional schemes , viz., Programme for Inspiring Inventors &

which focus  on development and promotion of innovations leading to technology transfer and their

4. COUNCIL OF SCIENTIFIC & INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH (CSIR)  
 
4.1 Created in  1942, the CSIR is an autonomous body under administrative control of 
the Department. The Council is known for its cutting edge R&D  knowledge base  in diverse 
S&T areas. A contemporary R&D organization having pan -India presence, CSIR has a dynamic 
network of 37 national  laboratories, 39 outreach centres, 1 Innovation Complex and 3 units. CSIR's 
R&D expertise and experience is embodied in about 3439 active scientists supporte d by about 
4193 scientific and technical personnel, along with about 2514 administrative staff. 
4.2. CSIR has two non -Central Sector Schemes, viz., (i) National Laboratories Scheme; and (ii)  
Capacity Building and Human Resource Development. While the former covers a wide range of R&D 

7 
 
and S&T aspects, latter deals with human resources and different awards. 
4.3 The Committee desired to know about the major achievement s of CSIR during the ye ar. 
The Department informed , during the meeting, that CSIR national labs are grouped together under 
eight sector-specific theme based clusters, with each cluster under a separate directorate. A few of the 
major achievements under these eight verticals during the year are as follow:-   
 
(i) HANSA-NG, India‟s first all -composite single engine light aircraft for flying, training, 
sport and hobby flying designed and developed by CSIR-NAL, successfully completed in-
flight engine relight test on 17 th May, 2022. The 2 -seater, low noise emissio n aircraft has 
completed initial certification, and is ready for flying. Tata Advanced Systems Ltd (T ASL), 
CSIR‟s production partner, has received order worth Rs. 220 crore  from HAL to make 
composite parts of series of Light Combat Aircraft Mk1A. Besides, CSIR developed multi-
copter drones which were utilized  during Covid times for drug delivery, are now also being 
utilized for fertilizer spray.   
(ii) As a part of its endeavo ur to address water security, CSIR has undertaken High Resolution 
Aquifer Mapping & Management in Arid Regions of North Western India to augment the 
groundwater resources. The Heli -borne geophysical  mapping technology of CSIR  which 
provides high resolution images enables mapping of water-rich areas as also arid regions. In 
phase –I, mapping of priority areas covering an area of 1 lakh sq.kms. has been completed. 
The ultimate a im of the project is to map potential sites for groundwater withdrawal and 
conservation. Further, CSIR is in the process of developing an integrated SMART water 
management system. 
(iii) In the area of energy – including generation, conversion and storage, CSIR has made 
significant strides. A CSIR -Innovation Centre for Next Generation Energy Storage Facility 
is being developed to meet the country's requirement for batteries, which aims to be the 
first in India to demonstrate Lithium battery fabrication up to 100  Mega Watt capacities. 
Once developed, it would help the Indian  industry to come up with Lithium battery 
fabrication facilities with environment -friendly, cost-effective, and energy-efficient 
technology. The proposed  facility would leapfrog next-generation technologies such as 
Sodium-ion, Lithium-sulfur and Solid-state batteries. The lead laboratory is  in the process 
of identifying the industrial partner. 
(iv) In view of the country‟s huge dependence on import of many chemicals, special ity 
chemicals and Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs), CSIR is giving special importance 
to speciality chemicals including leather and petrochemicals. Recently, one manufacturing 
unit of Hydrazine Hydrate in Gujarat was dedicated to the nation by the Prime Minister of 
India. CSIR has also made significant progress with respect production of Azelaic Acid and 
Isobutylene-based derivatives. 
(v) CSIR has developed a tissue culture technology for virus free apple root stock, which 
reduced the chilling time from 1,100 hours to 400 hou rs. These low chilling varieties of 
apple, which were earlier confined only to the Himalayan region, are now being 
popularized in the North -Eastern Region . Further, CSI R‟s „Purple  Revolution‟ under its 
Aroma Mission for introduction and promotion of Lavender  cultivation in  Jammu & 
Kashmir, is now in the process of being expanded to other states like Uttarakhand and 
Himachal Pradesh.  
(vi) After successful development of DNA v accines for the Covid – 19 pandemic, CSIR is 
slowly expanding interest towards mRNA vaccines, which will find application in respect 
of other diseases too, including cancer. CSIR is in the process of completely indigenizing 
the platform by means of which u pcoming pandemics can be easily understood, 

8 
 
predicted/forecast at the shortest possible time. 
(vii) CSIR has developed many waste-to-wealth technologies and products such as spent wash 
from distillery, industrial solid waste, brine sludge, e-waste, coal-based power industry 
waste, biomass/agri waste, fertilizer industry waste, lime sludge, marble waste, etc. These 
technologies have been transferred to more than 50 licencees and are at various stages of 
implementation with MSMEs, industries and other partners.  
4.4 The Committee applauds the contribution of the Department through CSIR and its 
network of laboratories in the pursuit of excellence across all sectors of scientific research and 
development. The Committee also notes that these endeavours of CSIR are  well-aligned to the 
economic, industrial and social priorities of the nation, as exemplified by their convergence with 
the Government's Mission Programmes  such as Atma Nirbhar Bharat, Make in India, Startup 
India, Swachh Bharat, focus on green growth, etc. 
4.5 The Committee is of the view that, although many new initiatives are being undertaken, a 
lot more needs to be done in order to successfully meet the challenges of the future. The 
Committee recommends that the Department should undertake meaningful ini tiatives to 
establish strong foundations to enable the country to become a global leader in scientific research 
and development.  While sufficient allocation of funds is an obvious pre -requisite to effectively 
pursue this goal, the Committee feels that i t is essential to let more private sector/industries on 
board to play a greater role in contributing to R&D in the country. The Committee, accordingly, 
recommends that more representatives of industries/companies should be motivated to partake 
in this endeavour, especially by way of capital investments.

6.  CSIR MISSION MODE PROJECT ON ‘WASTE TO WEALTH’  
6.1 The Committee was informed that, in 2023-24, the Department plans to launch a Mission Mode 
project through CSIR, to address a variety  of industrial and other crucial waste management issues 
with their proper disposal, including fossil fuel waste, biotic waste, metallic waste, non -metallic waste, 
and electronic  waste. The Mission is also  in alignment with the United Nation‟s „Sustainable 
Development Goals‟  and the Government‟s commitments towards environment conservation , 
mitigating climate change and adapting approaches of sustainable development. 
6.2 The Department, in the meeting, mentioned about some of the waste -to-wealth technologies 
developed by CSIR for converting various types of wastes into high, value added -end products. The 
Committee evinced keen interest in the success stories of the Department in this area, and sought to 
know more about the technology developed for conversion of steel slag as road making aggregates. In a 
written reply, the Department informed that , under the R&D project sponsored by Ministry of Steel 
along with four major steel industries, CSIR -Central Road Research Institute (CRRI), New Delhi 
developed customized steel slag valorisation technologies for conversion of different types of steel slag 
as processed steel slag aggregates for road making. The design and construction methodology for its 
utilization have been devised after various intrinsic challenges associated with the slag conversion and 
its possible environmental impacts were successfully addressed. 
6.3 Using this technology, India‟s first steel slag road (1.2 km long six lane) has been constructed at 
Hazira Surat. The road has 32% reduced thickness than conventional bituminous road section, with its 
structural strength four times better despite reduced thickness and caters to heavy commercial traffic 
without any sign of distress. Further, the construction cost is around 40 % cheaper than conventional 
bituminous road. So far, the technology has been used for construction of steel slag roads in other areas 
too, including the Sino -India Border Road in Aru nachal Pradesh (1 km. long, two lane); Jharkhand 
(six-lane road on NH -33 connecting Jamshedpur to Ranchi); Maharashtra (1 km. six lane road on 
Mumbai-Goa highway and another six lane Bhadara Bypass Section of NH -53); and Gujarat (NH -53, 
near Abhava village junction and Khajod village junction at Surat). 
6.4 The Committee was informed that there are many key benefits of thi s technology, such as eco -
friendly sustainable utilization of steel slag waste (19 million tons generated annually through various 
steel plants in the country, which will increase to 45 million tons by 2030); saving of natural aggregates 
and reducing unsustainable quarrying and mining; reduction of GHG emissions and carbon footprint of 
road construction, improved durability of road with better service life; higher load resistance capacity, 
etc. As per directives of Niti Aayog and Ministry of Steel, CSIR is preparing a comprehensive design 
guidelines and specifications for utilization of steel slag in road constructions. Apart from road 
projects, there are immense future prospects for using steel slags in construction of civil and defence 
runways and for usin g it as Railway Ballast. CSIR -CRRI is focused towards promotion of sustainable 
utilization side by side with upgradation of the technology for better outcomes, and aiming to extend 
this technological support to various SAIL and other steel plants in the country. 

11 
 
6.5 The Committee highly commends the efforts of the Department in the field of waste 
management and, in particular, is pleased to learn about the technol ogies developed for 
converting various wastes to wealth. Taking cognizance of the need for a we ll coordinated waste 
management strategy in the country for various types of wastes, the Committee recommends that 
the Department should make concerted efforts to ensure that the Mission project on waste to 
wealth is implemented with all sincerity  and in a  holistic manner. Apart from sufficient

7. MISSION PROJECT ON ACTIVE PHARMACEUTICAL INGREDIENTS (APIs) 
7.1 The Com mittee inquired about the steps taken by the Dep artment, if any, to reduce the 
country‟s heavy dependence on import of raw materials, intermediates, APIs and components for the 
pharmaceutical industry. In its reply, the Department submitted that, while  Indian pharmaceutical 
industry has established itself as a global player, it  is heavily depe ndent on key bulk/fine chemicals, 
solvents, salts and the excipients essential for drug formulations. Hence, there is an urgent necessity to 
invest in R&D not only to achieve greater heights in this field, but to sustain current levels of business. 
7.2 The Department informed that, so far,  CSIR has developed cost -effective processes for various 
APIs and their intermediates through different projects. Processes have been developed successfully for 
17 APIs with transfer of few molecules like α -Lipoic acid, Az elaic Acid and Paracetamol to 
pharmaceutical companies for production and commercialization. CSIR -Indian Institute of Chemical 
Technology (IICT), Hyderabad has established a kilo -lab facility which soon will be made a GMP 
accredited lab. Similarly, CSIR ha s stepped forward in developing indigenous, innovative and novel 
chemical processes to produce intermediates and final APIs and also repurposing drugs for Covid-19 
towards affordable health care. 
7.3 To continue R&D in this crucial domain,  CSIR has propose d to take up a Mission P roject on 
APIs, with an objective to develop viable, non -infringing routes of synthesis for selected APIs using 
advanced instruments such as automation, flow chemistry and follow ing green chemistry principles. 
The Government of Indi a had, during the beginning of Covid -19 pandemic, shortlisted close to 60 
APIs/bulk drugs for which the Indian pharma industry was critically dependent on imports of raw 
materials or Key Starting Materials (KSMs). Under the proposed Mission project on APIs , priority is 
being given to these KSMs depending upon essentiality, availability of raw -materials and supply chain. 
Some of them have been selected keeping the prior experience/expertise and the potential to bring 
down the cost of production through proce ss optimization to enhance productivity and robustness. The 
efforts will be focused on developing alternate synthesis with the use of indigenous and renewable 
sources of raw materials and flow synthesis. Based on their need for the country, around 20 APIs are 
being taken up for process development under the proposed mission project.  The project aims to serve 
the country with its contributions to „Make in India‟ program and towards better health for the society. 
7.4 The Committee is fully aware of current st ate of huge dependence of the Indian 
Pharmaceutical industry on import of majority of raw materials used in the pharmaceutical 
industry. The Committee, therefore, expresses its wholehearted support towards CSIR’s 
proposed Mission Project on APIs, and wishes the Department a speedy progress in this 
direction. 
7.5 The Committee recommends that specific targets, both short term and long term, should 
be set for reducing th e dependence on imported raw materials from around 80 per cent at 
present, to 30 or 4 0 per cent in the next five yea rs.  To achieve this, the Committee recommends 
that the proposed Mission project should be dovetailed with the initiatives being undertaken in 

12 
 
this area by other Ministries/Departments and the private sector, adequate funds s hould be 
earmarked for the purpose so that financial constrains do not hinder the much needed research 
work, and options should be explored for benefiting from latest emerging technologies such as 
Artificial Intelligence (AI), with the overall objective of achieving the desired outcomes within the 
shortest possible timeframe . The Committee would also like to be kept abreast of the progress 
made by the Department in this regard.

INTRODUCTION 
The Department of Science & Technology (DST) is the nodal agency in the country for 
strengthening science, technology and innov ation, identifying gap areas in S&T sectors, making 
planning and policy to meet the societal needs, promoting new areas of S&T in view of future 
demands. DST also serves in connecting the science and technology sectors with different Government 
horizontals and verticals, academia, R&D labs /institutions and industries. With the objective to 
strengthen the national S&T capacity and capability, DST provides the largest extramural research and 
development support in the country to scientists cutting across institutions and disciplines through a  
competitive mode reinforcing our country’s education system, scientific and industrial R&D and the 
overall Science, Technology and Innovation landscape of the country.  
1.2 The Department has been continuing efforts towards strengthening the national STI ecosystem 
to emerge as a forerunner to play a critical role in science and technology for bringing positive 
transformations towards a safe, secure, better society, and be well prepared for future disruptions.  
1.3 The Department also administers 25 autonomous bodies and two statutory bodies, namely 
Science & Engineering Research Board (SERB) and Technology Development Board (TDB). The 
autonomous bodies include 16 research institutions, 4 specialized knowledge and S&T service 
organizations and 5 profe ssional bodies. These institutions, with long and cherished history and their 
variety of activities, occupy an important place in the S&T eco-system of the country. 
1.4 The Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology, 
Environment, Forests and Climate Change considered the Demands for Grants (2023 -24) of the 
Department of Science & Technology in its meeting held on 21st February, 2023.

3.  KEY ACHIEVEMENTS OF THE DEPARTMENT DURING 2022-23 
 
3.1 The Department of Science & Technology has four Central Sector Schemes/Project s, namely, 
Science and Technology Institutional and Human Capacity Building; Research and Development; 
Innovation, Technology Development and Deployment; and National Mission on Interdisciplinary 
Cyber Physical System (NM -ICPS). The Department implements its wide -ranging programmes under 
these schemes. The Department, through written replies and presentation during the meeting, submitted 
some of the key achievements across its various programmes during the year 2022-23, as below – 
- The Fund for Improvement of S&T Infrastructure in Universities and Higher Educational 
Institutions (FIST)  programme has been restructured to orient it towards  the goal of 
Atmanirbhar Bharat. During the year, 525 fresh proposals were received in seven subject areas , 
out of which 90 projects have been recommended. With support pro vided by the 15 
Sophisticated Analyti cal Instrument Facilities (SAIFs ) in the country , approximately 2400 
research papers were published and about 33,000 users across India utilized and be nefitted from 
these facilities. Under Synergistic Training program U tilizing the Scientific and Technological 
Infrastructure (STUTI) , a total of 192 training programs were organized and around 6,500 
researchers have been trained. Similarly, u nder State S&T Programme, 31 S&T Councils are 
supported currently. Two Policy Research Cells (PRC s) have also been supported and around  
19 DST-STI fellows received fellowship under the DST-STI fellowship programme.  
- Under Promotion of University Research and Scientific Excellence (PURSE) , four new 
Universities have been identified for support. The Department also announced a special call for 
the unserved regions in the country, to provide basic infrastructure for promoting R&D 
activities in new and emerging areas, in the universities of North Eastern Region, Jammu & 
Kashmir, Chhattis garh, Madhya Pradesh, Jharkhand, Bihar, Haryana, Telangana, Himachal 
Pradesh and Rajasthan. Under the special c all, 12 new universities have been identified for 
support.  
- Under Women in Science & Engineering - Knowledge Involvement in Research Advancement 
through Nurturing ( WISE-KIRAN), a total of 293 projects out of 990 proposals have been 

7 
 
selected in 5 different streams under Women Scientists Scheme – A (WOS -A), while under 
WOS-B grant has been released for 9 ongoing projects  and more than 30 publications  have 
come out from these projects. A new post -doctoral fellowship for women has also been 
launched under the Women Scientists Scheme - Professional Development of Women in 
Science (WISE  - PDF). VigyanJyoti programme, which aims to encourage girls to pursu e 
higher education and career in Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM)  has 
been extended to 200 districts (including 13 aspirational districts) of 34 states/UTs of the 
country, thereby benefitting  approximately 18,000 girls.

Climate Change (NMSKCC) and National Mission for Sustaining the Himalayan Ecosystem

and Chandigarh (UT) resulting in the presence of SCCCs in 28 states/UTs across the country.

7. NATIONAL RESEARCH FOUNDATION 
7.1 On scrutiny of budgetary allocations of the Department for the financially year 2023 -24, it is 
observed that Rs. 2000 crore, i.e., almost 25 per  cent, has been earmarked for the head ‘National 
Research Foundation (NRF)’. The Committee sought details about the aims, objective and activities 
being planned under this head. In a written reply, the Department submitted that NRF is envisioned as a 
body with a mandate to set the overall research agenda at the national level and it will seed, grow and 
promote research and development (R&D) and foster a culture of research and innovation throughout 
India’s universities, colleges, research institutions and R&D laboratories. In addition, NRF will create a 
vibrant R&D framework for industries and other organizatio ns to work closely with academic and 
research institutions. Its objectives and goals include: 
- funding of competitive peer -reviewed grant proposals to indivi duals or groups of individuals 
across all S&T disciplines in all types of institutions;  
- assist in setting up research infrastructure and environment for scientific pursuit;  
- increase India’s role and participation in key areas of national and global importance;  
- coordinate across Ministries, State Governments, Industries, etc. to document and analyse 
expenditure on science research as well as their outcomes during each financial year; and 
- serve as a high -level think tank for the coordination and short -and long -term planning of 
research in the country  
 
7.2 The Department further submitted that NRF has a broad-based strategy to enlarge the scope of 
research funding and promote/facilitate growth in research in academic institutions across the country. 
Seeding research at State Universities and colleges at rural settings has been given top priority. 
Research Mentors (in the form of ‘NRF Professorships’) at Universities and Colleges where research is 
currently in a nascent stage, particularly State Universities, will be created by utilizing the expertise of 
serving or retired faculty. Bringing in young research talent will be key to developing research cultures 
at educational institutions. For this purpose, NRF will launch a large and prestigious system of 
postdoctoral fellowships to be used in our academic systems. Creating Centers of Excellence (CoE) & 
National Mission Projects are some other modes to develop and support areas o f  critical national 
importance, such as A rtificial Intelligence (AI) , Machine Learning, Environmental Science, Climate 
Change etc. Many of these  Centres will aim to work in an interdi sciplinary manner, while d edicated 
R&D platforms will be created in partnership with industry to support and improve linkages between 
R&D, academia and industry. 
7.3 The Department informed that the following programmes will be initiated during 2023-24: 
(i) Seeding Research at State Universities through NRF Professorships: One of the foremost aims 
of the NRF will be to seed research at Universities and Colleges where research is currently 
non-existent or in nascent stages, particularly State Universities, whe re over 90% of the 
country’s faculty and students work and study. 
(ii) Postdoctoral Fellowships: The NRF will initially select and fund Postdoctoral Fellowships to 
outstanding researchers across S&T fields. 
(iii) Centers of Excellence (CoE) & National Mission Projects: Each year, proposals will be invited 
for establishing Centres of Excellence/ National Mission Projects at academic institutions and 
National Labs in areas of critical national importance, such as Machine Learning, 
Environmental Science, etc. Many of these Centres will aim to work in an interdisciplinary 
manner. 
(iv) Funding of Grants: A major goal of the NRF will be to fund competent people with good ideas, 

13 
 
across fields, wherever they may be located. Proposals will be invited by the NRF from 
individuals and groups of individuals across institutions. The aim will be to increase the 
resource absorption capacity for high-quality research in the nation, over a period of time. 
7.4 Both domestic and International Projects will be undertaken under the Grant sy stem. Broadly 
these projects would have defining characteristics such as individual centric, competitive funding; high 
priority research around established research groups with complementary experti se from different 
departments/institutes; t ransformative a nd disruptive research concepts based on innovative and 
unproven hypothesis, possessing a high degree of uncertainty, yet having conviction to produce a 
lasting impact across discipline boundaries ; gender parity oriented; equity and e mpowerment focused; 
thematically oriented ; and State University/ College centric promotional competitive projects . In 
addition, there will be special window for addressing and funding industrial research engagement. 
Performing scientists will be recognized through National Fellowships. 
7.5  The Department submitted that the tentative physical targets for financial year 2023 -24 include 
- 10 NRF Professorships; 500 Postdoctoral Fellowships; a minimum of one CoE & National Mission 
Project; competitive funding of 1000 projects; Early  Career Research Support to 500 regular 
faculty/scientists; sanctioning of Homecoming Fellowship to  100 scientists from abroad; 100 Science 
Excellence Fellowships; 300 gender parity oriented programmes; 100 Special calls; and 50 Priority 
Research projects. 
7.6 The Committee desired to know as to what would be the nature of relationship between the 
Department of Science & Technology  and NRF, as also of other bodies under the Department such as 
the Technology Development Board (TDB) and Science and Engineeri ng Research Board (SERB) . In 
its response, the Department informed that NRF will be established as a statutory body through an Act 
of Parliament. While NRF will serve as a high-level think tank for coordination and short and long -
term planning of research in the country, funding of grant proposals to individuals, groups or 
institutions across all S&T disciplines in all types of institutions will be synergized with the EMR 
funding schemes of the Department . Further, considering that NRF has an expanded mandate covering 
activities over and above the activities of SERB, it is proposed SERB will be subsumed in NRF. 
7.7 The Committee takes due note of the visions, objectives and purpose of creation of the 
National Research Foundation. It believes that a cent rally established NRF that transparently 
seeds, funds, and coordinates research across institutions in the country - in all disciplines, in an 
integrated manner, with a special mandate to foster research and innovation in universities and 
colleges, includi ng inter -disciplinary research to provide practical solutions to societal, 
developmental, financial, techno -economic challenges of the nation,  is a much needed 
overarching mechanism. The Committee recommends that , in the process of implementing this 
programme, special consideration should be given towards under-funded as well as new and 
emerging areas of research, while also keeping under-served regions of the country in mind.

REPORT 
INTRODUCTION 
 The Government of India set up the Space Commission and the Depa rtment of Space (DOS) in 
1972. Department of Space is responsible for implementing the policies framed by the Space 
Commission. These are carried out through the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO), Indian 
National Space Promotion & Authorization Centre (IN -SPACe) and the Grant -in-aid institutions viz., 
Physical Research Laboratory (PRL), National Atmospheric Research Laboratory (NARL), North -
Eastern Space Applications Centre (NE-SAC), Semi-Conductor Laboratory (SCL) and Indian Institute 
of Space Science and Technology (IIST). 
1.2 The Secretariat of the Department of Space and the Headquarters of ISRO are located in 
Bengaluru. The Programme Offices at ISRO Headquarte rs co -ordinate the overall programmes like 
Satellite Communication, Satellite Navigation, Earth Observation, Space Transportation Systems, 
Space Science and Planetary Exploration, Climate & Atmospheric Programme, Disaster Management 
Support, National Natur al Resources Management System (NNRMS), International Co -Operation, 
Capacity Building, Media & Public Relations, Budget & Economic Analysis and Human Resources 
Development. 
1.3 The activities of Department of Space (DOS) are broadly organized und er four umbrella 
schemes namely 
 Space Technology - development of launch vehicles, satellites, manned space mission, R&D in 
Space Technology such as propulsion, navigational satellite systems, indigenization of Space 
materials & components, etc.  
 
 Space Applications - major Projects/activities such as Earth Observation Navigation Missions, Tele-
medicine, Tele-education, Disaster Management Support,etc are undertaken. 
 
 Space Sciences - projects towards Space sciences and planetary exploration are undertaken. Major 
projects undertaken under the scheme include Indian Lunar Mission - Chandrayaan-3, Aditya -L1 
mission, XPoSat, Space Docking Experiment.  
 
 INSAT Satellite Systems - This programme is envisaged to provide satellite based communication 
services in the country. 
1.4 Major Centres / Units of DOS/ISRO: 
a) Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre (VSSC), Thiruvananthapuram, provides the technology base for 
the country‟s indigenous launch vehicle (rocket) development 
b) Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre (LPSC), with its facilities locat ed at Bengaluru and 
Thiruvananthapuram, is responsible for development of liquid propulsion and cryogenic 
propulsion systems for satellite and launch vehicles 
c) Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC-SHAR) at Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh, is the spaceport of 
India providing launch base to indigenously built launch vehicles.  Also, it provides the facilities 
for processing of solid rocket motors 
d) Human Space Flight Centre (HSFC) is created with the responsibility to act as the lead centre for 
Human Space Flight Progra m. This centre is responsible for the execution of 
Gaganyaanprogramme that envisages sending a crew of astrounauts to space and bring back 
safely to earth.   
e) U R Rao Satellite Centre (URSC), Bengaluru, is entrusted with the prime responsibility for 
development of satellites     

2 
 
f) Space Applications Centre (SAC), Ahmedabad 
g) National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC), Hyderabad is responsible for satellite data acquisition 
and processing, data dissemination, aerial remote sensing and decision s upport for disas ter 
management 
h) The Laboratory for Electro-Optics Systems (LEOS), Bengaluru  
i) ISRO Propulsion Complex (IPRC), Mahendragiri 
j) ISRO Telemetry, Tracking & Command Network (ISTRAC) 
k) Master Control Facility (MCF), Hassan 
l) Indian Institute of Remote Sensing (IIRS), Dehradun  
m) ISRO Inertial Systems Unit (IISU), Thiruvananthapuram  
1.5 Organisations receiving Grants-in-aid: 
a) Physical Research Laboratory (PRL), Ahmedabad, an autonomous institution supported mainly 
by the Department of Space, carries out research in space sciences. 
b) The National Atmospheric Research Laboratory (NARL) set up at Gadanki near Tirupati, 
conducts atmospheric research. 
c) The North -Eastern Space Applications Centre (NE -SAC) established as an autonomous body 
under the Department of Space provides spac e technology inputs for developmental activities in 
the North-Eastern Region.  
d) The Indian Institute of Space Science and Technology (IIST) is an autonomous body under the 
Department with the objective of creating quality human resources tuned to suit the requirements 
of state-of-art space research programme.    
1.6 Government Companies under DOS:  
a) The Antrix Corporation Limited, Bengaluru, established in 1992, is a wholly owned 
Government Company for marketing space products and services.  
b) The NewSpace India Limited (NSIL), Bengaluru, is another commercial arm of Indian Space 
Research Organization, with the primary objective of enabling Indian industries to scale up high-
technology manufacturing and production base for Indian space programme.  
1.7 Indian National Space Promotion and Authorization Center (INSPACe) 
Recently, the space sector was opened up to promote, handhold, regulate and authorise private 
enterprises and start-ups to undertake space activities by creation of an independent nodal agency under 
Department of Space - the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorization Center (IN -SPACe). 
This will enhance the contribution of space technology towards boosting space economy within the 
country.

3. MAJOR ACHIEVEMENTS IN THE RECENT PAST 
 The Committee, with a view to gather information and the importance of the key achievements 
of the Department, enquired for the same. The Department of Space informed that   the Indian Space 
Research Organization (ISRO) is involved in science, engineering and technology to harvest the 
benefits of outer space for India and the mankind. ISRO is pursuing multidisciplinary Research and 
Developments (R&D) in various areas to fulfil the various national needs: 
3.1 Space Transportation System 
3.1.1. During the period 2020 -2022, the Department has performed nine launch vehicle missions 
including three dedicated commercial missions for NewSpace India Limited (NSIL), a CPSE under the 
Department. In  addition, the spare capacity available onboard the national missions of PSLV was 
utilized to launch 16 customer satellites as co -passengers along with experimental payloads from Indian 
space start-ups.  
3.1.2. LVM3, the heaviest launch vehicle of India, p erformed its first dedicated commercial mission 
for launching 36 satellites for the OneWeb constellation. 
3.1.3. ISRO completed the first developmental flight of Small Satellite Launch Vehicle (SSLV), which 
has a payload capability of 500 kg to planar Low Earth Orbit.  SSLV is designed to be a quick 
turnaround, launch on demand launcher for launching small satellites.   
3.1.4. The margin demonstration tests for the solid, liquid and cryogenic propulsion systems of the 
human rated launch vehicle were also co nducted during this period, thereby building confidence for the 
upcoming Gaganyaan mission. In addition, the Department has developed a Test Vehicle based on liquid 
propulsion to function as a platform for testing out critical technologies such as the Gaga nyaan Crew 
Escape System and stage recovery systems. The Test Vehicle is expected to have its first developmental 
flight in 2023.  
3.1.5. The Department has progressed in the development of engine subsystems for the high thrust 
Semicryogenic engine that wi ll power the Semicryogenic stage for LVM3, thereby resulting in higher 
payload capability. The engine is ready for testing in the intermediate configuration.  
3.1.6. With regard to the development of critical technologies for a Reusable Launch (RLV), the 
Department has completed several ground tests, simulations and helicopter sorties towards the RLV 
Landing Experiment, that is scheduled in the first quarter of 2023.  
3.2 Space Infrastructure 
3.2.1 In recent times, ISRO has realized advanced spacecraft for various applications ranging 
from Communications services, Earth Observation to Navigation. High throughput satellites, 
Earth Observation satellites for day night imaging, sub -meter resolution, multi -spectral 
capability, micro satellites with reduced reali zation time, and navigation satellites for accurate 
Position, Navigation & Timing Services with multiple frequencies. Further to that advanced 
technologies have also been developed for Deep space missions to facilitate multi wavelength 
observations, in-situ scientific experiments, sensors and soft landings, etc. 
3.3 Space Science and Inter-planetary missions 
3.3.1 The Chandrayaan-2 missions has facilitated hydration mapping on lunar surface at extended IR 
wavelength. This mission also achieved the first -ever global mapping of exospheric Ar -40, and global 
surface distribution of Na. Chandrayaan -2 observations have also led to the detection of trace elements 
like Cr and Mn. This mission houses the highest resolution (~0.25 m) camera for lunar surface studies.  

12 
 
3.3.2 The Mars Orbiter Mission, which served till 2022, studied the Martian exospheric neutral 
composition, which expanded our knowledge on the Solar forcing on evening side of the Martian 
exosphere. The mission has also conducted surface studies, including the study of the Martian polar caps 
and their variabilities. The mission is also credited with the imaging of the Martian natural satellites 
Phobos and Deimos.  
3.3.3 The AstroSat satellite, which is India‟s multi -wavelength astronomical observatory in space, is 
credited with several significant discoveries, which include the discovery of Ly -alpha photons from a 
galaxy 9.3 billion years away, solving the puzzle of a source bright in both UV and IR thereby leading to 
the discovery of a hidden white dwarf, discovery of extended emission (~3 times more) in butterfly 
nebula, FUV observation revealing hot stars in Stephen‟s quintet, complementing JWST observations, to 
name a few.  
3.3.4 ISRO has also made the planetary and astronomy data available for public, through its portal of 
the Indian Space Science Data Centre. The data from the Indian space science missions are used by 
several national and international scientists. 
3.3.5 In future, missions are being conceptualized to study the surface and atmosphere of Venus, and 
the upper atmosphere of Earth. Missions are also getting conceptualized in the domains of lunar polar 
volatile research, surface studies, as well as Astronomy missions in UV wavelengths. 
3.4 Space Applications 
3.4.1 Data products and services of EOS -04 (RISAT-1A) satellite was formally released for the user 
community. The data is being operationally used for a variety of applications across agriculture, wate r 
resources, disaster management support etc. 
3.4.2 The North Eastern Spatial Data Repository (NeSDR) NeSDR project has been awarded Silver; 
in Category V -Excellence in Adopting Emerging Technologies, under National Award for e -
Governance, 2022. NeSDR cons ists of ~1260 Geospatial layers, and 25 web & mobile applications for 
use by the State line departments for developmental planning and decision support. 
3.4.3 Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) and Department of Agriculture and Farmers 
Welfare (DoA&FW), signed the MoU on “Development, Demonstration, Deployment and Maintenance 
of Agri-DSS”. The Agri-DSS portal will leverage the capabilities of ISRO‟s VEDAS Geoportal towards 
implementing a web-based decision support system for Agriculture sector in India.  
3.4.4 Digital Agriculture & Support to PMFBY: Geospatial inputs are used for developing 
methodology for monitoring progress of sown area, cropping intensity, crop condition and yield 
modelling for Maharashtra and West Bengal States. 
3.4.5 Support to N ational Crop Weather Watch group of MoAFW, Govt. of India: Satellite and 
weather data products at fortnightly interval were generated to assess the drought situation in eastern 
India. 
3.4.6 Space based Information Support for Decentralized Planning (Update ) (for MoPR): Generation 
of updated thematic data on 1:10K scale (LULC, Drainage, Rail, Road) and integrating with MoPR 
Assets of entire country is in progress. 
3.4.7 Bhuvan-NHP portal (for MoJS) for dissemination of hydro-informatic products being developed 
under the NHP was launched.  
3.4.8 Spatial flood forecast models for Tapi& Godavari basins are run using real time rainfall data 
from IMD. Flood forecast alerts and spatial inundation simulations are disseminated through Bhuvan, 
NDEM and NHP geoportals.

3.7 Human Space Exploration 
3.7.1 At present, ISRO has undertaken and is actively pursuing the human spaceflight mission that is 
Gaganyaan which involves major technology elements such as Human rated launch vehicle, Crew 
escape systems, Habitable orbital module, Life support system, Crew m anagement activities. 
Demonstration of reentry flight of Crew Module (CARE) mission and Pad abort test for crew escape 
systems, testing of human rated launch vehicle propulsive stages i.e. solid boosters, liquid and cryo

before it is deemed qualified to be used in the first human spaceflight mission.

4. GLOBAL SPACE ECONOMY – INCREASING INDIA’S SHARE  
 Acknowledging the size of the Global Space Economy to be around $ 350 billion and the 
immense potential, economic and strategic position, that India can attain through increasing its share 
and participation, the Committee sought information from the Department about its vision and the steps 
being taken in this regard. The Committee was informed that through its various ag encies and 
especially through Indian National Space Promotion and Authorization Centre (INSPACe) and throug h 
New Space India Limited (NSIL), the Department is working out a strategy for increasing India‟s share 
in global space economy from the current 2 percent to 10 percent by 2030.  
4.2 INSPACe: 
4.2.1 The vision of IN-SPACe is to enable private sector participation in space activities, boost space 
economy of India and develop space force frontiers for a resurgent Aatmanirbhar Bharat. The 
mission of IN-SPACe is to act as the single window agency, to promote, enable, supervise and 
authorize Non -Governmental Entities (Private industries, start -ups, MSMEs, State/Central 
PSUs and academic institutions) in the country to take up innovations in space sector . The 
objectives of the IN -SPACe are to promote, permit and oversee the following activities of 
NGEs: 
 a) Space activities including building of Launch Vehicles & satellites and providing space 
based services as per the definition of space activities legislation. 
 b) Sharing of space infrastructure and premises under the control of DOS/ISRO with due 
regard to the on-going activities. 
 c) Establishment of temporary facilities under DOS/ISRO‟s control based on safety norms 
and feasibility assessment.  
 d) Establishment of new space infrastructure and facilities, by NGPEs, in pursuance of 
space activities based on safety norms and other statutory guidelines and necessary clearances. 
 e) Initiation of launch campaign and launch, based on readiness of launch vehi cle and 
spacecraft systems, ground and user segment 
 f) Building, operation and control of spacecraft for registration as Indian Satellite by 
NGPEs and all the associated infrastructure for the same. 
 g) Usage of spacecraft data and rolling out of space ba sed services and all the associated 
infrastructure for the same.  
 h) IN-SPACe shall draw-up an integrated launch manifest considering the requirements for 
ISRO, CPSEs and NGPEs based on priorities and readiness level. 
 i) IN-SPACe shall work out a suitabl e mechanism for promotion and hand holding, 
sharing of technology and expertise to encourage participation of NGPEs in space activities.   
 j) In order to carry out the space activities, capital intensive, high technology facilities will 
be required by NGP Es. These facilities, spread across ISRO centres, shall be permitted for use 
by NGPEs at a reasonable cost/free of cost. 
 k) The decision of IN-SPACe shall be final and binding on all stakeholders

 l) IN-SPACe will be chaired by a Secretary Grade officer and will have technical experts 
for space activities, safety experts, experts from Academia, Legal & Strategic experts from 
other department of Government of India.

6. RESOLVING IMPORT DEPENDENCIES – ACHIEVING STATE OF THE ART 
INDIGENIZATION  
 Noting that one of the main reasons for reduction in allocation during the R.E. 2022 -23 was 
delayed procurement of critical component due to g lobal supply chain disruptions, the Committee 
gathered information about the key import dependencies of the Department and the steps bein g taken 
for its indigenization as the schedule of satellite projects is dictated by the manufacturing lead time and 
availability of these components since the technologies are available with only a few global players. 
6.2 The Department informed that with regard to space transportation systems, continuous efforts 
by the Department has resulted in a reduction of the import content of 25 -30% in the development 
phase to about 8 -9% currently. Presently, the major import depende ncies are related to electronic 
components and high strength carbon -carbon fibres. With regard to satellite programme, the major 
import dependencies are for sourcing EEE components, space qualified Solar Cells, Detectors, Optics 
and Power Amplifiers. Currently, the import dependency for satellite programme is about 50-55% for a 
typical satellite. 
6.3 Some of the Measures taken to reduce dependency in realization of space systems include:  
 a) Careful planning of procurement activities and some amount of sto ckpiling has helped 
to mitigate the schedule risk.  
 b) Department has a continuous programme for indigenization and has achieved success in 
indigenizing some passive electronic components as well as critical components like processors 
and data converters in association with Semiconductor Laboratory, Chandigarh. 
 c) Indigenization programs for critical technologies such as Travelling wave Tube 
Amplifiers, Atomic Clock, Electronics packaging including LTCC (Low temperature co -fired 
ceramic) & HTCC (High temp erature co -fired ceramic) package technology for RF, Optical, 
and Digital systems, ASICs(Application Specific Integrated Circuits). 
 d) Indigenization targeted for Electro -optical Detectors development using indigenous 
design, RF high power GaN HEMT technology foundry development. 
 e) The imported items are published in the Procurement Live Register(PLR) portal of 
ISRO website to invite Expression of Interest (EoI) from Indian Industries for indigenous 
development. 
6.4 The Committee notes that the current import dependencies in satellite systems are to the 
tune of 45 -50 percent and that the Department is making earnest efforts in achieving higher 
indigenization. The Committee recommends that the Department collaborates more intensely 
with the Indian industry as well as with the Ministry of Electronics & Information Technology in 
finding out solutions towards creating the support ecosystem that enables domestic 
manufacturing of critical electronics components. This shall not only save expensi ve foreign 
reserves but also shuttle India into the orbit of semiconductors and related critical technologies.

INTRODUCTION 
 The Ministry of Environment, Forest & Climate Change is the nodal agency in the 
administrative structure of the Central Government for planning, promoting, co -ordinating and 
overseeing environmental, ecological, forestry and wildlife policies and programmes. Its main activities 
include: 
 conservation and survey of natural resources including flora, fauna, forests, wildlife, aquatic 
bodies and water resources and eco-systems 
 prevention and control of pollution and management of hazardous substances 
 protection of the environment and forests, including their biodiversity, mitigation and 
adaptation to climate change through measures that include afforestation, regeneration of 
degraded areas, and adoption of cleaner technologies 
 promoting sus tainable development and better environmental governance while protecting 
human, plants and animals life, health and welfare 
 Facilitate activities related to India‟s commitments and obligations with three Rio Conventions 
i.e. UNFCCC, UNCCD and CBD related reporting process 
 Facilitate activities related to Basel, Rotterdam, Stockholm Conventions and enable India to 
meet its commitments as per Montreal Protocol under the Vienna Convention. 
1.2 The main tools used to discharge its mandate include, inter alia, conducting surveys; collecting, 
compiling and disseminating data and information; undertaking scientific research, extension services 
and analyses; carrying out impact assessment of developmental projects and programmes; regulating 
use of natural resources ; undertaking regeneration programmes; extending technical, scientific, 
financial and administrative support to organisations and institutions in the subject fields; imparting 
education, training, building capacity and generating awareness among stakeholde rs and the public at 
large; and promoting international cooperation through bilateral, regional and multilateral initiatives in 
environment and ecology. 
1.3 The institutional set up of the Ministry includes a number of Directorates and Divisions 
assembled around the main thematic sectors of environment and ecology, forestry and wildlife, 
afforestation and eco -development.  The Ministry has 19 Regional Offices; ten Attached/Subordinate 
Offices ( such as the  Botanical, Zoological and Forests Surveys of India, Directorate of Forestry 
Education, Indira Gandhi National Forestry Academy, National Green Tribunal, Wildlife Crime 
Control Bureau etc.); Boards and Statutory Bodies (Commission for Air Quality Management, Central 
Pollution Control Board) and Authorities ( such as the  National Biodiversity Authority, National Tiger 
Conservation Authority, Central Zoo Authority) and Autonomous Institutions ( such as the  Indian 
Council for Forestry Research and Education, Wildlife Institute of India etc.). 
1.4 Consequent upon the decision to do away with the practice of classifying expenditure as „Plan‟

3. CONTROL OF POLLUTION 
 Environmental Pollution remains one of the most burning issues  impacting lives of Billions of 
citizens. With the increasing population load, industrialisation and growth of economic activity to cater 
to the needs of the ever growing population, the environmental ecosystem has been damaged to a great 
extent. Air and w ater quality, not just in large cities but also in smaller towns, has deteriorated 
drastically impacting hundreds of millions of lives. Recognizing the fact that  the ill effects of 
environmental pollution touches everyone‟s lives, the Committee desired to know about the measures 
taken by the Ministry towards control and ab atement of pollution. The Ministry informed that it had 
proposed a total financial outlay of Rs. 847.5 crore for the year 2023 -24 in the Expenditure Finance 
Committee (EFC) Note of the scheme. However, total budget of Rs. 756 crore has been allocated under 
the BE 2023-24.

2)     National Clean Air Programme (NCAP) 
The National Clean Air Programme (NCAP) is a comprehensive time bound action programme 
launched by Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEF&CC) in January 2019 with an 
objective to improve air quality in the Non – attainment cities. The cities which are exceedin g the 
National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) for 5 consecutive years are identified as Non -
Attainment cities by CPCB. 124 such NACs are identified by CPCB under NCAP. 
Fifteenth-FC has identified 42 cities / urban agglomerations (UA) with million pl us population 
on the basis of severity of air quality and population exposure for objective based grants for period FY 
2020-2026 under Million-Plus Cities Challenge Fund (MCF).  Out of these 42 MPCs/UAs, 34 cities are 
included in the list of 124 NACs being targeted in NCAP. Therefore, 132 cities (NACs and MPCs/UAs) 
are being targeted for improving air quality from NCAP and XV-FC funding and accordingly all the 132 
cities have prepared City Action plans (CAP) and approved by CPCB and is rolled out for 
implementation. 
 
The City Action Plan (CAP) of these 132 cities are to be implemented by coordinated action of 
state government and its agencies at state and city level. The funding for implementation of CAPs is to 
mobilised through convergence of resources from various schemes of Central Government such as SBM 
(Urban), AMRUT, Smart City Mission, SATAT, FAME -II etc. and resources from State/UT 
Governments and its agencies such as Municipal Corporation, Urban Development authorities and 
Industrial development authorities etc. 
 
The funding from NCAP/XV -FC is performance -based-supplemental grant for funding of 
activities of CAP for which adequate funding is not available from other sources and schemes. 
 
3)     Environmental Monitoring Programme  
The Ministry provides funding to Central Pollution Control Board for monitoring of air quality, 
water quality and noise monitoring across the country and to support the country wide network of air, 
water and noise monitoring network.

Government to improve air quality: 
 Vehicular Emission 
1. Leapfrogging from BS -IV to BS -VI norms for fuel and vehicles since April, 2018 in NCT of 
Delhi and from 1st April, 2020 for rest of the country. 
2. Network of metro rails for public transport are being enhanced and more cities are covered.  
3. Development of Expressway and Highways is also reducing the fuel consumption and pollution. 
4. Eastern Peripheral Expressway & Western Peripheral Expressway has been operationalized to 
divert non destined traffic from Delhi. 
5. Ban on 10-year-old diesel vehicles and 15-year-old petrol vehicles in Delhi NCR.  
6. Environment protection charges (EPC) have been imposed on diesel vehicles with engine 
capacity of 2000cc and above in Delhi NCR.  
7. Introduction of cleaner/alternate fuels like CNG, LPG, ethanol blending in petrol.  
8. Faster Adoption and Manufacturing of Electric Vehicles (FAME) -2 schemes have been rolled 
out. 
9. Permit requirement for electric vehicles has been exempted. 
10. Promotion of public transport and improvements in roads and building of more bridges to ease 
congestion on roads. 
 Industrial Emission 

14 
 
11. Ban on use of pet coke and furnace oil in NCR, use of pet coke in processes in cement plants, 
lime kilns and calcium carbide manufacturing units. 
12. Stringent emission norms for Coal based Thermal Power Plants (TPPs). 
13. Shifting of industrial units to PNG/cleaner fuel in Delhi 
14. Installation of online continuous emission monitoring devices in highly polluting industries. 
15. Shifting of brick kilns in Delhi- NCR to zig-zag technology for reduction of pollution 
 Air Pollution due to dust and burning of waste 
16. Notification of 7 waste management rules covering solid waste, plastic waste, e -waste, bio -
medical waste, C&D waste, hazardous waste and battery waste. 
17. Setting up infrastructure such as waste processing plants. 
18. Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) for plastic and e-waste management. 
19. Ban on burning of biomass/garbage. 
 Other measures for management of air quality  
20. Public Grievances and Response System (PGRS) is developed under NCAP 
21. Emergency Response System (ERS) has been prepared in NCAP cities. 
22. Air quality monitoring cell has been constituted across the country in NCAP Cities. 
23. Implementation of Air Quality Early Warning System for Delh i, Kanpur and Lucknow. The 
system provides alerts for taking timely actions. 
24. Public Complaints regarding air pollution issues in Delhi NCR are taken through „Sameer App‟, 
„Emails‟ (Aircomplaints.cpcb@gov.in) and „Social Media Networks‟ (Facebook and Twitter). 
25. At present ambient air quality is monitored through a network of 1296 manual and real time 
monitoring stations in 473 towns and cities across 28 states and 7 UTs in the country which is 
being further strengthened under NCAP. 
3.6 The following activities have been undertaken under the National Clean Air Programme  during 
the last three years: 
i. National Clean Air Programme (NCAP) has been launched by Ministry of Environment, Forest and 
Climate Change (MoEF&CC) in January 2019 with an aim to improve air quality in 131 cities covering 
24 States by engaging all stakeholders.  
ii. 95 cities out of 131 cities have shown improvement in air quality in terms of PM10 concentrations in FY 
2021-22 as compared to base levels of 2017. The improvement in PM10 concentrations in these 95 cities 
ranges up to 50 percent.  
iii. 41 cities out of 131 cities under NCAP are located in Indo -Gangetic plain. The cities located in Indo -
Gangetic plain, on account of typical geography and meteoro logy, have high base line levels of PM10 
concentrations. However, based on the on account of several measures taken by these cities over last few 
years, 29 cities have shown reduction upto 45 % in PM10 concentrations.    
iv. The action plans at City Level are primarily to be implemented through convergence of resources from 
schemes of Central Government such as, Swacch Bharat Mission, Smart City Mission, AMRUT, 
SATAT, FAME II, CESL Grand Challenge, National Biomass Mission and Nagar Van Yojana, 
resources of the State Government and Urban local bodies.  
v. The implementation of actions of city action plans under National level programmes being run by 
Central Government in the targeted cities over the period from 2021 -22 to 2025 -26 will result in 
intended reduction i n PM10 concentrations. The performance based funding mechanism under NCAP 
and XV th FC from year 2021 -22 to 2025 -26 will accelerate the implementation of action plans by the 
State governments, Municipal Corporations and other city level agencies.

vi. From year 2021-22, performance based grant is being released to 82 cities out 131 targeted cities under 
NCAP and to remaining 49 cities under XVth Finance Commission. Till date, total of Rs. 872 crores

Rs.7910 crore have been released under XV th Finance Commission from November, 2020 till date for 
funding critical gaps of their city action plans for improvement of air quality.

3.11 While the Committee underlines the efforts taken by the Ministry towards Control of 
Pollution and especially Air Pollution through the National Clean Air Programme, it 
recommends the Ministry to revisit its monitoring framework to ensure that the data captured is 
not just quantitative but also qualitative. The data provided by the Ministry seems very counter 
intuitive from what the public experiences at large. While d ata on PM10 levels suggests that 95 
cities out of the 131 non attainment cities have shown improvement, the public experience at 
large differs. It is therefore pertinent that the monitoring framework should also include a 
parameter on ‘public experience an d social audit’. This shall enable the Ministry to capture the 
public aspirations in a more holistic manner and shall be helpful in more efficient 
implementation of NCAP and other measures to control pollution.  
3.12 Further, the Ministry should engage with stakeholders, especially with the public 
representatives from each of these non attainment cities and establish a channel of two way 
communication. This 360 degree approach shall go a long way in making the fight ag ainst 
pollution a cumulative effort with increased public participation. Inclusion of matters relating to 
NCAP in the meetings of the District and State level DISHA Committees shall enable active 
monitoring of progress under NCAP.

monitored under the National Clean Air Programme more robustly across all cities.  In addition, 
the City Action Plans pertaining to the targeted cities are made available on public portals of the 
Ministry, promoted through social media, disseminated to schools, colleges, offices, RWAs, etc.

5. CONSTRUCTION ACTIVITIES IN ECOLOGICALLY SENSITIVE AREAS 
 Taking cognizance of the ongoing crisis in Joshimanth, Uttarakhand and reports of illegal 
construction activities in sensitive areas of Mussoorie, Dhanaulti without seeking clearances from the 
Forest Department, the Committee enquired from the Ministry about the extant practices of giving 
clearances to construction projects and mechanism for registration of complaints against those acting in 
defiance. The Ministry submitted that it  has delineated a detailed procedure for compre hensive 
assessment of environmental and social impacts of the project in the Environment Impact Assessment 
Notification, 2006, as amended; which inter-alia provides for four stages of consideration process i.e., 
Screening, Scoping, Public Consultation and Appraisal by the Expert Appraisal Committee (EAC), for 
assessment of environmental and social impacts taking into account the location of the Project and also 
for monitoring of projects. Study of the aforesaid and other related factors in the context of sp ecific 
projects forms the basis for preparation of the Environmental Impact Assessment/Environmental 
Management Plan. 
5.2 The EAC comprising domain area experts, after detailed examination and deliberations on 
various environmental and social aspects of the project including appraisal of the studies/information 
related to seismology, geological profile, study of landslide prone areas, risk analysis studies, 
recommend the project for grant of Environmental Clearance (EC) by suggesting suitable mitigation 
measures and Environment Management to minimize the environmental and social impacts associated 
with the project. It is only after such detailed study and analysis that environmental clearances are 
issued subject to compliance of necessary environmental saf eguards and general and specific 
conditions by the Project Proponent (PP) before undertaking construction of the project. 
5.3  Project specific conditions related to safety measures like installation of Early Warning 
Telemetric system,  implementation of Em ergency Preparedness Plan, Disaster Management Plan, 
Catchment Area Treatment plan, stabilization of muck disposal sites, rim plantation, pasture 
development, nursery development etc. are also prescribed in the Environmental Clearances.  
5.4 Projects invol ving forest land require Forest Clearance under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 
1980. Whenever, a proposal for diversion of forestland is received, it is examined and due diligence is 
exercised to avoid the use of forestland, or to keep it barest minimum.  The Ministry further submitted 
that issues pertaining to environmental non -compliance, violation or related negligence by the public 
officials are being reported to the Ministry vide complaint and Public Grievance received through the 
portal (https://pgpor tal.gov.in/). These complaints are processed by the Ministry as per the existing 
procedure.  
5.5 The Ministry is in the process of developing a web based system to automate the entire process 
of inspection and compliance monitoring. This system is expected  to reduce the time taken for 
monitoring, enhance coverage and transparency, reduce requirement of significant additional human 
resources even while ensuring comprehensive compliance of environmental conditions, thereby 
resulting in greater protection of the environment on a continuing basis.

5.10 The Committee notes the detailed procedure followed by the Ministry before giving 
clearances to construction and infrastructure projects and would like to emphasize on the fact 
that the role of the Ministry is to strike a balance between development and en vironment 
protection. The Committee also believes that a one size fits all approach to environment 
clearance should not be followed, especially for the ecologically sensitive areas of the country 
such as in Joshimath, Mussoorie, Dhanaulti, etc. , which requ ire a more meticulous approach 
with the only aim of furthering the environmental interests rather than economic interest.   
5.11 The Committee also highlights the tremendous increase of tourist activities in these areas 
which has put the natural resources under pressure. This has led to over -exploitation of natural 
resources and illegal construction of home stays, guest houses, resorts, hotels, rest aurants and 
other encroachments. In view of the imminent threat to ecological balance caused by these 
activities, it is pertinent that  a thorough assessment of illegal structures be undertaken in

illegal constructions, lest it results into a manmade crisis of huge proportions.

not paint a very rosy picture about the step s that the Ministry is taking towards addressing such 
complaints. While the idea to create an online mechanism for registration and tracking of 
complaints is a step in the right direction, the Committee recommends that the Ministry should 
take aggressive steps towards disposal of non -frivolous and serious complaints against violators 
of relevant laws. The Committee also recommends that the Ministry should undertake a review

with stakeholder institutions such as CPCB, NGT, State Government and redress these at the
