Department (Rs. 3,079.40 crore), though higher than the R.E. 2022 -23 allocation, is similar to the 
B.E. 2022-23 allocation.                                                                                                             (Para 2.2) 
 The Committee further observes that there has been a drastic reduction under the 
National Coastal Mission from Rs. 195 crore in B.E. 2022 -23 to only Rs. 4 crore in R.E. 2022 -23. 
Further an amount of Rs. 12.5 crore has been allocated under this head in B.E. 2023 -24. As 
regards the head ‘Control of Pollution’, the Committee observers that a budget of Rs. 460 crore 
was initially allocated during B.E. 2022 -23 which was revised upwards  to Rs. 600 crore in R.E. 
2022-23. The allocation under the head ‘Control of Pollution’ is Rs. 756 crore in B.E. 2023-24. 
(Para 2.3)  
 On perusal of Chart 1, the Committee observes that the B.E. and R.E. allocation across 
the years 2021-22 and 2022-23 have remained almost the same. Also, the B.E. 2023 -24 allocation 
is similar to that of B.E. 2022 -23. Although the allocation proposed by th e Department was Rs. 
4434.75 crore but only Rs. 3079 crore got allocated the Department in B.E. 2023-24.       (Para 2.5)  
  The Committee further observes that the Actual utilisation of the Ministry in 2022 -23 is 
Rs. 1707 crore (till January 2022 -23) against a R.E. allocation of Rs. 2478 crore. This amounts to 
about 69 percent budget utilisation which falls short of the 75 percent expenditure target set for 
3rd Quarter by the Ministry of Finance.                                                                                  (Para 2.6) 
 The Committee observes from Chart 2 that while the allocation under the Non -Scheme 
component in B.E. 2022-23 and R.E. 2022-23 remained almost the same, the allocation under the 
Scheme component was revised downwards in the R.E. stage. The allocation under the scheme 
component was Rs. 1893.26 crore during B.E. 2022 -23 which was reduced to Rs. 1396.45 crore 
during R.E. 2022-23.                                                                                                                  (Para 2.8) 
 The Committee is dismayed to note that financial utilization suffered because of a 
technicality in the manner of disbursement of f unds. While the change may have been brought 
with an intention of reducing parking of funds and loss on interest accrued, the approach should 
have been one with least collateral damage. The Committee recommends the Ministry to 
thoroughly review the status of States/Accounts on boarded and the pending disbursements be 
cleared as soon as possible, so that any projects which could not be initiated/completed due to 
unavailability of funds may be started/finished.                                                                   (Para 2.11)  
 The Committee observes from Chart 3 that the Ministry sought an allocation of Rs. 
4,434.75 crore in B.E. 2022 -23 whereas the Ministry received an allocation of Rs. 3079.40 crore. 
This amounts to a shortfall of Rs. 1,355.35 crore. It can also be observed that the major reduction 
in allocation is in the Scheme component – a reduction of about 1100 crore. Further, the 
Committee notes that the reduction under the National Coastal Management Programme  is 
drastic – from a proposed allocation of Rs. 723 crore to only Rs. 12.50 crore.                 (Para 2.13) 

26 
 
  The Committee is perturbed to observe that a reduction of almost 30 percent has been 
made in the proposed budgetary allocations requested by the Ministry. This may hamper the 
activities and initiatives of the Ministry across the entire gamut of Environmental protection and 
ecology management, forest & wildlife conservation as well as assistance to States and UTs. This 
may also lead to restricted implementation of ma ny initiatives of the Ministry pertaining to 
Climate Change, Pollution abetment and coastal development.                                         (Para 2.15) 
 The Committee is constrained to highlight the unpreparedness of the Ministry which is 
manifested in the fact that the Ministry depended on financial resources under the National 
Coastal Mission, from an outside agency. A setback in terms of administrative procedures from 
the agency has left the implementation of the initiatives of the Ministry in the loom. If resources 
are not made available timely, then the vast coastline of the country, the population dependent on 
it as well as the fragile coastal ecosyst em shall face the brunt. The Committee, therefore strongly 
recommends the Ministry to initiate a strategy and raise the deficit funds, either though the 
Ministry of Finance or by reaching out to other such agencies.                                         (Para 2.16) 
 On perusal of Chart 5, the Committee observes that ‘Green India Mission’ and ‘Control 
of Pollution’ which are key components of the Ministry’s initiatives towards Environment 
Protection and management of ecology, require additional budgetary support of Rs. 81 crore and 
Rs. 91 crore respectively.  Likewise, under Project Tiger & Elephant, an additional allocation of 
Rs. 43.2 crore is required. In addition, the Ministry is need of additional budgetary allocations to 
its institutions and autonomou s bodies engaged in Forestry research, survey and in -situ 
conservation.                                                                                                                            (Para 2.19) 
 The Committee underlines the requirement of an additional budgetary allocation of Rs. 
374 crore over and above the B.E. 2023 -24 quoted by the Ministry and recommends that the 
Ministry be given the additional allocation for them to continue with their set goals and 
objectives and ensure a timely and effective completion.                                                    (Para 2.20) 
 The Committee also recommends that the Ministry should reach out to the Ministry of 
Finance for additional funds at the R.E./ Supplementary stage and also look for raising t he same 
either through internal revenue or through reallocating funds from heads which have excess 
allocation, if any.                                                                                                                      (Para 2.21) 
 Chart 8 provides a clear picture of the status of utilisation of funds, till January 2023 (as 
percent of R.E. 2022 -23). The overall budgetary utilisation of the Ministry is around 69 percent, 
which is satisfactory. But a detailed examination reveals that a cross centrally sponsored and 
central sector schemes combined, the utilisation is only 54 percent (as percent of the R.E. 
allocation under these two heads). The combined R.E. 2022 -23 allocation was Rs. 1,369 crore out 
of which the utilisation till January 2023 has been only Rs. 792 crore. The Committee is 
astonished to observe that across crucial initiatives like Climate Change Action Plan and 
National Mission for Green India, the utilisation has been grossly suboptimal at 27 percent and 
55 percent respectively. Further, the Ministry has been able to utilise only 30 percent of the funds 
allocated to it under Project Tiger and Project Elephant combined.                                 (Para 2.29) 
 The Committee expresses its deep anguish and disappointment to wards the abysmally low 
utilisation of funds. While the reason, as stated by the Ministry, pertains to a procedural change 
in disbursement of funds, the Committee views this suboptimal utilisation as an opportunity lost. 
The Committee therefore recommends the Ministry to take strong, firm and quick actions to 
ensure that the funds under these heads are utilised to their fullest and that any shortfall in 
physical targets be compensated in the ensuing financial year.                                          (Para 2.30) 

27 
 
    CONTROL OF POLLUTION 
 The Committee observes from Chart 9 that there is a general upward trend in B.E. 
allocation under the ‘Control of Pollution’. Whereas the actual expenditure in 2020 -21 was Rs. 
267 crore, the B.E. allocation in 2023 -24 i s Rs. 756 crore. This is an increase of almost 200 
percent. The Committee is encouraged to see  and appriciates that the actions of the Ministry are 
being backed by a higher budgetary allocation year -on year. The Committee also notes the 
physical achievements of the Ministry during 2021-22 and 2022-23 which have been take towards 
strengthening of State Pollution Co ntrol Boars, NAMP stations assisted, initiatives taken for 
monitoring of pollution etc.                                                                                                      (Para 3.3) 
 While the Committee underlines the efforts taken by the  Ministry towards Control of 
Pollution and especially Air Pollution through the National Clean Air Programme, it 
recommends the Ministry to revisit its monitoring framework to ensure that the data captured is 
not just quantitative but also qualitative. The data provided by the Ministry seems very counter 
intuitive from what the public experiences at large. While data on PM10 levels suggests that 95 
cities out of the 131 non attainment cities have shown improvement, the public experience at 
large differs. It  is therefore pertinent that the monitoring framework should also include a 
parameter on ‘public experience and social audit’. This shall enable the Ministry to capture the 
public aspirations in a more holistic manner and shall be helpful in more efficient  
implementation of NCAP and other measures to control pollution.                                  (Para 3.10) 
 Further, the Ministry should engage with stakeholders, especially with the public 
representatives from each of these non attainment cities and es tablish a channel of two way 
communication. This 360 degree approach shall go a long way in making the fight against 
pollution a cumulative effort with increased public participation. Inclusion of matters relating to 
NCAP in the meetings of the District an d State level DISHA Committees shall enable active 
monitoring of progress under NCAP.                                                                                    (Para 3.11) 
 The Committee also recommends that levels of PM2.5 and smaller particles may also be 
monitored under the National Clean Air Programme more robustly across all cities. In addition, 
the City Action Plans pertaining to the targeted cities are made available on public portals of the 
Ministry, promoted through social media, disseminated to schools, colleges, offices, RWAs, etc. 
(Para 3.12)   
3.13 The Committee also recommends that levels of PM2.5 and smaller particles may also be 
monitored under the National Clean Air Programme more robustly across all cities. In addition, 
the City Action Plans pertaining to the targeted cities are made available o n public portals of the 
Ministry, promoted through social media, disseminated to schools, colleges, offices, RWAs, etc.   
(Para 3.13) 
PROJECT TIGER AND PROJECT ELEPHANT 
 The Committee notes that Project Tiger and Project Elephant are crucial to the initiatives 
of the Ministry relating to wildlife conservation, not just from an ecological standpoint but also 
for its societal and economic value. The initiatives of the Ministry, or the lack of it, have a direct 
bearing not just to the project but also to the human population living in these vulnerable areas. 
With increasing reports of man -animal conflicts , it becomes even more important that the 
Ministry sharpens its focus towards these projects and also allocate  more funds for meeting  
necessary expenditures are met. The Committee therefore recommends that the Ministry ensures 
that funds allocated in R.E. 2022 -23 be optimally utilized. Further, the Ministry should seek 

28 
 
additional allocation under this head so as to ensure that no conservation initiative i s left because 
of inadequacy of funds.                                                                                                              (Para 4.5) 
CONSTRUCTION ACTIVITIES IN ECOLOGICALLY SENSITIVE AREAS 
 The Committee notes the detailed procedu re followed by the Ministry before giving 
clearances to construction and infrastructure projects and would like to emphasize on the fact 
that the role of the Ministry is to strike a balance between development and environment 
protection. The Committee also  believes that a one size fits all approach to environment 
clearance should not be followed, especially for the ecologically sensitive areas of the country 
such as in Joshimath, Mussoorie, Dhanaulti, etc., which require a more meticulous approach 
with the only aim of furthering the environmental interests rather than economic interest.  
(Para 5.10)    
 The Committee also highlights the tremendous increase of tourist activities in these areas 
which has put the natural resources under pressure . This has led to over -exploitation of natural 
resources and illegal construction of home stays, guest houses, resorts, hotels, restaurants and 
other encroachments. In view of the imminent threat to ecological balance caused by these 
activities, it is pert inent that a thorough assessment of illegal structures be undertaken in          
co-ordination with local authorities and strict actions be initiated at the earliest against such 
illegal constructions, lest it results into a manmade crisis of huge proportions.               (Para 5.11) 
 The Committee is constrained to observe, from table 3 that against more than 5500 
complaints received in 2021-22, action could only be taken against 100 odd complaints. This does 
not paint a very rosy picture about the steps  that the Ministry is taking towards addressing such 
complaints. While the idea to create an online mechanism for registration and tracking of 
complaints is a step in the right direction, the Committee recommends that the Ministry should 
take aggressive st eps towards disposal of non -frivolous and serious complaints against violators 
of relevant laws. The Committee also recommends that the Ministry should undertake a review 
of all pending complaints especially pertaining to the State of Uttarakhand and devic e a strategy 
with stakeholder institutions such as CPCB, NGT, State Government and redress these at the 
earliest.                                                                                                                                      (Para 5.12) 
CENTRALLY SPONSORED SCHEME (CSS)- DATA REGARDING STATEWISE RELEASES 
(FY 2021-22) 
 The Committee observes from the data given by the Ministry that a total of Rs. 603.48 
crore were disbursed to States in F.Y. 2021 -22 through its Centrally Sponsored Schemes viz. 
Green India Mission, Integrated Development of Wildlife Habitats, Integrated D evelopment of 
Wildlife Habitats, Forest Fire Prevention and Management System, Biodiversity Conservation, 
Project Elephant and Project Tiger. The Committee also observes that six States namely, 
Maharashtra, Uttarakhand, Odisha, Karnataka, Mizoram and Madhy a Pradesh have received 
more than 50 percent of the total allocations to States in the year 2021 -22. Further, only Rs. 
206.40 crore could be disbursed to States in the year 2022-23 (till January 2023) which is only one 
third of what was disbursed in the ye ar 2021 -22.  Further, States like Jammu & Kashmir, 
Telangana, Goa have received almost negligible funds.                                                        (Para 6.4) 

29 
 
 While the Committee is aware of the fact that these disbursements are based on the 
Annual Plan of Operations submitted by the States, the Committee recommends that the 
Ministry actively pursues the underserved States and takes periodic assessment of their 
requirements under these CSS. Further, the Committee recommends that a mechanism of 
monitoring, targets achieved and scrutiny through public participation be devised by the 
Ministry which involves public representatives, legislators, MLAs and Hon’ble Members of 
Parliament.                                                                                                                                 (Para 6.5)

REPORT 
INTRODUCTION 
 The Ministry of Earth Sciences was established in the year 2006 by bringing all the agencies of 
meteorological and ocean developmental activities under one umbrella, to address holistically various 
aspects relating to earth system processes for improving f orecast of the weather, climate and various 
natural geo-hazards. The Ministry inter alia is also responsible for development of technology towards 
the exploration and harnessing of marine resources in a sustainable way for the socio -economic 
benefits of the country. The mission of the Ministry is to provide services for weather, natural hazards, 
climate, ocean and coastal state, seismology exploration and harnessing of marine living and non-living 
resources and exploration of the Polar Regions.  
1.2 The research & development and operational (service) activities of Ministry of Earth Sciences  
are carried out under the following six major umbrella schemes. A new scheme entitled Deep Oce an 
Mission has been implemented with effect from 2021-22. 
i). Atmosphere and Climate Research – Modelling, Observing Systems and Services 
(ACROSS). 
ii). Ocean Services, Modelling, Application, Resources and Technology (O-SMART) 
iii). Polar and  Cryosphere Research (PACER). 
iv). Seismology and Geosciences (SAGE). 
v). Research, Education, Outreach and Training (REACHOUT) 
vi). Deep Ocean Mission (DOM) 
1.3 The policies and programs of the Ministry are being primarily pursued through its centers viz., 
autonomous bodies, attached and subordinate offices. Currently there are 10 centre s / institutes under 
the Ministry to pursue programs/policies of the Ministry in different areas of Earth Sciences.  The 
institutions dealing with atmospheric sciences are the India Meteorological Department (IMD), 
National Centre for Medium Range Weather Forecasting (NCMRWF), Noida and Indian Institute of 
Tropical Meteorology (IITM), Pune. The institutions related to ocean science and technology are 
National Centre for Polar and Ocean Research (NCPOR), Goa, National Institute of Ocean Technology 
(NIOT), Ch ennai, Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS), Hyderabad, 
Centre for Marine Living Resources and Ecology (CMLRE), Kochi and National Centre for Coastal 
Research (NCCR), Chennai. The National Centre for Earth Science Studies (NCESS),  
Thiruvananthapuram and National Centre for Seismology (NCS), New Delhi are also part of the 
Ministry to conduct research on solid earth and earthquake monitoring. Each Centre of the Ministry has 
a well-defined mandate to conduct research and development in a specific area of Earth Sciences. 
1.4 The mandate of the Ministry includes overall policy, planning, coordination, implementation, 
evaluation and review of the schemes relating to meteorology, seismology, oceanography, ocean 
resources and technology, po lar science, cryosphere and geosciences not specifically allocated to any 
other Department or Ministry.

  3. Deep Ocean Mission 
 About 95 per cent of Deep Ocean remains unexplored. For India, with its three sides surrounded 
by the oceans and around 30 per cent of the country's population living in coastal areas, ocean is a 
major economic factor supporting fisheries and aquaculture, tourism, livelihoods and blue trade. 
Oceans are also storehouse of food, energy, minerals, medicines, modulator of weather and climate and 
underpin life on Earth. Considering importance of the oceans on sustainability, the United Nations 
(UN) has declared the decade, 2021 -2030 as the Decade of Ocean Science for Sustainable 
Development. India has a unique maritime position. Its 7517 km long coastline is home to nine coastal 
states and 1382 islands. The Government of India’s Vision of New India b y 2030 enunciated in 
February 2019 highlighted the Blue Economy as one of the ten core dimensions of growth. 
3.2 The Committee was informed that with a view to explore deep ocean for resources and develop 
deep sea technologies for sustainable use of ocean resources, Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs 
(CCEA) approved the proposal of Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES) on “Deep Ocean Mission” at an 
estimated cost of Rs. 4077.0 crore for a period of 5 years to be implemented in a phase -wise manner. 

11 
 
The estima ted cost for the first phase for the 3 years (2021 -2024) would be Rs.2823. 4 crore. Deep 
Ocean Mission will  be a mission mode project to support the Blue Economy Initiatives of the 
Government of India. Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES) is the nodal Ministry  implementing this 
multi-institutional ambitious mission. 
3.3 The Deep Ocean Mission consists of the following six major components:- 
1. Development of Technologies for Deep Sea Mining, and Manned Submersible:  A 
manned submersible will be developed to carr y 3 people to a depth of 6000 metres in the ocean 
with suite of scientific sensors and tools. Only a very few countries have acquired this 
capability. An Integrated Mining System will be also developed for mining Polymetallic 
Nodules from 6000 m depth in t he central Indian Ocean. This component will help the Blue 
Economy priority area of exploring and harnessing of deep-sea minerals and energy. 
2. Development of Ocean Climate Change Advisory Services:  A suite of observations 
and models will be developed to understand and provide future projections of important climate 
variables on seasonal to decadal time scales under this proof of concept component. This 
component will support the Blue Economy priority area of coastal tourism. 
3. Technological innovations f or exploration and conservation of deep -sea 
biodiversity: Bio- prospecting of deep -sea flora and fauna including microbes and studies on 
sustainable utilization of deep sea bio -resources will be the main focus. This component will 
support the Blue Economy priority area of Marine Fisheries and allied services. 
4. Deep Ocean Survey and Exploration:  The primary objective of this component is to 
explore and identify potential sites of multi -metal hydrothermal sulphides mineralization along 
the Indian Ocean mid -oceanic ridges. This component will additionally support the Blue 
Economy priority area of deep-sea exploration of ocean resources. 
5. Energy and freshwater from the Ocean:  Studies and detailed engineering design for 
offshore Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion (OTEC) powered desalination plant are envisaged 
in this proof of concept proposal. This component will support the Blue Economy priority area 
of off-shore energy development. 
6. Advanced Marine Station for Ocean Biology:  This component is aimed as 
development of human capacity and enterprise in ocean biology and engineering. This 
component will translate research into industrial application and product development through 
on-site business incubator facilities. This component will support the Blue Economy priority 
area of Marine Biology, Blue trade and Blue manufacturing. 
3.4 The Committee was further  informed that t he technologies required for deep sea mining have 
strategic implications and are not commercially available. Hence, attempts will be made to indigenize 
technologies by collaborating with leading institutes and private industries. A research vessel for deep 
ocean exploration would be built in an Indian shipyard whi ch would create employment opportunities. 
This mission is also directed towards capacity development in Marine Biology, which will provide job 
opportunities in Indian industries. In addition, design, development and fabrication of specialised 
equipment, ships and setting up of required infrastructure are expected to spur the growth of the Indian 
industry, especially the MSME and startups.

the next year.

provider in the Indian Ocean region and therefore, the Committee while emboldening the 
importance of the Deep Ocean Mission , recommends the Ministry to play a larger role in acting 
as the backbone of this cause.  
4. INITIATIVES FOR SOCIETAL BENEFITS 
 The Ministry, enlisting the various services it offers, provided details about the initiatives taken 
by it for societal benefits:  
4.1.1. Desalination: The Ministry is ensuring  availability of drinking water to the locals in 
coastal areas.  Project for 150 m3/day plants in Amini, Androth, Chetlat, Kadamat, Kalpeni, and 
Kiltan islands initiated with funding by UT Administration, M inistry of Home Affairs. Kalpeni 
and Amini Desalination plants are completed and water is being supplied lo cally since 1st June 
2022 and 29th December 2022, respectively.  Work is in progress at four more Islands Androth, 
Chetlat, Kadamat, and Kiltan Islands . It was also informed that desalinated sea water, which is  
fit for drinking is available at a cost as low as 40 paise per litre.  
4.1.2. Warnings Systems for weather phenomena : Provides forecasts and warnings against 
severe weather phenomena like tropical cyclones, dust storms, heavy rains , snow, cold & heat 
waves, earthquakes, tsunami and storm surge etc. which cause destruction of life and property. 
4.1.3. Farmers’ Awareness Programmes (FAPs):  The Ministry in collaboration with 
AMFUs and DAMUs organizes Farmers' Awareness Programmes  (FAPs) for the benefits of 
farmers in various parts of the country. 
4.1.4. Dissemination of information: In response to the query of the Committee  about 
initiatives taken by the Ministry to enhance the dissemination for information about its activities 
and achievements, the Ministry informed that it has launched several mob ile applications such 
as Meghdoot (Weather+Agriculture), Mausam (weather), Damini (Lightning), SAFAR AIR (air 
quality), SARAT (oil sleek pollution), RISEQ (now Bhookamp), Thoondil (for fishermen), 
which have helped disseminate real -time information on weat her, Ocean, and seismological 
services. The Ministry has also  developed the Gagan Enabled Mariner’s Instrument for 
Navigation and Information (GEMINI) for effective and seamless dissemination of ocean and 
weather information to fishermen and other maritime  users in the open ocean.  Further, it has 
also been apprised to the Committee that t he Ministry regularly uses the social media platform 
like You Tube, Twitter, Facebook, Instagram, Koo etc. to inform the general public about the 

14 
 
work being carried out at various Institutes of the Ministry as well as on the achievements of 
Ministry. A number of you tube videos have also been created and uploaded on the internet.  
4.1.5. Dissemination of Agromet Advisory Services: The Committee was informed that the 
Ministry provides agromet advisory for the benefit of farmers in the country. 9.76 million 
farmers receive agromet advisories through mobile APPs and private companies under Public 
Private Partnership (PPP) mode. Presently, about 6.5 million farmers in Madhya Pradesh, Tamil 
Nadu, Gujarat, Nagaland, Chhattisgarh, Haryana, Rajasthan, Odisha, Meghalaya and Uttar 
Pradesh are getting benefitted from weather forecast & agromet advisories. Weather forecast & 
agromet advisories a re being disseminated to approximately  1.3 m illion farmers of about 
1,20,000 villages through block -level Whatsapp groups. Approximately 2.8 lakh farmers are 
accessing District and Block -level weather forecast and agromet advisories through Meghdoot 
Mobile App. 
4.1.6. Atmospheric Research: To provide an experimental test bed for the study of important 
atmospheric processes particularly: a) Clouds and Convection;  b) Land-Atmosphere 
interactions; c) Aerosol and Radiation;  and d) thunderstorms, for developing and testing the 
parameterization schemes in weather and climate models by implementing advanced 
measurements of clouds, radiation, precipitation, dynamics and land -surface parameters in the 
core monsoon zone. 
4.1.7. Ocean Services: The Ministry provided information on the following fronts: 
i. Potential Fishing Zone Advisories and species -specific advisories to about 7.0 
Lakh fishermen daily. 
ii. Forecast on state of the ocean to about 9.45 l akh stake holders in India and also 
to 6 countries in the Indian Ocean. 
iii. High Wave Alerts to all the sea farers during extreme events. 
iv. Advisories on oil spill trajectories during the event of the oil spill to Indian Coast 
Guard. 
v. Alerts on the health of coral reefs and Harmful Algal Blooms (HABs). 
vi. Multi-Hazard Vulnerability Maps and Coastal Vulnerability Indices for all the 
coastal areas. 
vii. Tsunami Early Warnings for India and also to 25 Indian Ocean Rim Countries. 
Spearheading the Tsunami Ready community recognition programme – India 
first to implement in the Indian Ocean. 
 4.1.8. Coastal Protection and Shoreline Management : Acknowledging the fact that the 
Indian Coastline is vast and crucial as millions of lives depend on it, the Ministry carries out the 
following activities: 
i. Understanding of Coastal Pro cesses th rough Monitoring, Mode ling and 
prediction and development of Shoreline Management Plans along the Indian 
coast. 
ii. Assessment of Coastal Vulnerability due to Climate Change, Sea Level Rise and 
Natural Hazards. 

15 
 
iii. Monitoring of Shoreline Change along the Indian c oast including islands during 
normal and extreme events. 
iv. Understanding of nearshore processes through observations/modeling and 
estimation of sediment transport along the Indian coast in phased manner for 
better management of shoreline. 
v. Development of web based Coastal Change System to disseminate information 
related to coastal development, impact assessment of extreme events and climate 
change (SLR) on the shoreline and its management aspects. 
vi. Development of an operational Coastal Flood Warning System for flood prone 
coastal cities of the country and Impact based forecasting expert system for 
tropical cyclones and multi - coastal hazards in disaster prone areas of the 
country.

nodules; cobalt rich manganese crust and hydrothermal deposits.  Utilising this mineral wealth 
for the benefit of mankind will be the focus of ocean mining activities in future.  Polymetallic 
nodules have economically valuable metals such as Cop per, Cobalt, Nickel and Manganese and

REPORT 
Necessity is the mother of invention. The history of mankind is full of examples where 
scarcities and shortages led to inventions. The men behind these inventions were not always 
intellectuals hailing from affluent families. Instead, they came from ordinary walks of life and in 
many cases were illiterate and so poor that they did not have even two square meals a day. They 
burnt mid-night oil in order to help the mankind with the benefit of their inventions. They 
followed the ideals enshrined in what Sir Winston Churchill described in following woi:ds:-
"Heights of the great men were not attained in a single flight, they came up toiling upwards when 
their companions slept in the night" 
The domain of inventions is thus not the property of any intellectuals or enlightened or 
affluent sections of the Society alone. It belongs to one and all. 
Shri P. Ramar Pillai who shot in the news sometime back comes from ordinary walk of life. 
He was reported to have invented what he described as "Herbal Fuel". This gave him a world­
wide publicity, for his experiment could open. new vistas for the worlq and save the mankind 
from the near crisis in the field of energy with which we are confronted today. It has often been 
projected and rightly so that the oil reserves were not going to last long. It is thus incumbent on 
all of us to conserve · the oil resources in the best possible manner and at the same time our 
endeavour should be to aim at inventing the alternative and new sources of energy. 
It was in this background, that Shri P. Ramar Pillai of Kamrajar district, Tamil Nadu, 
attracted attention world-wide about his production of herbal fuel. History tells us that to Dr. 
Isaac Newton, it was a rude jolt by a falling apple which made him ponder about earth's 
gravitational pull whereas young Ramar did not have to undergo such an ordeal with the nature 
when the green leaves burnt with a frenzy, he knew they belonged to an extraordinary genre. 
According to Shri Ramar Pillai, while taking part in an annual picnic to the Western Ghats 
with other students of Mamsapuram's Sivanthi Petty Nadar High School, he had noticed that in 
the rice they had just cooked, a spark fell on the leaves and they caught fire. While this set him 
thinking, his other classmates were not carried by the significance that Shri Ramar Pillai

(Delhi) resembled commercial products with high olefinic content which are not found in 
straight ru!kproductsfrom crude oil but are generated during secondary conversion processes.

Institute of Petroleum on the solid and the liquid portions separated from the product 
sample obtained during the demonstration experiment for preparation of 'herbal fuel' on 
15th November, 1996 at Indian Institute of Petroleum, Dehradun clearly shows that it is a 
mixture of hydrocarbons boiling in kerosene range with dissolved camphor. 
The Committee has been further informed that the Indian Institute of Petroleum 
conducted a confirmatory experiment on 19th November, 1996 in order to further confirm 
the formation of the 'herbal fuel'. The steps followed were the same as in the demonstration 
experiment (Ramar experiment) carried out on 15th November, 1996. The data obtained in

1. Executive Summary 
1. A demonstration expecirnent on -the preparation what was described as Herbal fuel 
claimed by Mr. P. Ramar and his team was c<>nducted at the Indian Institute of Petroleum 
(liP) , Dehradun in the presence of the members of Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Science and Technology and Environment and Forests on 15th November, 1996. 
2. The experiment was conducted by the liP scientists as per the procedure lay down by 
Mr. Ramar. The end product burned with a sooty smoke and strong camphor like smell. 
The end product was handed over to liP for detailed analysis. 
3. In any scientific experiment, the inputs and outputs are analysed and measured as

(ii) The quantity of inputs 
(iii) The nature and detailed composition of outputs 
(iv) The quantity of outputs 
\ .

since separation of solid was observed when the so called Herbal fuel was allowed to cool to 
ambient temperature. Detailed analysis has been carried out on the solid and liquid portions . 
5. The laboratory analysis· by liP established that the product produced during the 
Ramar experiment is a mixture of hydrocarbons boiling in the kerosene range with dissolved 
camphor. 
6. Although, the nature of the inputs to the Ramar experiment were not allowed to be 
analysed , based on the fact that the solid input smelled strongly like camphor and the liquid 
input (so called essence) smelled strongly like kerosene, it is most likely that Ramar 
provided kerosene and camphor as inputs. Camphor dissolved in kerosene during the Ramar 
experiment with resultant increase in the volume of liquid. 
7. The hypothesis in Shri Ramar's experiment above was verified by liP in a 
confirmatory experiment where the same amount of camphor was mixed with the same 
amount of kerosene under the same experimental conditions leading to the same increase in 
volume with liquid having the same prope1 ty to burn as the so called herbal fuel produced in 
the Ramar experiment. 
8. It is finally concluded that the Ramar experiment carried out in liP was nothing other 
than mixing camphor, a combustible material, with hydrocarbons boiling in the kerosene 
range, also a combustible material, to obtain a solution of camphor in the hydrocarbons 

boiling in the kerosene range. This solution, claimed to be herbal fuel by Mr. Ramar, was 
obviously combustible. The herbal leaves used in the Ramar experiment had no role to play 
in the end product. 
We conclude that Ramar's claim of providing herbal fuel from herbal leaves and water 
is falacious.

paraffins mixture) is given ·n Figure 5 and the c:hromatogram of another reference mixture 
containing pure camphor in diethyl either is given in Figure-6. 
The relative per cent distribution of individual hydrocarbons calculated without 
incorporating response factors components is given in Table-9. Camphor has been identified 
on the basis of reference mixture. It is found to be 35% by wt. in the liquid portion . 
The identified J:tydrocarbons are between C7 to C16 carbon numbers suggesting the 
product is in the kerosene boiling range. Boiling points of the n-paraffins corresponding to 
C7 and C16 hydrocarbons are 98 deg. celcious and 287 deg. C. 
4.2.3. Mass spectral Analysis 
Mass spectra of liquid portion as such is shown in Fig.-7. The largest m/7 peak is at 226 
and peaks are present at each numbe{ towards lower mass range. The intense peaks are at 
152, 120, 109, 108, 105, 99, 97 and 95. Peak at IIliZ 95 is a little less intense than the base 
peak indicating large proportion of Camphor in this liquid product also. However , there are 
many peaks after subtracting the mass spectra of Camphor. 
There are peaks at IIliZ series 226, 212, 19!5, 184, 170, 156, 142 and 128 indicating 
presence of paraffins and veryintense peaks at IIliZ 85, 71, 57 and 43 (non -:normal paraffins) 
i.e.; fron nC9 to nC16. Similarly predominant peaks are also present at 224, 210, 140, 126 
and 112 supported by intense peaks at 55, 69, 83 and 97 indicating presence of 
monocycloparaffins in the same carbon range from C9-C16. Presence of condensed 
cycloparaffins are also indicated by the presence of peaks at 222 ·and 208. 
Inten se peaks at CnH2n-6 series IIliZ 190, 176, 120 and 106 supported by intense 
CnH2n-7 mass series at 133 and 91 indicate presence of alkyl benzenes in carbon range C8 
to C14. Peaks at mass .series CnH2n-8, i.e., 188 and 174-132 supported by fragment ion 
peaks at mass 159, 145 and 131 indicate presence of indanes/tetralins in carbon range_ C10-
C-14. This indicates that it is a complex mixture of hydrocarbons in carbon range C8 to C16, 
pointing· it to be a typical kerosene fraction along with large quantity of camphor.-
. fhe mass spectra of the three fractions of the jlbove liquid portion have been shown in 
fl~ . -8 . to 10. Mass spectrum of IBP-204 deg. C,Fig .-8 fraction has highest mass peak at l1l'Z 
170. It indicates presence of mixture hydrocarbons' in the C8-C12 ca·rbon range along with 
Camphor . However , in this mass spectrum, bl;l_Se peak of camphor at IIliZ 95 and all other 
peaks of camphor are not as intense as in ftg.-7. This points out that in this portion 
hydrocarbon mixture is predominant in camphor (maximum). 
' 
Mass spectrum of the fraction (204-208 deg. C) dissolved in acetone (Fig.-9) shows base 
peak at IIliZ 95 and all other intense peaks indicating large proportion of camphor in the 
sample. The highest mass peak in the spectrum is at mass number 198. This and the 
presence of other peaks at lower mass number indicates presence of hydrocarbon mixture in 
the carbon range C10-C14. However, low intensity ions of hydrocarbons, i.e., at 99 etc., 
indicate that C10 fraction of kerosene is 25% max. 
Mass spectrum of the fraction (218 deg. C+) is shown in Fig.-10. The highest peak is at 
mass 226 and all other peaks at lower mass range indicate the presence of hydrocarbon in 
carbon range Cll-C16. Hydrocarbon types present are paraffins, monocycloparaffin s., 

condensed cycloparaffins, benzenes, indanes/tetralins etc. This spectrum does not show 
much significant peaks at mass 95 (base peak of Camphor), indicating insignificant amount 
of Camphor in the mixture (fraction 218 deg. C+) 
4.2.4. lR Analysis 
The spectra of the liquid portion as such and a laboratory sample of Camphor are given 
in Fig. 11. Spectrum of the liquid portion also matches with th'at of Camphor except in 
aromatic band at 1608 cm-1 and few intensity variations of few band characteristics of 
hydrocarbons . The presence of the carbonyl band at 1742 cm-1 in the spectrum of the liquid 
sample confirms the presence of camphor in the sample. 
IR spectra of the three distillation cuts of the liquid portion are presented in Figs. 12-14. 
The spectra show that the Camphor content is substantial in the 204-218 deg. C cut. In ffiP-
204 deg. C cut, it is only lower than that in-204-218 deg. C cut. It is minimum in 218 deg. C 
+ cut . Bands of hydrocarbons are more predominant. The presence of the carbonyl band at 
1742 cm-t in the spectra of the distillate cuts: IBP (Initial Boiling Point, 137 deg. C) - 204 
deg. C, 204-218 deg. C and 218 deg. C+ of the liquid portion shows that camphor is present 
in · all the fractions. 
Material balance of the camphor separated from the product and the@amphor estimated 
in the liquid portion is compared with the total amount . of solid added during the 
demonstration experiment. The data given in Table-10 is in good agreement. 
S. Conclusions 
The detailed analysis carried out on the solid and the liquid portions separated from the 
product sample obtained during the demonstration experiment for preparation of what was 
described as herbal fuel on 15.11.1996 at liP clearly shows that it is a mixture of 
hydrocarbons boiling in kerosene range with dissolved camphor. 
Mr. Ramar, however , bad claimed that the so called herbal fuel obtained at the end of 
present experiment, if distilled, would yield petrol in the temperature range of 70--175 deg. 
C and diesel in the temperature range of 150--240 deg. C (see comments of Mr. Ramar in 
the report on the demonstralion on 15.11.1996 at liP). 
6. Confirmatory Experiment 
In order to further confirm the formation of the so called Herbal Fuel, a. confirmatory 
experiment was done on 19.11.96. The steps followed were the same as in thedemonstration 
experiment (Ramar experiment) carried out on 15.11.96. The steps are as foflows: 
1. A clean round bottom flask (2 litre) was washed with hot water. 
2. 750 ml water (corresponding to component A in Ramar experiment) was taken from 
Bisleri mineral water bottle in the flask. 
3. 230.1 gm of camphor (laboratory chemical) was weighed and transferred te the flask 
(corresponding to component C in Ramar experiment). 
4. Another 400 gm of camphor was weighed and transferred to the flask (corresponding 
to component B in Ramar experiment). 
5. 400 ml of kerosene fraction distilled from typical crude oil was measured and added 
to the flask (corresponding to component D in Ramar experiment, so called the essence). 
6. The flask containing all the components was closed With a stopper and heated in a 

mantle till the boiling started and continued for another five minutes intermittently openin~ 
the stopper to release excess pressure, total heating time was 28 minutes as was done in 
Ramar experiment. 
7. The flask was taken out from the mantle after the heating time and it was allowed to 
cool for some time. 
8. The contents of the flask were transferred to a separating funnel while they were stiR 
hot. While transferring the contents, 250 ml of Bisleri water was added simultaneously to the 
separating funnel. 
9. The two layers formed were transferred info two separate container s and their 
volume weights were recorded. The weight and volume of the upper liquid layer were 
720.1 g and 860 ml respectively as compared to 692.7 g and 850 ml for the so called herbal 
fuel obtained in the Ramar experiment. The weight and volume of the bottom layer in the 
confirmatory experiment were 998.0 g and 1010.0 ml as against 995.0 g and 1010.0 ml in the 
Ramar experiment (Table-11). 
10. Burning characteristics of the product obtained in the confirmatdry experiment were 
the same as that of the so called herbal fuel obtained in the Ramar experiment. 
The data obtained in the confirmatory experiment as well as in the demonstration 
experiment of what was described herbal fuel of Mr. Ramar (15.11.1996) are quite 
comparable in all respect s including the change in the liquid volumes and burning 
characteristics. 
7. Final Conclusions 
1. "Herbal fuel" obtained in the demonstration experiment (Ramar experiment) was 
separated into the solid and liquid portions. This step became necessary since separation of 
solid was observed when the so called herbal fuel was allowed to cool to ambient 
temperature. Detailed analysis has been carried out on the solid and liquid portions. 
2. The laboratory analysis by liP established that the product produced during the 
Ramar experime nt is a mixture of hydrocarbons boiling in the kero10ene range with disolved 
camphor. 
3. Although, the nature of the inputs to the Ramar experiment were not allowed to be 
analysed , based on the fact that the solid input smelled strongly like camphor and the liquid 
input (so called essence) smelled strongly like kerosene, it is most likely that Ramar 
provided kerosene and camphor as inputs. Camphor dissolved in kerosene during the Ramar 
experiment with resultant increase in the volume of liquid. 
4. The hypothesis in Shri Ramar's experiment above was verified by liP in a 
confirmatory experiment where the same amount of Camphor was mixed with the same 
amount of kerosene under the same experimental conditions leading to the same increase in 
volume with liquid having the same property to burn as the so called herbal fuel produced in 
the Ramar experiment.

OVERALL BUDGETARY DETAILS FOR THE FI NANCIAL YEAR 2022 -23 (BE, RE & 
ACTUAL EXPENDITURE) AND ALLOCATION FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR  2023-24 
Recommendations/Observations  
1.1 From Chart 1, t he Committee observes a general  increasing trend in BE allocations for the 
Department. While the BE allocation for 2021-22 was at Rs.27,795 crore, it has been increased by 
about 21 percent in BE 2023 -24. Similarly, for  the past two years,  i.e. 2021 -22 and 2022-23, the 
Department has been getting an additional allocation at the RE stage. The proposed BE allocation for 
2023-24 was Rs.42,092.20 crore but the Department was allocated only  Rs.35,262.49 cro re in 2023 -
24. This is a shortfall of Rs.6,829.71 crore.                                                 (Para 2.6 of the 373rd Report) 
Action Taken 
1.2 As observed by the Hon'ble Committee there has been  a consistent rise  in the BE allocations  
commensurate with the activities of the Department. There are budgetary cuts in the BE allocations in 
each year, however, the  Department has been  sanctioned additional  funds through Supplementary 
Demands for Grants at RE stage. The current shortfall of  Rs. 6,829.71 crore alongwith any further  
additionality, based on the budgetary requirements,  shall be sought at RE stage. 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
1.3 From the submission of the Department the Committee feels that the Department may  face 
challenges especially in its initiatives relating to Nuclear Recycle Board (NRB), Tata Memorial Centre  
(TMC), Nuclear Power  Corporation of India Limited  (NPCIL), Heavy Water  Board (HWB) and 
Bhabha Atomic Research  Centre (BARC).                                                                        (Para 2.11 ibid) 
 
1.4 The Committee underlines the requirement  of an additional budgetary allocation of Rs.3,150 
crore over and above  the BE 2023-24 quoted by the Department  and recommends that the Department 
be given the additional alloca tion for them to continue with their set goals and  objectives and ensure a 
timely and e ffective completion.  The initiatives of the Department under TMC, NPCIL  and BARC, 
amongst others, are crucial to the energy needs of the country  as well  as in  many healthcare and 
societal applications.  It is also necessary to ensure tha t the activities  of the Department do not suffer 
due to any lack of funds as it will have a bearing on India's strategic nuclear capacity.  
                                                                                                                                    (Para 2.12 ibid) 
 
1.5 The Committee also recommends  that the Department should reach  out to the  Ministry of 
Finance for additional funds  at the RE/Supplementary stage and al so look for  raising the same  either 
through internal revenue or  through reallocati ng  funds from heads which have  excess al location, if 
any.                                                                                                                                    (Para 2.13 ibid)

1.6 As advised by the Hon'ble Committee the Department shall  seek the additional funds of         
Rs.3,150 crore at the RE 2023-24/ Supplementary  Demands for Grants and ensure that the set Goals 
and objectives of the Department are achieved. 
Recommendations/Observations  
1.7 The Committee therefore recommends  that the Department be  diligent in managing  the 
expenditure as well as achieving the physical targets  that it has set out for  itself for  2023-24. The

Committee would  also like to recommend that the  Department should  ensure optimum utilisation of 
these funds.                                                                                                                        (Para 2.17 ibid)

targets indicated in  the major thrust areas of the Department/deliverables are acc omplished with the

Department has been able to utilise more than 99 percent of the funds in the previous years and shall 
continue to ensure optimum utilisation. 
Recommendations/Observations  
1.9 The Committee is of the view that even though  an increase of 40  percent i.e. from 4780 MW to 
6780 MW is substantial,  it is not commensurate  with the need of the  country for more clean energy. 
With nuclear energy having a share of only about 3 percent in the total  energy matrix of the country, it 
is high time that the contribution from nuclear power is  increased substantially. This is not just crucial

increasing power consumption.                                                                                         (Para 2.25 ibid)

ACTUAL EXPENDITURE) AND ALLOCATION FOR 20 23-24 
Recommendations/Observations  
2.1 From Chart 2 which depicts the share of Revenue and Capital allocation in BE 2023 -24 of the 
Department, across its various key sectors, t he Committee  observes that while the  share of revenue 
and capital expenditure allocations is almost  equal in the  total budget, capital  expenditure is  almost 
twice that of revenue for the Power Sector. On the other hand,  revenue expenditure is more than thrice  
of the capital expenditure  allocation under R&D Sector.                          (Para 2.7 of the 373rd Report) 
 
Action Taken 
2.2 Power Sector: The Department  provides Gross Budgetary Support under Capital Division for 
Power Sector  towards – Loans and Investments in PSUs.  Whereas, the Department  provides limited 
budgetary support under Revenue Division for Operation &  Maintenance purpose for e.g. Fuel 
Inventory, Interest on Heavy Water Pool Management etc. A  major portion of Revenue expenditure is 
incurred by the Power Sector  PSUs through internal sources. The Budgetary allocations under Capital 
Division (Loans and Inve stments) have increased due to the upcoming  Projects. Hence,  the Capital 
expenditure is  almost twice of the Revenue for the  Power Sector i.e.  NPCIL (Rs.6364  crore), 
Investments in NPCIL (Rs.3046  crore) and Loans to BHAVINI (Rs.200 crore). 
 
2.3 R&D Sector: The revenue expenditure of R&D sector comprises of Establishment expenditure 
(Rs.4410.80 crore) of all R&D Units viz. BARC, IGCAR, AERB, AM D, DCSEM, GSO, RRCAT and  
VECC. Grants to Autonomous Bodies and Aided Institute s (Rs.3240.40  crore) and Contribution to 
IAEA & Anunet charges (Rs.62.43 crores). As the employee strength in R&D units is 65% of the total 
staff strength of the Department, the establishment expenditure are commensurately on the higher side. 
Further, O&M expenditure of the  running Pl ants/R&D Reactors is also booked under  the Revenue 
Division. The allocations under the Capital  Division of R&D Sector are towards the ongoing  R&D 
Projects of BARC, IGCAR, RRCAT, VECC, GSO, AERB, DAE, DCSEM, and AMD as  per the 
budgetary requirements. Hence, the allocations towards revenue expenditure  are more than  thrice of 
the Capital expenditure under R&D Division. 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
2.4 The Committee observes and highlights the fact that even though India's rank is 6th in terms of 
numbers of nuclear power reactors being operated, we are still at number 11 and 14 when it comes to 
nuclear power produced and installed capacity respectively. This  is indicative of  the fact that the 
production capacity  per power plant is low. The Committee, therefore, recommends the Department to 
study the reasons for  this anomaly and also apprise the Commi ttee of  its findings. Further, the 

7 
 
Committee recommends that the  Department devices a  strategy to install higher production capacity 
power units so that the unit cost comes down and nuclear power becomes more affordable.    
                                                                                                                                           (Para 2.27 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
2.5 The small  size (200-220 MW) reactors were set up  in the early days of  the nuclear power 
programme in the country due to the limited capacity of the then existing regional electricity grids. 
Following the imposition of  international technology denial  and embargo regime in 1974, India placed 
thrust on achieving self-reliance in this high technology area. India mastered Pressurized Heavy Water 
Reactor (PHWR) technology,  evolved a standard 220 MW PHWR design and  setup a number of fully 
indigenous 220 MW reactors. With the evolution of the capacities of the Indian electricity  grids, a 540 
MW PHWR was designed in the 1980s and the first  540 MW PHWR commenced operation in 2005.  
Following the successful operation of the 540 MW size PHWRs, a larger  unit size - the indigenous 700 
MW standard design has been evolved and  the first  700 MW PHWR is  connected to  the grid, 
generating power.  Fifteen more reactors of 700MW size  PHWRs are under construction/pre-project 
activities, to be progressively commissioned  by 2031-32. These reactors will form the mainstay of the 
rapid expansion of  nuclear capacity in the  country in the near future. Large size reactors which were 
setup in some countries of the world in the 1980s and 1990s  could not be setup in India due to the 
technology denial  and embargo regime. However, with the fruition of international cooperation in 
nuclear energy and entering into of relevant agreements, large size reactors of 1000 MW capacity are 
being setup at Kudankulam in cooperation with Russian Federation . Discussions are also in progress 
with France and the USA to arrive  at project  proposals to  setup large size reactors at  Jaitapur, 
Maharashtra and Kovvada, Andhra Pradesh respectively. 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
2.6 The Committee therefore recommends that the Department should take utmost care in ensuring 
proper utilization of  funds and that the Department should  take extra effort to ensure optimum 
utilization under the three heads 'BARC', 'IGCAR'  and 'Nuclear Fuel Complex'.             (Para 2.30 ibid)

on Science and Technology, Environment, Forests and Climate Change deals with the action taken by  
the Government  on the recommendations/observations of the Committee contained in its ‘Three 
Hundred Seventy Fourth Report’ on ‘Demands for Grants (2023 -24) of the Department of 
Biotechnology’. The Report was presented to Rajya Sabha on the 15 th March, 2023 and laid on the 
Table of Lok Sabha on the 20th March, 2023.  
2. Action Taken Note s (ATNs) ha ve been received from the Department of Biotechnology  in 
respect of all the 21 recommendations/observations contained in the ‘Three Hundred Seventy Fourth 
Report’. The replies of the Department of Biotechnology have been categorized as follows:-  
Chapter I: Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the Government: 
Para Nos. 2.15, 3.5, 3.6, 4.9, 4.10, 5.6 and 6.2. 
 Total recommendations – 07

in view of the Government’s replies:

 Total recommendations – 14

have not been accepted by the Committee: ‘Nil’ 
Chapter IV:   Recommendations/Observations in respect of which final replies of the 
Government are still awaited: ‘Nil’ 
 
3. The details of the ATNs have been analyzed in the succeeding Chapters.

OVERALL BUDGETARY DETAILS FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2022-23 (BE, RE & 
ACTUAL EXPENDITURE) AND ALLOCATION FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2023-24. 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
1.1 The Commi ttee recognises the important contributions of the Department of Biotechnology 
across crucial sectors and the need for an additional allocation of at least Rs. 350 crore, over and 
above to the allocation of Rs. 2683.86 crore in B.E. 2023 -24, to sustain its  key programmes. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department may approach the Ministry of 
Finance/Department of Expenditure for seeking the requisite additional allocation of funds at the R.E. 
stage. The Committee further recommends that the D epartment should strive for greater revenue 
generation in the long term, especially through equity stake in incubated startups and through 
commercialization of products developed by the Department, and explore options to facilitate 
financing of some of its important projects and schemes through them.   (Para 2.15 of the 374th Report)  
Action Taken 
 
1.2 Department is thankful to the Committee for recognizing the important contributions of the 
Department across crucial sectors. As recommended by the Committee , the Department depending on 
the pace of expenditure may request for an additional allocation at the R.E. stage.   
1.3 With respect to revenue generation, it is submitted that the Department through its Public 
Sector Undertaking Biotechnology Industry Res earch Assistance Council (BIRAC) provides equity 
based funding to startups.  BIRAC has supported more than 140 startups through equity support under 
SEED and LEAP schemes. Out of these startups, more than 60% have raised follow on funding 
amounting to more  than INR 1000 Cr. There is an increasing number of startups getting investments 
from Angels, High Net Worth Individuals (HNIs), and early -stage Venture Capitals (VCs) contributing 
to the growth story of biotech industry. 
 
BIOTECHNOLOGY RESEARCH & DEVELOPMENT – MAJOR INITIATIVES 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
1.4 The Committee is of the considered view that setting of realistic and achievable targets, both 
short term and long term, as well as existence of a robust monitoring mechanism to monitor and review 
the progress of ongoing schemes and programmes, are extremely crucial. The Committee recommends 
that the Department of Biotechnology should ensure an effective monitoring and periodic review of all 
its schemes and programmes and take corrective measures, wh erever required, so that they proceed as 
per schedule.                    (Para 3.5 ibid)

and programmes undergoes both mid -term review during the finance commission period as suggested 
by DoE amd NITI Aayog. Further, the programs are being reviewed time to time by the respective 
expert committees. 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.6 The Committee recommends more collaboration with DARE/ICAR to acc elerate the R&D in 
agriculture, especially plant genomes, so that more productive, drought and flood resistant varieties of 
various important crops can be developed in the next 3-5 years.              (Para 3.6 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
1.7 The recommendations of the Committee have been noted. It is submitted that the Department is 
already collaborating with ICAR/NARs/SAU through its mission programmes and projects. In 
collaboration with ICAR institutions/SAU’s network projects are being funded towards development of 
drought and flood resistant varieties.

Recommendations/Observations 
 
1.8 While noting the not -so-encouraging fluctuations in figures of 2020 -21 and 2021 -22, the 
Committee is delighted to observe that, during 2022 -23, the Department has been able achieve its 
targets against almost all of the indicators, except just three parameters i.e., number of publications, 
number of genomes sequenced under Genome India and number of NE -specific germplasm collected. 
The Committee, in particular, takes note of the achievements in respect of the number of patents 
filed/granted and products/technologies developed, transferred or commercialized, as these are an

the number of genomes sequenced.                 (Para 4.9 ibid)

The Department will take requisite steps for achieving the targets during in FY 2023-24.

infrastructure, equipment, technical expertise, regulatory compliance requirements, etc. The concerned 
industry base, Angels/VCs investor pool are also domain centric rather than generic. Therefore, only 
6300+ biotech startups are there out of 95,000+ startups in the country. 
2.25 BIRAC’s model, best practices are shared and followed by peer ministries/departments at both 
Centre and State level. Duplication of efforts is avoided by having representation of officials in the 
monitoring and selection committees. BIRAC has an active engagement with all relevant National 
Mission programs. 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
2.26 The Committee especially recommends that the Department should ensure equitable 
distribution of resources/initiatives across the country, so that the benefits of its programmes aim ed at 
supporting start-ups and SMEs can reach the under-served regions of the country as well. 
          (Para 6.8 ibid)  
Action Taken 
 
2.27 Biotechnology Research Assistance Council (BIRAC) under the BIG programme has been 
instrumental in spurring the cre ation of biotech startups. More than 800 innovative ideas have been 
supported out of 10,000 applications received from across the country. The scheme has been able to 
aspire entrepreneurs across the country. The spread of aspirants covers 550+ cities and 3 8 aspirational 
districts pan India. More than 50% of the applications under BIG are from Tier 2 and 3 cities. 
2.28 BioNEST Bioincubation centres setting up is an ongoing activity. Currently, 75 incubation 
centres are located in 21 States/UTs. In the last f ew years, the numbers of new B ioincubation centres 
seeded in the Tier 2/3 cities have also increased significantly. 

11 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
2.29 The Committee recommends that the Department must carry out a detailed analysis on the 
investment in R&D over the last 10 years, the financial value created by the products, the potential 
revenue generated and the multiplier effect in the market.              (Para 6.9 ibid)  
Action Taken 
 
2.30 The recommendations of the Committee have been noted. Make -In-India Cell at Biotechnology 
Industry Research Assistance Council (BIRAC) has been mapping India’s BioEconomy since 2018 and 
publishes a professional India BioEconomy Report (IBER). This has monitored the growth from 
$44.47 Bn in 2017 to $93+ Bn in 2022. The I ndia Bioeconomy Report helps to determine the growth 
trajectory, and importantly set the target for India’s bioeconomy for 2025 as $150 Bn; for 2030 as $300 
Bn and 2047 as $3 trillion USD. 
 
 
HUMAN GENETICS & GENOME ANALYSIS 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
 
2.31 The Committee recognizes the immense potential that genetic research and gene therapy hold 
for altering the treatment paradigm of many genetic diseases, including those that are currently 
incurable. However, as it is a relatively new field of medical science, the many challenges still 
associated with it are not lost on the Committee. Despite the existing challenges, such as issues 
regarding delivery methods, safety and effectiveness concerns, potential long -term effects of genetic 
modification, high costs of developing and administering the therapy making it inaccessible to masses, 
etc., the potential benefits are far too significant to ignore and, therefore, it is highly essential to 
prioritize research in the area.                (Para 7.4 ibid) 
                 
Action Taken 
 
2.32 The Department has been facilitating research in this domain to make cell and gene therapy 
affordable. Since past one decade, the Department supported gene therapy programme, which led to the 
first-in-human gene therapy phase-I clinical trial for Hemophilia A patients.  Proof -of-concept studies 
have also been completed for development of novel lentiviral vectors which can be employed for gene 
addition (beta or gamma globin genes); gene modulation (BCL11A gene); and gene editin g approaches 
using CRISPR-Cas9 and base editing technologies. 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
2.33 The Committee appreciates the ongoing efforts of scientists and researchers in this field. The 
Committee recommends the Department to undertake deeper researc h in collaboration with other 
institutes under the government and private sector, explore avenues for using latest emerging 
technologies including Artificial Intelligence (AI), in order to fully explore the untapped potential of 
genetic research. The Commi ttee also recommends that adequate funds be earmarked for the purpose, 
so that financial constraints do not hinder the much-needed R&D. The Committee would also like to be 
kept informed about the progress made by the Department in this regard.            (Para 7.5 ibid) 

12 
 
Action Taken 
 
2.34 Department of Biotechnology under the Competitive Research Grant program considered 
Artificial Intelligence (AI) as one of the promising niche area and is supporting projects for application 
of AI in healthcare sector in t he areas of Cancer, Tuberculosis and Pulmonary Diseases, Diabetes & 
Cardiovascular Diseases, Ophthalmological Diseases, Neurological Disorders and Drug Development.
