TO THE DEPARTMENT OF ATOMIC ENERGY 
3.1 BHABHA ATOMIC RESEARCH CENTRE (BARC) 
 The Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) is India's premier 
multidisciplinary nuclear research institution under the Department of Atomic Energy 

13 
 
(DAE). Established in 1954 as the Atomic Energy Establishment, Trombay (AEET) and 
renamed BARC in 1966 in honour of Dr. Homi Bhabha, it has been instrumental in 
advancing nuclear science, technology, and energy security in India. BARC plays a 
crucial role in India's three-stage nuclear power programme, covering nuclear reactor 
research, fuel fabrication, waste management, isotope applications, and nuclear safety. 
The centre is also responsible for healthcare, agriculture, water purification, and 
radiation technology applications, reinforcing its impact beyond energy production. 
BARC is central to the implementation of India’s indigenous three-stage nuclear 
programme, designed to achieve energy security through the optimal utilisation of 
nuclear fuel resources. 
Stage I – Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors (PHWRs): BARC develops 
reactor safety technologies, nuclear fuel fabrication, and in-service reactor 
inspection tools to enhance the efficiency and safety of PHWRs. 
Stage II – Fast Breeder Reactors (FBRs): The centre contributes to spent fuel 
reprocessing, sodium-cooled fast reactor technology, and advanced fuel 
fabrication to sustain the second stage of the programme. 
Stage III – Thorium-based Reactors: BARC plays a vital role in research on 
Advanced Heavy Water Reactors (AHWRs) and Thorium fuel cycle 
technologies, leveraging India's vast thorium reserves. 
BARC has designed and operates research reactors such as Dhruva, Apsara-U, 
and KAMINI, which are essential for neutron beam research and isotope production. 
The centre is actively developing high-temperature gas-cooled reactors (HTGRs), 
molten salt reactors, and small modular reactors (SMRs) to explore future nuclear 
energy possibilities.BARC develops uranium and thorium fuel fabrication techniques, 
supporting India's expanding nuclear power infrastructure.The centre operates 
reprocessing plants for recovering plutonium and uranium, crucial for Fast Breeder 
Reactor technology. 
BARC is responsible for managing several research and industrial facilities that 
contribute to nuclear technology and allied fields. 
 (i) Research and Development Centres 
Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research (IGCAR): Focuses on Fast 
Breeder Reactor (FBR) technology, materials science, and reactor engineering. 
Raja Ramanna Centre for Advanced Technology (RRCAT): Specialises in 
lasers, accelerators, and advanced optics for nuclear applications. 
Variable Energy Cyclotron Centre (VECC): Engaged in particle accelerator 
research, medical isotope production, and high-energy physics. 
(ii) Industrial and Service Organisations 
Nuclear Fuel Complex (NFC): Manufactures fuel bundles for PHWRs and 
BWRs, producing fuel components for India's nuclear power plants. 
Heavy Water Board (HWB): Manages the production and supply of heavy 
water (D2O) for nuclear reactors and industrial applications. 
Board of Radiation and Isotope Technology (BRIT): Engages in radioisotope 
production, nuclear medicine, and radiation technology applications for 
agriculture and healthcare. 
 
 
 

14 
 
(iii) Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) Under DAE 
Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL): Responsible for the 
construction and operation of commercial nuclear power plants in India. 
Bharatiya Nabhikiya Vidyut Nigam Limited (BHAVINI): Develops and 
operates Fast Breeder Reactors, essential for India's nuclear energy future. 
Uranium Corporation of India Limited (UCIL): Engaged in uranium mining 
and processing, a critical part of the nuclear fuel supply chain. 
3.2 The Committee notes that during the year 2023-24, BARC focused on 
several key areas, including nuclear waste management, isotope production for 
medical applications, and reactor technology development. Notable projects 
included the fabrication and testing of heavy-water primary coolant heat exchangers, 
the installation of an Indian Pressurised Water Reactor (IPWR) test facility, and the 
development of an indigenous network security system. Additionally, R&D efforts in 
post-irradiation examination of reactor materials and isotope production for cancer 
treatment were prioritised. 
For 2024-25, BARC undertook several crucial projects, including upgrading 
nuclear waste reprocessing systems, enhancing reactor safety features, and conducting 
feasibility studies on new-generation nuclear reactors. The installation of high-dose 
neutron irradiation facilities and the expansion of computational research capabilities 
were also among the key activities. 
     BARC has outlined priority areas for the financial year 2025-26, including: 
 Upgradation and operation of research reactors such as Dhruva and Apsara-U 
for isotope production and nuclear research. 
 Advancing reactor technology to support the Indian Nuclear Power Program, 
including work on Pressurized Heavy Water Reactors (PHWRs), Fast Breeder 
Reactors (FBRs), and Advanced Heavy Water Reactors (AHWRs). 
 Strengthening fuel cycle infrastructure, including fuel fabrication and waste 
reprocessing. 
 R&D in material sciences, astrophysics, and nuclear safety, with investments in 
sensors, detectors, and reactor shielding technologies. 
 Deployment of nuclear applications in agriculture, food preservation, and cancer 
treatment through isotope-based technologies. 
 Expansion of water purification technologies and enhancement of nuclear 
medicine applications.

3.39 Bharatiya Nabhikiya Vidyut Nigam Ltd (BHAVINI) 
Bharatiya Nabhikiya Vidyut Nigam Limited (BHAVINI) is a Government 
Company under the administrative control of the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) 
incorporated on 22nd October, 2003 as Public Limited Company under the Companies 
Act, 1956 with the objective of constructing and commissioning the first 500 MWe Fast 
Breeder Reactor (FBR) at Kalpakkam in Tamilnadu and to pursue construction, 
commissioning, operation and maintenance of subsequent Fast Breeder Reactors for 
generation of electricity in pursuance of the schemes and programmes of Government 
of India under the provisions of the Atomic Energy Act,1962. BHAVINI is currently 
constructing a 500MWe Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) at Kalpakkam, 70 Kms 
away from Chennai. The PFBR is the forerunner of the future Fast Breeder Reactors 
and is expected to provide energy security to the country. The PFBR is being built with 
the design and technology developed at the Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research 
(IGCAR) located at Kalpakkam. The PFBR is a First-Of-Its-Kind (FOAK) reactor, 
designed to utilise plutonium-based mixed oxide (MOX) fuel and sodium as a coolant, 
paving the way for large-scale deployment of Fast Breeder Reactors (FBRs) in India. 
The objectives of BHAVINI emanate from the following mandate: 
Providing energy security for the nation through Fast Breeder Technology based 
power stations commencing with 500 MWe Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor. 
Demonstrating the techno-commercial viability of Fast Breeder Technology based 
nuclear power stations. Strengthening the public awareness programmes for enhancing 
and improving the public perception of Nuclear Power in the country. Strengthening the 
QA activities relating to Fast Breeder Technology based nuclear power programme 
within the organization and those associated with it and increasing the overall share of 
nuclear power. 
  BHAVINI’s 500 MW PFBR is in the advanced stage of integrated 
commissioning, with expected first criticality by 2025-26. Some of the key 
accomplishments are: 
 (i) Completion of major structural work: Reactor containment, sodium cooling loops, and steam 
generator systems have been installed.  
 (ii) Modifications to reactor components: 376 subassemblies were modified to address higher 
extraction force issues and ensure seamless handling.  
(iii) Deployment of high-temperature materials: Advanced materials have been incorporated to 
enhance reactor efficiency and safety.  
(iv) Operationalisation of the Demonstration Fast Reactor Fuel Reprocessing Plant (DFRP): 
This facility, capable of handling both carbide and oxide fuels, was commissioned in 2024 and has 
successfully completed two fuel reprocessing campaigns. 
(v) Indigenous production of medical isotopes (Strontium-89): The PFBR has been used for the 
pilot-scale production of radioisotopes, contributing to nuclear medicine and cancer treatment.

4. 100 GW Nuclear Energy Mission for Viksit Bharat 2047 
The Secretary, Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) made a presentation before 
the Committee, outlining the 100 GW Nuclear Energy Mission, an ambitious plan to 
achieve 100 GW of nuclear power capacity by 2047 in alignment with India’s energy 
security and decarbonization goals. The Committee was informed that this mission aims 
to leverage private sector participation, streamline regulatory frameworks, and scale up 
nuclear power production to meet India’s increasing energy demands. The Committee 
recognizes the strategic importance of this initiative in ensuring a sustainable, low-
carbon energy future but acknowledges significant challenges that need to be 
addressed to make this target achievable. 
4.2 The Department in a written reply informed the Committee that the present 
installed nuclear power capacity stands at 8.18 GW, with an additional 7.3 GW under 
construction/commissioning and 7 GW already sanctioned and currently undergoing 
pre-project activities. Upon completion of these projects, India’s nuclear power capacity 
is expected to reach 22.48 GW by 2031-32. Beyond this, NPCIL plans to add another 
15.4 GW through indigenous Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors (PHWRs) and 17.6 
GW through Light Water Reactors (LWRs) with foreign cooperation, bringing the total 
installed capacity to 55 GW. Additionally, BHAVINI is expected to contribute 3.8 GW 
through Fast Breeder Reactors (FBRs), while the remainder of the capacity will come 
from Small Modular Reactors (SMRs), Bharat Small Reactors (BSRs), and other 
advanced nuclear technologies developed with private sector collaboration. The 
Committee notes that scaling up from the projected 55 GW to 100 GW by 2047 
will require substantial investment, regulatory reforms, and policy interventions. 
4.3 On being asked about the capital investments in the 100 GW Mission, the 
Department informed that around 50% of the 100 GW target is expected to come from 
Public-Private Partnerships (PPP). However, the exact public-private and indigenous-
imported mix will emerge as amendments to the Atomic Energy Act and Civil Liability 
for Nuclear Damage (CLND) Act are introduced, along with necessary regulatory 
reforms. 
4.4 The Committee acknowledges that achieving 100 GW of nuclear capacity 
by 2047 requires a structured and phased approach. Instead of focusing solely on a 
long-term 100 GW target, the Committee recommends phased capacity additions, 
with clear short-term (2030), medium-term (2040), and long-term (2047) 
milestones. The Committee recommends that 2031-32 projection of 22.48 GW 

25 
 
should serve as a baseline, with subsequent capacity additions planned in 
alignment with investment inflows, policy reforms, and domestic manufacturing 
capabilities. 
4.5 The Committee notes that nearly 50% of the 100 GW capacity is expected 
to come from private sector participation and recommends establishing a robust 
financial model that includes Government incentives, Viability Gap Funding 
(VGF), and sovereign guarantees to attract both domestic and foreign investments. 
The Committee suggests that legislative amendments to the Atomic Energy Act 
and Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act should be expedited to encourage 
private investment in nuclear power generation. 
4.6 The Committee emphasizes the importance of Small Modular Reactors 
(SMRs) and Bharat Small Reactors (BSRs) in achieving the 100 GW target. The 
Committee recommends that SMRs and BSRs should be deployed in remote 
regions and industrial zones to support decentralized energy generation. The 
Committee also urges the Department to accelerate Fast Breeder Reactor (FBR) 
deployment, with the 500 MW Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) expected 
to attain first criticality by March 2026 and completion by September 2026.

8.2 The Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) plays a critical role in advancing 
India's nuclear research, energy generation, and scientific innovation. However, a 
review of its workforce distribution by the Committee reveals significant vacancies 
across its various units, which could affect efficiency and operational effectiveness. As 

31 
 
observed by Table 4 above, one of the most crucial institutions under the DAE, the 
Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC), has a sanctioned strength of 14,445 
personnel, but only 10,604 employees are currently in position, leaving 3,841 
vacancies. This results in a vacancy rate of 26.6%, indicating a substantial shortage of 
skilled personnel in key research and technical positions. Similarly, the Indira Gandhi 
Centre for Atomic Research (IGCAR), which is responsible for advanced nuclear 
research and fast breeder reactor development, has 2,134 employees in position against 
a sanctioned strength of 2,730, leaving 596 vacancies. This 21.8% vacancy rate could 
slow down research projects and affect the development of next-generation nuclear 
technologies. An even more concerning situation exists in the Heavy Water Board 
(HWB), which is responsible for producing and supplying heavy water for nuclear 
reactors. With a sanctioned strength of 3,872 personnel, only 2,015 employees are in 
position, leaving 1,857 vacancies. This represents a staggering 48% vacancy rate, which 
could impact reactor operations and nuclear fuel production. 
8.3 NPCIL which operates India’s nuclear power plants, has a sanctioned workforce 
of 15,088 employees, but only 10,745 are in position, leading to 4,343 vacancies. This 
represents a 28.8% vacancy rate, which could affect the efficiency and safety of nuclear 
power plant operations. The Atomic Minerals Directorate (AMD), responsible for the 
exploration of atomic minerals such as uranium and thorium, also faces significant 
shortages. With 2,495 sanctioned posts, only 1,699 employees are in position, leaving 
796 vacancies, translating to a 31.9% vacancy rate, which could impact India's ability to 
expand its nuclear fuel reserves.A notable concern is the vacancy rate at the Tata 
Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR), which is one of India's leading scientific 
research institutions. With a sanctioned strength of 1,448 employees, only 609 are in 
position, leaving 839 vacancies. This results in a 58% vacancy rate, reflecting a 
significant shortfall in scientific manpower. Such a high vacancy rate suggests that 
TIFR is heavily reliant on contractual and research-based staff rather than regular 
employees. Given the institute's crucial role in fundamental research, this issue requires 
immediate attention to ensure stability in long-term scientific projects. 
8.4 The Tata Memorial Centre (TMC), India's premier cancer treatment and 
research institution under the DAE, has a sanctioned strength of 6,229 personnel, with 
5,052 in position, leaving 1,177 vacancies. This results in a vacancy rate of 18.9%, 
which, although lower compared to other DAE institutions, still reflects a shortage of 
medical professionals and researchers who are essential for providing comprehensive 
cancer care and advancing oncology research. 
8.5 The DAE informed the Committee in its written reply that it has initiated a 
recruitment drive to mitigate workforce shortages. A Central Recruitment Agency 
(CRA) has been set up in the year 2022 to streamline recruitment across all DAE units. 
The Department further informed that a mission-mode recruitment drive in 2023-24 led 
to the hiring of 3,200 personnel, including scientific officers, technical staff, and 
administrative personnel. Trainee Scientific Officers (TSOs) are recruited annually for 
BARC Training Schools, and 180 officers were inducted in August 2024. The 
Department emphasized that Recruitment of Technical Officers, Scientific Assistants, 
and Paramedical Staff is ongoing, with empanelment of 2,269 technicians and 1,206 
scientific assistants. However, the Committee observes that recruitment delays still 
persist, and several advertised posts remain unfilled. 
8.6 The high vacancy rates across DAE institutions raise serious concerns 
about workforce planning, recruitment efficiency, and the overall sustainability of 
nuclear and research projects in India. The Committee expresses its concerns over 
these vacancies, especially in key operational areas such as nuclear power 
generation, research, and mineral exploration. The shortage of skilled personnel 
could lead to delays in research and development, inefficiencies in plant 
operations, and constraints in nuclear fuel production, ultimately affecting the 

32 
 
country's nuclear energy programme. To address this issue, the Committee 
strongly recommends an immediate recruitment drive to fill the existing vacancies. 
It is imperative that recruitment processes be streamlined to ensure timely hiring 
of personnel in technical, scientific, and operational roles. A review of existing 
workforce policies should be undertaken to identify areas where delays occur in 
the hiring process, and necessary reforms should be implemented. The DAE must 
adopt modern human resource management strategies to attract and retain talent, 
ensuring competitive salaries, career progression opportunities, and research 
grants for professionals in nuclear science, energy, and advanced research. 
8.7 The Committee observes with great concern contractual employment and 
temporary staffing, particularly in research institutions such as TIFR. The 
Committee urges a review of these employment practices and recommends 
converting long-term contractual positions into permanent roles wherever 
necessary. The Committee recommends that regularisation of employment will not 
only enhance job security for researchers and scientists but also ensure continuity 
in long-term research projects. Additionally, for institutions such as TMC, where 
medical professionals are in high demand, the Committee recommends expanding 
recruitment efforts and increasing budgetary support for healthcare staff and 
researchers.

potential uranium and thorium reserves in Jharkhand, Meghalaya, Andhra 
Pradesh, and Rajasthan and special attention should be given to monazite-bearing 
coastal areas in Odisha, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh for rare earth and 
thorium extraction. The Committee also expressed concerns over illegal mining of 
Atomic minerals and its impact on the cost of exchequer and national security. In 
parallel with exploration, the Committee recommends enhancing uranium ore 
processing plants at Jaduguda, Tummalapalle, and Narwapahar to improve the 
efficiency of domestic fuel production. The Committee recommends expedited 
approvals for the construction of AHWR and associated fuel reprocessing 
infrastructure. The Committee urges upon the DAE to have collaboration with 
international nuclear agencies for technological exchange on thorium reactor 
operations.                                                                                                       (Para 3.16) 
 The Committee recommends that AMD should collaborate with Indian 
Rare Earths Limited (IREL) and private mining firms to leverage expertise and 
accelerate exploration and processing.                                                         (Para 3.17) 

38 
 
 The Committee understands that given China’s dominance on production 
of global Rare Earth Elements (REE), India's lack of investment in domestic 
exploration and processing will keep the country vulnerable to supply chain 
disruptions. The Committee recommends the DAE to fast scale the exploration to 
reduce dependence on China-dominated REE supply chains. Given the increasing 
demand for nuclear and REE-based technologies, the Committee recommends 
establishing a strategic reserve for uranium, thorium, and REEs. The Committee 
observes that this will ensure long-term security and prevent supply disruptions in 
India’s nuclear and high-tech industries.                                                    (Para 3.18) 
The Committee observes that HWB has been allocated ₹6,478.07 crore, for 
the financial year 2025-26 with ₹3,322.31 crore earmarked for capital expenditure 
and ₹3,155.76 crore for revenue expenditure, a shortfall of ₹513.37 crore from its 
originally proposed ₹6,991.44 crore. The Committee observes that this reduction 
in allocation could adversely impact the modernisation of heavy water plants, 
delay the expansion of nuclear solvent production, and slow down critical research 
on deuterium-based pharmaceuticals. Given that heavy water is a strategic 
material crucial for India’s nuclear power programme, ensuring adequate funding 
is essential for energy security, industrial applications, and medical research.     
(Para 3.20) 
 The Committee expresses serious concern over the underutilisation of funds 
in 2024-25, particularly in facility upgrades, research initiatives, and procurement 
of essential materials for heavy water production. The Committee observes that 
HWB is pivotal in ensuring a steady supply of heavy water for Pressurised Heavy 
Water Reactors (PHWRs) and supporting India’s broader nuclear energy 
programme and it is imperative that funds be optimally utilised, and key projects 
be executed within stipulated timeframes. The Committee strongly recommends 
improved financial planning, closer monitoring of expenditure, and timely 
execution of planned projects to prevent further delays in critical infrastructure 
development and research activities.                                                            (Para 3.22) 
 The Committee recommends prioritisation of modernization of Heavy 
Water Plant and urges the DAE that up gradation to H₂S and ammonia-based 
heavy water plants should be fast-tracked, focusing on energy efficiency, 
automation, and operational safety. The Committee recommends ensuring timely 
commissioning of HWP, Tuticorin by the DAE and urges strict adherence to the 
April 2025 timeline for restarting the Tuticorin plant, an essential step towards 
maintainence of reactor-grade heavy water production. The Committee observes 
that increased investment in deuterium-depleted water (DDW) research is needed 
to explore its potential applications in cancer therapy and metabolic disorders.  
(Para 3.23) 
The Committee urges the Government to reinstate the funding shortfall, 
accelerate infrastructure modernisation, and prioritise R&D in nuclear medicine. 
Adequate funding and strategic planning are essential to ensure that India 
remains self-sufficient in heavy water production and nuclear fuel processing.  
(Para 3.24) 
  
The Committee recommends that continued investment in reactor safety, 
periodic maintenance, and component upgrades is necessary to sustain high 
availability and load factors. Reactor life extension programme should be 
prioritised for ageing units to maintain their contribution to clean energy 
generation. The Committee recommends expediting new reactor projects to 
increase installed capacity and further reduce CO₂ emissions. The Committee 

39 
 
recommends that with proven operational efficiency in large reactors, NPCIL 
should focus on the development and deployment of Small Modular Reactors 
(SMRs) to expand distributed nuclear energy solutions. The Committee is of the 
opinion that SMRs can enhance grid flexibility and support energy needs in 
remote areas where large-scale nuclear plants are not feasible.                (Para 3.27) 
The Committee expresses serious concern over the underutilisation of ₹1,465.71 
crore in 2024-25, which points to delays in project execution, inefficiencies in fund 
disbursement, and procurement-related bottlenecks. The Committee expresses 
concern over rising capital costs, extended regulatory approvals, and public 
hesitancy towards nuclear expansion. The Committee strongly recommends 
enhanced financial oversight, improved fund allocation mechanisms, and stricter 
monitoring of expenditure to ensure the timely execution of critical reactor 
projects.                                                                                                           (Para 3.29) 
 The Committee notes that land acquisition, community resistance and 
rehabilitation policies hinder project approvals and State-level delays in securing 
approvals further slow down progress. The Committee also notes that dependence 
on foreign suppliers for key reactor components results in extended lead times and 
increased costs. The Committee recommends the urgent need to prioritise 
domestic manufacturing for long-term self-reliance. The Committee agrees that 
concerns over nuclear safety and waste management impact project approvals and 
implementation and is one of the major challenges towards expansion. The 
Committee recommends that improved collaboration with state governments is 
necessary for land clearance acceleration and a proactive public outreach 
programme should be implemented to address nuclear safety concerns.   
 (Para 3.30) 
The Committee urges the Department to strengthen domestic nuclear 
equipment manufacturing and recommends that the Government should 
encourage Indian industries to produce nuclear reactor components. The 
Committee is of the view that exploring alternative procurement strategies for 
critical reactor-grade materials is essential. The Committee further recommends 
that priority must be given to completing KKNPP-3&4 and KKNPP-5&6 within 
the revised timelines and stronger oversight is needed to avoid unnecessary cost 
escalations. The Committee also recommends that expansion of research funding 
for Fast Breeder Reactors (FBRs) is essential for a transition to a thorium-based 
energy system.                                                                                                 (Para 3.31) 
The Committee notes that, the Budget Estimate (BE) for the financial year 
2024-25 was ₹3,627.97 crore (₹763.51 crore under the Central Sector Scheme and 
₹2,864.46 crore under Establishment Expenditure). This was later revised to 
₹4,491.74 crore at the Revised Estimate (RE) stage. However, actual utilization as 
of January 2025 stood at ₹4,000.22 crore. The Actual expenditure under Capital 
up to January,2025 is Rs.539.05 crore (78%) against RE 2024-2025 of Rs.690 
crores. For 2025-26, NFC proposed a Budget Estimate of ₹7,810.00 crore, but was 
allocated only ₹6,638.25 crore, reflecting a shortfall of ₹1,171.75 crore. The 
Committee notes that such a significant gap between the proposed and allocated 
budget could affect critical functions such as fuel supply, capacity expansion, and 
modernization efforts.                                                                                    (Para 3.33) 

40 
 
The Committee notes that delays in procurement, infrastructure 
development, and administrative approvals have impacted fund utilization. The 
Committee urges the Department to ensure timely execution of procurement 
contracts, enhanced financial oversight, and improved coordination with domestic 
suppliers to reduce reliance on imported raw materials.                           (Para 3.34) 
 The Committee appreciates NFC’s efforts in fuel fabrication and notes that 
it supplied 803.26 MT of nuclear fuel to NPCIL in FY 2024-25, underscoring its 
pivotal role in sustaining uninterrupted nuclear power generation. Despite NFC’s 
consistent operational performance, the budgetary shortfall of ₹1,171.75 crore in 
2025-26 raises concerns regarding the timely execution of critical infrastructure 
projects and procurement of essential raw materials such as zirconium and 
uranium compounds.                                                                                     (Para 3.35) 
 The Committee notes that cost escalations in uranium procurement and 
fuel fabrication materials pose significant financial challenges to NFC’s 
operations. The Committee strongly recommends that the Department prioritize 
additional budget allocations at the Revised Estimates (RE) stage to address 
funding gaps and prevent supply chain disruptions.                                  (Para 3.36) 
 The Committee observes that the funding shortfall may adversely impact 
NFC’s ability to sustain fuel production, which could lead to delays in supplying 
nuclear fuel to NPCIL and hinder planned expansion at NFC-Kota. The 
Committee urges the Department to ensure adequate financial support to meet 
production continuity requirements.                                                            (Para 3.37) 
 The Committee also urges the Department to strengthen NFC’s domestic 
production capabilities and recommends scaling up indigenous manufacturing of 
nuclear fuel materials to reduce reliance on foreign suppliers. The Committee 
recommends the Department to invest in R&D for next-generation nuclear fuels, 
including Thorium-based fuel fabrication for India’s three-stage nuclear program.  
(Para 3.38) 
 The Committee notes that, for BE 2025-26, BHAVINI has been allocated 
₹374 crore, significantly lower than the ₹600 crore in Revised Estimates (RE) for 
2024-25. This marks a reduction of ₹226 crore. However, the Committee observes 
that, in 2024-25, BHAVINI's actual expenditure of ₹390 crore was lower than RE 
of ₹600 crore, indicating underutilization of funds due to delays in commissioning 
process.                                                                                                            (Para 3.41) 
 The Committee urges the Department that BHAVINI should prioritise 
remaining integrated commissioning activities and ensure that criticality is 
achieved by 2025-26. Acknowledging the reduction of ₹226 crore in 2025-26 
allocations from ₹600 crore in RE 2024-25, the Committee recommends additional 
financial support at the RE stage to facilitate smooth commissioning and post-
criticality testing.                                                                                          (Para 3.42) 
100 GW Nuclear Energy Mission for Viksit Bharat 2047 
The Committee recognizes the strategic importance of this initiative in 
ensuring a sustainable, low-carbon energy future but acknowledges significant 
challenges that need to be addressed to make this target achievable.         (Para 4.1) 
 

41 
 
The Committee notes that scaling up from the projected 55 GW to 100 GW 
by 2047 will require substantial investment, regulatory reforms, and policy 
interventions.                                                                                                     (Para 4.2) 
The Committee acknowledges that achieving 100 GW of nuclear capacity 
by 2047 requires a structured and phased approach. Instead of focusing solely on a 
long-term 100 GW target, the Committee recommends phased capacity additions, 
with clear short-term (2030), medium-term (2040), and long-term (2047) 
milestones. The Committee recommends that 2031-32 projection of 22.48 GW 
should serve as a baseline, with subsequent capacity additions planned in 
alignment with investment inflows, policy reforms, and domestic manufacturing 
capabilities.                                                                                                       (Para 4.4) 
 The Committee notes that nearly 50% of the 100 GW capacity is expected 
to come from private sector participation and recommends establishing a robust 
financial model that includes Government incentives, Viability Gap Funding 
(VGF), and sovereign guarantees to attract both domestic and foreign investments. 
The Committee suggests that legislative amendments to the Atomic Energy Act 
and Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act should be expedited to encourage 
private investment in nuclear power generation.                                          (Para 4.5) 
 The Committee emphasizes the importance of Small Modular Reactors 
(SMRs) and Bharat Small Reactors (BSRs) in achieving the 100 GW target. The 
Committee recommends that SMRs and BSRs should be deployed in remote 
regions and industrial zones to support decentralized energy generation. The 
Committee also urges the Department to accelerate Fast Breeder Reactor (FBR) 
deployment, with the 500 MW Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) expected 
to attain first criticality by March 2026 and completion by September 2026.  
                                                                                                                            (Para 4.6) 
 
NUCLEAR ENERGY MISSION FOR R&D OF SMALL MODULAR 
REACTORS (SMRS) 
 To support SMR development, the Committee recommends prioritizing 
demonstration projects, ensuring that the first set of SMRs is successfully deployed 
and operational before scaling up production. Furthermore, international 
collaboration with established nuclear agencies should be pursued to adopt best 
practices in reactor design and safety protocols. The Committee also recommends 
prioritising domestic SMR research and pilot projects to ensure economic 
viability.                                                                                                             (Para 5.3) 
The Committee recommends that initial funding should focus on BSMR 
and GCMMR demonstration plants before large-scale commercialisation.  
 (Para 5.4) 
 
BHARAT SMALL REACTORS (BSR) AND PUBLIC-PRIVATE 
PARTNERSHIP IN INFRASTRUCTURE 
The Committee notes that the existing Atomic Energy Act and the Civil 
Liability for Nuclear Damage Act have been revised to facilitate private 
participation while ensuring safety and security standards are met. However, the 
Committee notes that several key concerns still remain. The Committee observes 
that ensuring strict compliance with nuclear safety protocols, waste management 
regulations, and radiation protection measures is crucial to avoid potential 

42 
 
hazards. The Committee expresses concern that regulatory uncertainties 
regarding liability and risk-sharing mechanisms could deter private investors.  
                                                                                                                (Para 6.2) 
                                              
The Committee also stresses that India’s strategic control over critical 
nuclear technologies must not be compromised through excessive reliance on 
private enterprises. To mitigate these risks, the Committee recommends that the 
Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) be strengthened to enforce stringent 
compliance measures for private sector entities. The Committee recommends that 
the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) must enforce compliance measures 
for private players. The Committee urges the Department to develop clear 
contractual frameworks and risk-sharing mechanisms. The Committee also 
suggests that clear contractual frameworks may be developed, ensuring 
transparent agreements that prioritise safety, security, and accountability in 
nuclear energy projects.                                                                                   (Para 6.3) 
TATA MEMORIAL CENTRE (TMC) 
The Committee notes that TMC's actual expenditure for 2023-24 was 
₹1688.93 crore, reflecting higher-than-expected financial utilisation. For 2024-25, 
the Revised Estimate (RE) was ₹1439.02 crore, with actual utilisation already 
reaching ₹1746.27 crore by January 2025, indicating an increase in spending on 
cancer care and research. The proposed BE 2025-26 for revenue (salary) was 
₹1164.55 crore, but only ₹980 crore was sanctioned, leading to a shortfall of 
₹184.55 crore. The Committee also notes that ₹1034.30 crore was proposed by the 
Department for BE 2025-26 but only ₹550 crore were sanctioned, reflecting a 
shortfall of ₹484.30 crore.                                                                                (Para 7.4) 
 The Committee acknowledges the effective financial management by TMC 
and recommends sustained funding to support ongoing and future initiatives. The 
Committee also recognises the importance of expansion of new cancer hospitals 
across the country and urges for timely completion of ongoing projects. The 
Committee commends TMC’s leadership in oncology research and recommends 
continued government funding for R&D.                                                      (Para 7.5) 
 The Committee recognises the Tata Memorial Centre’s outstanding 
contributions to India’s cancer care landscape. With consistent financial backing 
from DAE, TMC has expanded its network of cancer hospitals, pioneered new 
research in oncology, and strengthened preventive care initiatives. However, 
increasing cancer incidence necessitates further expansion of healthcare 
infrastructure, sustained investment in R&D, and enhanced public outreach 
programmes. The Committee urges the Government to ensure continued support 
for TMC’s initiatives to make cancer care affordable and accessible to all. 
(Para 7.6) 
 The Committee recommends increased Government funding for subsidised 
cancer treatment at TMC hospitals and affiliated institutions. The Committee also 
recommends that the National Cancer Grid (NCG) should be strengthened to 
ensure uniform pricing policies for cancer care across all NCG-affiliated hospitals 
to avoid cost disparities. The Committee urges the DAE that R&D in indigenous 
pharmaceutical production should be prioritised, focusing on generic versions of 
expensive cancer drugs to reduce dependence on costly imports. The Committee is 
of the opinion that TMC and the DAE should collaborate with Indian 
pharmaceutical industries to develop cost-effective versions of immunotherapy 
drugs, targeted therapies, and biologics for affordability.                           (Para 7.7) 

43 
 
 The Committee taking note of advancements in the field of radiotherapy, 
recommends increased investment in R&D under TMC and DAE for next-
generation chemotherapy and radiotherapy innovations to improve treatment 
outcomes and affordability. The Committee also recommends that Proton Beam 
Therapy (PBT) and Boron Neutron Capture Therapy (BNCT) should be 
expanded, as these offer precise tumour targeting with fewer side effects, reducing 
long-term treatment costs.                                                                               (Para 7.8) 
 The  Committee strongly recommends that TMC and DAE should engage 
with corporate entities and industry leaders to create dedicated CSR funds for 
subsidising cancer treatments.The Committee recommends introduction of 
Corporate-sponsored free treatment schemes, where large private enterprises can 
support treatment for underprivileged cancer patients in TMC hospitals. The 
Committee recommends fast-tracking the establishment of new TMC-affiliated 
cancer hospitals in tier-2 and tier-3 cities, ensuring better regional access to 
quality cancer care.                                                                                          (Para 7.9) 
 The  Committee recommends increased budgetary allocations to DAE and 
TMC for advanced oncology research, particularly in nuclear medicine, gene 
therapy, and radio-immunotherapy. The Committee urges the DAE to encourage 
institutional research collaborations between TMC, IITs, and AIIMS to develop 
low-cost, high-efficacy cancer treatments. The Committee also observes that 
Government-supported clinical trial funding should be enhanced, ensuring greater 
participation in global cancer research initiatives. The Committee firmly believes 
that TMC and DAE must adopt a multi-faceted approach to enhance cost-effective 
cancer treatment and therapies in India. Sustained government support, increased 
corporate participation, and advancements in research will ensure that high-
quality cancer treatment remains accessible to all sections of society.      (Para 7.10) 
 
HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT AND CAPACITY BUILDING 
  
However, the Committee observes that recruitment delays still persist, and 
several advertised posts remain unfilled.                                                       (Para 8.5) 
 
The high vacancy rates across DAE institutions raise serious concerns 
about workforce planning, recruitment efficiency, and the overall sustainability of 
nuclear and research projects in India. The Committee expresses its concerns over 
these vacancies, especially in key operational areas such as nuclear power 
generation, research, and mineral exploration. The shortage of skilled personnel 
could lead to delays in research and development, inefficiencies in plant 
operations, and constraints in nuclear fuel production, ultimately affecting the 
country's nuclear energy programme. To address this issue, the Committee 
strongly recommends an immediate recruitment drive to fill the existing vacancies. 
It is imperative that recruitment processes be streamlined to ensure timely hiring 
of personnel in technical, scientific, and operational roles. A review of existing 
workforce policies should be undertaken to identify areas where delays occur in 
the hiring process, and necessary reforms should be implemented. The DAE must 
adopt modern human resource management strategies to attract and retain talent, 
ensuring competitive salaries, career progression opportunities, and research 
grants for professionals in nuclear science, energy, and advanced research.  
(Para 8.6) 
  

44 
 
The Committee observes with great concern contractual employment and 
temporary staffing, particularly in research institutions such as TIFR. The 
Committee urges a review of these employment practices and recommends 
converting long-term contractual positions into permanent roles wherever 
necessary. The Committee recommends that regularisation of employment will not 
only enhance job security for researchers and scientists but also ensure continuity 
in long-term research projects. Additionally, for institutions such as TMC, where 
medical professionals are in high demand, the Committee recommends expanding 
recruitment efforts and increasing budgetary support for healthcare staff and 
researchers.             (Para 8.7)

9. The Chairman welcomed the Secretary, Department of Atomic Energy and his 
team of officers and asked them to give a brief presentation on the Demands for Grants 
(2025-26). Thereafter, The Secretary made a Power Point Presentation (PPT) which 
covered India's nuclear power expansion, detailing the current operational capacity of 
24 reactors (8,180 MW), with an additional 9 reactors (7,300 MW) under development. 
Further, it highlighted India's growing mining capabilities in lithium and rare earth 
elements, including a newly discovered 1,800-ton lithium reserve in Karnataka. Plans 
were also unveiled for a Titanium Slug Processing Facility in partnership with 
Kazakhstan, aimed at reducing dependence on foreign imports for critical minerals. The 
Secretary also informed the Committee that nine Tata Memorial Centres are operational 
across the country, with two more under construction. One in New Mumbai, Khopoli, 
will have 100 beds and will focus on Ayurvedic cancer treatment. The other, in 
Odisha’s Khurda district, will be a 400-bed hospital. Both centres are expected to be 
completed within one to two years. The Committee was also apprised that a new liquid 
formulation of mercaptopurine for treatment of acute lymphoblastic leukemia has been 
developed by Tata Memorial Centre. Approved by the Drug Controller General of 
India, it ensures precise dosing for children, is better absorbed than tablets, and has no 
food interaction. Priced at Rs. 864 per one-gram bottle (lasting 20 days), it is 
significantly cheaper than the $150 imported version, which is unavailable in India. 
This advancement has greatly improved pediatric cancer treatment and is now widely 
used by oncologists across the country. The Secretary, then, discussed the Bharat Small 
Reactors project, involving 220 MW pressurized heavy water reactors, which has been 
approved for private investment under the PPP model.

Northeastern region, measures taken by the Department for social outreach and 
awareness, amendment to the Atomic Energy Act and the Civil Liability for Nuclear 
Damage Act and cost-effective cancer therapies and medicines developed by Tata 
Memorial Centre.

1. INTRODUCTION 
1.1 The Department of Biotechnology (DBT) was established in 1982 as an independent board 
and later became a full-fledged department under the Ministry of Science & Technology in 1986. It 
is responsible for formulating policies, promoting research, and overseeing biotechnology-related 
manufacturing in India. DBT develops integrated biotechnology programs, ensuring their effective 
implementation and alignment with national priorities. It identifies and supports R&D initiatives, 
particularly in biologicals and biotechnological manufacturing, and establishes Centers of 
Excellence to advance research in critical areas. The department also functions as a regulatory and 
advisory body for the import, transfer, and approval of new biotech technologies and products. It 
develops safety guidelines for biotechnology research and production and serves as the central 
agency for importing genetically modified materials while promoting their domestic production. 
1.2 DBT plays a pivotal role in facilitating inter-ministerial and international collaborations, 
overseeing technology transfers, and supporting the development of recombinant DNA products, 
cell-based vaccines, and biotechnological diagnostics. A key mandate of DBT is human resource 
development in biotechnology, achieved through the administration of agencies, commissions, and 
research boards formed by the Government of India. Additionally, it serves as the primary body for 
bioinformatics, supporting training, infrastructure development, data collection, and knowledge 
exchange in biotechnology research. 
1.3 The Department oversees several autonomous institutions engaged in advanced research 
areas such as genomics, immunology, neuroscience, regenerative medicine, and bioresource 
management. It also manages the International Centre for Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology 
(ICGEB) in New Delhi. Furthermore, DBT supervises public sector undertakings that contribute to 
biotechnology innovation, vaccine production, and industry research assistance. These entities play 
a significant role in advancing India’s biotechnology sector. 
1.4 The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology, 
Environment, Forests and Climate Change considered the Demands for Grants (2025-26), Demand 
No. 90 of the Department of Biotechnology in its meeting held on 20th February, 2025.

3. BIO-RIDE: A UNIFIED FRAMEWORK FOR ADVANCING BIOTECHNOLOGY 
RESEARCH, ENTREPRENEURSHIP, AND BIOMANUFACTURING IN INDIA 
3.1 The Department of Biotechnology (DBT) was promoting research, development, and 
innovation across all sectors of biotechnology in India through the implementation of policies and 
programs under two umbrella Central Sector Schemes: (a) Biotechnology Research and 
Development, and (b) Industrial & Entrepreneurship Development. In a significant move, the Union 
Cabinet approved the merger of these schemes into a single, unified scheme titled “Biotechnology 
Research Innovation and Entrepreneurship Development (Bio-RIDE)”. This merger was based on 
the recommendations of the Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC). The EFC proposed the 

7 
 
integration of the two existing schemes with an additional new component, “Biomanufacturing and 
Biofoundry”, to be implemented during the 15th Finance Commission Cycle (2021-22 to 2025-26) 
with a total budget allocation of ₹9,197 crore. 
3.2 The Union Cabinet, in its meeting on 18th September 2024, formally approved the 
continuation of the DBT schemes under the consolidated Bio-RIDE scheme. This unified scheme 
now comprises three key components: 
1. Biotechnology Research and Development; 
2. Industrial and Entrepreneurship Development; and 
3. Biomanufacturing and Biofoundry (a newly introduced component). 
The total budget of ₹9,197 crore includes a dedicated allocation of ₹1,500 crore for the new 
Biomanufacturing and Biofoundry component. 
3.3 The Committee sought clarification on the rationale behind this merger of schemes. In 
response, the Department explained that the integration of earlier schemes under Bio-RIDE 
enhances flexibility and efficiency in resource allocation, enabling the Department to dynamically 
reallocate funds between the "Biotechnology Research & Development" and "Industrial & 
Entrepreneurship Development" components based on evolving program needs and priorities. This 
strategic approach will ensure optimal utilization of resources, promote innovation, research 
excellence, and entrepreneurship in biotechnology. 
3.4 The first component, Biotechnology Research & Development, aims to build a robust 
education, research, and translation ecosystem to position India as a global leader in emerging 
technologies. This component supports major programs such as capacity building, which includes 
human resource development and infrastructure enhancement, competitive research grants and 
mission programs, international cooperation, and biotechnology-based programs for societal 
development.  
3.5 The second component, Industrial & Entrepreneurship Development, focuses on enhancing 
the research and innovation capabilities of Indian biotech industries, particularly SMEs and 
startups, to drive affordable solutions for societal challenges. This component supports initiatives 
such as public-private partnerships (PPP), the Make in India Initiative, and the establishment of 
Biotech Parks. These efforts aim to stimulate innovation, foster entrepreneurship, and enhance the 
global competitiveness of Indian biotech industries, ensuring that they can address the needs of the 
largest sections of society through affordable and accessible products and services. 
3.6 The third and newest component, Biomanufacturing and Biofoundry, aims to enable a 
Circular-Bioeconomy by ‘Fostering High Performance Biomanufacturing’ in the country, with a 
strategic focus on: bio-based chemicals, Biopolymers and enzymes, functional food, smart proteins, 
precision biotherapeutics, climate resilient agriculture, carbon capture, futuristic marine and space 
research. The sectoral focus will be complemented by cross-cutting Enablers (मूलांक ु र Bio-Enablers) 
including Biofoundries, Biomanufacturing Hubs and Bio-Artificial Intelligence (AI) Hubs, 
powerful national platforms to accelerate biomanufacturing by enabling access to scale-up 
infrastructure, scientific data, technology platforms and biomaterial libraries. Major programs under 
this component include discovery and integrated network research, bridging the gap for scale-up, 
and setting up Bio-enablers to drive innovation and commercialization. 
3.7 On the basis of the information provided by the Department, some of the major 
programmes/initiatives, achievements and action plan for the future, under the newly launched 
component ‘Biomanufacturing and Biofoundry’ are:- 
 The Union Cabinet, approved India’s first Biotechnology Policy, the BioE3 (Biotechnology 
for Economy, Environment, and Employment) Policy for ‘Fostering High-Performance 

8 
 
Biomanufacturing’, marking a significant milestone in the country’s efforts to foster high-
performance biomanufacturing. This policy aims to position India at the forefront of a 
sustainable future by leveraging biomanufacturing processes to accelerate the development 
and production of bio-based high-value products. 
 Six thematic sectors were identified for the Biomanufacturing Initiative. These include bio-
based chemicals and enzymes, smart proteins and functional foods, precision 
biotherapeutics, climate-resilient agriculture, carbon capture and utilization, and futuristic 
marine and space research. A Strategic Roadmap has been formulated to implement these 
thematic verticals under the Biomanufacturing initiative.  
 As part of the BioE3 Policy, the Department is also setting up BioEnablers, including Bio-
Artificial Intelligence Hubs, Biofoundries, and Biomanufacturing Hubs, to accelerate 
innovation and scale-up efforts across thematic verticals. The first DBT-BIRAC joint call 
for proposals was given. Recommended projects are currently under implementation. In a 
landmark collaboration, a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) was signed between DBT 
and ISRO for joint efforts in Space Biotechnology and Biomanufacturing. 
 The Department is working to expand biomanufacturing efforts nationwide through Centre-
State partnerships. The Centre-State Partnership Conclave, held in New Delhi, brought 
together State representatives to strategize on the implementation of biomanufacturing 
initiatives across all States. As part of this collaboration, BioE3 Cells are proposed to be 
established across the country to align biomanufacturing initiatives with regional priorities 
while supporting national objectives. 
 The Department has also launched a new initiative, the DBT-BIRAC Amrit Team Grant, to 
support collaborative and innovative research programs. Simultaneously, Department 
remains committed to ongoing programs under the key components of Biotechnology 
Research & Development and Industrial & Entrepreneurship Development fostering 
advancements in medical, agricultural, and environmental biotechnology through basic and 
applied research, development, and innovation. 
3.8 The Committee appreciates the Department for integration of research, industrial 
development, and biomanufacturing under a unified framework. This will significantly 
enhance India's biotechnology capabilities and position the country as a global hub for 
innovation, sustainability, and bio-based industrialization.  
3.9 The Committee places its confidence in the Department’s ability to effectively 
implement the Bio-RIDE scheme and achieve its ambitious targets. The various initiatives 
under this scheme have the potential to drive transformative changes in healthcare, 
agriculture, environment, and industry. Most importantly, the Committee hopes that the 
advancements in biotechnology under this scheme will ultimately benefit the common man by 
providing affordable and accessible healthcare solutions, enhancing agricultural productivity, 
promoting environmental sustainability through carbon capture technologies and bio-based 
solutions and creating employment opportunities through bio-industrialization and 
entrepreneurship development. 
4. AUTONOMOUS INSTITUTIONS

established by an Act of Parliament, 1 Inter-Governmental Agency and 3 Public Sector 
Undertakings (PSUs) under its administrative domain. 
4.2 The Department informed the Committee that it has established an Autonomous Body, the 
Biotechnology Research and Innovation Council (BRIC), which consolidates the governance of 13 

9

groundbreaking advancements through multidisciplinary research, tackling complex scientific 
challenges and delivering affordable, impactful solutions. By expanding research scope and 
ambition, BRIC will strengthen institutional governance and propel India towards biotech 
excellence on the world stage.

institutions under the iBRIC+ framework has significantly enhanced the governance, 
collaboration, and impact of biotechnology research in India. The data provided reflects 
commendable progress in interdisciplinary research, education, biomanufacturing, and 
industrial partnerships. However, to amplify the outcomes, BRIC should scale 
interdisciplinary research into a nationwide innovation network with industry-aligned 
translational centres, broaden the i3c BRIC-RCB PhD Programme via global academic-
industry partnerships and merit-based fellowships, and develop regional Biomanufacturing 
Hubs for sector-specific bio-solutions. Prioritizing commercialization through streamlined 
regulatory approvals, incentives for startups, and centralized data-sharing platforms will 
expedite market readiness for innovations in diagnostics, biotherapeutics, and disease 
management. Strengthening mentorship programs, industry internships, and entrepreneurial 
fellowships will cultivate skilled talent, while leveraging breakthroughs. By scaling research 
initiatives, refining governance mechanisms, and deepening academia-industry synergies,

BRIC can position India as a global leader in biotechnology and biomanufacturing, fostering 
equitable and sustainable advancements in healthcare, agriculture, and environmental

4.7 The Department has following Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs): 
1.  The Biotechnology Industry Research Assistance Council (BIRAC) serves as a key 
industry-academia interface promoting public-private partnerships in biotech. It fosters 
innovation among startups and SMEs, supporting over 4,000 beneficiaries with ₹ 4,000 crore in 
direct funding and ₹ 2,600 crore through co-funding partnerships. With a growing national and 
international network, BIRAC has established 90+ biotech incubators spanning 9 lakh sq. ft., 
offering advanced infrastructure, mentorship, and business support. This has led to 1,300+ IP 
filings and the launch of 800+ biotech products. Today, BIRAC's ecosystem includes 9,000+ 
startups, 800+ biotech firms, and a vast network of entrepreneurs and experts driving 
innovation. 
2. Bharat Immunologicals and Biologicals Corporation Limited (BIBCOL) was incorporated in 
March 1989 as a public sector company in Bulandshahr, Uttar Pradesh to manufacture Oral 
Polio Vaccine (OPV) and other Immunologicals. In addition, BIBCOL has manufacturing 
facility of dispersible Zinc Tablet in pharmaceutical segment. BIBCOL is currently under 
financial crises, which leads to cessation of the production activities. The main reason for 
financial crisis in the company is single product i.e. Polio Vaccine for production and market 
competition with private companies. The proposal of revival package of BIBCOL is under 
consideration with the Department of Public Enterprises (DPE). The resumption of vaccine 
production is subject to the outcome of final decision of the said proposal. 
3. Indian Vaccines Corporation Limited (IVCOL) was incorporated in 1989 as a Joint Venture 
Company promoted by the Government of India (Department of Biotechnology), Pasteur 
Meraux Serum & Vaccines (PMSV) France and Indian Petrochemicals Corporation Ltd. (IPCL, 
now part of Reliance Industries Limited since 2007). With a paid-up capital of ₹ 18.78 crores, 
IVCOL aimed to manufacture (i) vaccines using Vero Cell technology and (ii) Injectable Polio 
Vaccines (IPV). However IPV did not get approvals from the World Health Organisation 
(WHO). As a result the Project of the IVCOL was put on hold in 1992. Following this setback, 
PMSV France exited the joint venture in 1998 by selling its shares to DBT. Subsequently, in 
1999, 46.20 acres of IVCOL’s land was leased for 30 years to the National Brain Research 
Centre (NBRC), an autonomous institution under DBT, at a nominal annual rent of ₹ 11.91 
lakhs. Presently, IVCOL has no commercial operations and is maintained by DBT from its 
CGO Complex office, ensuring site upkeep and compliance with statutory obligations under the 
Companies Act, 2013 
 
4.8 The Committee expresses deep concern over the current state of BIBCOL and IVCOL 
and urges the Department to take immediate and decisive action for their revival. 
Recognizing their immense potential, the Committee strongly believes that both PSUs can 
play a pivotal role in strengthening and transforming India’s vaccine manufacturing 
ecosystem. The Committee recommends that the Department proactively engage with the 
Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) and persuade them to secure a revival package for 
both BIBCOL and IVCOL. The Department could explore the possibility of merger of both 
the units to achieve efficiency. If the Department succeeds in securing the revival package 
from DPE, the Committee recommends that the Department should expand BIBCOL’s 
current product portfolio by initiating the production of critical vaccines. Additionally, the 
Department should actively seek technical collaborations with reputed international 
organizations to enhance manufacturing capabilities and technological expertise. The 
Committee acknowledges the Department’s ongoing efforts in developing vaccines for 
Dengue, Malaria, and Chikungunya and suggests that, upon receiving necessary regulatory 
approvals, these vaccines may be manufactured at BIBCOL and IVCOL. Reviving these 

12 
 
PSUs would not only contribute to ensuring affordable vaccine availability for citizens but 
also position them as key players in the global vaccine market. Once operational, these PSUs 
can leverage their infrastructure to support vaccine exports, further strengthening India’s 
presence in the international biopharmaceutical industry. 
5.  KEY INITIAVES AND ACHIEVEMENTS IN HEALTHCARE AND 
BIOTECHNOLOGY 
5.1 The Department of Biotechnology actively drives biomedical research and innovation to 
address human diseases, including emerging infections, antimicrobial resistance, non-
communicable diseases, genetic disorders, maternal and child health, and nutrition. Its efforts focus 
on early detection, prevention, vaccine development, novel therapies, healthcare systems, and 
biomedical devices. DBT has supported diverse R&D projects spanning bioengineering, cancer 
research, chronic diseases, drug development, human genetics, infectious diseases, public health & 
nutrition, stem cells & regenerative medicine, development of vaccines, women & child health, and 
genome editing & nanotechnology applications in healthcare. Its initiatives encompass mission-
driven programs and strategic interventions. 
5.2 The Department addresses key challenges through targeted initiatives, such as the UMMID 
Initiative, which focuses on inherited disorders. These efforts collectively enhance India's 
biomedical landscape, fostering cutting-edge research and healthcare solutions. Some of the 
significant achievements of the research and development supported during the period are: 
Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR) 
5.3 Considering Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR) as global threat, the Department initiated a 
“Mission program on Antimicrobial Resistance” with the vision to develop indigenous and cost-
effective therapies against AMR, categorization of AMR-specific pathogen priority list of India, 
establishment of Bio-repository for AMR-specific pathogens and development of rapid and cost-
effective diagnostic kits to identify AMR-specific pathogens. 
5.4 The Department announced a joint call with BIRAC in 2018 on AMR. This program aimed 
at tackling AMR under two specific categories: development of new antibiotics and development of 
alternatives to antibiotics which includes therapeutic antibodies, phage therapy, and anti-biofilm 
products. One successful example of this initiative is the development of antibiotic Nafithromycin. 
It is the country's first indigenously developed antibiotic aimed at tackling AMR. This innovation is 
designed to treat Community-Acquired Bacterial Pneumonia (CABP), a severe illness caused by 
Multi-Drug Resistant pathogens, which disproportionately affects vulnerable populations, including 
children and the elderly as well as immune compromised hosts like patients with diabetes, cancer 
etc. 
5.5 The Committee applauds the Department for its strategic foresight and decisive action 
in confronting AMR. Initiatives such as pioneering homegrown therapies, cataloguing 
priority pathogens, establishing AMR bio-repositories, and advancing rapid diagnostics 
underscore India’s resolve to mitigate this global health crisis. The Committee recognizes the 
breakthroughs like Nafithromycin — India’s inaugural indigenous antibiotic targeting drug-
resistant Community-Acquired Bacterial Pneumonia. This innovation exemplifies scientific 
excellence and addresses critical vulnerabilities among high-risk groups. The Committee 
emphasizes the need to expedite the deployment of such solutions through streamlined 
regulatory processes, scalable production, and inclusive partnerships. Strengthening AMR 
monitoring frameworks, broadening investigations into pathogen prioritization and 
integrating diagnostics into primary healthcare are vital next steps. 
 

13 
 
Development of Vaccines 
5.6 The National Biopharma Mission (NBM) being implemented by BIRAC, has supported the 
pre-clinical and clinical development of vaccines for Dengue & Chikungunya and also 
Translational Research Consortiums for vector borne diseases like Chikungunya, Dengue and 
Malaria. The details are as under: 
a) Indian Immunologicals Limited (IIL) has developed a freeze-dried, live-attenuated 
tetravalent dengue vaccine using four attenuated dengue virus strains (serotypes 1, 2, 3, and 4) 
provided by the National Institutes of Health (NIH), USA, under a 2016 agreement. Stability 
studies of the drug substance and product have shown stability under real-time conditions over a 
36-month period. NBM has supported the Pre Clinical Toxicology (PCT) studies and Phase I 
clinical trial for this vaccine. IIL has successfully completed the Phase I trial, which 
demonstrated the vaccine's safety for human use.  
b) The inactivated Chikungunya vaccine candidate BBV87, developed by Bharat Biotech, has 
demonstrated safety, tolerability, and immunogenicity. NBM has supported Phase II clinical 
trials for BBV87 in India. NBM is also funding Phase III trials, which have already received 
clinical protocol approval from the Drugs Controller General of India (DCGI). BBV87 has 
shown consistent safety and immunogenicity in India and internationally, with Phase II trials 
successfully conducted in Thailand and several Latin American countries, including Panama, 
Colombia, Guatemala, and Costa Rica, through collaboration with the International Vaccine 
Institute.  
c) Translational Research Consortiums (TRC) on Vector Borne Diseases has supported 
development of high throughput assays, animal models, biorepositories for clinical isolates & 
development of monoclonal antibodies. Malaria TRC project aims to develop multi-stage P. 
falciparum recombinant chimeric malaria antigens (rCMAs) consisting of leading pre-
erythrocytic and transmission blocking vaccine candidates, as novel malaria vaccines for 
preventing infection in man & minimizing community transmission.  
d) As part of the Ind-CEPI (India-Centric Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations) 
project, support has been provided for development of inactivated viral vaccine for 
Chikungunya (BBV87), whereby, GMP manufacturing of the vaccine in India and subsequent 
manufacture of clinical trial material for conducting Phase I/II clinical trial has been supported. 
The vaccine is presently in Phase II/III clinical trials. 
e) A low-cost Rotavirus vaccine (Rotavac) was indigenously developed and incorporated into 
the Universal Immunization Program (UIP), and India's first indigenously developed qHPV 
vaccine against cervical cancer (Cervavac) was granted market authorization. 
5.7 The Committee commends the Department for its laudable efforts under the National 
Biopharma Mission (NBM) in advancing indigenous vaccine development against critical 
diseases such as Dengue, Chikungunya, Malaria, and cervical cancer. The noteworthy 
progress in pre-clinical studies, clinical trials, and translational research, alongside strategic 
international collaborations, underscores India’s growing capacity to address global health 
challenges through innovation. 
5.8 The Committee urges the Department to expedite regulatory clearances, ensure robust 
post-trial protocols, and prioritize cost-effective manufacturing to facilitate the swift market 
entry of these vaccines. Emphasis must be placed on equitable access and affordability for all 
citizens, particularly vulnerable populations. The Committee expresses confidence that the 
timely deployment of these vaccines will significantly reduce disease burden, align with 
national health objectives, and reinforce India’s leadership in global vaccine equity.
