Unique Methods of Management of Inherited Disorders (UMMID) Initiative 
 
5.9 The Unique Methods of Management of Inherited Disorders (UMMID) Initiative was 
launched by the Department to tackle the challenges posed by genetic disorders in the country. It 
has three components: (i) NIDAN Kendras (setting up genetic diagnosis centres in Government 
hospitals); (ii) enhancing the skills of Government doctors; and (iii) outreach to aspirational districts 
for ante-natal and newborn screening and education about genetic pathways for rare disorders. The 
programme's focus is on improving maternal and neo-natal indicators in aspirational districts. The 
programme primarily focuses on promoting research and development and laying the groundwork 
for the anticipated ‘National Screening Programme’. The screening program primarily assesses 
pregnant women for hemoglobinopathies such as thalassemia, sickle cell disease, etc. and newborns 
for five key genetic disorders that require early intervention.  
5.10 In the first pilot phase, 5 NIDAN Kendras, 7 outreach centers, and 6 training centres were 
established. Over the past year, these active NIDAN Kendras and the outreach centers have offered 
screening to over 85,000 pregnant women and 25,000 newborn babies across five centers and nine 
aspirational districts. A total of more than 2,73,000 screenings of pregnant women and newborns 
were carried out in 1st phase wherein nearly 37000 positive cases were reported.  This has led to 
prevention of more than 34 hemoglobinopathy affected births, identification of more than 150 
carrier couples and more than 350 newborns received timely diagnosis of congenital metabolic 
disorders. During the last year, more than 20 faculty members from across the country have 
received training. NIDAN Kendras routinely conducts mass awareness programs about the 
prevention, screening, and management of inherited disorders at various levels, including 
workshops, lectures, and distribution of pamphlets in high schools, nursing colleges, and primary 
health centers, as well as the display of public hoardings.  
 
5.11 UMMID is presently undergoing nationwide expansion, aiming to encompass 
approximately 22 States/UTs by establishing around 70 UMMID components. Currently, 30 
aspirational districts have been covered and 30 NIDAN Kendras and 9 training centers have been 
established all over the country. The genetic disorders being covered in the NIDAN Kendra 
Component includes Beta thalassemia, sickle cell disease, and other hemoglobinopathies, Down 
syndrome and other aneuploidies, congenital malformations such as neural tube defects and other 
genetic disorders prevalent at a relatively higher rate in the region where the proposed NIDAN 
Kendra would be situated. Newborn screening for relatively common treatable genetic metabolic 
disorders including congenital hypothyroidism, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, galactosemia, 
biotinidase deficiency, G6PD deficiency, other treatable genetic metabolic disorders prevalent at a 
relatively higher rate in the region.  In phase-II expansion of the UMMID initiative some of the 
private hospitals like Sri Venkateswara Institute of Medical Sciences (SVIMS) Tirupati, Mahatma 
Gandhi Institute of Medical Science, Sevagram have been granted the NIDAN Kendras and training 
center has been established at Center for Human Genetics, Bengaluru.  
 
5.12 The Committee enquired whether the Department has initiated any research to determine the 
vulnerability of the population to genetic disorders and create a vulnerability index. The 
Department informed the Committee that UMMID is a pilot study for development of trained 
manpower, resources and to establish network in Government setup. However, the vulnerability of 
the population to genetic disorders and creation of vulnerability index can be taken up only when 
pan India study is carried out during the next level implementation in terms of setting up of a 
‘National Screening Programme’ for genetic disorders. 
5.13 The Committee extends its profound appreciation to the Department for the visionary 
launch and strategic implementation of the UMMID Initiative, a critical intervention to 
address the burden of genetic disorders in India. The initiative’s three-pronged approach —

15 
 
establishing NIDAN Kendras for genetic diagnosis, enhancing the capacity of healthcare 
professionals, and expanding outreach in aspirational districts — has demonstrated 
remarkable success in its pilot phase. The screening of over 2,73,000 pregnant women and 
newborns, identification of 37,000 positive cases, prevention of 34 hemoglobinopathy-affected 
births, and timely diagnosis of 350 newborns with congenital metabolic disorders underscore 
the programme’s transformative impact on maternal and neonatal health. Furthermore, the 
integration of mass awareness campaigns, skill-building workshops, and collaborations with 
educational institutions reflects a holistic model for tackling inherited disorders through 
prevention, early diagnosis, and community engagement. 
5.14 The Committee acknowledges the Department’s progress in scaling the UMMID 
Initiative, including its expansion to 30 aspirational districts, establishment of 30 NIDAN 
Kendras and 9 training centres, and the inclusion of private healthcare institutions such 
as SVIMS Tirupati and Mahatma Gandhi Institute of Medical Sciences, Sevagram, in Phase-
II. These efforts signify a commendable stride toward decentralizing access to advanced 
genetic screening and care. However, given the persistent challenges posed by genetic 
disorders—particularly in rural and underserved regions — the Committee urges the 
Department to expedite the pan-India expansion of the UMMID Initiative with a renewed 
focus on universal, time-bound screening coverage. This must include 100% screening of all 
pregnant women and newborns, irrespective of their access to private or Government 
healthcare facilities. The Committee also recommends that following the 100% screening, the 
Department should work upon creating a vulnerability index which would be helpful in 
assessing the susceptibility of specific demographic groups to various genetic disorders. 
Development of Biomedical equipments 
5.15 The Department promotes multi-disciplinary research involving application of science and 
engineering for development of innovative technologies and products leading to affordable 
healthcare. Major focus areas can be categorized as follows: a) Diagnostics - Bio sensors, in-vitro 
diagnostics, medical imaging, home care, wearables, etc. b) Therapeutics - Drug delivery vehicles, 
implants, tissue engineering, surgical robotics. c) Assistive technologies - Mobility aids, prosthesis, 
patient rehabilitation systems. Around 80% of the needs for medical devices are met through 
imports. Thus, the division is focused to support indigenization of biomedical devices and 
resources. The Department has established a Centre of Excellence for Minimally Invasive 
Cardiovascular Devices at Sree Chitra Tirunal Institute for Medical Sciences & Technology, 
Thiruvananthapuram. Some of the novels products developed / licensed under the Biodesign 
program are: 
a) InoHeal - Advanced Wound Healing Technology to facilitate accelerated healing of 
medically complex wounds like diabetic foot ulcers, pressure sores and infectious wounds 
etc. It overcomes the challenges of halted wound healing by removing exudate, reducing 
inflammation and oedema, enhancing cell proliferation and tissue perfusion and controlling 
microbial growth. 
b) Hip Pro - It is an elderly guardian smartbelt. It provides instant protection by automatic 
inflation of slim cushions with a simple press of a button. This ensures that the hips are 
cushioned before impact, reducing the risk of injury from falls. 
c) Urovib - A Catheter Associated Urinary Tract Infection (CAUTI) prevention device. It 
consists of two components: a reusable clip-on and a disposable coupler and works on dual 
synergistic mechanism. 
d) Preztic - Precision Needle Navigation System for the Ultrasound Machines. It is a small 
device that clips onto an existing ultrasound probe, keeping the needle constrained in the 
ultrasound plane and physically restricting it in the desired trajectory during insertion. 
Additionally, a camera in the device tracks the needle during the procedure. A computer 
vision algorithm computes the needle's position by tracking markers on the device. A 

16 
 
display tablet shows the real-time position of the needle tip and trajectory overlaid on the 
live ultrasound feed received from the ultrasound machine. 
5.16 The Committee commends the Department for its exemplary commitment to 
advancing multi-disciplinary research and innovation in the domain of biomedical science 
and engineering. The development of pioneering technologies such as InoHeal, Hip 
Pro, Urovib, and Preztic reflects a laudable effort to address pressing healthcare challenges 
through indigenous solutions. However, the Committee notes with concern that a major 
chunk of India’s medical device requirements continue to be met through imports, exposing 
vulnerabilities in healthcare security and economic sustainability. To address this critical gap, 
the Committee strongly urges the Department to intensify its focus on cutting-edge research 
and development in high-priority domains where import dependency remains acute. Priority 
areas could include the indigenous design and manufacturing of advanced imaging systems, 
such as CT scan machines and MRI systems, which are indispensable for modern diagnostics 
yet predominantly sourced from foreign markets. Similarly, the development of ophthalmic 
devices, including intraocular lenses for cataract surgery and retinal imaging equipment, 
must be prioritized to address the growing burden of vision-related ailments and reduce 
reliance on external suppliers. 
5.17 Furthermore, the Committee emphasizes the need for innovation in critical care 
equipment, such as ventilators, dialysis machines, and radiation therapy systems, which are 
vital for tertiary healthcare but remain largely imported despite rising domestic demand. 
Integrating emerging technologies like artificial intelligence and machine learning with 
medical diagnostics could further enhance precision, efficiency, and scalability, positioning 
India as a global leader in next-generation healthcare solutions. 
Mission Program on Pediatric Rare Genetic Disorders 
 
5.18 The Department has implemented a Mission Program on Pediatric Rare Genetic Disorders 
(PRaGeD) in 2022 for research and development in areas of Human Genetics. It aims to develop 
methods for diagnosis of difficult-to-diagnose pediatric rare genetic diseases, discover and 
characterize new gene/variants, provide counseling and to develop new therapies for pediatric rare 
genetic diseases in India. The Center for DNA fingerprinting & Diagnostics (CDFD) at Hyderabad, 
in collaboration with 15 centres across the country, aims to recruit patients and their families with 
rare genetic disorders for the study. The outcome of this study will not only provide a unique 
opportunity for the identification of novel genes for various known as well as unexplained inherited 
phenotypes but also help the patient and family with the management of disease and prenatal 
diagnosis. In addition, functional characterization of novel genes/variants using different metazoan 
model systems is likely to establish causality between the novel mutation and the phenotype. A 
database of sequence variants corresponding to phenotypes in Indian pediatric patients will serve as 
an invaluable resource for genetic diagnostics labs, clinicians and researchers across the globe. 
5.19 The Committee appreciates the mission program launched by the Department. It is a 
remarkable effort to address rare genetic disorders in children, combining research, 
diagnosis, and care. The program’s focus on identifying novel genes, improving diagnosis, 
enabling prenatal counselling, and developing targeted therapies reflects a transformative 
approach to addressing unmet medical needs. The creation of a pan-Indian database of 
genetic variants promises to empower clinicians and researchers globally while advancing 
precision medicine tailored to India’s diverse population. The Committee expresses 
confidence that PRaGeD will catalyze breakthroughs in understanding and managing rare 
diseases, reducing suffering through early intervention and innovative therapies. Sustained 
funding, capacity-building, and integration of research into clinical practice are critical to its 
success. The Department is urged to strengthen global partnerships, ensure ethical data-
sharing frameworks, and prioritize accessibility of outcomes for vulnerable families.

Research on Neurological Disorders: 
 
5.20 To enhance our understanding and improve outcomes for the neurological disorders, 
Dementia and Stroke, the Department is supporting cohort-based studies. The program also 
supports research and development initiatives that investigate the intricate structure, function, 
behavior, cognition, and development of the nervous system. 
5.21 The Department is supporting research on different neurological diseases including 
Parkinson’s, Alzheimer’s and Ataxia. Most of the ongoing research efforts are investigator driven 
research projects that have been supported under the Competitive Grant system. These include: 
a) Investigations into the impact of sleep deprivation on memory deficits through analysis of 
protein synthesis, and its implications in case of Alzheimer’s disease. 
b) Investigations into the effect of specific genetic variations on brain cells and their 
interactions in order to understand their implications for Parkinson’s disease. 
c) Investigations to get mechanistic insights into the biology of Spinocerebellar Ataxia. 
d) Investigations for finding a potential biomarker for detecting Parkinson`s disease using 
“Protein Misfolding Cyclic Amplification” technique. 
e) Design and development of cost-effective label-free detection of Alzheimer’s biomarkers 
using liquid crystals. 
5.22 The Committee appreciates the commendable efforts made by the Department in 
advancing research on neurological disorders, particularly through cohort-based studies and 
investigator driven projects. These initiatives are crucial in deepening our understanding of 
disease mechanisms and developing innovative diagnostic and therapeutic solutions.  
5.23 Keeping in view the rising prevalence of neurological disorders, particularly among 
the aging population, the Committee recommends that the Department should launch a 
dedicated mission to comprehensively research the most prevalent neurological diseases. This 
mission should be supported by substantial funding, targeted research programs, and 
strategic collaborations with leading healthcare institutions, academic centres, and industry 
partners to ensure a holistic approach to prevention, early diagnosis, and treatment.

6.3 The Committee sought details of the last recruitment exercise by the Department and it was

6.4 The Department informed the Committee that manpower shortage has increased work 
pressure on existing employees and causes unnecessary delays. To overcome this, Department has 
been hiring workforce on contractual basis, requesting cadre controlling authorities (DST and 
DoPT) for filling up the vacant posts, and removing the bottlenecks in hiring/recruitment process 
for the posts for which DBT is the cadre controlling authority. 
6.5 The Committee also sought details of the staff hired on contractual basis. The Department 
apprised the Committee that the Department currently employs nine Young Professionals and five 
Consultants on a contractual basis. This strategic hiring approach addresses workforce shortages 
and supports the efficient execution of departmental responsibilities. To bridge the staffing gap, 
retired Government employees are engaged as Consultants, leveraging their expertise for key 
advisory roles. Meanwhile, Young Professionals have been recruited to contribute to the Global 
Innovation and other Scientific Directorates in DBT, ensuring high-quality execution of scientific 
initiatives. In addition to these, the Department has also hired 31 Data Entry Operators, 6 Office 
Assistants, 18 Office Helpers, and 9 IT Specialists. The engagement of contractual office staff is 
essential to maintain operational efficiency in the absence of regular positions. IT specialists are 
recruited for their technical expertise, supporting the implementation and maintenance of 
application software and web portals, which are critical for the Department’s digital infrastructure. 
6.6 The Department informed the Committee that that a critical shortage of personnel across its 
network of autonomous institutions has severely hampered their ability to conduct routine 
operations and sustain scientific research initiatives. Persistent vacancies in key roles—spanning 
administrative, technical, and specialized scientific positions—have led to operational delays, 
diminished productivity, and a decline in the quality and output of research projects.  
6.7 The Committee expresses its deep concern over the acute staffing gaps plaguing the 
Department and autonomous institutions under it, condemning the systemic over-reliance on 
temporary contractual hiring to mask chronic manpower deficits. It underscores that such 
short-term stopgap measures erode institutional capacity, stressing that a robust, permanent 
workforce with specialized expertise is indispensable for driving scientific advancement and 
maintaining global competitiveness. To rectify this, the Committee urgently calls for the 
Department to prioritize filling all critical positions — scientific, technical, and administrative 
— through a mission-driven recruitment strategy.

COMPARATIVE BUDGET ANALYSIS 
 
 The Committee expresses deep concern over the sub-optimal utilization of funds by the 
Department, particularly in the context of the Central Sector Scheme, Bio-RIDE. This 
underutilization not only hampers the effective implementation of critical programs but also 
undermines the potential impact of the Department’s initiatives. The Committee strongly 
recommends that the Department take immediate and appropriate measures to address this 
issue and ensure the optimal utilization of funds allocated to it in the Budget Estimates (B.E.) 
for 2025-26. The Department should conduct regular reviews and take corrective actions to 
prevent delays and inefficiencies, thereby maximizing the impact of its programs and 
achieving the desired outcomes in a timely and effective manner.                              (Para 2.11)  
 
 Given the substantial allocation to Bio-RIDE, the Committee recommends that the 
Department must ensure optimal utilization of funds. Regular monitoring, timely 
implementation, and transparent reporting mechanisms should be established to avoid sub-
optimal utilization and maximize outcomes.                                                               (Para 2.15)

and urges the Department to take immediate and decisive action for their revival. 
Recognizing their immense potential, the Committee strongly believes that both PSUs can 
play a pivotal role in strengthening and transforming India’s vaccine manufacturing 
ecosystem. The Committee recommends that the Department proactively engage with the 
Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) and persuade them to secure a revival package for 
both BIBCOL and IVCOL. The Department could explore the possibility of merger of both 
the units to achieve efficiency. If the Department succeeds in securing the revival package 
from DPE, the Committee recommends that the Department should expand BIBCOL’s 
current product portfolio by initiating the production of critical vaccines. Additionally, the 
Department should actively seek technical collaborations with reputed international 
organizations to enhance manufacturing capabilities and technological expertise. The 
Committee acknowledges the Department’s ongoing efforts in developing vaccines for 
Dengue, Malaria, and Chikungunya and suggests that, upon receiving necessary regulatory 
approvals, these vaccines may be manufactured at BIBCOL and IVCOL. Reviving these 
PSUs would not only contribute to ensuring affordable vaccine availability for citizens but 
also position them as key players in the global vaccine market. Once operational, these PSUs 
can leverage their infrastructure to support vaccine exports, further strengthening India’s 
presence in the international biopharmaceutical industry.                                           (Para 4.8)

 The Committee commends the Department for its exemplary commitment to 
advancing multi-disciplinary research and innovation in the domain of biomedical science 
and engineering. The development of pioneering technologies such as InoHeal, Hip 
Pro, Urovib, and Preztic reflects a laudable effort to address pressing healthcare challenges 
through indigenous solutions. However, the Committee notes with concern that a major 
chunk of India’s medical device requirements continue to be met through imports, exposing 
vulnerabilities in healthcare security and economic sustainability. To address this critical gap, 
the Committee strongly urges the Department to intensify its focus on cutting-edge research 
and development in high-priority domains where import dependency remains acute. Priority 
areas could include the indigenous design and manufacturing of advanced imaging systems, 
such as CT scan machines and MRI systems, which are indispensable for modern diagnostics 
yet predominantly sourced from foreign markets. Similarly, the development of ophthalmic 
devices, including intraocular lenses for cataract surgery and retinal imaging equipment, 
must be prioritized to address the growing burden of vision-related ailments and reduce 
reliance on external suppliers.                                                                                        (Para 5.16)   
 Furthermore, the Committee emphasizes the need for innovation in critical care 
equipment, such as ventilators, dialysis machines, and radiation therapy systems, which are 
vital for tertiary healthcare but remain largely imported despite rising domestic demand. 
Integrating emerging technologies like artificial intelligence and machine learning with 
medical diagnostics could further enhance precision, efficiency, and scalability, positioning 
India as a global leader in next-generation healthcare solutions.                                (Para 5.17)   

23 
 
The Committee appreciates the mission program launched by the Department. It is a 
remarkable effort to address rare genetic disorders in children, combining research, 
diagnosis, and care. The program’s focus on identifying novel genes, improving diagnosis, 
enabling prenatal counselling, and developing targeted therapies reflects a transformative 
approach to addressing unmet medical needs. The creation of a pan-Indian database of 
genetic variants promises to empower clinicians and researchers globally while advancing 
precision medicine tailored to India’s diverse population. The Committee expresses 
confidence that PRaGeD will catalyze breakthroughs in understanding and managing rare 
diseases, reducing suffering through early intervention and innovative therapies. Sustained 
funding, capacity-building, and integration of research into clinical practice are critical to its 
success. The Department is urged to strengthen global partnerships, ensure ethical data-
sharing frameworks, and prioritize accessibility of outcomes for vulnerable families.  
(Para 5.19)   
 The Committee appreciates the commendable efforts made by the Department in 
advancing research on neurological disorders, particularly through cohort-based studies and 
investigator driven projects. These initiatives are crucial in deepening our understanding of 
disease mechanisms and developing innovative diagnostic and therapeutic solutions. 
 (Para 5.22)   
 Keeping in view the rising prevalence of neurological disorders, particularly among 
the aging population, the Committee recommends that the Department should launch a 
dedicated mission to comprehensively research the most prevalent neurological diseases. This 
mission should be supported by substantial funding, targeted research programs, and 
strategic collaborations with leading healthcare institutions, academic centres, and industry 
partners to ensure a holistic approach to prevention, early diagnosis, and treatment. 
(Para 5.23) 
HUMAN RESOURCE CHALLENGES 
 The Committee expresses its deep concern over the acute staffing gaps plaguing the 
Department and autonomous institutions under it, condemning the systemic over-reliance on 
temporary contractual hiring to mask chronic manpower deficits. It underscores that such 
short-term stopgap measures erode institutional capacity, stressing that a robust, permanent 
workforce with specialized expertise is indispensable for driving scientific advancement and 
maintaining global competitiveness. To rectify this, the Committee urgently calls for the 
Department to prioritize filling all critical positions — scientific, technical, and administrative 
— through a mission-driven recruitment strategy.                                                        (Para 6.7)

1.  INTRODUCTION 
1.1 The Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (DSIR) is one of the three 
Departments of the Ministry of Science and Technology. It was established in 1985, for the 
promotion of industrial research through indigenous technology promotion, development, 
utilization and transfer. The Department is entrusted with the following allocation of business:-  
(i) All matters concerning the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR). 
(ii) All matters relating to National Research Development Corporation (NRDC). 
(iii) All matters relating to Central Electronics Limited (CEL). 
(iv) Registration and Recognition of R&D Units. 
(v) Matters relating to UNCTAD and WIPO. 
(vi) National Register for Foreign Collaborations. 
(vii) Matters relating to creation of pool for temporary placement of Indian Scientists and 
Technologists. 
1.2. DSIR plays an instrumental role in accelerating the development of cutting-edge 
technologies by encouraging industries to significantly increase their investment in research and 
development. By facilitating the swift commercialization of laboratory innovations, DSIR 
effectively bridges the divide between scientific discovery and practical, real-world applications, 
ensuring that India remains at the forefront of technological progress. 
1.3. DSIR also functions through its attached autonomous institution, Council for Scientific and 
Industrial Research (CSIR) and the two public sector undertakings, National Research Development 
Corporation (NRDC) and Central Electronics Limited (CEL) to facilitate scientific and industrial 
research in the country. It also provides institutional host facilities to Asian & Pacific Centre for 
Transfer of Technology (APCTT). 
1.4. The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology, 
Environment, Forests and Climate Change considered the Demands for Grants (2025-26) of the 
Department of Scientific and Industrial Research in its meeting held on 20th February, 2025.

ensure the optimal deployment of resources within the remaining timeframe of the financial 
year. To preempt such inefficiencies in subsequent years, the Committee strongly advocates

lesser than its budgetary demand. Thus, here is an overall shortfall of ₹ 625.46 crore in the actual 
allocation to the Department. 
2.5 In response to a query about the likely impact of this shortfall in actual allocation over the 
proposed budget and the strategy of the Department for dealing with the challenges arising thereof,

potentially affect financial planning and participative performance of R&D projects in

2.8 During the meeting, the Department informed the Committee that in 2024-25, 62% of the 
allocated funds were spent on pensions and salaries, leaving only 38% for R&D and infrastructure. 
Within this, 7% supports capacity-building initiatives such as Junior Research Fellowships (JRF),

industry-ready technologies, repayable facility creation projects, and prioritized equipment 
upgrades. Despite these efforts, a funding shortfall persists, exacerbated by ageing infrastructure 
across CSIR’s 70 year old laboratories, necessitating urgent investments in R&D blocks, staff 
quarters, guest houses, and renovation of Director’s residences. The Department also informed that

be ₹600 crore to fully address the infrastructure gaps, support pilot plants for proof-of-concept

3.14 CEL is another PSE under the administrative control of the DSIR. It was established in 1974 
with an objective to commercially exploit the indigenous technologies developed by National 

10 
 
Laboratories and R&D Institutions in the country. It is carrying out commercial production as well 
as R&D in four fields: (i) Solar Photovoltaics (SPV) (ii) Railways Electronics (iii) Strategic 
Electronics (iv) Security & Surveillance Systems. It is the pioneer and leading manufacturer of SPV 
cells, modules and systems and Railway Safety Signaling Equipment. In the field of strategic 
electronics, it is the only indigenous manufacturer of phase control modules, which is a key element 
of phased array radar. 
 
3.15  The Committee enquired about the current product portfolio of CEL. The Department 
informed that CEL specializes in end-to-end manufacturing of technical ceramics, particularly 
ferrite-based components such as Phase Control Modules (PCMs), which are integral to defence 
systems like the Swathi Weapon Locating Radar and Troop Level Radar, with cumulative supplies 
exceeding ₹850 crore over 15 years. The company’s expertise extends to advanced defence 
applications, including the production of ceramic radar domes (radomes) for missile systems, which 
are placed on missile nose to primarily protect underlying electronics while maintaining technical 
requirement of the whole system. CEL further distinguishes itself through the indigenous 
development of critical import substitutes such as isolators, circulators, and Piezo Ceramics (PZT) 
for ammunition and civil applications, alongside strategic materials like Cadmium Zinc Telluride 
(CZT) substrates for advanced imaging systems in collaboration with DRDO. 
3.16 In the railway sector, CEL competes with private entities in manufacturing and upgrading 
digital axle counter systems, having supplied over 12,700 Single Section Digital Axle Counters 
(SSDAC), 6,100 High Availability SSDACs, and 10,700 detection points for Multi-Section Digital 
Axle Counters (MSDAC) since 2002. The company’s collaboration with Indian Railways includes 
the development of a Broken Rail Detection System for Delhi Metro, with potential for nationwide 
deployment. Concurrently, CEL has expanded its footprint in IT and smart infrastructure, delivering 
Integrated Security Solutions, IoT based systems for power and water management, and Blockchain 
driven recruitment automation platforms implemented in institutions such as AIIMS Delhi, UP 
Police Recruitment Board, and Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (DMRC). Notably, CEL has 
operationalized Smart Classrooms in 709 schools in Uttarakhand and established a production line 
for 65 and 75 inches Smart Boards, positioning itself as the sole PSU in this domain. Additionally, 
CEL’s legacy in renewable energy is marked by its pioneering role in developing country’s first 
solar cells and modules. The company continues to support the renewable sector through 
Engineering, Procurement, and Construction (EPC) services for solar projects, Project Management 
Consultancy, and maintenance of existing installations. 
3.17  The Committee also sought details of CEL's plans for technology development and 
innovation to maintain its competitiveness in the market. The Department informed that CEL has 
outlined a strategic roadmap for technology development and innovation to sustain its market 
competitiveness, anchored in proactive adaptation to emerging trends and collaborative 
partnerships. Recognizing the risk of technological obsolescence, particularly in defence 
applications, CEL is transitioning from legacy systems such as Passive Electronically Scanned 
Array (PESA) to advanced solutions like Active Electronically Scanned Array (AESA). This 
includes collaboration with a defence PSU to develop Transmit-Receive modules for AESA, which 
will replace the existing Phase Control Modules (PCMs) in phased manner, ensuring alignment 
with next-generation radar systems. To bolster innovation, CEL is strengthening ties with academic 
institutions and research organisations for technology transfers and joint development initiatives, 
particularly in defence and railway sectors. This collaborative framework supports the indigenous 
upgradation of existing products and the creation of new solutions tailored to dynamic market 
demands. In the IT domain, CEL is enhancing its Integrated Security and Surveillance Solutions 
through AI driven advancements, such as facial recognition, behaviour analysis, and real-time threat 
detection systems for smart cities, critical infrastructure, and corporate security. Concurrently, the 
company is expanding IoT-based security applications for power plants, transport hubs, and 
government facilities, alongside modernising CCTV technologies with higher resolution, cloud-

11 
 
based monitoring, and encrypted data protocols. Further, CEL is scaling its Smart Education 
portfolio by integrating AI-powered learning analytics into its smart board manufacturing line, 
enabling interactive and customized digital classrooms for educational institutions and corporate 
training programmes. The company is also prioritising e-learning platform development to broaden 
access to advanced educational tools.  
3.18 The Committee enquired regarding major challenges being faced by CEL and strategies 
being implemented to address these challenges. The Committee was informed that CEL had the 
mandate to commercialize technologies developed in the national laboratories. However, absence of 
any corresponding provision in the relevant guidelines/rules/provisions pertaining to those national 
laboratories creates an anomalous situation putting CEL in a disadvantageous situation. In the field 
of renewable energy, CEL despite being a promising initial player in the field of solar 
photovoltaics, has suffered huge losses to the tune of ₹ 280 crore cumulative in the last 10-11 years. 
Technological advancement in the area coupled with cheaper import products has dented the 
profitability and adversely affected the returns from the sector. While CEL’s defence, railway, and 
IT/security verticals remain profitable, these face risks of technological obsolescence, slow growth, 
and rising costs, exacerbated by competition from private and multinational entities. Despite 50 
years of operation, CEL’s turnover remains modest (₹150–340 crore), necessitating urgent strategic 
recalibration to avoid stagnation.  
 
3.19 To mitigate these challenges, CEL is pursuing a multipronged strategy. This includes 
deepening collaborations with national laboratories (CSIR, DRDO), defence PSUs (BEL, HAL), 
and State Governments to align with market needs and access emerging technologies. The company 
is diversifying its portfolio, leveraging its recent Mini Ratna status to expand into new domains 
such as AI driven surveillance systems, IoT based infrastructure solutions, and smart education 
technologies, including scalable smart board manufacturing with potential applications in IT 
hardware. Strategic partnerships with academia and industry aim to counter obsolescence through 
joint R&D and process modernization. CEL is transitioning from component manufacturing to 
subsystem and system-level supply to enhance revenue, while exploring Public Private Partnerships 
(PPP) for ventures like Tier III data centers. A proposed subsidiary is under consideration to 
streamline CSR activities, fostering community engagement in health, education, and skill 
development. Additionally, plans for public listing of shares, pending approvals, aim to raise capital 
for establishing an in-house R&D centre, ensuring sustained innovation. 
 
3.20 In its presentation during the meeting, the Department provided a brief overview of the 
financial turnaround of the company. CEL’s sustained operational excellence and improved fiscal 
performance were recognized through its elevation to "Mini Ratna" (Category-I) status. Over the 
period spanning FY 2019–20 to FY 2023–24, the company demonstrated robust growth, with its 
turnover rising from ₹246 crore to ₹344.03 crore, and projections indicating a further increase to 
₹500 crore in the current fiscal year. Concurrently, Profit Before Tax (PBT) surged from ₹6.36 
crore to ₹78.88 crore, reflecting enhanced operational efficiency and profitability. The net worth of 
the company also witnessed a substantial rise, escalating from ₹80.76 crore to ₹193.64 crore during 
the same period. In FY 2023–24, CEL contributed ₹11.87 crore as dividend to the Government of 
India, underscoring its renewed financial viability. Additionally, the company settled longstanding 
employee liabilities, disbursing ₹18 crore towards arrears of interest linked to the 2007 wage 
revision. These milestones collectively underscore CEL’s successful strides in stabilizing its 
financial health, aligning with national objectives of public sector revitalization and accountability. 
3.21 The Committee commends the Department for the successful revival of CEL, which 
was once a struggling PSU on the brink of disinvestment. The remarkable transformation of 
CEL stands as a testament to the potential of strategic interventions in revitalizing public 
sector enterprises. The Committee expresses its optimism that CEL will continue on this 
trajectory of growth and excellence, eventually attaining Maha Ratna status. CEL’s 

12 
 
resurgence serves as an exemplary model of how a well-executed turnaround strategy can 
reinvigorate a PSU, reinforcing its role in advancing national technological and industrial 
capabilities.  
3.22 In view of CEL’s strategic significance, the Committee strongly recommends that the 
Department provide consistent policy and financial support to enable CEL to overcome its 
current challenges and capitalize on growth opportunities. The Department should ensure 
that CEL receives adequate institutional backing to secure its position as a leading player in 
defence electronics, railway electronics, IT-enabled smart infrastructure, and renewable 
energy. The Committee further advises the Department to submit a detailed roadmap 
outlining the steps required to enhance CEL’s operational efficiency, financial viability, and 
technological competitiveness. Strengthening CEL’s capabilities will not only contribute to 
national self-reliance in critical technology sectors but also reinforce India’s public sector 
enterprises as key drivers of innovation and industrial growth.

 4.4 The Committee recognizes the pivotal role played by CSIR in driving research, 
innovation, and technological advancements across diverse domains. As one of the premier 
research organizations in the country, CSIR has contributed significantly to scientific 
breakthroughs, industrial applications, and the development of indigenous technologies that 
have strengthened national self-reliance. Its extensive research network, spanning multiple 
disciplines, has facilitated advancements in healthcare, engineering sciences, environmental 
sustainability, agriculture, and emerging technologies, thereby supporting India’s economic 
and strategic objectives. 
4.5 However, the Committee notes with concern that CSIR has substantial overlaps in 
research activities with other scientific institutions, including the Ministry of Earth Sciences, 
the Department of Biotechnology, the Department of Science and Technology, the Ministry of 
Electronics and Information Technology, the Indian Agricultural Research Institute, etc.. 
This duplication of research efforts leads to fragmentation of resources, inefficiencies in 
execution, and a lack of cohesive direction in national scientific pursuits. The Committee 
strongly recommends that CSIR undertake a comprehensive restructuring to optimize its 
research priorities, ensuring a sharper focus on projects that are highly critical, have a 
substantial impact, and align with the country’s strategic interests. The Committee urges 
CSIR to realign its research portfolio by concentrating on areas of national importance where 
it can deliver unparalleled expertise and breakthrough innovations. Rather than engaging in 
research that overlaps with other institutions, CSIR should collaborate with relevant 
Ministries and research organizations to ensure synergy rather than redundancy. By 
leveraging its strengths in cutting-edge technologies, translational research, and industrial 
applications, CSIR can maximize its contribution to India's scientific and economic 
development. The Committee also recommends that CSIR establish a clear roadmap to 
prioritize high-impact research, streamline its organizational structure, and enhance its role 
as a leader in addressing national challenges. A well-defined and strategic approach will not 
only enhance CSIR’s efficiency but also position it as a key driver of India’s scientific and 
technological advancement in critical sectors.

nine sector-specific theme based clusters, with each cluster under a separate directorate. The list of 
these thematic clusters is as follows:-

4.8 The Department informed the Committee that it requires ₹100 crore in FY 2025-26 to 
execute these nine projects. Additionally, it is working on 12 need based R&D projects, for which 
₹120 crore is needed. The Department is also constructing two Science Experience Centres in 
Ahmedabad and Hyderabad, requiring ₹80 crore. Furthermore, it plans to establish four pilot plants 
for translational and industrial-scale demonstrations—one for Engineering Sciences, two for 
Chemical Sciences, and one for Biological Sciences. These pilot plants aim to support start-ups, 
MSMEs, and industries, particularly in advancing indigenous technologies, with an estimated 
requirement of ₹100 crore. 
4.9 The Department is advancing next-generation benchmark facilities through five critical 
initiatives, requiring a consolidated investment of ₹500 crore. First, it is prioritizing the 
establishment of a secured and centralized data center to safeguard CSIR’s research data, ensuring 
robust storage and cyber security. Second, it is driving the development of nuclear batteries in 
alignment with national objectives related to Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) and Indo-US nuclear 
collaborations. CSIR has already initiated work on all-solid-state batteries and is seeking funding to 
accelerate progress in this technology. Third, it is setting up an indigenous chip fabrication facility 
focused on micro-LED displays. The Department has proposed collaborating with the Ministry of 
Electronics and Information Technology, aiming to match contributions and secure a total 
investment of ₹1,000 crore to strengthen India's global competitiveness in semiconductor 
manufacturing. Fourth, CSIR-National Physical Laboratory (NPL) is leading efforts in Indian 
meteorology and standardization by enhancing atomic clock precision, advancing quantum 
computing, and developing “Bharatiya Nirdeshak Dravya”—customized Indian standards for 
materials and measurements. Lastly, the Department is working on developing animal-free organoid 
models to replace animal testing with human cell-based alternatives, in line with ethical R&D 
practices and global trends. Despite CSIR’s existing capabilities, this project remains on hold due to 
funding constraints.

from the regular budget and introduced it as CSIR-Aerospace Projects of National Importance

5.4 The Committee is shocked to witness such a staggering number of vacancies in the 
Department, particularly in Group-I category of CSIR. It is concerning to contemplate how 
CSIR continues its research with such a skeletal workforce. Expecting optimal results from an 
understaffed organization is unrealistic. Human resources are the most important asset of any 
scientific organization and CSIR is critically lacking precisely in that. The Committee 
strongly recommends that the Department urgently fills up all vacant positions, particularly 
the Group-I vacancies in CSIR, in mission mode.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS-AT A GLANCE 
BUDGET ANALYSIS 
 The Committee notes with concern the sub-optimal utilization of funds under the 
Central Sector Scheme - ‘Industrial Research & Development’, as over half of the allocated 
funds remain unutilized as the current financial year enters its final quarter. In light of this, 
the Committee emphasizes the critical need for the Department to expedite expenditure and 
ensure the optimal deployment of resources within the remaining timeframe of the financial 
year. To preempt such inefficiencies in subsequent years, the Committee strongly advocates 
for the institutionalization of robust quarterly monitoring mechanisms.                      (Para 2.3) 
 The Committee finds merit in the Department’s request for an additional budgetary 
allocation to the tune of ₹ 363.92 crore, over and above the provision made in B.E. 2025-26. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department may seek the requisite 
additional allocation from the Ministry of Finance at the R.E. stage.                            (Para 2.9) 
 
CENTRAL SECTOR SCHEMES 
 The Committee expresses concern over the substantial gap between budgetary 
estimates and actual expenditures. The Committee observes that in several instances, the 
actual expenditure remains significantly lower than the budget estimates and even the revised 
estimates, indicating underutilization of allocated funds. Such underutilization may hinder 
the intended impact of these schemes and delay the realization of their objectives. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department take proactive measures to ensure 
effective fund utilization by addressing administrative bottlenecks, streamlining project 
approvals, and enhancing monitoring mechanisms.                                                        (Para 3.4) 
 The Committee appreciates the achievements made under these schemes. However, the 
Committee believes that a more robust approach is necessary to scale up these achievements 
and expand the reach of these schemes. The Department should consider increasing outreach 
efforts to encourage wider participation from start-ups, MSMEs, and research institutions, 
ensuring that more innovators benefit from these programs.                                         (Para 3.5) 
 The Committee acknowledges the vital role played by NRDC in facilitating the 
commercialization of technologies developed by CSIR, public-funded research institutions, 
universities, and autonomous research bodies. However, the Committee notes with concern 
the disparity between budgetary allocations, revised estimates, and actual expenditures across 
multiple financial years, particularly in the PIII scheme, where the actual expenditure has 
remained consistently lower than the allocated amount. The Committee recommends that the 
Department take necessary measures to ensure the optimal utilization of funds by enhancing 
project execution efficiency, streamlining approval processes, and addressing any institutional 
challenges that may be causing delays.                                                                            (Para 3.12)

Technology Scale-up Initiative (TSI) with its two major components, namely, the Technology 
Development Facility (TDF) and the Generic Startup Support Facility (GSSF). Given the 
critical role of start-ups in driving technological innovation and economic growth, the 
Committee emphasizes the importance of fostering stronger linkages between research 
institutions and start-ups to accelerate the commercialization of innovative technologies. The 
Committee recommends that the Department provide adequate financial and infrastructural 
support to ensure the successful implementation of this initiative, particularly in addressing 
the unique challenges faced by start-ups and women-led enterprises.                         (Para 3.13)

infrastructure projects are essential to support the recruitment of new scientists and to provide 
adequate facilities for existing staff. She projected a total requirement of Rs. 600 crores over five 
years to address these infrastructure needs. Additionally, she pointed out that the budget allocated 
for R&D is insufficient, with only Rs. 2,000 crores available out of the total budget of Rs. 6,600 
crores. She requested the Committee to recommend a minimum additional allocation of Rs. 350

within CSIR, including pilot plants, facility creation projects, and prioritized equipment. She 
explained that these initiatives are aimed at enhancing the capabilities of CSIR laboratories and 
ensuring that they can meet global benchmarks. She also highlighted the importance of need-based 
R&D, which focuses on addressing societal needs and industrial applications. She provided 
examples of projects such as the recovery of metals from e-waste, the development of sustainable 
aviation fuels, and the commercialization of sodium-ion batteries. Informing about the importance 
of promoting science and innovation among the younger generation through initiatives like the

Viksit Bharat initiative, with nine thematic groups working on various projects. These include 
precision medicine, geo-hazard mitigation, and the development of alternate fuels such as Dimethyl 
Ether (DME). She also highlighted the progress made in the field of sustainable aviation fuels, with

She emphasized the need for a policy framework to support the collection and processing of used 
cooking oil on a larger scale.

Thirty-ninth Report on Action Taken by the Ministry of Environment and Forests on the 
recommendations contained in the Ninth Report of the Committee on the Demands for

2. The Ninth Report of the Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and 
Forests was presented to Rajya Sabha on the 18th April, 1994. The Ministry furnished t.heir 
replies indicating action taken on the recommendations/observations contained in that 
Report on 27th March, 1995.

17th December, 1996. 
NEw DELHI;

V. NARAYANASAMY

REPORT 
CHAPTER-I: GENERAL 
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Ministry of 
Environment and Forests on the recommendations cont~iTled in the Ninth Report of the 
Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology, 
'Environment and Forests on the demands for Grants (1994-95) of the Ministry of 
Environment and Forests which was presented to the Rajya Sabha on 18th April, 1994. 
2. There are 13 recommendations contained in the Ninth Report of the Committee. 
Action Taken notes on the recommendations of the Committee, were received from the 
Ministry on 27th March, 1995. 
3. In the meeting held on 29th October, 1996 the Committee considered the Action 
Taken Report and decided to seek some clarificationslobserv3tions from the Ministry. The 
Ministry of Environment and Forests furnished their clarificatiom;/comments on 3rd 
December, 1996 which have been incorporated in this reports, in the succeeding paragraphs. 
RECOMMENDATION 
4. The Committee has also noted that in the Budget Estimates for 1993-94 the Non-Plan 
component of the Ministry was just over Rs. 52 crores which was subsequently revised to 
over Rs. 62 crores, thereby effecting an increase of about 20% but in the Budget Estimates 
for 1994-95, it has been shown as Rs. 58.27 crores, which represents a reduction of abot! ~ 
Rs. 4 crores over that of the previous year. While the Committee appreciates that the 
Ministry has sought lesser Non-plan allocation for 1994-95, it fails to understand as to what 
necessitated substantial increase in Non-Plan component in the Revised Estimates for 1993-
94. The Committee hopes that the Ministry would take due care and confine the Non-Plan 
expenditure to the amount as projected in the Budget Estimates for 1994-95 and the 
increase, if any, will be confil)ed to the barest minimum. 
(Para No. 5) 
ACTION TAKEN BY THE MINISTRY 
4.1 Against the Non-Plan Budget Estimates 1993-94 of Rs. 52.01 crores, a provision of 
Rs. 621.18 crores was asked for under the Revised Estimates 1993-94. An additional amount 
of Rs. 10.17 crores was projected for making reimbursement to the CentraYState Pollution 
Control Boards under the Prevention and Control of Water Pollution (Cess) and meet the 
additional requirement of Botanical Survey of India .for the following reasons:-
(a) In accordance with the Water Cess Act, 1977 as amended from time to time, 
CentraVState Pollution Control Boards collect the Water Cess which is deposited in the 
Consolidated Fund of India. The amount collected is then reimbursed to the CentraYState 
Pollution Boards under the prescribed formulae. 
The Water Cess Act, was amended in 1991 enhancing the Cess rates by nearly three 
times. This amendment came into effect from 1st February, 1992. While this led to a 
considerable increase in the total collection of Cess, it also correspondingly increased the 
total quantum of releases that bad to be made to the CentraVState Pollution Control 

Boards. This had an impact during 1992-'93; consequently an amount of Rs. 9.71 crores 
could not be reimbursed to State Pollution Boards during the said financial year and had to 
be carried forward for reimbursement to the subsequent year, i.e., 1993-94. As a result, an 
additional provision of Rs. 10.00 crores over and above the sanctioned grant of Rs. 16.30 
crores had to be kept for the purpose at the Revised Estimates stage during 1993-94. 
(b) An additional amount of Rs. 0.17 crores had to be provided for Botanical Survey of 
India to meet the additiona l requirement due to grant of Interim relief sanctioned during 
1993-94. 
Although the Non-Plan Revised Estiamte for 1993-94 for Rs. 62.18 crores had been 
accepted by the Ministry of Finance, keeping in view the need to ensure financial discipline, 
the Ministry had decided not to go in for a supplementary grant and instead endeavoured to 
remain .within the sanctioned Budget for 1993-94 by utilising the savings available under Plan 
through diversion. As no arrears for reimbursement of Water Cess pertaining to previous 
years were pending, the Budget Estimates for 1994-95 under Non-Plan were worked out on 
the basis of Actual requirement for the scheme of Prevention and Control of Water 
Pollution (Cess) which was therefore less than the provision made in Revised Estimates for 
the year 1993-94. 
COMMENTS 
4.2 The Committee finds that the Ministry did not take into consideration the 
recommendations of the Committee and again utilised the savings available under plan 
through diversion for Non-Plan expenditure. The Budget Estimates and Non-Plan provision 
were to the tune of Rs. 58.27 crores for the year 1994-95 but the Ministry spent Rs. 59.41* 
crores (actual) during the year 1994-95 obviously through diversion of Plan allocation. 
The Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation that the Ministry shou ld confine 
the Non-Plan expenditure to the amount projected in Budget Estimates. 
RECOMMENDATIONS 
5. The Committee feels that the Ministry through its R&D Units should concentrate on 
developing and providing low cost and fuel efficient energy for cooking so that the 
dependence of rural people on fuel wood from the forests is minimised substantially and the 
forests have unhindered growth. 
(Para No. 8) 
ACTION TAKEN BY THE MINISTRY 
5.1 The development of low cost and fuel efficient energy for cooking is the 
responsibility of the Ministry of Non-Conventional Energy Sources. That Ministry is 
implementing the following two national programmes since 1982-83:-
1. National Programme on improved chulha. 
2. National Programme on biogas development . 
National Programmes on improved cbulba: 
Various models of improved chulhas have been developed indigenously by 17 Technical 
Backup Units set up under this programme. At present, there are about 60 models of fixed 
chulhas and 20 models of portable chulhas under propagation, some of which cost as low as 
Rs. 351- with a thermal efficiency in the range of 25% to 45%. 
•Source:- Demands on Grants for Ministry of Environment and Forests 1996-97 showing actuals. 

National Programme on Biogas Development 
Cheaper models such as Deenbandhu and FRP models have been developed in the past 
and are being propagated by the MNES. Work on development of designs suitable for leafy 
biomass and agro-residues is in progress. 
These programmes are being implemented through State Government nodal 
departments and all India level agencies like Khadi and Village Industries Commission 
(KVIC) , National Dairy Development Board, State Forest Departments etc. Voluntary 
Organisations have also been involved in the implementation of these programmes. 
Till 1993-94, about 170 lakhs improved chulhas and 20 lakhs biogas plants have been 
installed . It is expected that about 132 lakhs tonnes of fuelwood will be saved annually. 
Ministry of Environment and Forests has also included the wood substitution and 
fuelwood conservation measures as one of the Project activities in its centrally sponsored 
scheme for Integrated Afforestation and Eco-Development Projects. Physical and Financial 
outlay as approved by the Planning Commission for this Scheme are as under:-

This Ministry has already taken several initiatives in the direction of fuelwood

COMMENTS 
5.2 The Ministry in its Action Taken Report has inter-alia stated that a Policy Advisory 
Group was constituted in 1990 to suggest measures for fuelwood conservation. The 
recommendations of this Group were circulated to the State Governments for

The Committee wanted the Ministry to furnish details of the recommendations and 
when these recommendations were communicated to the State Governments. Whether any 
follow-up action has been taken by the State Governments and if so, what is the outcome of 
that. If no follow up action has been taken by the State Governments, what are the reasons

RECOMMENDATIONS 
6. Forests are capital assets of the nation and the States do need central budgetary 
support in this vital sector. The central budgetary support can also be limited substantially if 
the States are encouraged to generate their own funds by utilising forest resources without, 
in any way, contributing to degradation. In this context the Committee observes that the 

Ministry of Environment and Forests can play an effective role in impressing upon the States 
to draw upon the experience of the State of Madhya Pradesh, which the Committee has 
been given to understand, is generating income from forests to the tune of Rs. 400 crores 
whereas its forest plan component is of the size of Rs. 50 crores. · · 
(Para No. 10) 
ACTION TAKEN BY mE MINISTER 
6.1 It is a fact that level of investment in the forestry sector in the country is not 
commensurate with the level of withdrawls from our forests. The Ministry has already taken 
up the issue of raising the forestry allocation with the Planning Commission and the State 
Governments. It has been found that many of the State Governments are not allocating 
sufficient funds for forestry development despite the fact that the revenue from forests from 
the States is considerable as is evident from the case of Madhya Pradesh. While the States 
with higher income from forests need to augment investments in order to sustainably 
manage, develop and utilise their forest resources, the States with lesser forest areas also 
need to allocate sufficient funds for forest development in order to ensure increased supply 
of goods and services for the benefit of community as well as for its environmental well 
being. The Plan allocation of forestry under Vlllth Plan is only 1% and there is urgent need 
to increase it upto 2% during the remaining years of the Vlllth Plan and to a level of 3% 
under IXth Plan. 
• COMMENTS 
6.2 In view of the reply of the Ministry, the Committee observes that there is need for 
more allocation for forestry. Planning Commission should consider the importance of the 
forestry and provide higher allocations in the IXth Plan period. 
RECOMMENDATION 
Paryavaran Vabini: 
7. Most of the schemes launched or contemplated by the Ministry of Environment and 
Forests such as Paryavaran Sudhar Pariyojna are of a peripheral nature and do not strike at 
the root of the problem. The idea behind setting up one Paryavaran Vahini for each 
identified district with a view to create environmental awareness and involvement of people 
through active participation , reporting of illegal acts pertaining to forests, wildlife, pollution 
and environmental degradation is no doubt good, but there appear to be many pitfalls in the 
scheme which is mainly to be administered through the District Collector who are supposed 
to take action on the complaints of the Members of the Vahini. There is an apprehension 
that the persons brought on these Vahinis may not be right sort of persons and the grant of 
Rs. 200 per month to each Member given through the State Governments may be pocketed 
by the persons who are not doing any worthwhile service. The Committee, therefore, feels 
that while the Paryavaran Vahini Scheme should be continued and adequate funds be made 
available therefor, there should be strict monitoring in respect of performance of these 
Vahinis. 
(Para No. 11) 
ACTION TAKEN BY THE MINISTRY 
7.1 This Ministry is making every effort to ensure that right kind of persons are selected 
as Members of the Paryavaran Vahinis. For this, the Ministry has provided detailed 
guidelines for selection of Members. Also, th! Regional Offices of, the Ministry are involved 
with process of selection and constitution of the Vahinis. Their representatives attend the 

Selection Committee meetings. Besides, the performance of these Vahinis is also monitored 
by the Regional Offices. 
(Para No. 11) 
COMMENTS 
7.2 The Committee feels that the Ministry should work and a mechanism in order to 
create awareness among the people to preserve the environment. The Ministry should 
examine as to how best the involvement of NGOs can be ensured. 
FURTHER ACTION TAKEN 
7.3 The Ministry of Environment and Forests in its drive for creating environmental 
awareness and to involve people in the preservation of environment and forests and wildlife 
has started a scheme known as 'Paryavaran Vahini'. It is meant to be a people's programme 
wherein persons!NGOs who are dedicated to the cause of environmental protection would 
be welcome to become members of the Paryavaran Vahinis. The objectives of the scheme 
are as follows:-
- Environmental awareness and involvement of people through active participation 
- Reporting on illegal acts pertaining to forests, wildlife, pollution and environmental 
degradation 
- Feed back regarding afforestation and survival of plants 
- Monitoring including collection of sample, analysis of ambient air and water quality 
including vehicular pollution 
The scheme is not an employment generating scheme and membership in the Vahini is 
of honorary nature and they are partially reimbursed the expenses incurred for the meetings. 
The meetings are held once every month. 
To involve people working at the grassroot levels in the Environment conservation 
efforts, Paryavaran Vahini has been constituted at the district level. 184 districts have been 
approved for constitution of Vahinis and by now, these have been constituted in 141 districts 
spread over 25 States and 4 Union Territories. These districts have been selected on the 
basis of high incidence of pollution, density of tribal population and forest cover. Each 
Paryavaran Vahini has about 20 members. Two States viz. Madhya Pradesh and Arunachal 
Pradesh have be.en covered 100% under the scheme. The members organise activities to 
create environmental awareness in their areas. 
Violation of activities like deforestation/illegal felling of trees/illegal mining! 
encroachment of forest land/wildlife poaching/cruelty to animals/violations of provisions of 
Environment Protection Act, 1986/Forest Conservation Act, 1980/Wildlife Protection Act, 
1972, causing environmental degradation · are reported and action is taken up on the 
complaints received from the various members by the District Magistrate. Action taken on 
various complaints is discussed in the subsequent meetings of Paryavaran Vahinis. 
Monitoring of scheme is being done through Regional Offices of the Ministry by way of 
quarterly reports received from district and field visits where Paryavaran Vahinis are 
working. 
RECOMMENDATION 
8. The Committee is of the view that any shortfall in achieving .the targets results in 
surrendering of allocated amount unless of course the funds themselves fall short and there 
is cost escalation, if the projects go heyond the periods earmarked for their completion. As 

regards Aerial Seeding Scheme it was submitted before the Committee that the results 
achieved under this scheme have not been that much satisfactory for various reasons such as 
lack of interest or the part of some States, non-checking of grazing and assistance from the 
people engaged in making soil fit for seeding because they do not have employment round 
the year. Nevertheless, the Ministry is in the process of identifying areas like Chambal 
ravines of U.P. and M.P. to bring them under Aerial Seeding Scheme. The Committee feels 
that there has not been any major R&D effort on the part of the Ministry in the field of 
Aerial Seeding and whole approach is of a lackadaisical. The Committee, therefore, urges 
upon the Ministry to strengthen R&D in this vital sector to make the Aerial Seeding Scheme 
more viable and meaningful. 
(Para No. 12) 
ACTION TAKEN BY THE MINISTRY 
8.1 As regards the Aerial Seeding Scheme ICFRE Dehradun have been asked to collect 
information regarding technological advances in the field of aerial seeding which ensure 
better penetration of seeds in soil and take care of characteristics of soil to secure plantation 
in difficult terrains. A techno-economic evaluation study for comparative analysis of manual 
and aerial seeding technique is also proposed to be carried out. 
COMMENTS 
8.2 The Committee is satisfied with the approach of the Ministry. However, the 
Committee would appreciate if the findings of the study conducted by the techno-economi c 
evaluation Group for comparative analysis of manual and aerial seedings technique are made 
known to the Committee. 
FURTHER ACTION TAKEN 
8.3 Subsequent to the observation of the Committee there has not been any major R&D 
effort on the part of the Ministry in the field of aerial seeding, Indian Council of Forestry 
Research and Education (ICFRE) was asked to carry out the evaluation of the aerial seeding 
scheme. A meeting was held at the level of the then Ministry of Environment and Forests on 
5.9.94 to discuss the technological improvements possible in the scheme. ICFRE was 
assigned the task of collectiqg available information in other countries particularly with 
regard to latest technologies of aerial seeding as experimented in the country in the past has

RECOMMENDATION 
9. It is of utmost importance that monitoring and evaluation aspects of prescribed 
targets are taken due care of and mechanism provided therefore is suitably strengthened. In

~ystem during 1994-95. Since the Ministry proposes to acquire equipment such as Digital

(Para No. 13)

9.1 Under this head, evaluations that are mounted to sample check the saplings planted

9.2 The Committee wanted the Ministry to apprise it of the present position ':1 this

FURTHER ACTION TAKEN 
Status Note on Digital Cartographic System 
The main objective in acquiring Digital Cartographic System was to have an operational 
forest mapping and monitoring system, which would be used to produce forest vegetation 
map at 1 : 250000 scale at a two year cycle and thematic map at 1 : 50000 scale at a ten year 
cycle for the whole country. Alongwith Digital Satellite Data, digitized forest maps and 
other ancillary data would be used as an input to the· Digital Cartographic System with an 
objective to build up a geographic information system for forest development planning. The 
main functions of the system are:-
- map digitization. 
- storage and Management of large volumes of spatial data. 
- manipulation and editing of all graphic features. 
- overlaying of classified data with map. 
- high quality map plotting. 
- printing of copies of thematic maps as required. 

The purchase of Digital Cartographic System was approved in the EFC Memo under the 
Scheme, Forest Survey of India-Application of Remote Sensing Techniques in the Survey 
of Forests on 16th November, 1994. The approval of Ministry of Finance could be obtained 
only in late March, 1995. The Digital Cartographic System has since been procured in 
August, 1996 at a cost of Rs. 7,755 crores and is being commissioned at Forest Survey of 
India, Dehradun. 
The Digital Cartographic System includes a package of sophisticated computer systems 
intended to produce digital vegetation and thematic maps. At present , they are being 
commissioned. Once commissioned, they shall provide Forest Survey of India the capability 
to achieve in time its present mandate of publishing a biennial report called "State of Forest 
Reports", as well as National Vegetation Map digitally. The digital photogrammetic 
subsystem alongwith analytical one shall allow Forest Survey of India to update existing 
thematic maps as well as produce new maps/reports containing species, volume and growing 
stock information. Several important studies like monitoring hot spot areas like highly 
deforestation prone or fire prone area can also be undertaken which were hitherto not 
possible. 
During its visit to Forests Survey of India, Dehradun on 16th November, 1996 the 
Committee was given to understand that the pace of acquisition of Digital Cartographic 
System was rather slow depending on the availability of funds in a given year. The 
Committee is not happy with the snail's pace at which the system is being acquired. 
RECOMMENDATION 
10. The efforts of the Central and State Governments at afforestation , preventing 
deforestation and extending forest area by developing wastelands cannot succeed unless the 
critical area of ravaging fires is tadued on a war footing. A major fire in a forest may cause 
devastation as recently happen ed in the Nagarhole forests. Such fires virtually reduce to 
naught years of efforts of Ministry of Environment and Forests and the State Forest 
Departments in just minutes. In the course of the evidence of the Secretary and other 
officials of the Ministry taken by the Committee, it came to light that in controlling fires, the 
Ministry is still depending upon conventional methods such as collecting the villagers and 
providing fire fighting tools to them to undertake the gigantic task of controlling forest fires. 
In the Budgetary estimates for 1994-95, a provision of just 2 crores of rupees has been made 
for introduction of modern forest fire control methods in the country. Even if it be assumed 
that this outlay will be further supplemented by State allocations, still this amount looks 
ridiculous when we talk of introducing modern methods of fire control. It has come to the 
notice of the Committee that close on the heels of a major fire in the Nagarhole forest, 
another devastating fire has been caused in vast areas of Orissa's Simlipal Wildlife Sanctuary 
which went on raging for over 15 days with still no sign of it being controlled. On a total 
area of 2,200 sq. kms. of the sanctuary at least 200 sq. kms. was reported to be in the grip 
of fire and the loss was expected to run into millions of rupees. The Committee feels that 
forest wealth worth crores of rupees is lost in fires and accordingly would like to impress 
upon the Ministry to examine whether it could not be worth spending a small amount on 
employing modem methods of fire control like spraying chemicals with the help of 
aeroplanes as is being done in some of the advanced countries. Besides, the Committee 
recommends that law should be made more stringent with deterrent penalties for chose who 
deliberately set the forests on fire and huge losses of national wealth.

To replicate the methods in the fire prone forest areas , and with the objectives to

productivity of forests by reducing the incidence and extent of fire. The Centrally Sponsored

Year Plan period was Rs. 5 crores only. Till 1993-94 the Centrally Sponsored Scheme 
"Modem Forest Fire Control Methods" was limited to only eleven States of Andhra

13.3 Central PoJiution Control Board, State Pollution Control Boards and Pollution Control 
Committee 
The Central Pollution Control Board , the State Pollution Control Boards in the States, and 
the Pollution Control Committees in the Union Territories, are the controlling agencies of air 
and water pollution. They are statutory bodies. They were constituted under section 4, 5, 6 and 
7 of the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974. These Boards and Committees 
are responsible for implementation of Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution), Air 
(Prevention and Control of Pollution, Cess and the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. 
Under Section 17(n) of the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 and 
Section 17(h) of the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act. 1981, the State Pollution 
Control Boards are to advise the respective State Governments with respect to the location of 
any indu stry carrying on of which is likely to pollute water and air. 
No Objection Certificate or "Consent to Operate" 
Under section 25 of the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974, and section 
21 of the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981, an industry is required to obtain 
"consent to operate", where it is a statutory obligation of the industry to comply with the 
pollution control norms stipulated by the State Pollution Control Boards. 

As per provisions of the Water t.•td Air Acts, the "No Objection Certificates I Consent 
to Operate.. are given by the respective State Pollution Control Boards and the Pollution 
Control Committees in the Union Territories. The requirement and procedure for seeking 
environmental clearances of projects and industries are listed in Schedule-! of the 
~otification issued by this Ministry dated 17.1.94 (as amended on 4.5.94). The issuance of 
clearance, which also includes public hearing, take~ upto four months. 
Procedural Delays and Check on Malpractices 
In order to reduce procedural delays, several State Boards have simplified the 
procedure for issue of "No Objection Certificate". For non-polluting industries and those 
complying with their location in conforming areas, are either exempted or issued with long 
term consents. For selected category of industries, clearances from "single window concept" 
has been introduced. In some States categorisation of industries into "Red", "Orange" and 
"Green" is done depending on pollution potential of the units. The Green category of 
industries in non-polluting and units under such category are issued clearances expeditiously 
for longer periods upto 15 years. 
The "No Objection Certificates" I "Consent to Operate" are given with the concurrence 
of respective State Pollution Control Boards, by a Committee which consists of 17 members 
(the Chiarman and the Member-Secretary of the State Pollution Control Board are full-time 
members) and the others are nominated by the respectives State Boards. This helps in 
keeping a watch over indiscriminate issuance of NOCs.

15. The Committee feels that in order to fulfil the tasks expected of the Ministry, it is 
necessary to have technical personnel with the appropriate experience at the highest level of 
administration in the Ministry rather · than operate it largely as an administrative Ministry. 
This Ministry by itself cannot be expected to perform all the major tasks relating to 
environmental and forestry, even with the assistance of related agencies of the State 
Governments. The role of the Ministry is to perform promotional and catalytic activities that 

show the way for society to implement meaningful programmes. For this it is necessary that
