of the Ministry and the actuals of the Budget. 
(Para No. 20) 
ACTION TAKEN BY THE MINISTRY 
15.1 The Committee's observations that the Ministry should perform catalytic activities 
that show the way society to implement meaningful programmes are undisputed. However, it 
is doubtful whether this purpose can be achieved merely by placing technical personnel at 
the highest level of administration in the Ministry. Identification of promotional and catalytic 
activities that can effectively motivate the society comes more out of administrative 
experience rather than handling of frontier technologies. Any administrative officer selected 
to head the Ministry is, in addition to his administrative experience, undoubtedly endowed 
with as much technical awareness of environmental issues, if not more than, any other 
enlightened citizen of the country. Technical knowledge higher than that level of awareness 
is not a pre-requisite to identify the catalytic activities that can mobilise the society. Any 
higher technical knowledge of environmental science is necessary for a researcher exploring 
new horizons to enlarge the human knowledge base, but such academic excellance may most 
often inhibit effective leadership to stimulate the ground level application of such scientific 
knowledge. 
Further, the Ministry of Environment and Forests deals with a wide range of subjects 
associated with .environment and forests. In fact, it is a multi-disciplinary Ministry which has 
to interact not only with scientific institutions but also with a large spectrum of institutions 
dealing with administrative, social, economic, academic, legal and various other aspects of 
programmes in different sectors of the nation. There has, therefore, to be a balanced 
appreciation of these related programmes of the Government while ensuring that the 
Ministry of Environment and Forests discharges its responsibilities meaningfully in 
conformity with the priorities of the nation. In addition, the Ministry has extensive 
international interactions and obligations and is often called upon to take positions from not 
only scientific angle but also developmental and diplomatic angles keeping in view the 
international conventions an9 commitments of the country. All this requires that the 
Ministry is headed by an administrative officer who possesses varied experiences of different 
programmes of Government and is familiar with the overall policy thrust of the 
Government. 
It may be appropriate to mention that Research and Development has received due 
attention since the inception of the Ministry of Environment and Forests (and the erstwhile 
Department of Environment created in November, 1980). 
Research and Development Programmes of the Ministry are supported in 
multidisciplinary aspects of environmental protection, conservation and development . The 
journey of the research efforts in a decade and a half has been one of preliminary 
assessments of the status of the various environmental parameters to those of 
characterisation of the problems and organisms in different eco-systems. 
From its modest start in the late Seventies, the programme of research has progressed 
from preliminary estimations to futuristic impact studies both in manifestations and 
ecological insights. 

The programme of Research in the Research Division is e~sentially undertaken through 
three major researches viz. 
(i) Man and Biosphere Research Scheme. 
(ii) Environment Research Scheme. 
(iii) Integrated Action Oriented Research and Demonstration Projects in the Western 
and Eastern Ghats. 
During the period of operation of these schemes more than 600 research projects in 
multi-disciplinary aspects of Environmental Management has been supported all over the 
country through Universities , R&D Institutions and non-governmental organisations. 
These schemes have significantly contributed to the 
(a) Advancement of the Scientific knowledge 
(b) Creation of Scientific Manpower 
(c) Creation of Research Facilities in the Institutions. 
The research studies, in the first instance, have contributed to the advancement of 
scientific understanding of the complex processes, systems and development of 
methodologies for studies. Secondly, the research the multidisciplinary aspects and, thirdly , 
through the research schemes, capability of institutions has beP-n built up in terms of modern 
equipment and the capability ·of undertaking research problems. 
The research results, more often than not, are not directly applicable to problems of 
environmental management, but do immensely contribute towards attempting solutions to 
environment problems in helping to devise strategies for protection, conservation and 
management of the environment. 
In order to achieve this summaries of the completed research projects have been 
published in two volumes and have been widely circulated for appropriate use. 
The Eighth Plan orientation of the Research Programmes is to intensify activities in 
development of low cost solutions to environmental problems and long-term monitoring 
studies, a mixture of immediate to medium and long-term needs.

1. INTRODUCTION 
1.1 The Department of Science & Technology (DST) stands as the premier nodal agency in 
India dedicated to fortifying the nation's Science, Technology, and Innovation (STI) landscape. It 
plays a pivotal role in identifying critical gaps within the S&T sectors, formulating strategic plans 
and policies to address societal needs, and fostering emerging areas of science and technology to 
meet future demands. DST acts as a vital bridge, connecting the science and technology domains 
with various Government horizontals and verticals, academia, Research and Development (R&D) 
laboratories, institutions, and industries, ensuring a cohesive and collaborative ecosystem. 
1.2 With the overarching goal of enhancing India's S&T capacity and capability, DST 
spearheads the largest extramural R&D support in the country. This is achieved through three 
comprehensive umbrella schemes: (i) Science and Technology (S&T) Institutional and Human 
Capacity Building, (ii) Research and Development, and (iii) Innovation, Technology Development, 
and Deployment. These schemes are designed to empower scientists across diverse institutions and 
disciplines through a competitive framework, thereby reinforcing India's education system, 
scientific and industrial R&D. 
1.3 In a significant move to streamline operations and enhance flexibility in fund allocation, 
these three umbrella schemes have been consolidated into a single, unified initiative named ‘Vigyan 
Dhara’. This integration ensures a more efficient and adaptive flow of resources across programs, 
fostering greater innovation and impact. 
1.4 DST remains steadfast in its mission to strengthen the national STI ecosystem, positioning 
India as a global leader in science and technology. By driving positive transformations, DST aims 
to contribute to a safer, more secure, and prosperous society, while proactively preparing for future 
challenges and disruptions. Through its relentless efforts, DST continues to catalyze advancements 
that not only address current societal needs but also pave the way for a sustainable and 
technologically advanced future. 
1.5 The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology, 
Environment, Forests and Climate Change considered the Demands for Grants (2025-26) of the 
Department of Science & Technology in its meeting held on 19th February, 2025.

3. RESEARCH, DEVELOPMENT & INNOVATION FUND 
3.1 In the Interim Budget for the fiscal year 2024-25, a ₹1 lakh crore corpus was announced to 
promote private sector research and innovation in deep tech and sunrise sector. This corpus was 
intended to provide long-term financing or refinancing at low or zero interest rates through a 50-
year interest-free loan. 
3.2 Building on this initiative, the Budget for FY 2025-26 introduced the Research, 
Development, and Innovation (RDI) Fund with a budgetary allocation of ₹20,000 crore. This fund 
is designed to facilitate long-term financing or refinancing with extended tenors and minimal or 
zero interest rates for science, technology, and other research-driven initiatives. The objective is to 
incentivize the private sector to expand its research endeavors and position India as a global leader 
in research, development, and innovation within emerging domains. The fund aims to support 
programs that leverage the potential of India's youth and technological advancements. 
3.3 Under this scheme, a Special Purpose Fund would be set up and implemented by 
Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF) for funding Startups and private sector 
corporates. The focus and coverage of RDI Scheme is envisaged to be in sunrise sectors which are 
likely to have transformative and strong ripple impact on the economy, besides having potential for 
high growth and commercial success. The identification of sectors and sub-sectors, for the purpose 
of funding, will also account for the Indian context including the economic landscape, level of 
technological advancement and the societal needs. The relevance for global value chain integration 
as well as potential for creating market access shall also be considered. 
3.4 The Department submitted that the specific sectors and sub-sectors to be supported by the 
Scheme would be identified upfront.  Some of the sunrise sectors have been identified for 
consideration of funding under the Scheme which may  subject to further refinement include 1) 
Energy security/transition and climate action 2) “Deep Technology” including quantum 
computing, robotics and  space  3) Artificial Intelligence and its application to Indian problems 
including  in agriculture, health, and education  4) Biotechnology, biomanufacturing, synthetic 
biology, pharma, medical devices  5) Digital economy including Digital agriculture, technologies 
whose indigenization for strategic reasons or for economic security and any other sector or 
technology where it is deemed necessary in  public interest. 
3.5 The Department plans to allocate ₹20,000 crore as a 50-year interest-free loan to a special 
purpose fund. This fund will be managed by second-level fund managers, including alternate 
investment funds, fund of funds, and non-banking financial companies (NBFCs). These managers 
will invest in deep tech sectors such as clean energy, bio-manufacturing, quantum computing, AI, 
sustainable agriculture, gene therapy, and computational drug discovery, either through loans or 
equity investments in start-ups and private companies. A key condition is that private sector

5. NATIONAL QUANTUM MISSION (NQM)  
5.1 The Department informed the Committee that one of the thrust areas for the year 2025-26 is 
National Quantum Mission (NQM). It was approved by the Union Cabinet on 19th April 2023 at a 
total cost of ₹6003.65 crore for a period of eight years from 2023-24 to 2030-31.  
 
5.2 Under the Mission, four Thematic Hubs comprising of 14 Technical Groups having 17 
Project Teams across India, involving nearly 152 researchers from 43 institutions have been 
established, each dedicated to a specific technology vertical:  
(i) Quantum Computing at IISc. Bengaluru; 
(ii) Quantum Communication at IIT Madras in association with C-DOT, New Delhi; 
(iii) Quantum Sensing & Metrology at IIT Bombay; and 
(iv) Quantum Materials & Devices at IIT Delhi 

10 
 
5.3 The Mission objectives include developing intermediate-scale quantum computers with 20-
50 physical qubits in 3 years, 50-100 physical qubits in 5 years and 50-1000 physical qubits in 8 
years in various platforms like superconducting and photonic technology. Satellite-based secure 
quantum communications between ground stations over a range of 2000 kilometers within India, 
long-distance secure quantum communications with other countries, inter-city quantum key 
distribution over 2000 km as well as multi-node Quantum networks with quantum memories are 
also some of the deliverables of the Mission. The National Quantum Mission will focus on 
developing magnetometers with high sensitivity in atomic systems and atomic clocks for precision 
timing, communications, and navigation. It will also support the design and synthesis of quantum 
materials such as superconductors, novel semiconductor structures, and topological materials for the 
fabrication of quantum devices. Single photon sources/detectors, and entangled photon sources will 
also be developed for quantum communications, sensing, and metrological applications. The 
Mission would greatly benefit various sectors including communication, health, financial, energy 
with applications in drug design, space, banking, security etc. The Mission will also provide a huge 
boost to National priorities like Digital India, Make in India, Skill India and Stand-up India, Start-
up India, Self-reliant India and Sustainable Development Goals (SDG). 
5.4 The Committee enquired about the physical achievements of the Mission, and was informed 
that IIT Bombay has established the section – 8 Company in the area of Quantum Sensing & 
Metrology namely Qmet Tech Foundation in October 2024. Similarly, IIT Madras in association 
with C-DoT, New Delhi has established IITM CDOT Samgnya Technologies Foundation in 
December 2024 in the area of Quantum Communication. 
5.5 The Committee notes that the ₹ 427 crores were allocated in B.E. 2024-25 which were 
significantly reduced to ₹ 86 crores and Department could spent only 64.30 per cent of the 
R.E. till 31st January, 2025. Even after such gross under-utilization of funds, ₹ 600 crores has 
been allocated for this Mission in B.E. 2025-26. The Committee enquired about the increased 
budget allocation for the National Quantum Mission (NQM) in B.E. 2025-26 and the 
Department informed that the increased allocations will play a pivotal role in expanding and 
scaling up ongoing initiatives while accelerating the development of a robust quantum 
technology ecosystem in India. A significant portion of this funding will be dedicated to 
strengthening the four established Thematic Hubs (T-Hubs), each focused on a key vertical—
Quantum Computing, Quantum Communication, Quantum Sensing & Metrology, and 
Quantum Materials & Devices. The enhanced funding will empower these T-Hubs to fulfill 
their mandates effectively by: Technology Development, Human Resource Development, 
Entrepreneurship Development and Industry Collaborations and International 
Collaborations. 
5.6 The Committee acknowledges that the launch of a dedicated Mission for research in 
Quantum Technologies is a strategic and forward-looking initiative, aligning with global 
technological advancements. However, the underutilization of allocated funds raises concerns 
about the Department's commitment and operational efficiency. The Committee emphasizes 
the need for the Department to adopt a more proactive and results driven approach to ensure 
the Mission's success. Rather than merely playing catch-up to Google’s Willow and 
Microsoft’s Majorana 1, the Committee strongly recommends that the Department adopt an 
ambitious vision to position India as a global leader in Quantum Technology.

6.10 The Committee recognizes the Indian Institute of Astrophysics (IIA) as a premier 
institution dedicated to research and development in Astronomy, Astrophysics, and 
Astronomy Instrumentation. The successful fabrication and verification of the first 1.44-
meter mirror segment for the international Thirty Meter Telescope (TMT) at the India-TMT 
Optics Fabrication Facility is a significant achievement, demonstrating India's capability in 
high-precision optics and advanced astronomical instrumentation. 
6.11 The Committee recommends that the Department extend continued support to IIA for 
the successful completion of India’s commitments to the TMT project and other international 
collaborations in astrophysics. Additionally, the Committee urges the Department to explore 
opportunities for further strengthening indigenous expertise in astronomical instrumentation, 
including the development of next-generation telescopes and space-based observational 
facilities. Ensuring adequate funding, infrastructure, and skilled workforce development will 
be crucial for positioning India as a global leader in cutting-edge astronomical research and 
technology. 
D. Raman Research Institute (RRI), Bengaluru 
The Raman Research Institute (RRI) was founded by Indian Science Nobel Laureate Sir C V 
Raman in 1948, marking 2023 as its Platinum Jubilee Year (PJY). The research at the Institute 
spans mind-boggling spatial and temporal scales from the very large- galaxies, galaxy clusters and 
beyond, to the very small – on the scale of atoms; from processes that happen over millions and 
billions of years to ultrafast processes that occur in attoseconds. The Institute has designed and built 
POLIX, world's first instrument designed to operate in the medium X-ray band of 8 to 30 kilo 
electron Volt (keV) energy. It was launched onboard XPoSat mission by ISRO on 1st January, 2024. 
It is designed to detect the scattered X-rays, enabling X-ray polarisation measurements. After initial 
calibrations and tests, the first light was obtained in early February and since then, the instrument 
has been making scientific observations. 
6.12 The Committee commends the Raman Research Institute (RRI) for its outstanding 
contributions to scientific research across vast spatial and temporal scales, from cosmology to 
atomic physics.  
6.13 The successful design and development of POLIX, the world's first instrument 
operating in the medium X-ray band (8 to 30 keV), and its launch onboard ISRO’s XPoSat 
mission on 1st January 2024, is a remarkable achievement in space-based X-ray astronomy. 
The Committee appreciates the Institute’s efforts in pioneering X-ray polarisation 
measurements, which hold immense potential for advancing our understanding of high-
energy astrophysical phenomena. In light of these achievements, the Committee recommends

The Committee also emphasizes the need for sustained funding, enhanced infrastructure, and 
skilled human resources to propel future discoveries and innovations in this critical domain.

mode approach to expeditiously fill all vacant positions. This will ensure the availability of a 
competent and stable workforce, essential for advancing scientific research and institutional

training initiatives, skill development, and continuous learning opportunities. Additionally, 
the Department should actively explore and establish collaborations with internationally 
renowned scientific institutions to facilitate knowledge exchange, exposure to global best

INTRODUCTION 
 The Government of India has set up the Space Commission and the Department of 
Space (DOS) in 1972. Department of Space is responsible for implementing the policies 
framed by the Space Commission. These are carried out through the Indian Space Research 
Organisation (ISRO), Indian National Space Promotion & Authorization Centre (IN-SPACe) 
and the Grant-in-aid institutions viz., Physical Research Laboratory (PRL), National 
Atmospheric Research Laboratory (NARL), North-Eastern Space Applications Centre (NE-
SAC), Semi-Conductor Laboratory (SCL) and Indian Institute of Space Science and 
Technology (IIST). 
1.2 The Secretariat of the Department of Space and the Headquarters of ISRO are located 
in Bangalore. The Programme Offices at ISRO Headquarters co-ordinate the overall 
programmes like Satellite Communication, Satellite Navigation, Earth Observation, Space 
Transportation Systems, Space Science and Planetary Exploration, Climate & Atmospheric 
Programme, Disaster Management Support, National Natural Resources Management System 
(NNRMS), International Co-Operation, Capacity Building, Media & Public Relations, 
Budget & Economic Analysis and Human Resources Development. 
1.3 The activities of Department of Space (DOS) are broadly organized under four 
umbrella schemes namely 
 Space Technology - development of launch vehicles, satellites, manned space mission, 
R&D in Space Technology such as propulsion, navigational satellite systems, 
indigenization of Space materials & components, etc.  
 
 Space Applications - major Projects/activities such as Earth Observation Navigation 
Missions, Tele-medicine, Tele-education, Disaster Management Support, etc are 
undertaken. 
 
 Space Sciences - projects towards Space sciences and planetary exploration are 
undertaken. Major projects undertaken under the scheme include Indian Lunar Mission - 
Chandrayaan-3, Aditya-L1 mission, XPoSat, Space Docking Experiment.  
 
 INSAT Satellite Systems- This programme is envisaged to provide satellite based 
communication services in the country.  
1.4 Major Centres / Units of DOS/ISRO: 
a) Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre (VSSC), Thiruvananthapuram, provides the 
technology base for the country’s indigenous launch vehicle (rocket) development 
b) Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre (LPSC), with its facilities located at Bangalore and 
Thiruvananthapuram, is responsible for development of liquid propulsion and 
cryogenic propulsion systems for satellite and launch vehicles 
c) Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC-SHAR) at Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh, is the 
spaceport of India providing launch base to indigenously built launch vehicles.  Also, 
it provides the facilities for processing of solid rocket motors 

2 
 
d) Human Space Flight Centre (HSFC) is created with the responsibility to act as the 
lead centre for Human Space Flight Program. This centre is responsible for the 
execution of Gaganyaan programme that envisages sending a crew of astrounauts to 
space and bring back safely to earth.   
e) U R Rao Satellite Centre (URSC), Bangalore, is entrusted with the prime 
responsibility for development of satellites     
f) Space Applications Centre (SAC), Ahmedabad 
g) National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC), Hyderabad is responsible for satellite data 
acquisition and processing, data dissemination, aerial remote sensing and decision 
support for disaster management 
h) The Laboratory for Electro-Optics Systems (LEOS), Bangalore  
i) ISRO Propulsion Complex (IPRC), Mahendragiri  
j) ISRO Telemetry, Tracking & Command Network (ISTRAC) 
k) Master Control Facility (MCF), Hassan 
l) Indian Institute of Remote Sensing (IIRS), Dehradun  
m) ISRO Inertial Systems Unit (IISU), Thiruvananthapuram  
1.5 Organisations receiving Grants-in-aid: 
a) Physical Research Laboratory (PRL), Ahmedabad, an autonomous institution 
supported mainly by the Department of Space, carries out research in space sciences. 
b) The National Atmospheric Research Laboratory (NARL) set up at Gadanki near 
Tirupati, conducts atmospheric research. 
c) The North-Eastern Space Applications Centre (NE-SAC) established as an 
autonomous body under the Department of Space provides space technology inputs 
for developmental activities in the North-Eastern Region.  
d) The Indian Institute of Space Science and Technology (IIST) is an autonomous body 
under the Department with the objective of creating quality human resources tuned to 
suit the requirements of state-of-art space research programme.    
1.6 Government Companies under DOS:  
a) The Antrix Corporation Limited, Bangalore, established in 1992, is a wholly owned 
Government Company for marketing space products and services.  
b) The NewSpace India Limited (NSIL), Bangalore, is another commercial arm of 
Indian Space Research Organization, with the primary objective of enabling Indian 
industries to scale up high-technology manufacturing and production base for Indian 
space programme.  
1.7 Indian National Space Promotion and Authorization Center (INSPACe) 
Recently, the space sector was opened up to promote, handhold, regulate and 
authorise private enterprises and start-ups to undertake space activities by creation of an 
independent nodal agency under Department of Space - the Indian National Space Promotion 
and Authorization Center (IN-SPACe). This will enhance the contribution of space 
technology towards boosting space economy within the country.

4.  Establishment Expenditure of the Centre 
4.1    IN-SPACe 
  The Department in a written reply informed the Committee about the vision, mission 
and objectives of INSPACe. IN-SPACe aims to boost private sector participation in space 
activities, strengthen India’s space economy, and promote self-reliance in space technology. 
As a single-window agency, it facilitates start-ups, MSMEs, industries, and academic 
institutions in innovation and commercialisation within the space sector. Its key functions 
include:  
 
(i) Enabling private sector involvement in launch vehicle and satellite development. 

20 
 
(ii) Granting access to ISRO’s infrastructure for research, manufacturing, and testing. 
(iii) Overseeing the establishment of new space facilities by private players while ensuring 
compliance with safety and statutory guidelines. 
(iv) Facilitating launch campaigns and satellite registration for Indian private entities. 
(v) Encouraging technology sharing and collaboration to strengthen India’s space 
ecosystem. 
(vi) Managing an integrated launch manifest to align priorities of ISRO, public sector 
units, and private entities. 
(vii) Providing affordable access to ISRO’s high-tech facilities for private sector research 
and   development. 
The Department further informed that IN-SPACe actively promotes skill development 
and talent acquisition through short-term training courses in satellite technology, propulsion, 
and space communications to bridge industry skill gaps; academic partnerships with IIT 
Roorkee and universities to integrate space technology education; Pre-Incubation 
Entrepreneurship (PIE) Program, launched in June 2024, to mentor and support early-stage 
start-ups and recognition by NCVET as an awarding body, setting industry standards for 
space-related vocational education and training. 
4.2 The Department of Space highlighted the following key initiatives/actions under taken 
to support & enable the private-sector engagement in space activities:  
i. Regulatory and Policy Framework for Indian Space Sector 
Indian Space Policy – 2023 (ISP-2023) was brought out in April 2023, has identified 
the range of Space Activities undertaken by private players that require Authorization 
by IN-SPACe. 
Subsequently, IN-SPACe has brought out the Norms, Guidelines and Procedures 
(NGP) document for streamlining the authorization processes. 
Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) policy provisions for the Space sector have been 
liberalized in prescribed sub sectors/activities, to attract potential foreign investors to 
invest in Indian companies in space sector. 
ii Enabling Access to Critical Infrastructure & Technical Facilities 
IN-SPACe enables & facilitates NGEs to access ISRO’s capital intensive testing 
facilities and launch infrastructure. IN-SPACe also facilitates NGEs to access & 
utilize standard test facilities at the IN-SPACe Technical labs established exclusively 
for developing and testing their technologies. All these facilities are offered to the 
Start-up and MSME at a price support. 
IN-SPACe in collaboration with ISRO, facilitates the opportunity to host payloads on 
POEM (PSLV orbital experimental module) platform to strengthen / complement the 
space-based research activities taking place in industry/academia within the country. 
IN-SPACe has also setup mechanisms to provide expert mentorship, and guidance to 
help NGEs develop & commercialize space technologies. 
iii Financial Support & Handholding for Space Startups and MSEs 
To accelerate promising start-ups, IN-SPACe had launched Seed Fund scheme to 
provide initial financial assistance to Indian early-stage space start-ups through a 

21 
 
grant of up to INR 1 cr. Under this scheme so far six (06) start-ups qualified for seed 
funding. 
Venture Capital Fund for Indian Space Sector: RFP for selection of Fund Managers to 
manage ₹1,000 Crore Venture Capital Fund for the Indian Space Sector issued in 
November-2024. Four (4) bids are received and are under evaluation. 
Technology Adoption Fund (TAF), a scheme to promote Indian Enterprise towards 
commercialization of early-stage technologies in the space sector is announced. 
iv Transfer of Technology (ToT) 
IN-SPACe, ISRO and NSIL have initiated the process for transfer of Small Satellite 
Launch Vehicle (SSLV) technology to Indian Entity. Good number of responses to 
the RFP is received. Further evaluation is in progress.  
v Access to Orbital Resources & Standardization

4.10  ISRO Head Quarters 
The Committee notes that the allocation for ISRO Headquarters has decreased 
marginally by 4.88% from ₹226.08 crore in RE 2024-25 to ₹215.05 crore in BE 2025-26. The 
Committee inquired into the factors that have contributed to this reduction. The Committee 
asked the Department the manner in which it plans to optimize costs and maintain efficiency

subhead ISRO headquarters is mainly on account of reduced requirement towards online

administers the activities of ISRO Centres / Units and projects and provides programmatic 
directions for different verticals of space programme such as space transportation systems,

administrative and operational activities of ISRO headquarters. In case of additional 
requirements, the Department would approach the Ministry of Finance for additional funds at 
RE stage and through the mechanism of supplementary Grants. 
4.11  The Committee recommends that ISRO Headquarters should continue 
streamlining expenditure through improved cost optimisation measures, particularly in 
areas such as IT infrastructure, subscriptions, and operational expenses. The

spectrograph, positioning India among a select group of nations with exoplanet detection 
capabilities; PRL’s Alpha Particle X-ray Spectrometer (APXS) on Chandrayaan-3’s Pragyan

5.3   National Atmospheric Research Laboratory (NARL)  
NARL conducts advanced research in atmospheric and space sciences, focusing on 
monitoring atmospheric processes, high-resolution weather modelling, and scientific 
observations to support space missions and other applications. It has developed high-power 
radio and optical instruments, many of which have been patented and transferred to industry. 
The Department informed that observatories in Hyderabad and Kolkata have been established 
to study key national issues, while the Venus Advanced Radar and Differential Absorption 
Lidar have been developed for planetary and atmospheric studies. NARL has also introduced 
AI/ML-based techniques for weather forecasting and atmospheric data analysis, built GNSS 
receiver networks for ionospheric and meteorological research, and improved rocket launch 
weather forecasting models. The airglow laboratory in Hyderabad and spectrograph in 
Gadanki contribute to studying atmospheric dynamics and space weather. Over 6.8 TB of 
climate data has been shared with scientists, and 184 research papers have been published in 
peer-reviewed journals. The institute has produced 17 PhDs and 97 dissertations, with many 
faculty members receiving national and international honours, including recognition from 
Stanford University, INSA, and the International Commission for Optics. Looking ahead, 
NARL aims to expand its research facilities, setting up more observatories across the country 
and establishing a national-level observational network. It seeks to develop indigenous 

26 
 
ground-based and space-borne instruments, enhance weather forecasting through water 
vapour and ionospheric mapping, and study the impact of rapid urbanisation on atmospheric 
conditions. The institute is also committed to strengthening collaboration with academic and 
national laboratories to achieve significant advancements in atmospheric and space research.

6. Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) Activities in the Department of Space 
The Committee notes that Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) activities within the 
Department of Space are carried out by two Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs), 
namely Antrix Corporation Ltd and NewSpace India Limited (NSIL), in compliance with the 
Companies Act, 2013. Both entities allocate CSR funds to various social development 
projects, following strict guidelines to ensure transparency, accountability, and effective 
implementation. 
6.2 Antrix primarily implements its CSR projects through State Government 
Departments, allocating over 75% of its CSR funds for such initiatives. The selection of 
implementing agencies is conducted through rigorous due diligence, ensuring proven 
experience in social issues, strong governance, financial transparency, and robust monitoring 
mechanisms.  
6.3 NSIL, on the other hand, has established a Corporate Social Responsibility and 
Sustainable Development (CSR & SD) Committee, responsible for recommending CSR 
expenditure, monitoring CSR policies, and formulating an annual action plan. The selection 
of CSR projects follows a structured approach, including inviting proposals through its 
website and from ISRO centres/units. The approval of CSR projects is based on the 
feasibility of implementation, availability of skilled manpower, and previous experience. 
CSR activities may be carried out by the company itself or registered entities such as trusts, 
societies, or government-established organisations that meet the necessary legal and financial 
criteria. 
6.4 The Committee appreciates the structured approach adopted by both Antrix and 
NSIL in implementing CSR initiatives. However, it recommends that greater emphasis 
be placed on monitoring and evaluating the long-term impact of these projects. Given 
that Antrix spends the majority of its CSR funds through State Government 
Departments, the Committee recommends that a performance assessment framework 
be developed to track the effectiveness of these projects. 
6.5 The Committee acknowledges the role of the CSR & SD Committee in 
streamlining CSR initiatives under NSIL but recommends greater outreach to 
underrepresented communities, particularly in rural areas, to ensure that space 
technology and innovation contribute to broader societal benefits. The Committee also 
urges greater collaboration between NSIL and academic institutions, start-ups, and 
ISRO units to leverage space-based applications for social development projects. 
Furthermore, the Committee highlights the importance of ensuring that all CSR-
implementing agencies maintain high standards of governance, transparency, and 
efficiency. The Committee recommends that third-party audits and impact assessments 
be conducted regularly to ensure CSR funds are being utilised effectively and delivering 
measurable outcomes.

7.2 The Committee inquired into the manner in which this shortage will affect the 
efficiency and performance of ISRO and its affiliated PSUs, CPSEs, and Autonomous Bodies 
and the measures being taken to ensure that the Department's missions and projects are not 
impacted due to manpower shortages. The Department acknowledges the pressing issue of 
manpower shortages across ISRO, PSUs, CPSEs, and Autonomous Bodies, which currently 
stands at 3,927 vacancies. The Department informed the Committee that this shortage has 
impacted the operational efficiency and timely execution of projects, particularly as ISRO 
gears up for major missions such as the Bharatiya Antariksh Station (BAS), lunar sample 
return, and human spaceflight to the Moon by 2027. The Department informed the 
Committee that the accumulation of vacancies was primarily due to disruptions caused by 
COVID-19, sectoral reforms, and recruitment policy revisions, leading to a one-year delay in 
hiring. Additionally, security concerns in examination halls led to a four-month halt in 
recruitment activities in 2023, further compounding the backlog. The Department highlighted 
the key measures taken to expedite filling of vacancies which are as follows: 

30 
 
(i) The Department has initiated actions to fill about 1,950 posts before June 2025, with 
written tests and interviews for 1,060 posts underway and reporting planned for 889 selected 
candidates. However, administrative vacancies remain significantly high (2,008 out of 3,062 
positions), indicating challenges in processing personnel recruitment. 
(ii) To  meet the rising demands of space exploration and mission complexity, ISRO has 
proposed augmenting its workforce by at least 500 additional S&T personnel and increasing 
IT personnel by 80 posts to strengthen cyber security monitoring. 
(iii) The Department has implemented a centralised recruitment process under which 
hiring for general disciplines is conducted annually, covering about 70% of staffing needs. 
Additionally, quarterly recruitment monitoring exercises have been introduced to identify and 
resolve bottlenecks in hiring. 
7.3 The Committee recommends expediting the recruitment process to ensure that 
vacant posts, particularly for Scientists/Engineers and technical staff, are filled within 
the next six months. A dedicated recruitment task force should be established to oversee 
hiring efficiency, identify process bottlenecks, and ensure compliance with recruitment 
timelines. The Committee recommends that the Department must develop a structured 
workforce planning model, forecasting staffing needs for the next decade in alignment 
with ISRO’s Vision 2047. The Committee is concerned about the high vacancy rate in 
NSIL and Antrix, as it may impact India’s growing commercial space sector. It 
recommends an industry-specific recruitment approach to attract talent from both 
public and private space technology domains, ensuring that PSEs remain competitive 
and capable of supporting ISRO’s missions. 
7.4 The Committee supports the Department’s plan to engage S&T personnel on a 
tenure basis but recommends that flexible hiring models be expanded to include 
project-based contracts for emerging space technologies. 
7.5 The Committee notes that the backlog in hiring was caused partly due to delays 
during the COVID-19 period and recruitment policy revisions. It recommends 
increasing the frequency of centralised recruitment drives to ensure that vacancies do 
not accumulate in the future. Quarterly recruitment monitoring exercises should be 
conducted to track hiring progress and address any procedural challenges.

9. The Chairman welcomed the Secretary, Department of Space and his team of officers 
and asked them to give a brief presentation on the Demands for Grants (2025-26). Thereafter, 
The Secretary began his presentation by providing an overview of the Department of Space, 
highlighting its major components, including the Indian Space Research Organisation 
(ISRO), the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorization Centre (IN-SPACe), and the 
New Space India Limited (NSIL). He explained that ISRO, being the primary component, is 
responsible for research and development in launch vehicles, satellite applications, planetary 
exploration, and the human spaceflight program. He then presented the major 
accomplishments of the Department of Space over the years, starting from the first sounding 
rocket launch in 1963 to the recent successful missions such as Chandrayaan-3, Aditya-L1, 
and the XPoSat satellite. He highlighted that India has launched 4,002 sounding rockets, 
accomplished 100 launch vehicle missions, and built 131 satellites, including the heaviest 
satellite, GSAT-11, weighing 6,000 kg. He also mentioned that India has launched 433 
satellites for 34 foreign countries, demonstrating its capability in the global space arena. He 
elaborated on the recent achievements of ISRO, including the successful launch of the 
XPoSat satellite on January 1, 2025; INSAT-3DS meteorological satellite and  the successful 
docking experiment conducted in January 2025, which positioned India as the fourth country 
to achieve this feat. He stated that this experiment is crucial for future missions, including the 
development of a space station and the Gaganyaan human spaceflight program. He further 
highlighted the progress in the Gaganyaan program, including the human rating of launch 
vehicles, the development of the orbital module, and the crew escape system. He mentioned 
that the first uncrewed mission is planned for 2025, followed by two more uncrewed missions 
and a crewed mission. While informing about the development of a Next-Generation Launch 
Vehicle (NGLV) capable of placing 30,000 kg into low Earth orbit, he explained that the 
NGLV would use a liquid oxygen and methane propulsion system, which is reusable and 
more cost-effective. Additionally, he highlighted the development of atomic clocks and 
Traveling Wave Tube Amplifiers (TWTAs), which are critical for navigation and 
communication satellites. He also informed about the Department’s plans for India's first 
space station, with the first module targeted for launch by 2028 and the complete space 
station by 2035. He further elaborated on the Chandrayaan-4 and Chandrayaan-5 missions, 
which aims to bring back lunar samples and conduct more advanced lunar exploration.

for green propulsion technology and the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in satellite 
health monitoring and disaster management, underutilization of funds in previous years and

1 
 
REPORT  
INTRODUCTION 
The Ministry of Environment, Forest & Climate Change (MoEF&CC) is the nodal 
agency in the administrative structure of the Central Government for planning, promoting, 
coordinating and overseeing environmental, ecological, forestry and wildlife policies and 
programmes. Its main activities include conservation and survey of natural resources 
including flora, fauna, forests, wildlife, aquatic bodies and water resources and eco-systems, 
prevention and control of pollution and management of hazardous substances, protection of 
the environment and forests, including their biodiversity, mitigation and adaptation to 
climate change through measures that include afforestation, regeneration of degraded areas, 
and adoption of cleaner technologies, and promoting sustainable development and better 
environmental governance while protecting human, plants and animals life, health and 
welfare.  
1.2 These objectives are well supported by a set of legislative and regulatory measures, 
aimed at the preservation, conservation and protection of the environment. Besides the 
legislative measures, a National Conservation Strategy and Policy Statement on 
Environment and Development, 1992, National Forest Policy, 1988, a Policy Statement on 
Abatement of Pollution, 1992 and a National Environment Policy, 2006 also guide the 
Ministry’s work.  
1.3 The main tools used to discharge its mandate include, inter alia, conducting surveys; 
collecting, compiling and disseminating data and information; undertaking scientific 
research, extension services and analyses; carrying out impact assessment of developmental 
projects and programmes; regulating use of natural resources; undertaking regeneration 
programmes; extending technical, scientific, financial and administrative support to 
organisations and institutions in the subject fields; imparting education, training, building 
capacity and generating awareness among stakeholders and the public at large; and 
promoting international cooperation through bilateral, regional and multilateral initiatives in 
environment and ecology. 
1.4 The institutional set up of the Ministry includes a number of Directorates and 
Divisions assembled around the main thematic sectors of environment and ecology, forestry 
and wildlife, afforestation and eco-development. The Ministry has 20 Regional Offices; ten 
Attached/Subordinate Offices (e.g. Botanical, Zoological and Forests Surveys of India, 
Directorate of Forestry Education, Indira Gandhi National Forestry Academy, National 
Green Tribunal, Wildlife Crime Control Bureau etc.); Boards and Authorities (e.g. Central 
Pollution Control Board, National Biodiversity Authority, National Tiger Conservation 
Authority, Central Zoo Authority) and Autonomous Institutions (e.g. Indian Council for 
Forestry Research and Education, Wildlife Institute of India etc.). Provision has been made 
in the Demand for Grants for the year 2025-26 for its attached/ subordinate/ autonomous 
organisations and other bodies. 
FUNCTIONING AND ACTIVITIES OF THE MINISTRY 
1.5 The Mission of Ministry of Environment, Forest & Climate Change is to plan, 
promote, co-ordinate and oversee the implementation of India’s environmental and forestry 
policies and programmes related to conservation of the country’s natural resources including 
its lakes and rivers, its biodiversity, forests and wildlife, ensuring the welfare of animals, 
and the prevention and abatement of pollution. The Ministry seeks to ensure inclusive 
economic growth guided by the principles of sustainable development and enhancement of 
human well-being.

5. CONTROL OF POLLUTION 
5.1 The Ministry of Environment, Forest & Climate Change administers the Central 
Sector Scheme-‘Control of Pollution’ to curb environmental pollution since 2018-19.  For 
the FY 2025-26, the total budget (under BE) of the scheme is Rs.853.9 crore.  The main 
objective of the Control of Pollution scheme is to monitor air quality across the country and 
take appropriate air pollution mitigation measures, besides monitoring water quality and 
noise levels in the country. The components under the scheme are as under: 
(a) Assistance for Abatement of Pollution to weaker SPCBs/PCCs-Under this 
component State Pollution Control Boards (SPCBs)/Pollution Control 
Committee (PCCs) are supported to meet the expenditure requirements for taking 
pollution abatement activity including pollution assessment (Source monitoring, 
monitoring of ambient air, water and noise), technical studies for R&D, survey 
and documentation for creation of environmental database and consultation in 
the area of pollution abatement of air, water & noise, scientific research and 
studies on issues of waste management, inventorisation of wastes, training and 
mass awareness, education, seminars/workshops/conference, lab upgradation/ 
procurement of equipment,  E- Governance and IT applications including online 
consent management, online emission/effluent monitoring systems, development 
of IT infrastructure. 
(b) National Clean Air Programme (NCAP): The National Clean Air Programme 
(NCAP) was launched by Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change 
in January 2019 with an aim to improve air quality in 130 cities (Non-Attainment 
cities and Million-Plus cities) in 24 States/Union Territories (UTs) by engaging 
all stakeholders. The NCAP envisages reduction by 20-30% in PM10 
concentrations by 2024-25 over baseline in the year 2017-18. Target has been 
revised to achieve reduction in PM10 level up to 40% over baseline in the year 
2019-20 or achievement of national ambient air quality standards (60 
microgram/cubic meter) by 2025-26. Annual PM10 reduction target of 4-15% has 
been assigned to each city to improve air quality through implementation of City 
Action Plans. The Ministry has issued guidelines for release and utilization of 
funds under the sub-component. Further, in case of 48 Million-Plus cities /Urban 
Agglomerations funded under 15th Finance Commission Air Quality Grant, 15% 
reduction in PM10 concentrations and 15% improvement in good days (Air 
Quality Index<200) w.r.t. previous year have been considered.   
(c) Following Components come under Environmental Monitoring Network 
Programme:- 

12 
 
i. Operation and Maintenance of National Air Quality Monitoring 
Programme (NAMP) stations 
ii. Operation and Maintenance of Continuous Ambient Air Quality 
Monitoring Stations (CAAQMS) 
iii. National Ambient Noise Monitoring Network (NANMN) – strengthening 
and establishment of New Stations in Million Plus Cities 
iv. National Water Monitoring Programme (NWMP)                      
(d) Research and Outreach Programmes - The Ministry is providing funds to the 
projects which have impact for prevention and control of pollution. Under 
this component of the scheme, the Ministry proposes to provide funds to the 
Research and Development (R&D) projects, which can advance emerging 
technologies and solutions in control and prevention of pollution and 
implementing decision support systems. This component also includes 
developing indigenous facilities for certification, testing and calibration of air 
quality monitoring equipment, and National Environmental Health Profile 
(NEHP) study. NEHP study aims to assess impact of air pollution on human 
health in selected cities across the country.

5.3 The Committee was surprised to observe that out of the RE 2024-25 allocation of 
Rs.858.00 crore for ‘Control of Pollution’, only an amount of Rs.7.22 crore was spent upto 
31.1.2025.  The Committee desired to know the reasons therefor from the Ministry.  In their 
reply, the Ministry informed that the utilisation of majority of the funds in the scheme for 
the financial year 2024-25 could not be made till now as the approval for the continuation of 
the ‘Control of Pollution’ scheme till FY 2025-26 is awaited. Planning for disbursement and 
utilization of the funds are already in place and will be executed as soon as approval is 
received.  Further, the Ministry intends to spend the budget of Rs.853.00 crore for FY 2025-
26 under Control of Pollution Scheme under various components of the scheme as per the 
approval. 
5.4 The Committee is of the view that pollution, whether it be air, water or noise, 
has gone beyond permissible limits during the last few years and has serious 
consequences for the health and well being of the citizens of the country. Air pollution 
has assumed gigantic proportions and has become a national issue.  Although Delhi has 
been in the news because of it ever-deteriorating air quality, other cities in the country 
are also not left behind and are experiencing high AQI levels.  In such a scenario, the 
Committee is shocked to note that amount to the tune of Rs. 858.00 crore allocated for 
‘Control of Pollution’, which is 27.44% of the annual RE allocation of the Ministry, 
remains unutilized since the approval for continuation of Control of Pollution Scheme 
till 2025-26, is awaited, even at the fag end of the financial year.  The rising 
environmental pollution in the country not only results into a number of pollution 
related human diseases and health conditions but negatively impact our ecology too.  
The scenario of air pollution in the country is indeed very grim and has been affecting 

13 
 
one and all.  At a time when the Ministry is required to address the grave and critical 
challenge of deteriorating air quality, the Ministry has not been able to decide the 
continuation of the concerned scheme, as a result of which not even 1% of the funds 
allocated for the scheme have been utilized so far.  The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry needs to introspect and take a serious note of the 
reasons for this gross underutilization.

Development of Wildlife Habitats 
6.3 The ‘Development of Wildlife Habitats’ (DWH) is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme. 
The overall objective of the scheme is conservation and management of PAs, recovery of 
endangered species, mitigating man-animal conflict, and voluntary relocation of families 
for creating inviolate space for wild animals, healthier ecosystem and repository as source 
for gene pool.  The Protected Area (PA) network in country comprises of 106 National 
Parks, 573 Wildlife Sanctuaries, 123 Conservation Reserves and 220 community reserves 
extending over an area of 1,78,640.69 sq.km., which is 5.43% of the geographical area of 
the country.  The components of the scheme are (i) Support to Protected areas, (ii) 
Protection of Wildlife outside Protected Areas and (iii) Recovery Programmes for saving 
Critically Endangered Species and habitats.  
Project Tiger & Elephant 
6.4 The Ministry provides financial assistance to the States/UTs under the Centrally 
Sponsored Scheme Project Tiger & Elephant for the protection of elephants, their habitats & 
corridors, welfare of captive elephant and mitigation of human elephant conflict.

are fulfilled through several programmes and schemes; mostly financed through annual 
budget of Government of India.  34 States/Union Territories (UTs) prepared State Action 
Plan for Climate Change (SAPCC); and 12 States and UTs updated in line with NAPCC. 
The Committee was further informed that on 30th December, 2024, India submitted its 4th 
Biennial Update Report to the UNFCCC.  The Ministry also provided the following 
information on India’s quantitative NDCs and NDC Update:

7.2 It was informed that India is on track to meet its global commitments towards global 
collective efforts to combat climate change and that some of the Targets under India first 
NDC, submitted in 2015, have been achieved ahead of stipulated timeline (2021-30). 
7.3 The Committee desired to know from the Ministry that given the commitments 
under India’s Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) to the Paris Agreement, how 
does this budget support India’s goal of achieving a 45% reduction in emissions intensity by 
2030?  In response, the Committee was informed that India is a Party to three treaties 
governing the International Climate Regime; namely the United Nations Framework 
Convention on the Climate Change (UNFCCC), its Kyoto Protocol and Paris Agreement. 
Under the Paris Agreement of the UNFCCC, India has submitted and subsequently updated 
its Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) to the UNFCCC. India’s current NDC is for 
the period of 2021-2030. In addition, India has also submitted its Long-Term Low Carbon 
Development Strategy to reach net-zero by 2070. 
7.4 The Government earlier committed to finance India’s climate action, which cuts 
across various sectors important for our economy, through annual budget exercise.  On 
these lines, and like the previous budgets, Union Budget 2025-26 has provisioned series of 
measures including those for energy sector reforms, nuclear energy development, clean 
technology manufacturing, lithium-ion battery production, and increase in budgetary 
allocations for the Ministry of Power and the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy from 
the previous year and for enhancing climate resilience. Some of the salient announcements 
are as under:  
(a) A “National Manufacturing Mission” to cover small, medium, and large industries is 
announced. Recognizing our commitment to climate-friendly development, the 
Mission will also support Clean Tech manufacturing. The aim is to improve 
domestic value addition and build our ecosystem for solar PV cells, EV batteries, 
motors, and controllers, electrolyzers, wind turbines, very high voltage transmission 
equipment and grid scale batteries.  
(b) Nuclear Energy Mission for Viksit Bharat: -The Budget recognizes the importance 
of nuclear energy in reaching to net-zero. Towards this, the Budget has provisioned 

18 
 
development of at least 100 GW of nuclear energy by 2047. It is essential for our 
energy transition efforts. For an active partnership with the private sector towards 
this goal, amendments to the Atomic Energy Act and the Civil Liability for Nuclear 
Damage Act have been proposed. A Nuclear Energy Mission for research & 
development of Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) with an outlay of Rs. 20,000 crore 
is proposed through which at least 5 indigenously developed SMRs will be 
operationalized by 2033. 
(c) The budget also emphasizes expanding the electric vehicle ecosystem, strengthening 
domestic battery manufacturing, supporting startups, and enhancing green financing 
for EV adoption and energy storage solutions. In the context of battery 
manufacturing; the Budget has announced Mining sector reforms, including those 
for minor minerals, including a policy for recovery of critical minerals from tailings. 
The Budget has also proposed to add to the list of exempted capital goods, 35 
additional capital goods for EV battery manufacturing, and 28 additional capital 
goods for mobile phone battery manufacturing. This is to boost domestic 
manufacture of lithium-ion battery, including those required for electric vehicles. 
(d) For enhancing the resilience of agriculture sector, the Budget has proposed Prime 
Minister Dhan-Dhaanya Krishi Yojana; 6-year Mission for Aatmanirbharta in 
Pulses; Comprehensive Programme for Vegetables & Fruits; National Mission on 
High Yielding Seeds; and Mission for Cotton Productivity. The Budget also 
proposes a framework for sustainable harnessing of fisheries from Indian Exclusive 
Economic Zone and High Seas.   
(e) To further enhance India’s action towards adapting to the climate change in water 
sector, the Budget has announced the extension of the Jal Jeevan Mission until 2028 
with an enhanced total outlay. 
7.5 The Committee is of the view that Climate change is a global concern and India, 
being amongst the most populous countries, needs to be concerned about that. Our 
National Action Plan for Climate Change (NAPCC) has missions in areas like solar 
energy, energy efficiency, water, human health, sustainable agriculture, Himalayan 
ecosystem, sustainable habitat, and strategic knowledge of climate change. We must 
cooperate with other countries globally, as climate summits, after the Paris Agreement, 
have shown slow progress.  While taking progressive steps, India must correlate her 
efforts with other countries. The Committee notes that the new U.S. administration's 
withdrawal from climate funding is a matter of concern, as they had committed to 
contributing $100 billion to the climate fund under the Paris Agreement.  Not only 
have they backed out, but even the international organizations, like, the WHO has 
shown its reservations. Under these circumstances, India, being a large country and 
being a major player in climate change mitigation, must take responsibility and work 
towards achieving its goals. 
7.6 During the meeting, the Committee also drew attention of the Ministry to the 
reports that in view of the recent climatic trends, the coming months of the year 2025-
26 are likely to see temperatures soaring to 1-3°C higher than the average 
temperatures recorded in the past across various cities and terrains of the country, 
especially Delhi where the temperature may be abnormally high during the summer 
season of 2026.  The Committee is extremely concerned over such alarming reports. 
The Committee is of the view that, if this happens, it will have devastating 
consequences for human habitats, birds, animals, and the environment.  The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Environment, Forest & 
Climate Change should immediately formulate and implement a national-level Heat 
Action Plan (HAP) to mitigate the heatwave conditions that the citizens of India are 
likely to face in the coming months.  

19 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS-AT A GLANCE 
BUDGETARY DETAILS FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2024-25 AND 
ALLOCATION FOR 2025-26 
 The Committee observes that the Ministry had been able to utilize more than 
96% of the allocated funds during the year 2022-23 and 2023-24.In 2024-25, against the 
BE allocation of Rs.3330.00 crore, a reduced RE allocation of Rs.3125.96 was made to 
the Ministry.  However, the Committee is constrained to note that the actual 
expenditure of the Ministry upto 31.1.2025 was only Rs.1712.48 crore which is merely 
54.78% of the RE allocation.  During the presentation made before the Committee on 
19.2.2025, the Secretary of the Ministry further informed the Committee that the 
Ministry has utilized 69% of the funds as on that date.  However, the Committee is of 
the view that the utilization of funds by the Ministry during 2024-25 is not satisfactory.  
With hardly 40 days left in the completion of the financial year, the Ministry is yet to 
make use of more than 30% of the funds allocated to it.  This is in sharp contrast to the 
utilization of funds by the Ministry during the past two financial years when the 
Ministry was able to utilize more than 96% of the budgetary allocations.  The 
Committee is of the view that the Ministry must make proactive efforts to optimally 
utilize the funds made available to it during the financial year 2024-25.          (Para 2.3) 
 
BARE MINIMUM REQUIREMENTS IN BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS FOR 
SUSTAINING KEY PROGRAMMES 
 The Committee takes note of the challenges projected by the Ministry in Budget 
allocation in Key programmes and the bare minimum budgetary requirements 
projected by it for sustaining certain key programmes.  Though the Committee is in 
agreement with the requirements projected by the Ministry, the utilization of funds by 
the Ministry in 2024-25 are not encouraging enough for the Committee to make any 
positive recommendations in this regard.  The Committee would, however, like to 
recommend that in 2025-26, the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change 
should make proactive efforts to ensure that the physical targets of the Ministry in 
respect of the above schemes/programmes are on schedule and the allocation made at 
BE is utilised to the maximum so that it is on a firm ground to seek additional funds at 
the Supplementary and RE stage in respect of the schemes/programmes stated above.  
(Para 2.5) 
MAJOR THRUST AREAS  
 The Committee is of the opinion that the launching of the campaign to plant 
trees on the occasion of World Environment Day is indeed laudable.  The Committee 
feels that the campaign to plant a tree in honour of a mother would certainly create a 
lasting legacy that nurtures both the environment and a greener, prosperous future.  
The Committee notes that 118 crore had already been planted as on 19th February 
2025 and hopes that the Ministry would be able to achieve its target of planting 140 
crore trees by 31st March 2025.                                                                              (Para 3.4) 
 The Committee would, however, like to point out that although a number of 
plantation activities are undertaken on various occasions, the mortality rate of such 
plants is very high.  There is a need not only to plant the trees but also to ensure that 
once planted, they are looked after well and continue to survive and grow.  The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should not only undertake 
plantation activities but should also ensure that the survival rate of these plants 
remains high so that they continue to contribute to the environment and the society. 
This also needs to be emphasized to the youth/children etc. when organizing 
workshops, exhibitions, campaigns, competitions etc. by the concerned 

20 
 
Central/State/UT authorities.  There is also a need for audit of the plantation activities, 
so that the allocations made in this regard are utilized optimally.                     (Para 3.5) 
The Committee is also of the view that Centrally-funded schemes are crucial 
because they provide funds to other States for improving their systems. Facilitating 
research and development and investing for the same are extremely important for the 
development of any nation and for a developing country like India, the critical 
importance of environmental education, awareness, Research and Development cannot 
be overemphasized, as education and awareness only can help finding practical 
solutions to problems of environmental protection and management and for developing 
policies, strategies, action plans and in better management and conservation of natural 
resources. The Committee feels that the allocation of Rs. 101.96 crore allocated for 
‘Environment Education, Awareness, Research and Skill Development’ is not adequate 
and the Ministry should consider allocating additional funds to this head.       (Para 3.6) 
NATIONAL COASTAL MISSION 
 The Committee is not convinced with the reply furnished by the Ministry with 
regard to the allocations made to the National Coastal Mission during the last few years.  
The allocation was reduced from Rs.196.00 crore (BE) to Rs.4.00 crore (RE) in 2022-23.  
In 2023-24, the allocation was increased from Rs.12.50 crore (BE) to Rs.43.30 crore

crore (RE), out of which the Ministry has been able to spend only 13.8% i.e. Rs.1.10

are being allocated and utilized in an adhoc and unplanned manner.  The Committee is 
of the view that, keeping in view the importance of the Mission, the Ministry should 
holistically plan the execution of the scheme and ensure that the funds are suitably 
allocated and optimally utilized.                                                                                (Para 4.4) 
CONTROL OF POLLUTION 
 The Committee is of the view that pollution, whether it be air, water or noise, 
has gone beyond permissible limits during the last few years and has serious 
consequences for the health and well being of the citizens of the country. Air pollution 
has assumed gigantic proportions and has become a national issue.  Although Delhi has 
been in the news because of it ever-deteriorating air quality, other cities in the country 
are also not left behind and are experiencing high AQI levels.  In such a scenario, the 
Committee is shocked to note that amount to the tune of Rs.858.00 crore allocated for 
‘Control of Pollution’, which is 27.44% of the annual RE allocation of the Ministry, 
remains unutilized since the approval for continuation of Control of Pollution Scheme 
till 2025-26, is awaited, even at the fag end of the financial year.  The rising 
environmental pollution in the country not only results into a number of pollution 
related human diseases and health conditions but negatively impact our ecology too.  
The scenario of air pollution in the country is indeed very grim and has been affecting 
one and all.  At a time when the Ministry is required to address the grave and critical 
challenge of deteriorating air quality, the Ministry has not been able to decide the 
continuation of the concerned scheme, as a result of which not even 1% of the funds 
allocated for the scheme have been utilized so far.  The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry needs to introspect and take a serious note of the 
reasons for this gross underutilization.                                                                 (Para 5.4)

 The Committee notes that the financial performance of the Ministry under this 
scheme had been satisfactory during the last three years.  The Ministry was able to

21 
 
January 2025.  The Committee hopes that the Ministry would be able to fully utilize 
the allocations under this head by the end of the financial year.                       (Para 6.2) 
INTEGRATED DEVELOPMENT OF WILDLIFE HABITATS 
 The Committee observes that state governments receive funds under centrally 
sponsored schemes such as Project Tiger and Elephant and the scheme for 
Development of Wildlife Habitats for the maintenance of protected areas notified

Committee is of the view that no amount of compensation can compensate the loss of a

should be on minimizing and mitigating the human-animal conflict rather than merely 
providing adequate compensation to the victims of the conflict. The Committee further 
recommends that the Ministry should impress upon all the State Governments to take 
necessary action in this regard so that the loss of human lives / injuries due to the 
attack by wild animals is reduced to the minimum.  There is also a need to 
clarify/reiterate the role of the State Forest Officials in such cases so that the required

INTRODUCTION 
 
 Earth System Science deals with all the five components of the Earth 
System, viz., Atmosphere, Hydrosphere, Cryosphere, Geosphere, and 
Biosphere, and their complex interactions. The Ministry of Earth Sciences 
(MoES) holistically addresses all the aspects relating to the Earth System 
Science for providing weather, climate, ocean, coastal state, hydrological, and 
seismological services. The services include forecasts and warnings for various 
natural disasters like tropical cyclones, storm surges, floods, heat waves, 
thunderstorms, and lightning; alerts for Tsunamis and monitoring of 
earthquakes, etc. In addition, the ministry also has the mandate to develop 
technology for ocean surveys and exploration of living and non-living 
resources from the ocean and exploration of all three poles (Arctic, Antarctic, 
and Himalayas). The services provided by the ministry are being effectively 
used by different agencies and state governments to save human lives and 
minimize damages due to natural disasters. 
 
1.2 The mandate of the ministry includes overall policy, planning, 
coordination, implementation, evaluation and review of the schemes relating to 
meteorology, seismology, oceanography, ocean resources and technology, 
polar science, cryosphere and geosciences not specifically allocated to any 
other Department or Ministry.  The overarching vision of the Ministry is 
“Excelling in Earth System Science to make lives better through world class 
services for weather, climate, ocean, coastal and natural hazards; sustainable 
harnessing of ocean resources and exploration of the polar regions”.  The 
Objectives of the Ministry are as under :- 
i. To provide Weather and Climate Services for various sectors like 
disaster management, agriculture, aviation, water resources, power, 
tourism, health, air quality, public safety etc. 
ii. To undertake the Science of Climate Change- Regional Climate Change 
Scenarios. 
iii. To provide Early warnings for Hazards such as Cyclones, Heavy 
Rainfall, Heatwave, etc. 
iv. To provide Ocean Services, which include Tsunami warnings, Potential 
Fishing zone advisories, Ocean State Forecasts, Oil Spill Advisories, 
Coastal Research, and Coastal Protection. 
v. Harnessing of non-living ocean resources - Water, Energy and Minerals 
vi. Ocean living resources mapping, Marine biodiversity, Marine 
Biotechnology

vii. Survey and Exploration of Exclusive Economic Zone and Continental

viii. Earthquake Detection and information, Deep Scientific drilling, Crustal

ix. Scientific exploration of the three poles (Arctic, Antarctic and

x. Develop deep sea technologies for sustainable use of ocean resources, 
and improve our understanding of deep sea. 
xi. R&D and development of technology leading to weather intervention 
xii. To support various Extra-Mural R&D activities, Outreach and 
Awareness activities and Capacity Building in the field of Earth 
Sciences. 
 
1.3 The policies and programs of the Ministry are being primarily pursued 
through its 10 Institutes viz., autonomous bodies, attached and subordinate 
offices.  The institutions dealing with atmospheric sciences are the India 
Meteorological Department (IMD), National Centre for Medium Range 
Weather Forecasting (NCMRWF), Noida and Indian Institute of Tropical 
Meteorology (IITM), Pune.  The institutions related to ocean science and 
technology are National Centre for Polar and Ocean Research (NCPOR), Goa, 
National Institute of Ocean Technology (NIOT), Chennai, Indian National 
Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS), Hyderabad, Centre for 
Marine Living Resources and Ecology (CMLRE), Kochi and National Centre 
for Coastal Research (NCCR), Chennai. The National Centre for Earth Science 
Studies (NCESS), Thiruvananthapuram and National Centre for Seismology 
(NCS), New Delhi conduct research on solid earth and earthquake monitoring. 
Each Centre of the Ministry has a well-defined mandate to conduct research 
and development in a specific area of Earth Sciences.

5. Deep Ocean Mission 
5.1 As a Maritime nation with a coastline of about 7500 km and around 30% 
of the country's population living in coastal areas, oceans play an important 
role in the Indian economy. The Government of India’s Vision of New India by 
2030, enunciated in February 2019, highlighted the Blue Economy as one of 
the ten core dimensions of growth. With a view to exploring the deep ocean for 
resources, developing deep-sea technologies for sustainable use of ocean 
resources, and improving our understanding of the deep sea, the Government 
of India launched the “Deep Ocean Mission” at an estimated cost of Rs.4077.0 
crore for a period of 5 years. This mission mode project will support various 
priority areas illustrated in the Blue Economy policy document of the 
Government of India. Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES) is the nodal 
implementing Ministry for this multi-ministerial, multi-institutional mission.   
5.2 Deep Ocean Mission (DOM) aims to explore deep-oceanic resources and 
develop technologies for their sustainable use. The Mission consists of six 
major themes, namely (i) Development of Technologies for Deep Sea Mining, 
Manned Submersible, and Underwater Robotics; (ii) Development of Ocean 
Climate Change Advisory Services; (iii) Technological innovations for 
exploration and conservation of deep-sea biodiversity; (iv) Deep Ocean Survey 
and Exploration; (v) Energy and freshwater from the Ocean and (vi) Advanced 
Marine Station for Ocean Biology. The mission involves mapping of floors of 
Deep Oceans and development of technologies like a manned submersible with 
6000m water depth rating, mining system for deep sea mining, sustainable 
utilization of deep-sea bioresources and developing engineering designs for 
offshore thermal energy-driven desalination plants. Human capacity will be

6. Prithvi Vigyan (PRITHVI) 
6.1 Ministry of Earth Sciences is mandated to translate Science to Services 
for Society in providing services for weather, climate, ocean and coastal state, 
hydrology, seismology, and natural hazards; to explore and harness marine 
living and non-living resources in a sustainable manner for the country and to 
explore the three poles of the Earth (Arctic, Antarctic and Himalayas).  
PRITHVI Scheme deals with the study of various aspects of Ocean, Polar and 
Cryosphere with Special emphasis on the Antarctic, Arctic, Southern Ocean 
and Himalayas, Seismological and Geo-science as well as Research Education, 
Training and Outreach.  All the earlier schemes, viz. Ocean Services, 
Modelling Application, Resources and Technology (O-SMART), Polar Science 
and Cryosphere Research (PACER), Seismology and Geosciences (SAGE) and 
Research, Education, Training and Outreach (REACHOUT) have been merged 
together in the PRITHVI scheme.   
6.2 The overarching scheme of PRITHVI will holistically address all the 
five components of earth system to improve the understanding of the Earth 
System Sciences and to provide reliable services for the country.  The major 
Objectives of the Prithvi Scheme are:  
 Augmentation and sustenance of long-term observations of the 
atmosphere, ocean, geosphere, cryosphere and solid earth to record the 
vital signs of the Earth System and change 
 Development of modelling systems for understanding and predicting 
weather, ocean and climate hazards and understanding the science of 
climate change 
 Exploration polar and high seas regions of the Earth towards the 
discovery of new phenomena and resources;  
 Development of technology for exploration and sustainable harnessing 
of oceanic resources for societal applications 
 Translation of knowledge and insights from Earth systems science 
into services for societal, environmental and economic benefit.

7. Mission Mausam  
7.1 This scheme has been designed to enhance India's weather and climate 
forecasting capabilities across various critical sectors, including agriculture, 
aviation, urban planning, defense, sports, and disaster preparedness. The 
mission seeks to leverage cutting-edge technologies, high-performance 
computing, and advanced modeling techniques to revolutionize weather 
monitoring, prediction, and data analysis. By advancing weather surveillance, 
incorporating next-generation radars and satellites, and utilizing artificial 
intelligence and machine learning, Mission Mausam aims to provide more 
accurate and timely forecasts, addressing the challenges of extreme weather 
events and climate change. The program also focuses on building robust 
infrastructure, fostering innovation, and ensuring that weather-related 
information reaches the public effectively, contributing to national 
development, disaster management, and climate resilience. Through its 
comprehensive approach, Mission Mausam aims to establish an integrated 
framework for advanced weather and climate prediction in India.   
7.2 The Government of India has approved the Mission Mausam with a 
financial outlay of ₹ 2000 crore with Rs. 1500 crore being additional 
allocation, and the remaining Rs.500 crore is drawn from the PRITHVI scheme 
(ACROSS sub-scheme) of the MoES, which was approved earlier.

Mission Mausam is designed to provide highly accurate forecasts across 
multiple time scales: 
(i) Short-Term (up to 72 hours): High-resolution forecasts using data 
from advanced observation systems like radars, wind profilers, and 
satellites, combined with real-time computational models for rapid 
prediction. 
(ii) Medium-Term (3 to 15 days): Enhanced weather predictions utilizing 
advanced modeling techniques and HPC resources for greater 
accuracy.

weather and climate patterns over months or seasons.

Mausam will have a profound impact on sectors like agriculture, disaster 
management, and transportation, enabling better preparedness and more 
effective responses to climate and weather events. The mission’s integrated 
approach will help deliver more precise, timely, and actionable forecasts,

8. High-Performance Computing System 
8.1 The High-Performance Computing (HPC) systems deployed across 
various institutes of the Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES) in previous plan 
periods have been crucial in enhancing the accuracy of weather forecasts and 
advancing research and development over the past decade. These HPC systems 
have facilitated seamless data assimilation and the generation of precise 
forecasts with extended lead times from both global and regional Numerical 
Weather Prediction (NWP) models, leading to significant improvements in 
weather, climate, and ocean state predictions. The proposed scheme aims to 
establish a petaflops-scale HPC facility for MoES institutes to support 
numerical modelling for weather and climate forecasting, basic research, and 
data assimilation. It will also provide computational resources to the academic 
and R&D community, to undertake research and development and enable 
improvements in operational forecasting systems and enhance forecast skill.

visualization environment to support state-of-the-art Big Data Analytics and
