COUNCIL OF SCIENTIFIC & INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH (CSIR) 
 
Recommendation/ Observation 
 
2.7 The Committee recognizes the pivotal role played by CSIR in driving research, innovation, 
and technological advancements across diverse domains. As one of the premier research 
organizations in the country, CSIR has contributed significantly to scientific breakthroughs, 
industrial applications, and the development of indigenous technologies that have strengthened 
national self-reliance. Its extensive research network, spanning multiple disciplines, has facilitated 
advancements in healthcare, engineering sciences, environmental sustainability, agriculture, and 
emerging technologies, thereby supporting India's economic and strategic objectives. 
(Para 4.4 ibid) 
 
Action Taken: 
 

 
11 
 
2.8 The Department along with CSIR sincerely acknowledges the Committee’s appreciation 
and recognition. 
 
Recommendation/ Observation 
 
2.9 However, the Committee notes with concern that CSIR has substantial overlaps in research 
activities with other scientific institutions, including the Ministry of Earth Sciences, the 
Department of Biotechnology, the Department of Science and Technology, the Ministry of 
Electronics and Information Technology, the Indian Agricultural Research Institute, etc. This 
duplication of research efforts leads to fragmentation of resources, inefficiencies in execution, and 
a lack of cohesive direction in national scientific pursuits. The Committee strongly recommends 
that CSIR undertake a comprehensive restructuring to optimize its research priorities, ensuring a 
sharper focus on projects that are highly critical, have a substantial impact, and align with the 
country's strategic interests. The Committee urges CSIR to realign its research portfolio by 
concentrating on areas of national importance where it can deliver unparalleled expertise and 
breakthrough innovations. Rather than engaging in research that overlaps with other institutions, 
CSIR should collaborate with relevant Ministries and research organizations to ensure synergy 
rather than redundancy. By leveraging its strengths in cutting-edge technologies, translational 
research and industrial applications, CSIR can maximize its contribution to India's scientific and 
economic development. The Committee also recommends that CSIR establish a clear roadmap to 
prioritize high-impact research, streamline its organizational structure, and enhance its role as a 
leader in addressing national challenges. A well-defined and strategic approach will not only 
enhance CSIR's efficiency but also position it as a key driver of India's scientific and technological 
advancement in critical sectors. 
(Para 4.5 ibid) 
 
Action Taken: 
 
2.10 CSIR acknowledges the Committee’s concerns regarding perceived overlaps in research 
activities with other scientific institutions. However, it is important to clarify that what may appear 
as duplication is, in many instances, a reflection of necessary convergence in addressing complex, 
multidisciplinary national challenges. Scientific research today, by its very nature, involves 
intersecting domains where coordinated efforts are essential to generate comprehensive and 
impactful outcomes. 
CSIR’s research programs are designed with a focus on translational and industrial applications, 
aiming to deliver end-to-end solutions, develop indigenous technologies, and enhance national 
self-reliance. Thus, CSIR’s mandate centers on converting knowledge into deployable 
technologies, prototypes, and processes that serve India's industry, strategic sectors, and societal 
needs. This translational emphasis distinguishes CSIR’s contributions from those of other 
organizations working in similar areas. A part of CSIR’s activities that seemingly overlap with 
other agencies (such as genome sequencing initiatives with DBT, etc.) are specifically meant to 
generate redundancy, aiming towards improving the quality and robustness of data. 
CSIR actively collaborates with other scientific ministries and agencies, including MoES, DBT, 
DST, MeitY, and ICAR, through joint initiatives, co-funded programs, and shared platforms. 
These partnerships ensure synergy and resource optimization as well as effective exchange of 
scientific knowledge among sister ministries/departments. Few of the examples about inter 
departmental/ ministerial collaboration are as below: 
 

 
12 
 
1. CSIR has been undertaking a nationally important project entitled “Indian Breast Cancer 
Genome Atlas’ in collaboration with Dept. of Biotechnology Institute -National Institute of 
Biomedical Genomics (NIBMG) Kolkata. 
  
2.  CSIR is also partnering with All India Institute of Medical Science (AIIMS), New Delhi, 
Ministry of Health & Family Welfare to work jointly for identified healthcare related research 
projects. 
  
3. CSIR has initiated a new Scheme titled Aerospace Projects of National Importance to undertake 
much needed R&D in National aerodynamic testing facilities, Civil and Military aircraft including 
electric aircraft. 
  
4. CSIR is also partnering with the Ministry of Civil Aviation to develop a National Drone 
Mission. 
  
5. CSIR is in collaboration with the Department of Space, Department of Defence (MoD) for 
various High Technology research and development for national programs. 
  
6. CSIR has entered into Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Ministry of Micro, Small 
and Medium Enterprises (MoMSME) on June 27, 2025. Both the organizations will work jointly to 
meet the needs and demands of MSMEs under the diversified areas of Science & Technology.  
  
7. CSIR is implementing mission mode projects CSIR Aroma mission and CSIR Floriculture 
Mission. The activities being undertaken under these projects are implemented in collaboration 
with Indian Council of Agricultural Research (Krishi Vigyan Kendra), Directorate of Floriculture, 
Pune and Department of Horticulture, ICAR-IARI, New Delhi across the country.  
  
8.  Under CSIR Floriculture Missions, apiculture has been integrated in collaboration with KVIC, 
wherein the Bee boxes and colonies are provided by KVIC to the clusters established by CSIR 
under these missions. Besides, CSIR is also partnering with agencies like APEDA, TRIFED, State 
Horticulture Departments, FFDC (MSME), Central and State Agriculture Universities etc. 
  
9. Under another mission mode project, which aimed at the development of genetically modified 
cotton resistant to insect pests especially Pink bollworm, CSIR collaborated with ICAR institutes 
and Punjab Agricultural University for validation of the technology in containment. 
  
10. In line with direction of the NITI Aayog, CSIR is pursuing a project under mission mode 
aimed at identification of potential sites for commercial cultivation of seaweeds across the coastal 
states and union territories of the country and their valorisation through downstream processing to 
several value added products. Earlier CSIR had worked with the Department of Fisheries, GoI and 
several state Fisheries departments for this purpose under PMMSY and other schemes. 
 
2.11 Further, in line with the Committee’s recommendations, CSIR has already been conducting

check. Projects are chosen and evaluated through a cross-disciplinary committee of experts drawn 
from peer institutions. CSIR remains committed to continuously evolving its strategy to stay 
aligned with India’s scientific and economic goals, while reinforcing its active role in addressing

REPORT 
The Action Taken Report (ATR) of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Science and Technology, Environment, Forests and Climate Change deals with the 
action taken by the Government on the recommendations/observations of the Committee 
contained in its ‘Three Hundred Ninetieth Report’ on “Demands for Grants (2025-26) of the 
Department of Science and Technology.  The Report was presented to/ laid on the Table of both 
the Houses of Parliament on the 25th March, 2025. 
2. Action Taken Notes (ATNs) have been received from the Department of Science and 
Technology in respect of all the 16 recommendations/observations contained in the ‘Three 
Hundred Ninetieth Report’. The replies of the Department of Science and Technology have been 
categorized as follows:- 
Chapter I: Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the 
Government: Para Nos.:- 2.8, 3.6, 4.5, 5.5, 5.6, 6.6, 6.7, 6.8, 6.9, 6.10, 6.11, 
6.12, 6.13 and 7.6  
 Total recommendations – 14 
Chapter II: Recommendations/Observations which the Committee does not desire to 
pursue in view of the Government’s replies:  
  Para Nos.:- 2.10 and 7.4 
  Total recommendations – 02  
Chapter III:  Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the 
Government have not been accepted by the Committee: NIL 
Chapter IV:  Recommendations/Observations in respect of which final replies of the 
Government are still awaited: NIL 
3. The details of the ATNs have been analyzed in the succeeding Chapters.  
  

2 
 
CHAPTER-I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
GOVERNMENT 
OVERALL BUDGETARY DETAILS FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2024-25 (BE, RE & 
ACTUAL EXPENDITURE) AND ALLOCATION FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2025-26  
Recommendation/Observation 
1.1         A significant restructuring has taken place in the funding mechanism for institutional and 
human capacity building. The previously existing three schemes under this category have been 
merged into a single entity called 'Vigyan Dhara,' which has now been allocated ₹1,425 crore for 
the upcoming year. This consolidation suggests a move towards greater efficiency in fund 
utilization and streamlined administration. While this restructuring is intended to simplify 
processes, it will be crucial to ensure that it does not lead to disruptions in existing projects. 
 
(Para 2.8 of the 390th Report) 
  
Action Taken: 
 
1.2 The merger of three schemes; into a single unified scheme “Vigyan Dhara” is aimed to 
simplify the process, provide flexibility in reappropriation of fund among the programmes 
towards greater efficiency in fund utilization and streamlined administration. The Department is 
taking adequate measures to avoid any adverse impacts of this merger. 
 
RESEARCH, DEVELOPMENT & INNOVATION FUND 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.3         Although the Committee acknowledges the bold initiatives undertaken by the Department 
to encourage private sector participation in cutting-edge research in deep tech and sunrise 
sectors, it also recognizes certain concerns. These include the potential risk of fund misallocation, 
the competence of fund managers in identifying suitable recipients and impactful projects, 
implications for national security, the limited rate of return on investment, the possibility of 
private entities benefiting disproportionately at the Government’s expense, and the extent to 
which the outcomes of such research will ultimately benefit the common citizen. The Committee is 
also concerned that such a substantial allocation of funds could have yielded a significant impact 
if directed towards Government institutions. Therefore, the Committee strongly recommends that 
the Department should keep these apprehensions in mind while formulating the detailed 
framework and guidelines to implement this scheme. 
(Para 3.6 ibid) 
  
Action Taken: 
 
1.4 Research, Development & Innovation:       Department appreciates the 
acknowledgement of committee for the initiative to encourage the private sector participation in 

3 
 
deep tech and sunrise sectors. Research Development, and Innovation (RDI) Scheme has been 
conceptualized to establish a corpus of ₹1 lakh crore for providing long-term financing or 
refinancing with long tenors and low or nil interest rates to encourage the private sector to scale 
up research, development and innovation in sunrise domains. As the lead ministry, the 
Department of Science and Technology (DST) convened a post-budget webinar with India’s 
leading industrialists, venture capitalists, and startup founders to gather strategic insights for the 
effective rollout of the RDI scheme in March 2025.  
The detailed framework and guidelines for implementation process is currently underway to 
operationalize the fund in a structured and impactful manner. 
 
ANUSANDHAN NATIONAL RESEARCH FOUNDATION 
 
Recommendation/ Observation 
1.5         The Committee acknowledges and appreciates the establishment of the Anusandhan 
National Research Foundation (ANRF) as a significant and progressive initiative to strengthen 
research and innovation in the country. However, the Committee is of the view that the 
Department could have demonstrated greater foresight in expediting the procedural formalities 
and operationalization of the ANRF. With better planning and timely execution, a portion of the 
allocated funds could have been effectively utilized during the financial year. The Committee, 
therefore, urges the Department to ensure a more structured and time-bound approach in the 
future to optimize the utilization of budgetary allocations, thereby facilitating the timely 
implementation of research initiatives under ANRF.  
(Para 4.5 ibid) 
  
Action Taken: 
 
1.6 Anusandhan National Research Foundation: The government has established the 
Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF) through ANRF Act of 2023. The 
Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF) has been operationalized since February 05, 
2024. The first meeting of the Governing Board (GB) of ANRF was held on 10th September, 
2024 which discussed about India’s Science and Technology landscape and redesigning of 
research and development programmes. As per the recommendation of the GB, ANRF has 
launched multiple programmes aiming to position India as global player in select key sectors, 
driving scientific advances and innovation ecosystem, and for promoting the research and 
innovation in partnership with the private sector. These include Prime Minister's Early Career 
Research Grant (PM-ECRG) to assist young researchers for initiating their research career; EV-
Mission program under MAHA (Mission for Advancement in High-impact Areas) to promote 
research & development of Electric Vehicle (EV) adoption in India; Partnerships for Accelerated 
Innovation and Research (PAIR) in line of Hub and Spoke model, as a first step towards 
fostering research across a broader range of institutions; and  Inclusivity Research Grant (IRG) 
to provide funding support to researchers belonging to the Scheduled Caste /Scheduled Tribe for 
undertaking research in frontier areas of science and engineering. 

4 
 
ANRF endeavors to take all possible measures with better planning and timely execution for the 
effective, efficient and impactful utilization of its fund.  
 
NATIONAL QUANTUM MISSION (NQM) 
Recommendation/ Observation 
1.7 The Committee notes that the ₹ 427 crores were allocated in B.E. 2024-25 which were 
significantly reduced to ₹ 86 crores and Department could spent only 64.30 per cent of the R.E. 
till 31st January, 2025. Even after such gross under-utilization of funds, ₹ 600 crores has been 
allocated for this Mission in B.E. 2025-26. The Committee enquired about the increased budget 
allocation for the National Quantum Mission (NQM) in B.E. 2025-26 and the Department 
informed that the increased allocations will play a pivotal role in expanding and scaling up 
ongoing initiatives while accelerating the development of a robust quantum technology ecosystem 
in India. A significant portion of this funding will be dedicated to strengthening the four 
established Thematic Hubs (T-Hubs), each focused on a key vertical—Quantum Computing, 
Quantum Communication, Quantum Sensing & Metrology, and Quantum Materials & Devices. 
The enhanced funding will empower these T-Hubs to fulfill their mandates effectively by: 
Technology Development, Human Resource Development, Entrepreneurship Development and 
Industry Collaborations and International Collaborations.  
(Para 5.5 ibid) 
 
1.8         The Committee acknowledges that the launch of a dedicated Mission for research in 
Quantum Technologies is a strategic and forward-looking initiative, aligning with global 
technological advancements. However, the underutilization of allocated funds raises concerns 
about the Department's commitment and operational efficiency. The Committee emphasizes the 
need for the Department to adopt a more proactive and results driven approach to ensure the 
Mission's success. Rather than merely playing catch-up to Google’s Willow and Microsoft’s 
Majorana 1, the Committee strongly recommends that the Department adopt an ambitious vision 
to position India as a global leader in Quantum Technology.  
(Para 5.6 ibid) 
  
Action Taken: 
 
1.9 The concerns of the Committee regarding the underutilization of allocated funds in 
National Quantum Mission in the previous financial year are duly noted. The Department would 
like to submit the following clarifications and forward-looking commitments: 
  
1. Initial Underutilization: 
 The year 2024–25 marked the foundational phase of the Mission, during which the 
selection and establishment of the four Thematic Hubs (T-Hubs) was carried out. 
 The time-intensive nature of establishing these hubs at premier academic 
institutions, ensuring due diligence contributed to a slower pace of fund utilization. 
2. Corrective Measures and Acceleration: 

5 
 
 Following the establishment of the T-Hubs, the Mission has now entered its 
implementation phase with clearly defined technology development targets. 
 Robust mechanisms have been instituted for monthly monitoring, milestone-based 
disbursements, and timely approvals, ensuring improved fund absorption. 
3. Strategic Vision for Global Leadership: 
 The Department supports the Committee’s view that India must not merely play 
catch-up to international players but also work toward global leadership in 
Quantum Technologies. 
 To this end, the enhanced allocation of ₹600 crores in B.E. 2025–26 will directly 
support technology development, human resource development, entrepreneurship 
and startup ecosystem and international collaborations. 
  
PERFORMANCE OF THE AUTONOMOUS INSTITUTIONS UNDER THE 
DEPARTMENT DURING 2024-25 
 
Sree Chitra Tirunal Institute for Medical Sciences & Technology (SCTIMST), 
Thiruvananthapuram 
 
Recommendation/ Observation 
1.10 The Committee commends the efforts of Sree Chitra Tirunal Institute of Medical Sciences 
and Technology (SCTIMST) in advancing biomedical technology development, fostering industry 
collaboration, and translating research into commercially viable products. The successful 
development and market launch of innovations such as the AG Chitra Tuberculosis Diagnostic 
Kit, Titanium Nitride (TiN) coated coronary stent, Automatic Contrast Injector, and Automated 
Trolley e-drive highlight the Institute’s significant contributions to the healthcare sector.  
(Para 6.6 ibid) 
 
 
1.11         Given the impact of these developments, the Committee recommends that the 
Department extend greater financial and infrastructural support to SCTIMST to further 
strengthen its research and development capabilities. Additionally, the Committee urges the 
Department to facilitate wider adoption and deployment of these indigenous technologies across 
healthcare institutions in India, ensuring affordability, accessibility, and scalability. The 
Committee also emphasizes the need for an enabling ecosystem to promote industry partnerships 
and expedite regulatory clearances, thereby accelerating the commercialization of innovative 
medical technologies for the benefit of the healthcare sector and the common citizen. 
(Para 6.7 ibid) 
 
 
Action Taken: 
 
1.12 1. There has been a 12% increase in financial allocation to SCTIMST for FY 2025-26 when 
compared to the FY 2024-25. The Department is providing necessary support for improving the 
infrastructure to strengthen the R&D capabilities of the Institute.  

6 
 
2. SCTIMST has a dedicated 'Technology Business Division' (TBD) to take care of the 
deployment of indigenous technologies developed by the research team of the Institute. TBD-
SCTIMST co-ordinates the various activities related to the commercialisation of the know-how 
and technologies developed at the Institute and liaison between the Institute and industry. The 
information about new technologies and other developments are disseminated through SCTIMST 
Website and social media handles.  
3. The products developed at the Institute are publicized through an Expression of Interest for 
Technology Transfer whereby the medical device industry can collaborate and take ahead the 
products into commercialization. Such collaborations have happened with TTK Healthcare Ltd, 
Terumo Penpol, HLL Lifecare Ltd, Anabond Stedmann Pharma Ltd, Basic Healthcare Ltd, Meril 
Lifesciences, Wipro 3D, Biorad Medisys Pvt Ltd etc.  
4. Many of the technologies like heart valve, blood bag, oxygenator, dental and orthopaedic 
composites, Intrauterine Device, Vein veiwer, bioceramic beads to treat bone infections, bioink 
for 3D bioprinting, etc have been commercialized to benefit the patient population.  
5. The Institute provides all kind of technical support to the industry partner for regulatory 
submissions. The Regulatory cell interacts with the Technology partner and guide on regulatory 
submissions wherever required.  
6. The testing services of the Institute offer various preclinical evaluations including 
physicochemical, biocompatibility and large animal safety and functional evaluations to the 
medical device industry for submission to the regulatory authorities.  
7. The incubator facility of the Institute SCTIMST TIMed supports the medical device industry by 
providing the incubates with seed funds and mentoring for the development of their devices.  
8. SCTIMST, being a pioneering institution in MedTech research, creates an enabling ecosystem 
for MedTech translation. The Institute has implemented Medical Device Regulatory Compliance 
Facility (MDRCF), Industry Institute Partnership Cell (IIPC) and the Technology Business 
Incubator (TIMed) from the period 2016-17 onwards. This system has catered to many 
entrepreneurs and other R&D setups, through direct interactions and facilitations in product 
translation.  
International Advanced Research Centre for Powder Metallurgy & New Materials (ARCI), 
Hyderabad 
Recommendation/ Observation 
1.13  The Committee acknowledges the significant contributions of the International 
Advanced Research Centre for Powder Metallurgy and New Materials (ARCI) in advancing 
research across critical domains such as energy storage, nanomaterials, engineered coatings, 
additive manufacturing, and advanced powder metallurgy. The successful development and 
technology transfer of battery-grade Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP) as a cathode material for Li-

7

1.15

 Indian Institute of Astrophysics (IIA), Bengaluru 
 
 
Recommendation/ Observation 

8 
 
 
1.16 The Committee recognizes the Indian Institute of Astrophysics (IIA) as a premier 
institution dedicated to research and development in Astronomy, Astrophysics, and Astronomy 
Instrumentation. The successful fabrication and verification of the first 1.44-meter mirror segment

1.18

India’s commitments to the TMT project and other international collaborations in

Raman Research Institute (RRI), Bengaluru 
 
Recommendation/ Observation 
1.19 The Committee commends the Raman Research Institute (RRI) for its outstanding 
contributions to scientific research across vast spatial and temporal scales, from cosmology to

(Para 6.13 ibid)

further advancements in space based astronomy and astrophysics. RRI’s quest to understand the

explosive events in the universe. RRI also has a dedicated program to study the early high energy

HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT AND CAPACITY BUILDING 
Recommendation/ Observation 
 
1.22       The Committee observes that the existing provisions for capacity building and skill 
enhancement are inadequate in effectively cultivating scientific talent. To address this gap, the 
Committee strongly recommends that the Department formulate a comprehensive policy dedicated 
to capacity building programs for its staff. This policy should focus on structured training 
initiatives, skill development, and continuous learning opportunities. Additionally, the 
Department should actively explore and establish collaborations with internationally renowned 
scientific institutions to facilitate knowledge exchange, exposure to global best practices, and 
advanced research training.  
  
(Para 7.6 ibid) 
  
Action Taken: 
 
1.23 For capacity building and effectively cultivating scientific talent several efforts are being 
undertaken in the DST, which are as under: 
 For implementation of National Programme for Civil Service Capacity Building 
(NPCSCB) - Mission Karmayogi - Finalization of Annual Capacity Building Plan 
(ACBP), the department has formulated the ACBP calendar by identified level-wise 
courses (based on competencies i.e. Domain, Functional and Behavioral) on iGOT 
Karmayogi Platform. 
 Seven (07) Training Sessions  have been organized in DST under Rashtriya karmayogi 
training initiative of Capacity Building Commission to instil “Seva Bhav” in the 
officials/scientists. So, far total of 254 employees of DST have been trained under this 
initiative.  
 14 Lectures/talks were also conducted in the Department. Two immersion programme 
were also conducted for the newly recruited scientists at INST, Mohali  and WIHG, 
Dehradun. 
  Learning Hour is observed in DST on every Monday from 4:30 PM to 5:30 PM. 
 Seven (07) mandatory  courses of iGOT Karmayogi Portal have been identified in DST for 
all the officials of DST. 
A sub committee has been formed for exploring the potentiality of collaborations with 
internationally renowned scientific institutions to facilitate knowledge exchange.

CHAPTER – II 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT 
DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE GOVERNMENT'S REPLIES 
 
OVERALL BUDGETARY DETAILS FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2024-25 (BE, RE & 
ACTUAL EXPENDITURE) AND ALLOCATION FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2025-26 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.1         The Committee emphasizes the need to ensure that administrative and procedural 
challenges do not become significant obstacles to the Department's planned activities in the long 
term. It, therefore, recommends that the Department exercise due diligence in managing its 
expenditures to guarantee optimal fund utilization for 2025-26 while ensuring the successful 
achievement of its set objectives. Furthermore, the Committee urges the Department to make 
every possible effort in the current financial year to compensate for the suboptimal performance 
recorded during 2024-25. 
 (Para 2.10 of 390th Report) 
  
Action Taken: 
 
2.2 Based on the lessons learnt in the past, the department is taking all possible efforts towards 
optimal fund utilization during 2025-26 towards smooth execution of the planned activities 
boosting the impetus of research & development in the country.  
 
HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT AND CAPACITY BUILDING 
Recommendation/Observation  
2.3       The Committee expresses deep concern over the significant number of vacancies in the 
Department, as well as in the Autonomous Institutions (AIs) under its administrative control. It is 
particularly dismayed by the persistent reliance on contractual appointments as a stopgap 
measure to address short-term manpower shortages. The Committee firmly believes that a highly 
skilled and dedicated workforce is the cornerstone of any scientific institution’s success and 
output. Therefore, it strongly recommends that the Department adopt a mission-mode approach to 
expeditiously fill all vacant positions. This will ensure the availability of a competent and stable 
workforce, essential for advancing scientific research and institutional excellence. 
(Para 7.4 ibid) 
  
Action Taken: 
 
2.4 Most of the vacancies in Group A, Group B and Group C posts of DST Secretariat, pertain 
to CSS, CSCS, CSSS and CS (OL) cadres for which the Department of Personnel & Training 

12 
 
(DOP&T) and Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) are the Cadre Controlling Authorities. This 
Department has been requesting DOP&T and MHA time and again to allocate manpower as per 
the sanctioned strength and DOP&T and MHA have been posting officials of these cadres on an 
ongoing basis. For filling up other vacant posts, recruitment processes have been initiated in this 
Department which are at various stages of recruitment. 
  
It is submitted that the Autonomous Institutions get various extra mural research projects funded 
by government and industry funded projects and the existing permanent manpower is not 
sufficient to execute these projects. Hence, project staff are appointed on tenure and contractual 
basis for implementation of these projects. However, efforts are underway by all the AI’s to fill 
the vacant positions and many AI’s in the recent past has added young and dynamic researchers 
who have now gone on to establish research groups on par with the best in the world. The AI’s are 
making substantial efforts and several AI’s had initiated recruitment to fill up vacant permanent 
posts following the reservation roster for permanent recruitment, which is under process.

CHAPTER-I 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE GOVERNMENT 
 
OVERALL BUDGETARY DETAILS FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2024-25 (BE, RE 
& ACTUAL EXPENDITURE) AND ALLOCATION FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 
2025-26 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.1 The Committee observes that the Budget Estimate (BE) for 2024-25 was ₹13,042.75 
crore, but this was revised downwards substantially by 10.09% to ₹11,725.75 crore at the 
Revised Estimate (RE) stage. As of December 2024, actual expenditure stood at ₹8,296.38 
crore, a mere 71% utilisation of RE allocations. For the year 2025-26, the Department 
projected a requirement of ₹15,983.37 crore, but was allocated ₹13,416.20 crore, reflecting 
a shortfall of ₹2,567.17 crore that could impact some planned initiatives. While the increase 
in allocation over the previous year suggests continued government support for space 
activities, the reduction from the projected requirement raises concerns about the 
Department’s ability to execute all planned projects efficiently. (Para 2.2 of the 391st Report) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.2 At the end of the FY 2024-25, the Department was able to utilise 98% of the RE 
allocations – expenditure of ₹11,518.64 crore incurred against RE allocations of ₹11,725.75 
crore.  
 
1.3 An amount of ₹13,416.20 Crore has been allocated to the Department in BE 2025-26 
against the projection of ₹15,983.37 crore. The Department has ensured that key projects / 
programmes are sufficiently funded based on the budgetary resources made available in 
2025-26. Depending on the progress of on-going missions, R&D projects and facility build-
up, the Department would approach Ministry of Finance for additional funds at RE stage and 
through the mechanism of supplementary Grants. 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.4 The Committee observes from Chart-2 & 3, for RE 2024-25, an overall utilization 
rate of 70.75% across all schemes. Space Technology, a key sector, has utilized 70.95% of its 
allocated funds while Space Sciences shows the lowest utilization rate at 46.10%, indicating 
significant underutilization. The Committee notes that Space Applications, which includes 
Earth Observation, GIS-based services, and disaster management applications, has a 
utilization rate of 73.09%. This suggests a relatively strong performance in project execution, 
particularly in satellite-based services for agriculture, urban planning, and environmental 
monitoring. INSAT Satellite Systems has seen 60.10% utilization, reflecting slower spending. 
Establishment Expenditure stands at 65.53%, pointing to stable spending on administrative 
functions, infrastructure maintenance, and research facility operations. Other Central Sector 
Expenditure, including initiatives supporting private sector participation and space-sector 
reforms, has the highest utilization at 75.76%.                                         (Para 2.7 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.5 Department incurred expenditure of ₹11,518.64 crore against RE allocations of 
₹11,725.75 crore during FY 2024-25. (~98% of RE allocations).

Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.7 The Committee observes from Charts 4 & 5 that there has been a significant 
reduction in revised allocations for 2024-25 under some of the crucial schemes of the 
Department. The Scheme- ‘Gaganyaan Programme’ India’s human spaceflight mission, 
experienced a significant budget reduction at the R.E. 2024-25 stage, from ₹1200 crore to 
₹847.35 crore, indicating a cut of ₹352.65 crore. The actual expenditure till December 2024 
stood at ₹627.05 crore, reflecting delays in hardware realisation and milestone-based 
payments. However, B.E. 2025-26 has been restored to ₹1200 crore, suggesting that higher 
spending is expected in the coming year. The Committee expressed concern over the repeated 
fund reductions and emphasised that predictable financial allocations were crucial  for 
maintaining mission timelines.                                                                             (Para 2.9 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.8 At the end of the financial year, the Department has utilised an amount of ₹826.96 
crore under the Gaganyaan programme, which is about 98% of RE allocations. 
 
1.9 Gaganyaan Programme involves development of several new technologies such as 
Human Rated Launch Vehicle, Crew Escape System, Crew Module, Service Module, 
Environment Control & Life Support System and Human Centric Products. The budgetary 
projections and expenditure patterns have been affected by the complex technology 
development cycle involving multiple design iterations and extensive flight/ ground testing to 
meet the stringent human rating requirements. In addition to these, extrinsic factors such as 
global pandemic and disruptions in supply chain of semiconductors & raw materials have 
also impacted the programme in recent past. 
 

4 
 
1.10 As ISRO is preparing for the first 4nscrewed mission after the completion of some of 
the major ground qualification tests, there is greater clarity on the overall outlay plan and 
yearly budgetary requirements. This is expected to result in higher expenditure in the coming 
years for flight hardware realisation and mission related activities. Further, expenditure 
monitoring through regular reviews is being carried out. Based on this cash-flow assessment, 
the BE 2025-26 provision for the programme is restored to ₹1200.00 crore. 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.11 The Committee observes that the Joint ISRO-NASA Mission to the ISS faced a 
substantial budget cut at the R.E. stage, reducing its allocation from ₹715 crore to ₹412 
crore, reflecting a ₹303 crore reduction. The actual expenditure till December 2024 was 
₹413.14 crore, exceeding the R.E. allocation. However, the B.E. for 2025-26 has been 
drastically reduced to ₹135 crore, reflecting the deferral of the mission to a later date. The 
Committee expresses concerns over further delays in India’s collaboration with NASA and 
recommends that DoS maintain strong international engagement to ensure mission stability.
                                                                                                                 (Para 2.10 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.12 The mission has been rescheduled by NASA from FY 2024-25 to FY 2025-26 due to 
its internal scheduling constraints. Accordingly, the associated payment milestones and 
expenditure plan has been revised. The mission was successfully launched on June 25, 2025. 
 
1.13 ISRO and NASA teams continue to have regular bilateral engagements to plan and 
review the collaborative activities being undertaken as part of this mission. 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.14 The Committee observes that the Scheme –‘Semi- Cryogenic Engine Development’ 
was allocated ₹190 crore (B.E. 2024-25) which was revised to ₹115 crore (R.E. 2024-25), 
reflecting a ₹75 crore cut. The actual expenditure till December 2024 was ₹76.67 crore, 
highlighting slower-than-expected project execution. However, B.E. 2025-26 has been 
increased to ₹150 crore, indicating renewed funding support for this critical propulsion 
technology.                                                                                                     (Para 2.11 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.15 The BE 2024-25 allocation for ‘Semi-cryogenic Engine Development’ & ‘Semi-
cryogenic Stage Development’ was ₹190.00 crore. Against RE 2024-25 allocation of ₹115.00 
crore, the actual expenditure was ₹120.63 crore. The reasons for reduced budget utilisation 
with respect to BE is mainly due to the geopolitical situation in Ukraine as a result of which 
the engine tests are now being conducted at IPRC, Mahendragiri.  Further, payments 
pertaining to SIET fluid servicing system, Strain gauge equipment for tank proof pressure 
tests spilled over to the next financial year.  
 
1.16 The BE 2025-26 allocation under ‘Semi-cryogenic Engine Development’ & ‘Semi-
cryogenic Stage Development’ is ₹150.00 crore to meet the project milestones for 
commissioning of SIET stage test bay, Engine and stage sub-systems realisation, spill over 
payments etc.  
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 

5 
 
1.17 The Committee observes from Chart 4 that the budget for IN-SPACe (Indian National 
Space Promotion and Authorization Centre), which is tasked with promoting private sector 
participation in space activities, was reduced from ₹96 crore (B.E. 2024-25) to ₹58 crore 
(R.E. 2024-25), reflecting a cut of ₹38 crore. The actual expenditure till December 2024 was 
₹30.19 crore, significantly below the allocated funds. However, B.E. 2025-26 has been set at 
₹70 crore, showing partial restoration of funding. The Committee recommends that the 
Department should provide clear demarcation in future budget proposals between 
establishment and operational expenses and promotional activities for IN-SPACe. The 
Committee also recommends that a separate budgetary subhead under IN-SPACe should be 
considered to ensure transparency in fund allocation and utilisation, preventing confusion in 
financial reporting.                                                                                            (Para 2.12 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.18 At the end of the financial year 2024-25, the actual expenditure incurred by IN-
SPACe was ₹41.36 crore against the RE allocations of ₹58 crore. 
1.19 As recommended by the Committee, a clear demarcation is made between the 
establishment and operational expenses and promotional activities for IN-SPACe in BE 
2025-26.  
1.20 Budget provision of ₹70.00 crores is provided towards establishment and operational 
expenses of IN-SPACe. The budget provision of ₹165.00 crore for promotional activities / 
schemes has been provided under the minor head ‘Space Technology’- Promotional activities 
of IN-SPACe. Hence, the total allocation for operational and promotional activities of IN-
SPACe has been enhanced to ₹235.00 crores in BE 2025-26 (₹70.00 crore under ‘Direction 
and administration’ and ₹165.00 crore under the minor head ‘Space Technology’). 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.21 The Committee notes that the Scheme- ‘GSLV Operational & Continuation 
Programme (Phase-4)’ faced a budget reduction at the R.E. stage 2024-25, from ₹350 crore 
to ₹249.12 crore, reflecting a cut of ₹100.88 crore. The actual expenditure till December 
2024 was ₹191.16 crore. However, B.E. 2025-26 has been restored to ₹350 crore. The 
Committee is concerned that such reductions could impact India's ability to meet its launch 
manifest commitments and urges DoS to ensure better alignment between projected and 
actual expenditures.                                                                                         (Para 2.13 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.22 The actual expenditure incurred during 2024-25 under the ‘GSLV Operational & 
Continuation Programme (Phase-4)’ is ₹249.56 against RE allocations of ₹249.12 crore.  
 
1.23 In line with the programmatic targets planned during 2025-26, BE provision is 
restored to ₹350 crore. The Department will make all efforts to ensure complete utilization of 
the allocated funds in BE 2025-26. 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.24 The Committee strongly recommends that additional funds be allocated to Space 
Sciences at the R.E. 2025-26 stage, ensuring that critical planetary and interplanetary 

6 
 
missions proceed without disruption. The Committee also recommends that the ₹1,488.60 
crore reductions in Space Technology be re-evaluated, as it could slow down key 
advancements in satellite launch capabilities, propulsion systems, and indigenous space 
innovation. The Committee recommends that the Department should improve its financial 
forecasting for major space research and technology projects to avoid significant funding 
shortfalls at the final allocation stage. The Committee also recommends that while cuts in 
Establishment and Other Central Expenditures are reasonable, critical infrastructure and 
capacity-building expenses should not be compromised.                            (Para 2.17 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.25 As recommended by the Committee, the Department would approach Ministry of 
Finance for additional funds at RE stage and through the mechanism of supplementary Grants 
especially for the Space Sciences and Space technology schemes based on the progress of the 
missions.  
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.26 The Committee observes that the capital expenditure allocation for the Department of 
Space (DoS) has increased significantly from ₹4,728.37 crore (R.E. 2024-25) to ₹6,103.63 
crore (B.E. 2025-26), an increase of ₹1,375.26 crore (29%).                         (Para 2.19 ibid) 
 
Action Taken

b) Newly approved projects such as Next Generation Launch Vehicle, Venus Orbiter

1.55 Under the aegis of Indian Space Policy-2023, ISRO/DoS has implemented ‘Earth 
Observation (EO) Data Dissemination Guidelines’ on 22nd November 2023. Under the EO 
Data Dissemination Guidelines, ISRO is providing ‘Free and Open’ access to Indian Remote 
Sensing Data & products to all the users including academic institutions start-ups and 
industries. All the remote sensing data acquired by ISRO through its ground stations in India 
and abroad since 1988, having spatial resolution 5m & coarser, is made accessible on ‘free 
and open’ basis to all. The data of resolution finer than 5m resolution is available free of cost 
to Government entities, and at a fair pricing to non-governmental entities.  
 
1.56 ISRO/DoS is making continuous efforts in developing advanced EO based solutions 
for automatic crop mapping, monitoring crop health and crop yield/production forecasting. 

12 
 
ISRO/DoS has developed and transferred the methodology to Mahalanobis National Crop 
Forecast Centre for operational, in-season mapping of 10 major crops. ISRO has developed a 
processor called “SASYA” (Satellite-based crop mapping System with Automl) for mapping 
crops using time series SAR data through automatic Machine Learning (ML) algorithms. 
Attempts are ongoing to update the processor to map other Kharif crops.  
 
1.57 ISRO has developed algorithm for Surface Soil Moisture (SSM, @500m, 17-day 
repetivity) product generation using EOS-04 (RISAT-1A) data and the operational products 
are released through Bhoonidhi portal since December 2023. These SSM product are useful 
for drought assessment, irrigation monitoring, land hydrological modelling etc. ISRO also 
plans to enhance the temporal/spatial resolution of SSM product utilizing SAR data from 
upcoming NISAR satellite. The concurrent SAR data from EOS-04 and NISAR missions is 
expected to increase the efficacy as well as resolution of SSM products.  
 
1.58 ISRO has developed and tested GNSS-Reflectometry payload onboard EOS-
08/Microsat-2C (launched on 16th August 2024). The payload utilizes signals from GNSS 
satellites as signal-of-opportunity to map the earth surface including oceans. The data from 
this payload was processed and evaluated to assess its potential for soil moisture retrieval. 
Soil moisture retrievals from Microsat-2C correlated well with incidence of high rainfall and 
irrigation areas, demonstrating promising potential for future utilization. ISRO is exploring 
possibility of operating constellation of this payload to enhance the temporal and spatial 
coverage of the GNSS-R data and soil moisture products derived from it. 
 
1.59 ISRO/DoS has prepared the National level hydrological modelling framework under 
National Hydrology Project to facilitate dynamic computation of water balance components. 
ISRO provides daily products on surface runoff, evapotranspiration, soil moisture as 
operational outcome of the project. ISRO has also developed a web-based interactive 
hydrological modeling system to help user to build, execute and store the model results 
online, to reduce user’s dependence on software and computational infrastructure. ISRO is 
also making efforts towards developing techniques for assimilation of Indian EO data in 
hydrological models for improving the model performance.

Advanced propulsion systems: 
Hathor Rockets- Semi Cryo Engine- 
 
Hathor Rockets is a space propulsion startup incubated at the Indian 
Institute of Space Science and Technology (IIST), focused on the

reusable launch vehicles and affordable access to space. The start-up is

the long term, Hathor Rockets aims to scale its propulsion systems and

ISRO’ Scramjet Project- HAVA- IIST’s involvement- 
 
ISRO is actively pursuing the development of horizontal-flight scramjet 
engines with longer test durations, with the intention of integrating them 
with other propulsion systems to enhance launch vehicle reusability. The 

25 
 
practical implementation of scramjet flights remains challenging due to 
issues such as combustion stability, rapid fuel-air mixing, and reliable 
ignition under extreme aerodynamic conditions. A critical component of the 
scramjet engine is the fuel injection system, which must deliver a finely 
atomized liquid fuel to ensure efficient evaporation and mixing within the 
millisecond-scale residence times available in the combustor. The 
effervescent strut injection strategy is one of the successful configurations 
implemented by ISRO as well as other agencies worldwide to sustain 
supersonic combustion in real time scramjet flights. The spray 
characteristics of the actual flight strut hardware is investigated and tested 
at APLD Lab, IIST using advanced optical based diagnostic techniques like 
high-speed shadowgraph, Mie scattering and phase Doppler measurements. 
IIST is fully involved in the optimizing the Scramjet injector in ISRO’s 
mission.

1.144 One such initiative is NSIL’s collaboration with the Cochin University of Science and 
Technology (CUSAT) to develop an Automated Warning System for Landslides in the 
susceptible zones of the Meenachil River Basin, Kerala. This project effectively demonstrates 
the application of space technology for addressing critical societal challenges. 
 
1.145 NSIL is also executing a range of projects aimed at empowering rural and tribal 
communities such as Skill development and market linkage programs for underserved rural 
girls and women to promote sustainable livelihoods, Nutritional enhancement support for 
Tribal families, Education and vocational training in the apparel sector for rural youth, etc.  
Additionally, NSIL is sponsoring equipment support to the Indian Institute of Technology 
(IIT), Madras for the development of a Human Autoantibody Atlas. This initiative aims to aid 
in the profiling of autoimmune diseases and facilitate the advancement of personalized 
medicine, thereby contributing significantly to public health and societal well-being. 
 
1.146 As recommended by committee, NSIL is committed to ensure high standards of 
governance, transparency and efficiency by all CSR implementing agencies through regular 
monitoring. Furthermore, third-party audits and impact assessments will be undertaken as per 
approved DPE guidelines. 
 
HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT AND CAPACITY BUIDING  
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
1.147 The Committee observes that the Department faces a 20.48% vacancy rate, which 
may impact operational efficiency. The Committee notes that out of 19,178 sanctioned posts 
in ISRO, 3,927 remain vacant, with the most significant gaps in administrative staff (2,008) 
and Scientists/Engineers (1,032). While recruitment actions for 1,950 posts are in progress, 
there is a pressing need to accelerate hiring, particularly for S&T roles. The Public Sector 
Enterprises (PSEs) under DoS, such as Antrix and NSIL, also report a concerning vacancy 
rate (265 out of 323 sanctioned posts), which may hinder their efficiency in commercial 
space activities. Similarly, Autonomous Bodies (NARL, NESAC, PRL) and IIST also face 
recruitment challenges, although to a lesser extent.                                             (Para 7.1ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.148 As of end of May 2025, the vacancies in Scientist/Engineer category remains revised 
to 876 posts. Recruitment action to fill up the S&T vacancies are taken in Campaign mode. 
Majority of Scientist/Engineers posts are being filled up through Centralised process for 
common disciplines (457 posts) and expected to complete the recruitment process before 
November 2025 (factoring the requirement of conducting PAN India level written test & 
interview). Also, for recruitment with specialised fields, advertisements are released / 
advance stage of releasing, for which recruitments are expected to be completed before 
December 2025.   
 
1.149 In the administrative area, recruitment actions are completed for 451 posts (against 
advertised 553 posts), reporting is pending C&A verification. Next advertisement for 
centralised recruitment is being finalised. Further, as mentioned previously, majority 
vacancies are in erstwhile Group D posts which is proposed for category change as part of 2nd 
cadre review exercise (proposal submitted to DoE, queries being addressed). 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 

29 
 
1.150 The Committee supports the Department’s plan to engage S&T personnel on a tenure 
basis but recommends that flexible hiring models be expanded to include project-based 
contracts for emerging space technologies.                                                        (Para 7.4 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.151 The scheme for engaging S&T personnel on tenure basis while factoring the above 
recommendations has been generated and currently under active consideration. 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
1.152 The Committee notes that the backlog in hiring was caused partly due to delays 
during the COVID-19 period and recruitment policy revisions.  It recommends increasing the 
frequency of centralised recruitment drives to ensure that vacancies do not accumulate in the 
future. Quarterly recruitment monitoring exercises should be conducted to track hiring 
progress and address any procedural challenges.                                              (Para 7.5 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.153 The Department takes note of the Committees recommendations to increase frequency 
of centralised recruitment drives and quarterly monitoring of the activities to address any 
challenges. 
 
 
 
 
 
  

30 
 
 
CHAPTER-II 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT 
DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE GOVERNMENT’S REPLIES 
 
OVERALL BUDGETARY DETAILS FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2024-25 (BE, RE 
& ACTUAL EXPENDITURE) AND ALLOCATION FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 
2025-26 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
2.1 The Committee observes from Chart 6 that the Budget Estimates (B.E.) for 2025-26, 
including projected allocations and actual allocations, highlights significant discrepancies 
across various schemes of the Department. The Committee notes with concern the shortfall of 
approximately 16% of the total projected budget for 2025-26 which was ₹15,983.37 crore, 
whereas the actual allocation made to the Department was ₹13,416.20 crore, indicating a 
substantial reduction of ₹2,567.17 crore. The Committee notes significant reduction of 
₹505.14 crore (from ₹876.14 crore to ₹371 crore) in Space Sciences. The substantial 
reduction of projected demand, of over 57% in Space Sciences funding raises concerns 
regarding India’s deep space exploration, interplanetary missions, and astrophysics 
research. The Committee believes that this cut might delay major projects related to 
planetary studies and space observatories, thereby impacting India's standing in global space 
science research. Similarly, the Committee notes that the ₹1,488.60 crore reductions in Space 
Technology funding could affect crucial R&D activities, such as reusable launch vehicles, 
semi-cryogenic engine development, and human spaceflight missions.     (Para 2.15 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
2.2 The Department has ensured that all ongoing projects/ programmes/ schemes are 
sufficiently funded and the requirements for the newly approved projects have been 
optimized to stay within the budgetary ceilings communicated for BE 2025-26.  
 
2.3 Depending on the progress of the missions, the Department would approach Ministry 
of Finance for additional funds at RE stage and through the mechanism of supplementary 
Grants. 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
2.4 The Committee acknowledges the increased capital allocation towards IN-SPACe for 
promotion of private-sector participation in space activities. The Committee recommends 
that for full utilization of the potential of private enterprises in the space sector, a well-
structured incentive framework should be introduced to support start-ups and industry 
players engaged in space applications, satellite development, and launch services. The 
Committee urges upon the Department that IN-SPACe should create dedicated incubation 
hubs within ISRO centres, where private firms can collaborate with ISRO scientists to refine 
their technologies.                                                                                         (Para 2.23 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
2.5 IN-SPACe has created a limited version technical centre phase-1 attached to IN-
SPACe within the SAC/ISRO campus to provide the private firms access to space systems’ 

31 
 
design and analysis software tools, electronics systems assembly, integration and testing 
facilities including climatic chambers, thermovac & vibration test facilities, cleanrooms. The 
private firms are provided with mentorship through retired ISRO scientists. Currently, we are 
working on phase-II of establishing  full-fledged dedicated Technical centre collocated with 
SAC campus which is expected to be commissioned in 2027. The objective of this centre is to 
nurture private space 31tilize3131 and entrepreneurs by providing technical and legal 
mentorship, guidance to create innovative ideas into viable commercial products.  
 
2.6 IN-SPACe has launched the Pre-Incubation Entrepreneurship development program, 
where the identified start-ups can be incubated/guided by the experts from 
industries/academia/ research institutes/incubators. 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
2.7 In view of the fact that NSIL has now become the primary commercial arm of ISRO, 
the Committee recommends that it should proactively engage with international clients, and 
secure more commercial contracts for satellite-building and launch services. The Committee 
expresses concern over the sharp decline in INSAT/GSAT transponder lease earnings. The 
Committee recommends that the Department should identify market demand, explore 
partnerships with telecom operators and OTT service providers, and secure long-term 
transponder leasing agreements. The Committee recognizes that the launch services market 
remains a key revenue generator. The Committee recommends that ISRO should strengthen 
its commercial launch portfolio, offer competitive pricing, and leverage reusable launch 
vehicle (RLV) technology to reduce costs and attract global customers.          (Para 2.25 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
2.8 NSIL has been very proactively engaging with international customers for securing 
launch service contracts for launching customer satellites onboard PSLV, SSLV and LVM3. 
Global Launch Service market has been extremely competitive as some of the US launch 
service providers have been offering services at much reduced cost in comparison to Indian 
launchers.  
 
2.9 Inspite of the stiff competition, NSIL could secure several dedicated PSLV and 
LVM3 launch contracts.  As on date, NSIL has successfully accomplished 5 dedicated PSLV 
missions and 2 dedicated LVM3 missions for international customers, besides launching 
several international customer satellites as co-passengers.   Till date, NSIL has launched 64 
customer satellites onboard PSLV. NSIL has three Dedicated launch contracts in-hand, one 
for launching US customer satellite onboard LVM3, one for launching Singapore customer 
satellite onboard PSLV and other for launching Australian customer satellite onboard SSLV.  
 
2.10 In addition, NSIL has several co-passenger satellite launch service contracts in-hand. 
NSIL is making all efforts to secure many more dedicated launch service contracts.  
 
2.11 DTH market is undergoing disruption due to increase in OTT services and NSIL is 
putting its efforts to improve the Satcom business by providing end-to-end solutions to its 
customers in addition to working towards long term leasing agreements and newer 
partnership models with operators. 
 
 
 
 
 

32 
 
CENTRAL SECTOR SCHEMES OF THE DEPARTMENT OF SPACE 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
2.12 The Committee notes with concern that allocation under the Scheme- ‘INSAT Satellite 
Systems’ has decreased from ₹218.44 crore in R.E. 2024-25 to ₹207 crore in B.E. 2025-26.                          
(Para 3.20 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
2.13 The allocation towards INSAT Satellite Systems have been reduced in BE 2025-26 in 
view of the programmatic realignment of INSAT satellite programme in line with the space 
policy 2023. 
 
2.14 As per the space policy, NSIL will act as the exclusive public-sector aggregator for 
both demand and supply of space assets on a commercial basis. Space assets related to 
INSAT Satellite systems have been transferred to NSIL to own and operate on commercial 
basis to provide communication services to various users. 
 
ESTABLISHMENT EXPENDITURE OF THE CENTRE 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
2.15 The Committee acknowledges the significant strides made by IN-SPACe in promoting 
private sector participation in the Indian space sector. The Committee recommends that IN-
SPACe should develop a structured framework for private sector access to ISRO’s 
infrastructure, including transparent guidelines on facility usage charges, eligibility criteria, 
and priority allocation for research and commercial activities. In view of the fact that 75 
Technology Transfer (ToT) agreements have been signed since 2020, the Committee 
recommends that IN-SPACe should expand its industry outreach, conduct awareness 
programs, and streamline ToT processes to increase private sector adoption of ISRO-
developed technologies. The Committee notes that IN-SPACe has issued 56 authorisations 
and received 480 applications from 382 Indian entities. To streamline processes and ensure 
timely approvals, the Committee recommends that IN-SPACe should establish clear 
timelines, a digital tracking system, and a public dashboard for real-time updates on 
authorisation requests and approvals.                                                                (Para 4.5 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
2.16 IN-SPACe has put in place Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) to process the 
applications from private entities for various support from IN-SPACe. A dashboard has been 
created in the IN-SPACe digital platform giving the status of the applications of NGE and 
real time updates on authorisation requests and approvals. 
 
2.17 IN-SPACe released the Norms, Guidelines and Procedures for implementation of the 
Indian Space Policy 2023 (‘ISP-2023’) in respect of Authorization of Space Activities 
(“NGP”) on May 3, 2024 which is readily available online on IN-SPACe Digital Platform 
(IDP www.inspace.gov.in). The Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) to process the 
Authorization applications is clearly brought out in the NGP and provides clarity on the 
timelines established & transparency in the authorization process. 
 

33 
 
2.18 Also, all applications to IN-SPACe are received digitally through IDP portal where 
their progress can also be seen. Additionally, a separate page is hosted publicly on the 
dashboard of IDP, displaying details of all Authorization issued by IN-SPACe. 
 
2.19 IN-SPACe is not able to meet the desired timelines.  A detailed review is being 
undertaken to further streamline the process, identify the reasons for delay and thus speed up 
the process.  There is a dependency on several Departments for doing so. 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
2.20 The Committee notes IN-SPACe’s ongoing efforts to establish space-based Earth 
Observation (EO) services under a Public-Private Partnership (PPP) model and the 
development of common technical facilities in space manufacturing clusters with a funding 
cap of ₹100 crores per state. The Committee recommends that modalities for these initiatives 
should be finalised at the earliest and that a structured implementation roadmap with 
periodic progress reports should be made available. The Committee also recommends that 
the Investment Incentive Scheme for private-sector manufacturing of space systems should be 
formulated with clear eligibility criteria and incentive structures.                   (Para 4.8 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
2.21 IN-SPACe is following a due EOI/RFP process for identifying an Indian Entity to 
establish of space based EO services under a Public Private Partnership. The final selection of 
Indian Entity is targeted by 15 August 2025.  
 
2.22 IN-SPACe has communicated to all the state governments seeking interest in 
establishing space manufacturing clusters (SMC). As on 01 June 2025, four states have 
communicated their willingness to establish SMC (viz., Government of Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, 
Karnataka and Chhattisgarh). IN-SPACe has signed framework MoU with Governments of 
Gujarat, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka and discussions have been initiated for establishing 
Common Technical Facilities within the SMC. A Detailed Project Report for each Common 
Technical Facility would be prepared by IN-SPACe and submitted to the empowered 
committee for final approval for implementation. 
 
2.23 IN-SPACe has prepared a Detailed Project Report for the Investment Incentive 
Scheme detailing the scope, incentive structure, eligibility and evaluation criteria. As 
recommended by the Space Commission, the DPR will be submitted to Department of 
Expenditure for approval. 
 
2.24 Based on the direction of the PSC, IN-SPACe will work with the companies to better 
understand how we can support them better and implement initiatives. 
 
HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT AND CAPACITY BUIDING  
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
2.25 The Committee recommends expediting the recruitment process to ensure that vacant 
posts, particularly for Scientists/Engineers and technical staff, are filled within the next six 
months. A dedicated recruitment task force should be established to oversee hiring efficiency, 
identify process bottlenecks, and ensure compliance with recruitment timelines. The 
Committee recommends that the Department must develop a structured workforce planning 
model, forecasting staffing needs for the next decade in alignment with ISRO’s Vision 2047. 
The Committee is concerned about the high vacancy rate in NSIL and Antrix, as it may 

34 
 
impact India’s growing commercial space sector. It recommends an industry-specific 
recruitment approach to attract talent from both public and private space technology 
domains, ensuring that PSEs remain competitive and capable of supporting ISRO’s missions.
                                                                                                                     (Para 7.3) 
Action Taken 
 
2.26 Periodic review of recruitment activities by ISRO HQ is put in place, which is 
addressing the bottlenecks and compliance to the timelines. All concerned recruitment 
agencies in ISRO are sensitised on the need to have advance recruitment plan for ensuring 
least vacancies at any given point of time.  
 
2.27 As part of S&T workforce planning exercise for the period 2025-2030, ISRO has 
proposed for augmentation of its S&T staff strength by 500 posts in a phased manner (spread 
over three years). Further assessment of requirement beyond 2030 is planned to be taken up 
as next phase requirement assessment during 2029-2030.

THE GOVERNMENT 
 
OVERALL BUDGETARY DETAILS FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2024-25 (BE, RE & 
ACTUAL EXPENDITURE) AND ALLOCATION FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2025-
26 
Bare minimum requirements in budgetary allocations for sustaining key programmes 
Recommendation/Observation  
1.1 The Committee takes note of the challenges projected by the Ministry in Budget 
allocation in Key programmes and the bare minimum budgetary requirements projected by it 
for sustaining certain key programmes.  Though the Committee is in agreement with the 
requirements projected by the Ministry, the utilization of funds by the Ministry in 2024-25 are 
not encouraging enough for the Committee to make any positive recommendations in this 
regard.  The Committee would, however, like to recommend that in 2025-26, the Ministry of 
Environment, Forest and Climate Change should make proactive efforts to ensure that the 
physical targets of the Ministry in respect of the above schemes/programmes are on schedule 
and the allocation made at BE is utilised to the maximum so that it is on a firm ground to seek 
additional funds at the Supplementary and RE stage in respect of the schemes/programmes 
stated above.                                                                                    (Para 2.5 of the 392nd Report)  
 
Action Taken 
1.2 The suggestions of the Committee have been noted for compliance. The Ministry will 
make best efforts to ensure that the physical targets of the Ministry in respect of the concerned 
schemes/programmes are on schedule and the allocation made at BE is utilised to the 
maximum, so that the demand of additional funds at the RE/Supplementary Stage could be 
justified. 
 
Major thrust areas  
Recommendation/Observation 
1.3 The Committee is of the opinion that the launching of the campaign to plant trees on the 
occasion of World Environment Day is indeed laudable.  The Committee feels that the 
campaign to plant a tree in honour of a mother would certainly create a lasting legacy that 
nurtures both the environment and a greener, prosperous future.  The Committee notes that 118 
crore had already been planted as on 19th February 2025 and hopes that the Ministry would be 
able to achieve its target of planting 140 crore trees by 31st March 2025.             (Para 3.4 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 

 
3 
 
1.4 (i)  As informed by National Afforestation & Eco- Development Board division, the 
target of planting 140 crores seedlings under “EkPedMaaKeNaam” campaign 
was successfully achieved by 31st March, 2025. 
(ii)  Intensive efforts had been made in collaboration with States/UTs, local bodies, 
educational institutions, civil society organisations, and community groups to 
ensure the momentum continues and the campaign concludes successfully. 
 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.5 The Committee would, however, like to point out that although a number of plantation 
activities are undertaken on various occasions, the mortality rate of such plants is very high.  
There is a need not only to plant the trees but also to ensure that once planted, they are looked 
after well and continue to survive and grow.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the 
Ministry should not only undertake plantation activities but should also ensure that the survival 
rate of these plants remains high so that they continue to contribute to the environment and the 
society. This also needs to be emphasized to the youth/children etc. when organizing workshops,

Human-Animal conflict 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.13 The Committee observes that the cases of attacks on humans by wild animals and 
consequential severe injuries/ death of human beings are increasing too. The Committee is of 
the view that no amount of compensation can compensate the loss of a human life.  The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the focus of the Ministry should be on minimizing and 

 
6 
 
mitigating the human-animal conflict rather than merely providing adequate compensation to 
the victims of the conflict. The Committee further recommends that the Ministry should impress 
upon all the State Governments to take necessary action in this regard so that the loss of human 
lives / injuries due to the attack by wild animals is reduced to the minimum.  There is also a 
need to clarify/reiterate the role of the State Forest Officials in such cases so that the required 
necessary action is taken immediately by the concerned authorities.                 (Para 6.13 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.14 Incidences of human-wildlife conflict have been reported from various parts of the 
country. The important steps taken by Government for protection of wildlife and to address 
human-wildlife conflict include the following: 
(i)  The Central Government provides financial assistance to State/Union Territory 
Governments under the Centrally Sponsored Schemes, ‘Development of Wildlife 
Habitats’ and ‘Project Tiger and Elephant’ for management of wildlife and its habitat 
including management of human-wildlife conflict in the country. The activities supported 
under the schemes include construction/erection of physical barriers such as solar 
powered electric fence, bio-fencing, boundary walls etc. to prevent the entry of wild 
animals into crop fields. 
(ii)  An advisory on dealing with human-wildlife conflict has been issued by the Ministry in 
February 2021. The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change has also issued 
guidelines to States/UTs on 3rd June, 2022 on managing human-wildlife conflicts 
including damage to crops. The Advisory recommends coordinated interdepartmental 
action, identification of conflict hot spots, adherence to Standard Operating Procedures, 
establishment of rapid response teams, formation of State and District level committees 
to review the quantum of ex-gratia relief, and issuing guidance/instructions for expedited 
payments etc. 
(iii)  The Ministry has also issued species-specific guidelines to deal with human-wildlife 
conflict situations on 21.03.2023. 
(iv)  The Section 11 (1) (a) of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, empowers the State Chief 
Wild Life Wardens to grant permits for hunting animals listed in Schedule I of the Act, 
which become  dangerous to human life. Further, the Section 11 (1) (b) of the Act 
empowers State Chief Wild Life Warden or any authorized officer to grant permits for 
hunting of wild animals falling under Schedule-II of the Act, if such animals have 
become dangerous to human life or property. 
(v)  A network of protected areas namely, National Parks, Sanctuaries, Conservation 
Reserves and Community Reserves covering important wildlife habitat have been created 
all over the country under the provisions of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 to 
conserve wild animals and their habitats. 
(vi)  In accordance with provisions contained under Section 33 of the Wild Life (Protection) 
Act, 1972, the Ministry has issued guidelines for the process of management planning for 
protected areas and other landscape elements. 
(vii)  Periodic awareness campaigns to sensitize guide and advise the general public on human-
wildlife conflict, including dissemination of information through various forms of media 
is carried out by the respective State Governments/Union Territory Administrations.
