Climate Change 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.15 The Committee is of the view that Climate change is a global concern and India, being 
amongst the most populous countries, needs to be concerned about that. Our National Action 
Plan for Climate Change (NAPCC) has missions in areas like solar energy, energy efficiency, 
water, human health, sustainable agriculture, Himalayan ecosystem, sustainable habitat, and 
strategic knowledge of climate change. We must cooperate with other countries globally, as 
climate summits, after the Paris Agreement, have shown slow progress.  While taking 
progressive steps, India must correlate her efforts with other countries. The Committee notes 
that the new U.S. administration's withdrawal from climate funding is a matter of concern, as 
they had committed to contributing $100 billion to the climate fund under the Paris Agreement.  
Not only have they backed out, but even the international organizations, like, the WHO has 
shown its reservations. Under these circumstances, India, being a large country and being a 
major player in climate change mitigation, must take responsibility and work towards achieving 
its goals.                                                                                                                   (Para 7.5 ibid)  
 
Action Taken 
1.16 (i)  The Government stands committed in combating climate change and have already 
put in place various ambitious programs, schemes and initiatives to deal with 
challenge of climate change, and the environmental problems.   
 (ii)  India submitted its Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) under the Paris 
Agreement and communicated to the United Nations Framework Convention on 
Climate Change (UNFCCC) in 2015 and subsequently updated it in August, 2022. 
India's updated NDC seeks to enhance India’s contributions towards achievement of 
the strengthening of global response to the threat of climate change, as agreed under 
the Paris Agreement.  Such action will help India usher in low emissions growth 
pathways.  It would protect the interests of the country and safeguard its future 
development needs based on the principles and provisions of the UNFCCC.   
 (iii) India now stands committed to reduce Emissions Intensity of its GDP by 45 percent 
by 2030, from 2005 level and achieve about 50 percent cumulative electric power 
installed capacity from non-fossil fuel-based energy resources by 2030. The decision 
on enhanced NDCs demonstrates India’s commitment at the highest level for 
decoupling of economic growth from greenhouse gas emissions. India’s NDC is 
currently being implemented over the period 2021-2030 through programs and 
schemes of relevant Ministries /Departments and with due support from States and 
Union Territories.  
  
 (iv)  India submitted India’s Long-Term Low-Carbon Development Strategy to UNFCCC 
in November 2022. The document lays out India's approach to low-carbon 
development pathway, taking note of the development challenges in the context of 
climate change and cognizant of its historical traditions and culture that seeks 
harmony and balance between human society and nature. 
  
 (v)  The Government is implementing the National Action Plan on Climate Change 
(NAPCC). It is the overarching policy framework and comprises of nine national 
missions in specific areas of solar energy, enhanced energy efficiency, water, 
agriculture, Himalayan eco-system, sustainable habitat, health, green India and 

 
8 
 
strategic knowledge on climate change.  All the nine Missions under National 
Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC) has been updated and revised to align 
with India’s NDC and emerging scientific knowledge. Each National Mission is 
being anchored by respective Ministries/Departments. Ministry of Environment, 
Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) is anchoring the National Mission for a 
Green India (GIM).   
 (vi)  To support the objectives of NAPCC, as on date, 34 States and Union Territories 
have already prepared their State Action Plan on Climate Change (SAPCC) to 
address State specific actions. States/UTs have been asked to revise the SAPCC. 
Under the Climate Change Action Plan, a grant of 20 lakhs per State/UT is 
sanctioned for revision of SAPCC.  
 (vii) India submitted its Initial Adaptation Communication to the United 
Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) in 2023, 
highlighting the adaptation priorities, strategies, policies and programmes of the 
country along with implementation support needs for adaptation action.  India has 
been diligently working towards adaptation in mission mode. Several policies and 
measures have been put in place across key economic sectors, keeping in mind the 
wide scope of adaptation activities. India has been spending significant amount of 
resources on adaptation relevant actions, despite the competing demands for limited 
resources in a developing economy.  
 (viii) India, despite its pressing development imperatives, has accorded a prominent focus 
to the sustainability aspects in its accelerated economic growth. India recognizes 
adaptation is inevitable and imperative for its development process and has been 
undertaking several efforts to increasingly mainstream adaptation efforts while 
furthering developmental requirements through a range of schemes/ projects/ 
programmes of several Ministries/ Departments to improve adaptive capacities and 
reduce socioeconomic vulnerabilities of the people.  
 (ix)  Some examples of India's efforts to transition to a more sustainable and self-reliant 
energy sector are:- 
  (a) The National Green Hydrogen Mission which focuses on domestically producing 
and utilizing green hydrogen, a clean fuel derived from renewable sources, to 
decarbonize industries and reduce fossil fuel dependence. 
  (b) Green sovereign bonds are debt instruments used by the government to finance 
green infrastructure projects, including those related to renewable energy and energy 
efficiency. 
  (c) Nuclear Energy Mission- India has a significant nuclear power program. The 
mission aims to increase nuclear energy generation to meet the growing energy 
demand and reduce reliance on fossil fuels. This could involve the development of 
advanced reactor technologies and the expansion of existing nuclear power plants. 
  (d) India has committed to achieving 500 GW of non-fossil energy capacity by 
2030 and sourcing 50% of its energy from renewable sources by the same year.  
  (e) India aims to reduce projected carbon emissions by one billion tonnes by 2030 
and lower the carbon intensity of its economy by 45% compared to 2005 levels, 
also by 2030. 

 
9 
 
  (f) India has pledged to reach net-zero emissions by 2070.  
  (g) India has also launched initiatives like "Lifestyle for the Environment" and 
implemented policies for protecting regional glaciers, greening the railway system, 
and reducing single-use plastic. 
  (h) The Government of India has taken several steps to promote electric vehicles 
(EVs) and address climate change, including financial incentives, infrastructure 
development, and policy changes. These efforts aim to reduce emissions from the 
transportation sector and transition towards a sustainable mobility ecosystem.  
 (x) In nutshell the Government of India stands committed to protect, vulnerable 
populace from impacts of climate change, and the environment. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.17 During the meeting, the Committee also drew attention of the Ministry to the reports 
that in view of the recent climatic trends, the coming months of the year 2025-26 are likely to 
see temperatures soaring to 1-3°C higher than the average temperatures recorded in the past 
across various cities and terrains of the country, especially Delhi where the temperature may 
be abnormally high during the summer season of 2026.  The Committee is extremely concerned 
over such alarming reports. The Committee is of the view that, if this happens, it will have 
devastating consequences for human habitats, birds, animals, and the environment.  The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Environment, Forest & Climate Change 
should immediately formulate and implement a national-level Heat Action Plan (HAP) to 
mitigate the heatwave conditions that the citizens of India are likely to face in the coming 
months.                                                                                                                     (Para 7.6 ibid) 
        
Action Taken 
1.18 (i) In the context of Heat Waves, it is submitted that heat waves are one of the 
severe weather phenomena for which Indian Meteorological Department (IMD) issues colour

 (ii) IMD in collaboration with National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) and 
local health departments have started Heat Action Plans (HAPs) in many parts of the country to 
forewarn about the heat waves and also advising action to be taken during such occasions.  
 (iii) At present the HAPs have been implemented in 23 States that are prone to high 
temperatures leading to heat-wave conditions.  
  
 (iv) The heat wave bulletin is issued to provide heat wave forecast and warnings with 5-
day forecasts. Impact of heat wave expected over a region is being mentioned in colour codes

Centres at district levels.  Meetings are conducted by concerned departments of central and 
State Governments to review preparedness for the ensuing heat wave season.  
 (v) NDMA has taken all measures including holding Annual Workshop with Ministry of 
Earth Sciences, 23 Heat wave prone States/ UTs, selected districts, and key sectors like Health, 

 
10 
 
Water, Agriculture, Railways, and the civil society. They are also following the best practices of

 (vi) NDMA runs Awareness Generation campaign using Radio (Helpline FM Rainbow), 
TV (special episode of Aapdaka Samna, regional DD channels), eVidya DTH TV channels, and 
social media.  Short-term preparedness to long-term mitigation taken by NDMA are as follows: 
  (a) Comprehensive Mitigation Framework 
  (b) NDMA Manual on Cool Roof: technologies to reduce indoor temperature. 
  (c) Advanced Meteorological Services and operational forecasts for temperature, 
       wind, humidity, and heat index to inform mitigation strategies. 
  (d) Ecosystem and Water Management: green cover, water bodies

  (f) Integrating Heat wave Mitigation in Urban Planning: cool roofs, greenery,

  (g) Technological solutions: Construction technology, monitoring system. 
 (vii)  M/o Health and family welfare - issued Advisories to State Health Department on

The arrangements to deal with situation of heat waves are in place.

Control of pollution 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
2.5 The Committee is of the view that pollution, whether it be air, water or noise, has gone 
beyond permissible limits during the last few years and has serious consequences for the health 
and well being of the citizens of the country. Air pollution has assumed gigantic proportions 
and has become a national issue.  Although Delhi has been in the news because of it ever-
deteriorating air quality, other cities in the country are also not left behind and are 
experiencing high AQI levels.  In such a scenario, the Committee is shocked to note that amount 
to the tune of Rs.858.00 crore allocated for ‘Control of Pollution’, which is 27.44% of the 
annual RE allocation of the Ministry, remains unutilized since the approval for continuation of 
Control of Pollution Scheme till 2025-26, is awaited, even at the fag end of the financial year.  
The rising environmental pollution in the country not only results into a number of pollution 
related human diseases and health conditions but negatively impact our ecology too.  The 

 
13 
 
scenario of air pollution in the country is indeed very grim and has been affecting one and all.  
At a time when the Ministry is required to address the grave and critical challenge of 
deteriorating air quality, the Ministry has not been able to decide the continuation of the 
concerned scheme, as a result of which not even 1% of the funds allocated for the scheme have 
been utilized so far.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry needs to 
introspect and take a serious note of the reasons for this gross underutilization.                                                                 
                   (Para 5.4 ibid)

I, the Chairman of the Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and Forests, having been authorised
 by the Committee to present the report on its behalf, present this Fourth Report of the Committee. This Report deals
 with issues contained in the Annual Report of the Department of Electronics for the year 1992-93.
2. The Committee held in all four meetings on 24th, 25th June, 22nd September and 16th December, 1993
 (Appendix). In the meeting held on 24th June, 1993, the representatives of the Department of Electronics gave an
 overview of various activities of the Department. On 25th June and 22nd September, 1993 the Committee discussed in
 detail the activities of the Department.
3. The Committee expresses its appreciation for the officials of the Department for their cooperation and making
 available the material whenever required by the Committee.
4. The Committee considered and adopted the draft report at its meeting held on the 16th December, 1993.

R E P O R T
Introductory
Electronics is all pervasive, ubiquitous and universal. It has become a symbol of the progress and prosperity of a
 nation. It is one of the fastest growing industries. Electronics Industry on the one hand, is concerned with inputs which
 lead to the improvement of productivity of other sectors of economy and on the other hand, provides products of direct
 benefit to the consumer. It plays a vital role in industry, agriculture, communication, strategic sectors of Security,
 atomic energy, space, transportation, education, banking and many other areas. It has a tremendous potential for
 improving the living standards of the people. In India, Electronics has been gaining momentum over the past quarter of
 a century. Today one sees extensive use of component electronics in homes in the form of consumer Electronics, in
 offices as office support systems (PCs), Fax machines, etc. and in industry in terms of measurement and control
 systems.
2.         Keeping in view the importance of Electronics Industry, the Committee decided to examine the Annual Report
 of the Department of Electronics (1992-93). The Deptt. of Electronics was created in 1971 to implement the policies
 laid down by the Electronics Commission. After the abolition of the Electronics Commission in 1989, the said
 Department has been given the responsibility of policy-making as well as implementing the same. During the course of
 its deliberations, the Committee heard the views of the Secretary and other officials of the Department of Electronics.
General Overview
3.         The Secretary of the Department of Electronics placed before the Committee a broad picture of the functioning
 of the Department and stated that electronics and information technology, with the use of computers, etc. can make
 significant contributions towards social development and national prosperity, particularly through promoting industrial
 growth in saving energy and time, and bringing about improvement in productivity. Highlighting the achievements, the
 Secretary cited the example of introduction of computerised reservation in Railways which has not only brought down
 substantially the time taken in getting the booking done but also checked corruption to a great extent and thus
 contributed to public convenience. He also informed the Committee about the implementation of another project in the

4th REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/4threport.htm[29-08-2018 16:09:51]
 Department of the Posts for transfer of money order through satellite communication which would curtail to the extent
 of seven days the time usually taken in transmitting the money orders.
4.         As regards electronics production, the Committee was informed that consumer electronics constitutes nearly 30
 per cent, which is a substantial portion. Communication and broadcast equipments constitute about 25 per cent. During
 the Seventh Plan, the achievement of the consumer electronics industry was 170 per cent of the target. The growth of
 colour TV network, which was introduced in 1982, covered the whole country by 1984. It not only exceeded the target
 but also provided a base for the growth of the component industry of colour television during that period.
5.         It was also submitted that the share of Electronics Sector in GDP of the country is 2% it provides jobs to 4 per
 cent of the employment force; its contribution to the exports is 3 per cent which roughly comes about Rs.1260 crores.
 By 1995-96, this is likely to go up to 8 per cent. In order to develop indigenous technology, the Department has been
 operating Technology Development Council (TDC), National Radar Council (NRC), National Microelectronics
 Council (NMC) and Electronics Materials Development Council (EMDC). The TDC has so far funded 350 projects and
 quite a few of these technologies have been commercialised. Since its inception in 1974, NRC has supported 133
 Technology Development Projects in 44 institutions located in 14 States. So far 103 projects have been completed by it.
 Through NMC the Department of Electronics has sponsored R&D projects in academic institutions, laboratories and
 industries. These projects have made a positive impact on establishment of technology base, development of systems
 and trained manpower. Likewise, EMDC has also supported R&D projects in thrust areas like industry-oriented
 projects, advance material technologies and infrastructure building. During the year 1992-93, 28 projects were under
 implementation and out of which 6 projects have been completed.
6.         Government have also set up 21 laboratories for maintenance of quality of electronic goods. With a view to
 competing with foreign countries an emphasis has been given on quality control aspects, for which the Standardisation,
 Testing and Quality Control Directorate have entered into an agreement with the British Standard Institution to set up
 the ISO 9000 standard. This would help Indian Industries to get internationally recognised standard certification. The
 Centres at Bombay, Delhi and Calcutta have been authorised to give that certification. Government have also set up
 Electronics Research and Development Centres at Trivandrum and Pune. At present, the Department is implementing a
 World Bank Project of Rs.78 crores for upgrading the hardware in 32 institutions which includes about 14 electronics
 industries and about a dozen colleges and centres for electronic testing. This account represents a small part of the
 efforts of the Department of Electronics and index of the progress of electronics in India.
7.         The Committee took up for consideration the various subjects mentioned in the Annual Report (1992-93) and
 made certain recommendations thereon as per details given in the succeeding paragraphs.
Promotional Policy Measures
8.         Realising the importance of electronics in improving productivity and accelerating economic growth,
 Government have been announcing from time to time, a number of promotional policy measures and incentives for
 building a vibrant electronics industry. The most significant step taken was the introduction of Liberalised Exchange
 Rate Management System (LERMS) in place of EXIM scrip mechanism, under which certain categories of consumer
 electronics exports which had been granted flexible EXIM scrip earlier, were given special import licences.
 Simultaneously, the new Export and Import Policy simplified foreign trade regulations making it far more transparent
 than before. Promotion of electronics depends greatly on the quality of products for which the Department has launched
 its Standardisation Testing and Quality Control Programme which aims at inculcating consciousness for quality and
 reliability, thereby upgrading the overall quality of Electronic products manufactured in the country.
9.         The effect of these policy changes was felt immediately across the spectrum of electronics sector. As the import
 compression of the previous year was reduced substantially, the electronics industry started a slow recovery. The
 growth rate which had dropped to 5.7 per cent in 1991, rose to 17.2 per cent in 1992
10.       The Committee expressed concern over the slow progress in the export of electronic goods in comparison with
 other countries like Hungary, Taiwan who are exporting 20 times more than India and wanted to know the reasons for
 not capturing the export market even after the announcement of New Industrial Policy and various liberalisation
 measures. The Secretary replied that main reasons for poor performance of our export market are procedural constraints
 and tariff barriers. In July 1991, seventy such restrictions and procedural problems were identified. Some of them relate
 to the Customs and Excise, banking procedures and formalities and many other relate to State Governments. The matter
 was discussed in the meetings of Secretaries and some of the problems have been removed. Highlighting the procedural

4th REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/4threport.htm[29-08-2018 16:09:51]
 impediments, the Secretary cited the instance of Singapore where documents for imports/exports are cleared within 15
 minutes through the introduction of Electronics Data Change Network, as against 3 days' time taken in our country.
 Similarly, the Duty Drawback is given in South Korea in 3 days whereas in our country it takes more than 3 months.
 While summing up, the Secretary submitted that India can become a super Japan provided such type of environment is
 created in our country. The Secretary also submitted that one of the basic needs for software export is High Speed Data
 Communication which was not available in our country till 1990. Now the facility has been made available and the
 Satellite Earth Station has been set up in Bangalore from where Video Conference with U.S. is possible. Hyderabad,
 Gandhinagar, Trivandrum and Bhubaneshwar are also proposed to be covered during the current year. High Speed Data
 Communication facilities are being provided in Delhi, Bombay and Madras for which the funds are being provided by
 French Government.
11.       The next area of problem relates to dealing with the State Governments where every industrialist has to go
 through the hurdles of getting so many NOCs for setting up of the industry and such formalities take about 18 months.
 With a view to overcoming such difficulties, a suggestion was made to the State Governments to give priority for the
 industry and to provide grace period of 3 years during which other formalities can be completed. But no State
 Government has responded so far.
12.       The Secretary also informed that they are in constant touch with the Ministry of Finance to reduce the Customs
 Duties on electronics goods with a view to bringing down the cost of the products. Steps are also being taken to ensure
 investment on a large scale and for that purpose, the scheme of Electronics Hardware Technology Parks (EHTPs) has
 been brought forward, which allows 40% sale in India so as to achieve globalisation. Department of Electronics has
 also taken up the task of issuing concessional customs duty certificates for raw materials, components, piece parts etc.
13.       The Committee notes that the Government have taken a number of promotional policy measures to boost exports
 and attract foreign investment in the country, but the desired results have not been achieved so far while there are
 procedural impediments as stated by the Department, this is not the whole story. Some of our electronics products are
 not as good in terms of quality compared to those which are imported from outside. The Committee recommends that
 Government should immediately strive to remove the procedural hurdles and simplify the Rules and Regulations,
 specially relating to the Customs and Excise which are creating lot of harassment to exporters. State Governments
 should be directed to ensure that the industrialists/exporters are not forced to run from pillar to post to complete
 formalities. Single window system should be introduced in order to attract foreign investment as significant expansion
 of the electronics  industry will be facilitated through foreign investment. Apart from taking these administrative
 actions, the Committee feels that the Department should make serious efforts to identify areas of its strength and
 weakness. In areas where India can easily compete in export market, we should give more attention so that the export
 potential of the country is increased. In this regard the Department can make serious efforts to improve the quality of
 electronics components. The area of weakness may also be given special treatment so that the Department of
 Electronics becomes a vital agency in developing electronics in the country.
Software Technology Parks
14.       The scheme of Software Technology Park (STP) was introduced in 1986 with the prime objective of promoting
 software exports from the country and in pursuance thereof, the first Technology Park was set up which became
 operational in 1987. Department of Electronics has so far set up 7 STPs. Till March, 1993, 71 companies were accorded
 approval to operate under the Scheme from their, own premises as private STP units. The Government of Kerala has set
 up STP which is known as Techno Park on 150 acres of land around Kerala University. The construction work is in
 progress. The State Government of Haryana have also taken some steps for setting up a STP. One STP each has been
 set up in Jaipur and Calcutta by the respective State Governments.
15.       The companies operating under the STP Scheme exported software worth Rs.16 crores up to December 1992 as
 against India's total software export of Rs.675 crores at the end of 1992-93.
16.       The Committee was informed that a scheme for allowing legal reproduction of international software has been
 devised in order to bring down the cost of software in India. The scheme envisages the import of the master copy and
 on payment of royalty, reproduction of software can be undertaken within India. Automatic approval for the royalty
 payment will be granted by the foreign exchange dealers provided the royalty payable does not exceed 30 per cent of
 the Indian published price for the software. It is stipulated that at least 75 per cent of the savings should be passed on to
 the Indian customers by the person/company authorised to reproduce software on payment of royalty. The scheme
 would enable the Indian companies to provide software approximately 40 per cent cheaper in comparison to the

4th REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/4threport.htm[29-08-2018 16:09:51]
 international price. The Committee was further informed that as per the World Bank Report in the total software market
 of $250 b the share of countries like India is not more than 3% to 4%. The World Bank Report also suggested that it is
 possible to raise software export from $ 660 million as per present trends to lb by 1996 if the facility of High Speed
 Telecommunication and adequately trained manpower are made available.
17.       The Committee expressed its concern over the India's meagre share in the world software market and
 recommends that Government should take urgent steps to increase the domestic production. There has to be significant
 technology development of software and India should make advances in this field. We should develop our own strength
 in the area of software. We should also create suitable climate to attract NRIs for setting up industries in India. Priority
 should be given to the development of High Speed Communication System so as to enable the exporters to send out the
 products within the shortest period and interact suitably. There should be less regulation and more support so that these
 companies bring large amount of foreign exchange for the country. Besides, the software companies should not be
 asked to obtain a pollution certificate as these units do not cause any pollution. There should be an income-tax holiday
 at least for the period of five years.
Electronics Hardware Technology Park
18.       The Department of Electronics announced the Electronics Hardware Technology Park Scheme (EHTPs) to
 facilitate the transition of Indian manufacturers to a globalised environment and to attract sizeable international
 investments in the field of electronics. This Scheme is designed to correct some of the lacunae that exist in the Export
 Processing Zone/EOU policy when applied to high-tech field such as electronics. The main objective of the scheme was
 that entrepreneurs require much greater operational flexibility when operating in an industry which is characterised by
 rapidly changing technologies. This scheme has been made particularly attractive for investments in electronics raw
 materials and components, which have been a major weakness of the Indian electronics industry.
19.       The scheme provides the policy environment. The actual implementation of the Parks requires close co-
operation of State Governments. The EHTPs can be set up either by State Governments or by private or public sector
 companies. So far six proposals received from the State Governments for setting up of EHTPs have been approved and
 infrastructure is being set up there. 45 proposals have been given approval for setting up of private EHTP Units
 involving an investment of Rs.1852.4 crores with Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) of US $ 28.3 millions.
20.       The Committee hopes that under the scheme, large number of industries where value addition may be less than
 20% would be set up which would create more jobs. It would boost the production of electronics goods and enable the
 industries to compete with the foreign countries which would result in the earning of foreign exchange. The Commit,
 tee recommends that limitations like high cost, delays, red-tapism should be removed so as to enable our industries to
 operate like a unit in Singapore and Hong Kong where facilities of electronic Data Change Network and Duty
 Drawback are available for their exporters.
Technology Development
21.       The Technology Development Council (TDC) was set up in 1973 to generate indigenous technology. Since its
 inception, the Council has funded about 350 projects spread over about 100 organisations and a large number of
 technologies have been transferred to the industry during 1992-93. These include: Microprocessor Based Pan
 Monitoring System, Micro-Teimic System for Monitoring and Controlling the Temperature and MAPCON System for
 Sugar Industry, Axle Counters for Indian Railways, Zirconium Oxygen Sensor, Ultrasonic Flow Meter, Route
 Interlocking System for Indian Railways, etc.
22.       The Committee while appreciating the achievements made by the Department of Electronics in the field of
 technology development, wanted to know the details of amount spent by the Department on R & D projects like Centre
 for Materials for Electronics Technology (C-MET) alongwith the number of technologies developed by the Societies of
 the Department of Electronics. The Secretary replied that 63% of the Budgetary Grants is spent in providing assistance
 for technology research and development activities. He also submitted that 82 technologies were developed by these
 societies which have been commercialised. As regard C-MET, the Secretary replied that it is a new organisation
 operating through its Laboratories located at Pune, Thrissur and Hyderabad. The Hyderabad Laboratory has been
 assigned the task relating to high purity metals and alloys, semiconductor crystals related products. The Pune
 Laboratory deals with thick films materials, photocrests, MOS-MOCVD chemicals, basic chemicals for electronics
 components and related products. C-MET, Thrissur deals with electronic ceramics, ferrites, high purity rare earth
 materials and related products. Presently, C-MET is handling four projects with a total outlay of approximately Rs.72.5

4th REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY

 lakhs sponsored by Government agencies such Electronics Materials Development Council (EMDC), National
 Photonics Council and Ministry of Non-Conventional Energy Sources. C-MET has also attracted four projects with an
 outlay of Rs.7.45 lakhs from the Private Sector industries. The Secretary further submitted that assistance is provided to
 such institutions for development of indigenous technologies but they do not monitor their performance.
23.       The Committee observes that a large amount of money is being spent by the Department of Electronics on the
 funding of various societies like C-MET which are engaged in research and development but no machinery has been
 evolved to assess their performance. The Committee recommends that the Department should set up a cell to monitor
 the performance of societies and stop the funding where performance of the society is not upto the mark.
Semiconductor Complex Limited
24.       Semiconductor Complex Limited (SCL) started commercial production in 1984 and has been manufacturing
 LSI/VLSI devices and sub-systems for consumer, telecom, industrial and strategic sectors. With the liberalisation of
 Indian economy and to keep pace with the changing market scenario, SCL has been making efforts to diversify into
 new areas during the year.
25.       The Company has projected a sales turnover of Rs.65.01 crores with a cash profit of Rs.4.76 crores during 1992-
93. The company has achieved a sales turnover of Rs.51.00 crores against a target of Rs.55.71 crores till February,
 1993.
26.       VLSI Project: As part of the second phase of the project super structure of water fabrication plant has been
 constructed during the year. Work pertaining to clean room and equipment procurement has been kept in abeyance
 pending approval of the revised project proposal by the Government. Work on 66 KV sub-station, 11 KV load centre
 and Nitrogen gas plant is progressing as per the schedule. Some of the major electrical equipments are being installed
 and the 66 KV Power Transmission line is being laid. Civil construction work of Nitrogen gas plant has been going on
 parallely.
27.       On a point raised by the Committee about the availability of sufficient funds for the SCL and delay in its
 completion, the Secretary of the Department of Electronics informed the Committee that the Semiconductor Complex
 which is meant to make chips required for Defence and Space and other requirements, was set up initially at a cost of
 Rs.100 crores. In February, 1989 there was a fire in that facility. In 1990, Government agreed for Rs.183.29 crores for
 reconstruction. Then, in 1991 because of devaluation and restriction on import of components, the project cost from
 Rs.183.29 crores went up to Rs.315.13 crores which was approved on 18 March 1993. The Ministry of Finance was
 requested to provide Rs.97.09 crores during the current year for this project but the Ministry have advised the
 Department of Electronics to manage that expenditure within the budgetary grant for 1993-94 of Rs.137 crores, which
 the Department feels is not even sufficient to meet other expenditure. The Secretary submitted that this additional fund
 of Rs.97.09 crores during this year is absolutely necessary in order to enable the Department to reconstruct this facility.
 As regards the delay in the completion of project, the Committee was informed that an enquiry Committee was
 appointed to go into the cause of fire in the project. The Committee came to the conclusion that there was no sabotage
 but pointed out certain deficiencies like excess use of wood in the facility. Immediately after the submission of the
 report, Government adopted the Austrian Micro System in the foundry facility and also derided to have modern 6"
 Water facility instead of 4" Water facility. The said scheme was worked out in July 1990 but in early 1991 two major
 developments took place on the financial side. One was that Government put a lot of conditions for opening of L.C. for
 imports and secondly, the devaluation of the rupee. Since lot of imported equipments were required for the facility, the
 cost of which had substantially increased on account of devaluation of Indian currency, a revised estimate was
 submitted to the Ministry of Finance for approval which took more than a year. The Committee was further informed
 that the Company had been earning profits and whatever money was available, was utilised for civil works which is
 now, complete. The Committee was also told that the Company is functioning without a regular Chairman since June
 1989. In 1992, a lot of suggestions were made that the Government should not spend on the SCL and that the private
 sector should enter this area and the Government should not be in this business at all. In these circumstances, the matter
 could not be processed further. However, after a good deal of deliberation, Government have decided that this should
 be done through Public Investment Bureau and the revised estimates of Rs.315.13 crores was approved on 18 March,
 1993.
28.       Keeping in view the seriousness and importance of the SCL, the Committee strongly feels that inordinate delay
 has taken place in the finalisation of the project and as a result thereof cost escalation has taken place which could have
 been avoided had the decision to restructure the facility been taken promptly. The Committee wishes to emphasise that

4th REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/4threport.htm[29-08-2018 16:09:51]
 micro-electronics is a vital area and by loosing time on this project, the Department has, in fact, lost an opportunity of
 assuming leadership in the field. The Committee recommends that an additional fund of Rs.97.09 crores which has
 already been approved by the Government, must be released during the current year in order to enable the Department
 of Electronics to complete the project by the third quarter of 1994. The Committee also feels that such an important
 public sector unit should not be kept without top executive for such a long time.
Technology Missions
29.       Government have announced a number of schemes to give filip to electronics industry. Besides enhancing the
 flow of Technology from abroad, it has been decided to launch the following eight Technology Missions, essentially to
 strengthen the technology-base infrastructure and to commercialise the indigenous technologies to improve the
 performance of selected industries :--
(1) Information Highway: To develop the technologies required for an inter-connected information highway and
 implementing the same for networking of distributed institutions in India and abroad for collaboration research and
 resource-sharing. Under this project Indian Technological Institutions are proposed to be linked by a computer network
 which will give the facility for data-base access document transfer, Electronic Mail, etc. Total cost of this project is
 Rs.100 crores and budgetary allocation during the year 1993-94 is Rs.1 crore.
(2) Future Air Navigation System (FANS): To develop and productionise all equipment needed for satellite-
based navigation system for the aviation sector. By the end of the century, the entire aviation sector, both military and
 commercial, will shift from ground-based systems to satellite-based systems. Total cost of the project is Rs.23 crores
 and the budgetary provision during the year 1993-94 is Rs.1 crore.
(3) Retrofit Automation in Economic Sectors: To improve the efficiency and competitiveness of the key
 economic sectors of the Indian economy such as fertilizers, textiles, power, paper and pulp through the application of
 electronics in high-visibility demonstration projects. Total cost of the project is Rs.21 crores and there is no allocation
 of funds during the year 1993-94.
(4) Massively Parallel Supercomputer: To develop a high performance Parallel Supercomputer in the teraflop
 range with all necessary supporting hardware and software for both strategic and commercial applications. Total cost is
 Rs.48 crores and allocation for 1993-94 is Rs.3 crores.
(5) Microelectronics: To develop and productionise microelectronics (the basic building blocks of all
 electronics) which are of critical importance for strategic and industrial requirements. Total cost is Rs.87.42 crores and
 allocation is Rs.2 crores during 1993-94.
(6) Photonics/Optoelectronics: To develop photonics/optoelectronics core technologies and applications which
 are of critical importance of present and next generation of electronics, computers and communication system. Total
 cost is Rs.116 crores and budgetary provision is Rs.1 crore for the year 1993-94.
(7) New Electronics Materials: To develop technologies for selected electronics materials which are critical for
 the electronics industry to establish a competitive edge, and also to meet strategic and futuristic requirements. Total
 cost is Rs.21 crores and allocation is Rs.2 crores during 1993-94.
(8) Special Components (Strategic & Non-Strategic):  To develop in an integrated manner certain selected
 critical components (Strategic and non-strategic). These are at the cutting edge of technology and tend to be closely
 held. Total cost is Rs.102.35 crores and there is no allocation of funds during the year 1993-94.
30.       The representative of the Department informed the Committee that only 6 Missions out of 8 have been taken up
 because funds to the extent of Rs.10 crores against the total requirement of Rs.519.17 have been made available during
 the year 1993-94. Again, because of funds restriction, even within these missions, only limited projects have been taken
 up this year for implementation.
31.       The Committee appreciated the decision of the Department of Electronics for launching of Technology Mission
 for strengthening the technology-base  infrastructure, commercialisation of indigenous technologies for improving the
 performance of selected industries and their competitiveness, etc. The Committee, however, feels that in view of the
 financial constraints it will be possible only to take up certain specific Missions. Even these can be taken up if
 minimum fund is provided. For example, the Technology Mission on Micro-electronics which is considered as heart of
 the electronics industry, a sum of Rs.2 crores has been provided during 1993-94 as against its total requirement of

4th REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/4threport.htm[29-08-2018 16:09:51]
 Rs.87.42 crores. The Committee, therefore, recommends that a few Missions which are crucial should be identified and
 taken up first for implementation and no efforts should be spared in completing them within the prescribed time frame.
Manpower Development and Training
32.       A trained manpower is one of the basic requirements for the growth of domestic software industry and software
 exports of India. The Department of Electronics have undertaken various programmes to meet the future requirement of
 qualified technicians. Under the DOE-UGC programme, 11 Universities were approved for starting M.Sc. (Electronics
 Science) programme. 10 Universities were given the full amount of Rs.22 crores for equipments and books.
33.       The Committee was told that the Electronics Industry Development Project (Manpower Component) (IMPACT)
 assisted by the World Bank continued this year also and a sum of Rs.34.5 crores was earmarked by the Department of
 Electronics, Rs.77 crores by the World Bank and Rs.4 crores by the Government. 12 poly-technics, 14 colleges and 6
 Centres of Electronics Design and Technology (CEDTs) all over the country have been selected for improving
 infrastructural facilities. New syllabus is being chalked out and teachers are being trained in order to equip them with
 the skill to teach up-dated technology. The project was reviewed twice by the World Bank. The Government have also
 entered into an agreement with EEC and a sum of Rs.11 crores has been provided for Software Support System and
 Education Centre being set up in Bangalore where the students will be given training in Software details.
34.       The Department has also recommended for an assistance of about Rs.290 crores to the World Bank. Out of that
 Rs.175 crores will be given to different institutions like Aligarh Muslim University for improving both software and
 hardware infrastructure and for training purpose. The World Bank has already recommended the setting up of a
 Software Development Board for manpower development. Apart from that the Education Department under the
 Ministry of Human Resource Development had constituted the Reddy Committee which has made some suggestions
 for manpower development. An amount of Rs.292 crores is required for this aspect of improving educational
 infrastructure. A credit of $ 220 millions from the World Bank would also be available for the purpose.
35.       The Committee is happy to note that the Department of Electronics has drawn up a number of schemes and taken
 up programmes to provide infrastructure facilities for manpower development and training which will ensure a certain
 degree of uniformity in the standards throughout the country and improve the basic infrastructure for manpower
 development. The Committee recommends the Department of Electronics should evolve programmes which can ensure
 greater involvement of State Governments. Areas should also be identified where the Government can have the co-
operation of private sector. In view of financial constraints, the Committee feels that involvement of State Governments
 as well as of private sector would lessen the burden of the Central Government and it will also ensure the better use of
 resource with decentralised monitoring system. The Committee wishes to emphasize that India's great strength lies in
 her human resource. When we train our people, we would be getting trained manpower at relatively low cost.
 Therefore, the training of manpower in the field of electronics should be treated as thrust area by the Department. The
 Department should also develop mechanism to provide continuing education and refresher courses to its existing
 technical personnel to keep them a breast of the latest technological development in the field of electronics.
36.       The Committee was informed that Electronics is an employment oriented industry in which there is less
 investment as compared to areas like Petro-chemicals, steel, power-generation, shipbuilding, etc. It is possible to think
 of new employment opportunities by using electronics technology like Videographic Data Bases which provides
 World-wide satellite communication network system, wherein large number of educated unemployed persons can be
 engaged not only in cities but also in rural areas and small towns. The Committee, therefore, recommends that priority
 should be given to such electronics industry as would definitely solve the unemployment problem to some extent.
National HVDC Programme
37.       The National HVDC Project Stage-I 100MW/100 KV system between Lower Sileru in Andhra Pradesh and
 Barsoor in Madhya Pradesh was an R&D Project and has completed more than one year of continuous successful
 operation commercially exchanging power between the two States. This is one of the most significant achievements of
 India as the technology in this area is available with only 5 countries/consortia namely, ABB (Sweden), Seimens
 (Germany), GEC (UK) and Alsthom (France) consortium, Japan and Russia. This was an R&D project funded jointly
 by the Ministry of Defence, Department of Heavy Industry and Department of Atomic Energy. It was a fine example of
 team work.
38.       The Committee appreciated the work done by the Department of Electronics in implementing the HVDC project
 Stage-I and desired to know about its future programme in this regard. The Committee was informed that the success of

4th REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/4threport.htm[29-08-2018 16:09:51]
 the National HVDC Project Stage-I (100MWA00KV) has paved the way for HVDC Stage-I (200MW/200KV) to be
 implemented as an operational project with concurrent Reserach & Development activities in hardware, new control
 concepts, etc. and jointly funded by the Departments of Heavy Industry, Electronics, Power, BHEL ABSEB and MPEB
 at a total cost of Rs.105 crores. An Inter-Ministerial Committee under the Chairmanship of Member, Power System,
 CEA has also recommended the entrusting of either the 500 MW Jeypore-Gazuwaha or 2×250 MW Mau Bihar Sharif
 two commercial HVDC Back to Back projects identified as 8th Plan as Projects whichever is decided earlier to BHEL
 to enable it to execute a commercial project with independent responsibility based on the strengths built through
 NHVDC Stage-I. The estimated cost of this project is approximately Rs.400 crores and funds availability is creating
 difficulties in taking a decision. Hence, Power Grid Corporation has issued a global tender for the 500 MW Jeypore-
Gazuwaha Project which calls for financial package of soft loan/grant which will inhibit BHEL to capitalise on the
 strengths built through NHVDC Stage-I. The Committee was also informed that if funds are made available for
 implementation of this project it will help India to establish the capability of independently handling commercial
 HVDC projects with associated performance guarantee. It would also increase indigenous contents in future projects
 and create an opportunity to earn foreign exchange. In case the funds are not made available, it is likely to result in the
 inability to consolidate on the strength built so far and lose the opportunity to enter global market which an HVDC
 Stage-I has got both nationally and internationally. In view of this, the Committee recommends that adequate funds
 should be made available to implement 500 MW Jeypore-Gajuwaha project independently by BHEL/Power Grid
 Corporation.
General Observations
39.       Electronics is one of the few factors which permeates Atomic energy, Defence, Railways, Industries, Chemicals
 etc. Accordingly, the Department is required to play an important role to bring about electronification and electronic
 culture in the country and if co-ordination with other Ministries like Finance, Railways, Defence, Planning
 Commission, etc. could have been better, the progress of electronics industry would have been certainly at a higher rate
 than what is it presently. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Department of Electronics should
 play the promotional and catalytic role by coordinating with different Ministries and Departments which are engaged in
 the development of the new technologies and also in the production of electronics items in various hi-tech areas.
 Government should also look into the matter seriously and revive the Electronics Commission.
40.       The Committee also recommends that every Department should earmark a fixed about of budget for its
 electronification in view of the universal nature of Electronics.
Action Taken on the Recommendations Contained in the First Report of the Lok Sabha Committee on Science &
 Technology (1993-94)
41.       The First Report of the Committee on Science & Technology (1993-94) of the Lok Sabha which deals with the
 Department of Electronics focussing specially on imports and indigenisation, was presented to the Lok Sabha on 29th
 March, 1993 and recommendations of that Committee contained in the Report were referred to the Department of
 Electronics for compliance.
42.       The Committee enquired from the Secretary about the decision taken on the various recommendations contained
 in the Report.
43.       The Secretary told the Committee that out of the 85 recommendations, 60 relate to other Ministries which have
 been referred to them for necessary action, but no reply has since been received from those Ministries. The Committee
 was also informed that the Department of Electronics has accepted the remaining recommendations with the exception
 of these recommendations contained in para 3.30, 3.37 and 4.28 of the Report for which the Secretary of the
 Department explained the position to the Committee. The Committee hoped that with regard to the recommendations
 made in the First Report of the Committee on Science and Technology with which other Ministries and Departments
 are concerned, the Department of Electronics would inform the Committee about the implementation of those
 recommendations.

REPORT 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Science and Technology, Environment and Forests, having been authorised by the 
Committee, do hereby present on its behalf, this 40th Report of the Committee. This 
report deals with the programmes and functioning of the Department of Bio-technology 
with special emph asis on the role of Bio-technology in Agriculture and Allied areas on the 
basis of 'Mid- Term Appraisal' undertaken by the Committee. 
2. In the meeting of the Committee held on the 27th January, 1997, the Secretary and 
other officers of the Department of Bio-technology gave an overview of the various 
activities of the Department and the Committee sought clarifications on the various aspects 
of the functioning of the Department particularly about the activities relating to the fields 
of Crop Biotechnology , Biofertilizer, Biopesticides , Sericulture, Plant Tissue Culture, 
Acquaculture, Biosafet y, financial aspects, etc. 
3. The Committee wishes to express its appreciation to the officers of the Department 
of Biotechnology for their coo peration and making available the material requisitioned by 
the Committee on various aspects on programmes undertaken by the Department. 
4. The Committee conside red and adopted the draft report at its meeting held on the 
5th March, 1997. 
5. After the decipherment of the structure of DNA molecule by Watson and Crick in 
1953, major breakthroughs have taken place in the field of Mole cular Biology lead ing to a 
better understanding of origin of life and life processes. All the characteristics of the living 
organisms from single cell microbes and viruses to multicellul ar organisms e.g. pla nts , 
animals and hum an being are determined on the basis of information coded in the ir nucle ic 
acid, the basic genetic material which is mainly the template Deoxyn ibon ucleic Acid 
(DNA) assisted chiefly by anothe r nucleic acid e.g. Ribon ucleic Acid (RNA). It is now 
possible to isolate, splice and clone and even tra nsfer genes of interest from microbes, 
plants, animals and humans and get them expressed in any other organism or cell derived 
from them. Scientists have unfolded the secrets of genetic code, deciphered the mechanism 
of protein synthesis in living cells, identified and located spec ific genes and have learnt to 
establi sh the genetic reasons of many diseases like siekel cell anaemia, Beta Thalassemia or 
phenylketonuria etc . As a result, a large number of biotechnology industries have come 
up , specially in the pharmaceutical sector all over the world. It has been fully recognized 
that to have biotechnol ogy based industrial development , it would be esse ntial to bring 
together the disciplines of Medicine, Biology, Chemistry , Engineering and other areas. It 
was with a view to explo it the potential of biotechnology revolution and to derive 
econOinic benefits of the same in India , that the Department of Biotechnology was set- up 
in Februa ry, 1986. 
6. The Se<.:rctary. Department of Biotechnology in her presenta tion before the 
Committee. gave an overview of the thrust areas in wh~{ h the Department was engaged 
durin g the year 1996-97 particularly the applicat ion df Biotechnology in the field of 
agriculture and allied areas for the overall Socio-econom ic progress. The thrust of the 
Department had been in Research & Development in ident ified areas of modern biology 

and biotechnology; demonstration and technology transfer; human resource developoment; 
creation of infrastructural facilities; industrial biotechnology; support to autonomous 
research institutions; and international Collaborations. The Secretary informed the 
Committee that during the last ten years of its existence, a unique feature of the Department 
has been to involve the scientific community of the country through a number of technical 
task forces, advisory committees and as individual experts in identification, formulation, 
implementation and monitoring of various programmes and activities. The task forces in 16 
identified areas namely - crop biotechnology and plant molecular biology, plant tissue 
culture, basic research, medical biotechnology, medicinal and aromatic plants, microbial 
biotechnology, environment and biodiversity conservation, aquaculture and marine 
biotechnology, human genetics, food biotechnology, biological control of pests and diseases, 
biotechnology of silkworms and host plants, process engineering and bioinformatics have 
been the main strength of the scientific programmes. In addition, individual expert 
committees like steering committee on biofertilisers, immunological approaches to fertility 
control, neurosciences and immunodiagnostics development have also been guiding the 
programmes in these areas. Biotechnology based projects for SCIST and weaker sections 
have made significant impact on the target population. 
7. In order to realise the full potential of Biotechnology in the field of agriculture and 
allied areas, technology transfer and product generation have been supported in the areas 
relating to agriculture and allied fields covering: Crop Biotechnology and Plant Molecular 
Biology; Bio-fertilizers and Bio-control. Plantation Crops; Animal Biotechnology and 
Aquaculture; Seribiotechnology; Medicinal and Aromatic Plants and Food-Biotechnology. 
The Committee was informed that about 225 projects have been funded in these areas and 
55-60% funds were invested. The Department was working in dose collaboration with 
Indian Council of Agricultural Research (!CAR), Ministry of Agriculture. State Level 
Institutions, Agricultural Universities, NGOs and other R & D Academic institutions. Most 
of the projects were being implemented by the !CAR institutions. Joint monitoring 
mechanisms had been instituted. There was a DBT - !CAR Committee and small sub­
groups which met regularly for identification of joint programmes, their expeditious 
implementation and monitoring. It was stated that every effort was being made to avoid 
duplication. 
8. The Department, the Committee was informed , has tried to develop new plant 
varieties with novel traits by strengthening plant breeding programmes and initiating plant 
research and crop improvement packages at its 7 centres for plant molecular biology 
(CPMBs). Twenty R & D projects on four priority crops namely rice. wheat. chickpea and 
rape mustard have been launched by Jawaharlal Nehru University, New Delhi; Madurai 
Kamraj University, Madurai; Tamil Nadu Agriculture University, Coimbatore; Bose 
Institute, Calcutta; Osmania University, Hyderabad; National Botanical Research Institute. 
Luck now and Delhi University, Delhi. Two multi-institutional projects: (i) the development 
of transgenic cotton varieties resistant to insect pests; and (ii) quality improvement in wheat 
have also been launched. The Secretary apprised the Committee of some salient 
achievements of these projects as under:-
A gene encoding for a protein of lysine and containing amino acid from Amaranthus 
has been cloned sequenced and transferred in to potato with the objective of 
improving the nutritional quality (JNU, New Delhi); 
Transgenic tobacco plants expressing Bt gene have been tested for insect susceptibility 
in. R2 and R3 generations. Also transgenic plants with CpTl gene in Ro population are 
under investigation; gene conferring insect resistance / tolerance have been transferred 

in to mustard chickpea and rice. Transgenic plants and the stable lines would be soon 
subjected to tests for insect resistance (National Botanical Research Institute , 
Lucknow and Bose Institute, Calcutta); 
Several somatic hybrids of Brassica using protoplast hybridization developed between 
B. Juncea and wild spp. for introgressing genes for CMS and disease resistance 
through cytogenetic manipulation. Hybrids were confirmed through molecular analysis. 
Plants resistant to Alternaria blight and white rust were selected among the progenies 
of somatic hybrids and backcrossed with B. Juncea and B. napus (Indian Agricultural 
Research Institute, New Delhi; Bose Institute, Calcutta); 
In mungbean, transformation has been successfully carried out through co-cultivation 
with Agrobacterium tumefaciens and putative transgenic plants raised in laboratory 
condition (Calcutta University); 
Blackgram has been successfully transformed with npt II (neomycin phostransferase II) 
marker gene (MKU, Madurai); and 
In cotton, a method for production of multiples standardized. The chemic al synthe sis 
of Cry lA (c) designed for high level expression and transformation work initiated. 
9. The Mission Mode project on "Technology Development and Demonstration of 
Biofertilizers - Blue Green Algae (including Azolla) and Rhizobium " and thirty R & D 
projects have been supported ; large scale production technologies have been developed and 
standardised for indoor and outdoor production of BGA. Alternate carrier materials like 
rice/wheat/maize straw/sugarcane waste/corn dust and rice husk have been successfully 
introduced. Polyalkene bioreactors have been used for scaling up of genetically pure 
cultures. Large scale production technologies have been developed and standardised for 
indoor and outdoor production of BGA. The improved new technologies include live algal 
cultures in polybags called "Flexibioreactors ". The carriers like pulverized straws of wheat , 
rice , maize and dried powder of sugarcane leaves, Mont Morillonite Clay were found to be 
potential carrier. Several algal biofertilizer parks have been established in the States of 
Mahaiashtra and Tamil Nadu. 
9.1 The Committee recommends that in order to ensure production and distribution of 
adequate quantities of quality based Bio-fertilizers efforts should be made to open atleast one 
centre during the year 1996-97 in each of the States/Union Territories . The Department 
should ensure the availability of mother culture of micro-organisms from research centres/ 
universities sponsoring for large scale commercial production of biofertilizers through 
appropriate public/co-operative and non-governmental agencies. It should also launch a 
nation-wise awareness programme for dissemination of basic information on biofertilizers 
intelligible to common population. 
10. The Department established a Biocontrol Network Programme in 1989 initially with 
10 R & D projects. Presently, the programme is stated to be running with about 60 R & D 
projects at various institutes/universities throughout the country. The biocontrol agents and 
biopesticides include microbial pesticides (baculoviruses), parasitoids , predators , antagonistic 
fungi and bacteria for use under Integrated Pest Management System (IPM). 
The Committee was informed that the efficacy of biocontrol agents have been 
demonstrated in farmers ' field at multilocations covering an area of 11,700 ha. throughout 
the country. Mass production technologies have been developed for NPV of Heliothis 
armigera, NPV of Spodopter4 litura , GV of Chilo infuscatellus , Trichogramma, Chrysopa, 
Trichoderma viridae and other species , Gliocladium virens and Pseudomonas fluorescens and 

their efficacy have been demonstrated in the fields of cotton, chickpea, tobacco, sugarcane, 
groundnut, sunflower, blackgram, greengram, pigeonpea and other pulses, sesame and 
cauliflower and other vegetables. A baculovirus based technology at Kerala Forest Research 
Institute, Trissur for the management of teak defoliator, a serious pest of teak plantation in 
India and a protocol of cheap mass production of NPV is being standardized. 
10.1 The Committee is of the view that popularisation of Bio-pesticides Technology is an 
important component of Integrated Pest Management System. The Committee recommends 
that mass awareness programmes should be undertaken in all the States of the country 
including setting up of demonstration units. The feedback from the farmers, who are the 
ultimate users be analysed and improved in light of the feedback. In order to achieve the 
above objective more production units should be set-up in coordination with or by other 
concerned Ministries in different States with the help of willing entrepreneurs. The 
Department should also take initiatives to identify biological control of crops having significant 
export potential. 
11. The Committee was apprised of some of the drought resistant varieties of certain 
crops including Sorghum and Bajra. It was stated that the Department has also initiated 
research in plantation crops including Pepper, Tea and Coffee. A successful project on Oil­
Palm demonstration in the State of Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Maharashtra has been 
completed. 
11.1 The Committee feels that keeping in view the requirements of different Agro-climatic 
regions of the country efforts should· be made to involve more and more States in various 
projects. The Committee recommends that in order to expedite research for technology 
transfer in the areas of drought resistant varieties and cover more areas for Palm-Oil 
cultivation. The Committee notes that although the DBT had generated several result oriented 
technologies much was left to monitor the transfer of results of various researches after field 
testing to the user Ministries/Departments particularly that of agriculture. The Committee 
feels that there is need for minimising the time gap between the results of research and its 
application. . 
12. The Committee took note of the position regarding patenting in Biotechnology in the 
country. The DBT started promoting patenting of inventions from the middle of 1994 and has 
already filed 17 patent applications. 7 patent applications are under process. The Committee 
is of the view that the research institutes need to be encouraged to protect their inventions 
before the same are published. Perhaps many projects lose their importance before they are 
commercially exploited. There is therefore need to choose the research projects with abundant 
caution keeping in view their viability and importance in the specialised fields. 
12.1 The Committee feels that DBT should make sufficient financial provisions and 
strengthen in-house expertise to provide both financial and technical assistance to DBT funded 
investigations for securing inventions made by them in India and abroad. In order to catalyse 
large scale dissemination and commercialization of technologies, the scale up and 
demonstration need to be undertaken with the active involvement of industries and 
enterpreneurs along with research institutions and DBT. Some professional interface 
organisations like the Biotech Consortium India Ltd., (BCIL) and National Reseach 
Development Corporation (NRDC) · could also be brought in to the forefront to assist the 
process. 
12.2 Although the DBT has generated technologies and processes which can be utilised by 
the industry, the response of the latter to commercially exploit them had not been 
encouraging. The Committee feels that this could be attributed to a variety of factors 
including the weak linkages between the industry and research institutions. The Committee 

recommends that the DBT should carry out join~ development work tegether with the industry 
and the user institutes so that a closer liaison is established on the utility of the projects. 
13. During the last 10 years of its existence , the Department of Biotechnology has not 
set up many of its own research institutions. Instead it has made use of the existing 
infrastructure in the country; the national laboratories , state level research institutions and 
the universities. This has resulted in strengthening the expertise and capability and in 
capacity building in the field of biotechnology. Keeping in view the number of research 
publications and the work being done in the advance areas of molecular biology in 20 to 25 
reputed research institutions in the country there is need for the personnel with tremendous 
amount of experience in diverse fields. Even while considering support in terms of 
consu mable , research requirement etc. based on identified research programmes, the 
question of availability of trained manpower would continue to be a serious concern. 
13.1 The Committee is of the view that the Department should make every effort to have 
a dialogue with the host institutions as well as other scientific agencies, UGC and State 
Government Departments to take over technically trained personnel and creat more positions 
for their regularisation and absorption . In training the manpower, the country has made 
considerable investment in advance areas of research, development and application and losing 
this manpower would entail huge national loss. The Department should be consious of the fact 
that more often a potential Scientist goes abroad as a student and subsequently spends all or 
most of his/her working life abroad which is the crux of the problem of brain-drain.

REPORT 
 
 
The Action Taken Report (ATR) of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Science and Technology, Environment, Forests and Climate Change deals with the 
action taken by the Government on the recommendations/observations of the Committee contained 
in its ‘Three Hundred Ninety Third Report’ on ‘Demands for Grants (2025-26) of the Ministry of 
Earth Sciences. The Report was presented to/laid on the Table of both the Houses of the 
Parliament on the 25th March, 2025.  
2. Action Taken Notes (ATNs) have been received from the Ministry of Earth Sciences in 
respect of all the 11 recommendations/observations contained in the ‘Three Hundred Ninety Third 
Report’. The replies of the Ministry of Earth Sciences have been categorized as follows:-  
Chapter I: Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the 
Government: Para Nos. 2.3, 2.6, 3.3, 6.5, 7.7, 8.5, 9.3, 10.5, 11.5 
 Total recommendations – 09  
Chapter II:    Recommendations/Observations which the Committee does not desire to 
pursue in view of the Government’s replies: 
Para Nos. 5.4, 7.4 
 Total recommendations – 02 
Chapter III: Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the 
Government have not been accepted by the Committee: Nil 
Chapter IV:   Recommendations/Observations in respect of which final replies of the 
Government are still awaited: Nil 
  
3. The details of the ATNs have been analyzed in the succeeding Chapters. 

 
2 
 
CHAPTER-I 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
GOVERNMENT 
 
 
Budgetary details for the financial year 2024-25 and allocation for 2025-26 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.1 The Committee observes that the utilization trend of the Ministry during the last three years 
has not been very encouraging.  The Ministry could utilize merely 76.8% and 83.4% of the 
allocated funds during the years 2022-23 and 2023-24. In 2024-25, against the BE allocation of 
Rs.3064.80 crore, an increased RE allocation of Rs.3632.78 crore was made to the Ministry.  
However, the Committee is constrained to note that the actual expenditure of the Ministry upto 
21.01.2025 was only Rs.1952.75 crore which is merely 53.75% of the RE allocation.  During the 
presentation made before the Committee on 20.2.2025, the Secretary of the Ministry further 
informed that the Ministry has utilized Rs.2261.69 crore as on 13.02.2025, which still remains only 
62.30% of the RE allocation.  The Committee is of the view that the utilization of funds by the 
Ministry during 2024-25 in also not satisfactory.  With hardly 40 days left in the completion of the 
financial year, the Ministry is yet to make use of nearly 38% of the funds allocated to it.   The 
Committee is of the view that the Ministry must make proactive efforts to optimally utilize the funds 
made available to it during the financial year 2024-25.     
(Para 2.3 of the 393rd Report) 
Action Taken 
1.2 As suggested by the committee, the Ministry has adopted proactive efforts and optimally 
utilised Rs. 3389.54 Crores (93.3% of RE allocation) of the funds made available during the 
financial year 2024-25. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
  
1.3 The Committee notes that the Ministry has assured that they would be able to spend a large 
chunk of amount available with them within the current financial year.  The Committee hopes that, 
as assured by the Ministry, they would be able to make use of the remaining budgetary allocation 
available with them during 2024-25.  The Committee is of the view that instead of dragging their 
activities till the end of the financial year, the Ministry must make proactive efforts to optimally 
utilize the funds made available to it well in time. 
 (Para 2.6 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.4 As suggested by the committee, the Ministry has adopted proactive efforts and optimally 
utilised Rs. 3389.54 Crores (93.3% of RE allocation) of the funds made available during the 
financial year 2024-25. 
 
Budgetary Allocations for 2025-26 

 
3 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.5 The Committee notes that the Ministry has been, to a large extent, able to get the allocation 
required by them for the year 2025-26.  The Committee also observes that there has been no 
reduction at all in the funds requested by the Ministry for its various Schemes and the reduction 
has only been in case of Autonomous bodies and Establishment Expenditure.  The Committee 
hopes that having been allocated the sum as desired for its various schemes,  the Ministry would 
now plan and execute all activities in respect of all its schemes with the desired outcomes and 
efficiency and make full utilization of the funds allocated to them for the next financial year.  
(Para 3.3 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
1.6 The Ministry will take all the necessary measures and will ensure the full utilization of 
funds allocated during FY 2025-26. 
 
 
Prithvi Vigyan (PRITHVI) 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.7 The Committee observes that the Ministry has been able to utilize 74.01% of the allocated 
amount upto 13th February 2025.  The Committee hopes that the Ministry will be able to optimally 
utilize the allocation made to this scheme by the end of the financial year.  The Committee is also 
of the view that the overarching scheme of Prithvi Vigyan will enable development of integrated 
multi-disciplinary earth science research and innovative programs across different MoES 
institutes and the integrated R&D efforts will help in addressing the grand challenges of weather 
and climate, ocean, cryosphere, seismological science and services and explore the living and 
non-living resources for their sustainable harnessing.  
(Para 6.5 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.8 Out of the total allocation of Rs. 695 Crores under PRITHVI scheme, an amount of Rs. 
667.38 Crores (97.42 %) was utilized by the end of FY 2024-25 
 
 
Mission Mausam 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.9 The Committee hopes that with the requisite budget allocation at their disposal, the 
Ministry would make all out efforts to ensure that all the objectives of the Mission planned for the 
next financial year are achieved in a time-bound manner and allocation utilized optimally.  The 
Committee feels that by improving weather prediction accuracy, Mission Mausam will have a 
profound impact on sectors like agriculture, disaster management, and transportation, enabling 
better preparedness and more effective responses to climate and weather events. The mission’s 
integrated approach will help deliver more precise, timely, and actionable forecasts, thus 
contributing to improved safety, economic stability, and climate resilience for India.  
(Para 7.7 ibid) 

 
4 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.10 Mission Mausam aims to enhance weather monitoring and forecasting across India and 
surrounding regions by leveraging state-of-art observational, computing technologies and 
advanced data assimilation and modelling techniques for improved weather and climate services. 
 
1.11 Mission Mausam will help in building the “Early Warnings For All” Initiative and mitigate 
the impact of climate change-induced extreme weather events and strengthen the resilience of the 
communities, with the ultimate goal of making Bharat a "Weather-ready and Climate-smart" 
nation. 
1.12 It will help better equip all the stakeholders, including citizens and last-mile users, to tackle 
extreme weather events and the impacts of climate change. 
 
High-Performance Computing System 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.13 The Committee is happy to note that the High Performance Computing System (HPC) was 
commissioned in September 2024 and the financial commitments for the same would also be 
completed within this financial year.  The Committee hopes that HPC would not only enable the 
institutes of the Ministry to fulfil the desired objectives of supporting numerical modelling for 
weather and climate forecasting, basic research, and data assimilation but also provide 
computational resources to the academic and R&D community, to undertake research and 
development and enable improvements in operational forecasting systems and enhance forecast 
skill.  
(Para 8.5 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
1.14 The Ministry is pleased to report that the High-Performance Computing System (HPC) was 
successfully commissioned in September 2024. A capital expenditure of approximately ₹714.31 
crore has been made in FY 2024–25 for the system. 
1.15 Currently, the National Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasting (NCMRWF), 
Noida, and the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology (IITM), Pune, are in the process of 
transitioning their operational models to the new HPC infrastructure. The Ministry is ensuring that 
the system operates with an uptime of 99.99% to support continuous and reliable performance for 
weather and climate forecasting, as well as basic research and data assimilation. 
 
Autonomous Bodies 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.16 The Committee notes that the financial performance of all the autonomous institutions 
under the Ministry has been satisfactory during the years 2022-23 and 2023-24.  In 2024-25, the 
allocations made to NIOT, NCPOR and NCESS were increased at the RE stage.  The Committee
