CHAPTER – 3 
CENTRAL ELECTRONICS LIMITED (CEL) 
   
 Central Electronics Limited (CEL) is a Mini Ratna Category-I Central Public Sector 
Enterprise (CPSE) under the Department. It was established in 1974 with an objective to 
commercially exploit the indigenous technologies developed by National Laboratories and R&D 
Institutions in the country. The ccompany specializes in the manufacturing of strategic electronic 
components critical for defence applications of national importance. In addition, CEL produces 
advanced railway signalling systems, security and surveillance solutions, smart classroom systems, 
and solar photovoltaic products. The operations of the Company are organized into four major 
verticals, namely:  
a) Defence Business Group,  
b) Railway Signalling Systems,  
c) Solar Photovoltaic Group, and  
d) Integrated Solutions for Security & Surveillance 
3.2 Through these verticals, CEL has established a strong presence in both strategic and 
commercial sectors. As part of its diversification and long-term growth strategy, CEL is 
establishing a fully automated Solar Module Manufacturing Plant with an annual capacity of 200 
MW under the Public-Private Partnership (PPP) model. This initiative is expected to enhance 
domestic solar manufacturing capacity and strengthen the Company’s footprint in the renewable 
energy sector. Further, civil works have commenced for setting up a Green Tier-III Data Centre at 
Sahibabad, Ghaziabad under the PPP model, with a planned capacity of 30 MW. The Data Centre is 
envisaged to generate consistent revenue streams and significantly improve profitability in the 
coming financial years. 
3.3 The financial performance of CEL during FY 2024–25 reflects sustained growth and 
operational efficiency. As on 31st March 2025, the paid-up share capital of the Company stood at 
₹84.37 crore, and the Company remains completely debt-free, holding no secured loans. The Net 
Worth increased significantly to ₹266.94 crore in 2024-25 from ₹193.64 crore in the previous year, 
while Reserves & Surplus rose to ₹182.57 crore from ₹119.47 crore. The Company achieved its 
highest ever turnover of ₹390.01 crore during FY 2024–25 as compared to ₹344.03 crore in FY 
2023–24. PBT (Profit Before Tax) increased to ₹103.12 crore from ₹78.88 crore, while Profit After 
Tax rose to ₹74.96 crore from ₹58.87 crore in the previous financial year, reflecting better project 
execution, financial discipline, and strengthened business performance. During the year, the 
Company also met financial commitments from internal accruals, including a payment of ₹11.39 
crore towards interest on wage arrears from 2007. The Defence Business Group recorded its highest 
ever turnover of ₹148 crore, and the Company maintained a nil overdraft position with banks, 
demonstrating sound liquidity management. In view of the Company’s strong performance and 
profit earning during the financial year 2024-2025, it paid an interim dividend of ₹248 per equity 
share of ₹1,000 face value, aggregating to ₹20.92 crore for the financial year. Furthermore, it also 
paid a final dividend of ₹18.55 per equity share, aggregating to ₹1.57 crore. The financial

3.6 The Committee asked the Department that how CEL does collaborate with CEERI, Pilani

3.9 The Committee learnt through the replies to the detailed questionnaire sent to the

3.10 The Committee observes that the revival of this loss-making Public Sector 
Undertaking stands as a remarkable success story, transforming its trajectory to emerge as a 
growth-oriented entity operating in strategic sectors. Having acknowledged this 
commendable turnaround, the Committee notes with concern that the allocation of a meager 
₹3.03 crore for a PSU which has just been revived, is currently in its critical growth phase, 
and functions in areas of national importance, appears insufficient and warrants more 
proactive support from the Government. The Committee therefore strongly recommends that 
CEL should prepare a comprehensive future roadmap outlining its strategic direction along 
with its corresponding financial requirements, and should subsequently approach the 
Government to secure a significant increase in its budget allocation to sustain its growth 
momentum. In this context, the Committee also feels that the decision to pursue listing in the 
capital markets is a step in the right direction, as this will provide CEL with the much-needed 
visibility, enhance operational transparency, and grant the Company access to market capital 
for funding its future expansion plans. The Committee recommends for early listing along 
with focus on contemplating other business opportunities to make CEL a truly flagship 
electronics PSU. 
3.11 The Committee further recommends that CEL should establish a more structured and 
intensive collaborative framework with CEERI, Pilani, given that both institutions operate

grants it an exclusive, pre-emptive right of first refusal for all technologies, innovations, and

indigenous technologies developed at significant public expense are first offered to a

CEL with a competitive advantage in accessing cutting-edge technologies but also accelerate

reliance within the departmental ecosystem.

CHAPTER – 4 
COUNCIL OF SCIENTIFIC & INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH (CSIR) 
 
 Established in 1942, CSIR operates as an autonomous body under the administrative 
framework of the Department. It is widely recognized for its pioneering Research and Development 
(R&D) capabilities spanning a broad spectrum of scientific and technological domains. As a 
modern R&D institution with a extensive pan-India presence, CSIR's infrastructure comprises a 
formidable network of 37 national laboratories, 39 outreach centres, one Innovation Complex, and 
three specialized units, reflecting its extensive engagement in scientific advancement. 
4.2 In its background submitted before the Committee, the Department informed that CSIR did 
not operate any Central Sector Scheme or Centrally Sponsored Scheme from FY 2017-18 onwards. 
As per the rationalization process of Central Government expenditure, the budgetary outlay for 
autonomous bodies was allocated under "Other Central Sector Expenditure – Autonomous Bodies" 
to meet establishment and administrative expenses as well as project requirements. Under this 
arrangement, CSIR received financial support for its two Non-Central Sector Schemes, namely the 
National Laboratories Scheme and the Capacity Building and Human Resource Development 
Scheme, until FY 2025-26. The National Laboratories Scheme encompasses the entire gamut of 
CSIR's R&D and S&T activities, while the Capacity Building and Human Resource Development 
Scheme focuses on national S&T human resource development and various awards.  
4.3 However, as per the recent direction of the Ministry of Finance, DSIR and CSIR have been 
directed to review the categorization of their schemes and shift them from "Other Central 
Expenditure" to "Central Sector Scheme," with only establishment expenditure to remain under the 
former category. In order to implement this directive, CSIR is in the process of re-categorizing its 
National Laboratories Scheme and Capacity Building and Human Resource Development Scheme 
as Central Sector Schemes, and the EFC documents for the same are under active preparation. 
4.4 Under the re-categorized National Laboratories Scheme, three major sub-schemes are being 
conceptualized and proposed to continue supporting CSIR's R&D, S&T, and related intellectual 
activities. The first sub-scheme, CSIR Research for Industrial, Scientific and Societal Progress 
(CRISP), focuses on delivering innovation-driven solutions through developed intellectual property 
that targets specific industrial and national requirements while fostering essential skill sets. Its 
objectives include enhancing quality of life through innovative S&T initiatives, advancing 
technology readiness from TRL 3 to 8, reducing trade deficits through technology development, 
preparing human resources by kindling interest in industrial R&D among school children, 
supporting ecosystem development through robust IP protection systems and access to scientific 
resources, and promoting global collaboration. CRISP will provide financial support to priority 
programmes across CSIR laboratories under components including Core R&D and Mission 
Projects, Outreach and Skill Development Initiatives like CSIR Jigyasa, Modernisation of Scientific 
Infrastructure under MASS (Modernization of Assets for Sustainable Science), Human Resource 
Training programmes, Intellectual Property Management and Commercialisation Support, and 
Access to Scientific Knowledge Resources including the One Nation One Subscription initiative, 
apart from supporting global mobility of scientists. 

16 
 
4.5 The second sub-scheme, Unit & Laboratory In-house Projects (ULIP), aims to provide S&T 
outputs directly relating to individual CSIR unit or laboratory mandates while catering to specific 
stakeholders and society. ULIP seeks to nurture early-stage, exploratory, and mandate-specific 
research, strengthen in-house R&D capabilities, and support innovative ideas through objectives 
such as developing sector-specific innovations, establishing a solid fundamental research 
foundation for future needs, building skilled human resources for translating innovation from lab to 
market, strengthening the CSIR intellectual property base, bridging industry gaps through 
technology transfer, and aligning research initiatives with national missions and sustainable 
development goals. 
4.6 The third sub-scheme, Science Coordination, Outreach, Utilization and Technology 
Transfer (SCOUT), facilitates the global translation of research into industry applications through 
IT-enabled technology demonstration and dissemination, appropriate planning, human resource 
development, and management. Its major objectives include aligning research under CRISP and 
ULIP to avoid duplication and create complementary strengths around thematic priorities, 
facilitating interdisciplinary teams and shared infrastructure aligned with Government of India 
priorities, building and deepening international partnerships, attracting diverse talent to strengthen 
the CSIR S&T base, capturing and turning CSIR IP into strategic national assets while enabling 
commercialization through licensing and spin-offs, coordinating technology demonstration and 
advising on business enhancement for multi-laboratory projects, sparking curiosity and 
foundational scientific understanding among school students through outreach, widening the future 
STEM talent pipeline, and utilizing modern ICT practices to improve S&T planning and 
monitoring. 
4.7 In response to a query regarding major thrust areas of the Department, the Committee was 
informed that for the years 2025–26 and 2026–27, CSIR has identified nine thematic areas for 
advancements in research, scientific excellence, fostering technological innovation for responding 
effectively to national and societal needs with a focused, comprehensive and outcome-driven 
approach. These thematic areas are as follows:-  
1. Aerospace, Electronics, Instrumentation & Strategic Sectors 
2. Civil Infrastructure & Engineering 
3. Earth, Oceanography & Water 
4. Ecology, Environment & Sustainability 
5. Mining, Minerals, Metals & Materials 
6. Chemicals (including Leather) and Petrochemicals 
7. Energy (Conventional and Non-Conventional) and Energy Devices 
8. Agriculture, Nutrition & Biotechnology 
9. Healthcare 
 
4.8 Within these themes, CSIR is pursuing several priority research and development initiatives. 
In aerospace and strategic sectors, efforts focus on indigenous aviation platforms such as the 
SARAS 19-seater aircraft, RTA-70, the new-generation HANSA aircraft and UAV/MAV systems. 
Defence-related R&D includes fibre Bragg grating sensors, aerospace biofuels, advanced wind 
tunnel facilities and structural health monitoring technologies. Electronics and instrumentation 
research covers IP core development, MEMS accelerometers, gyrotrons, high-power klystrons, 
metrology, cybersecurity, IoT and advanced sensing systems. Materials research targets 
thermoplastic composites, carbon fibres, stealth coatings, and thermal barrier coatings while 
mechanical systems development encompasses aircraft subsystems, actuators, valves, and 
gearboxes. In civil infrastructure and engineering, CSIR emphasizes affordable housing, heritage 

17 
 
conservation, disaster mitigation, smart cities, and sustainable construction technologies. Robotics 
and automation initiatives support agriculture, Industry 4.0 applications and green manufacturing. 
Agriculture and biotechnology research prioritizes crop productivity, mitigation of malnutrition,

petrochemical research promotes import substitution, specialty chemicals, and green chemistry

and advanced energy devices. Environmental initiatives focus on water purification, waste 
management, emission reduction, and sustainability, while Earth sciences research addresses 
natural resources, geohazards, and biodiversity. The 4M domain (Mining, Minerals, Metals, and

4.8 The Committee sought details of the budget demanded and budget allocated to CSIR for FY 
2026-27. The Committee was informed that CSIR demanded Rs. 7953.90 crore but was allocated

4.9 The Committee then enquired about the absolute bare minimum increase needed in the 
budgetary allocations of the CSIR for the year 2026-27 to sustain its key programmes with the 
desired outcomes and efficiency. The Committee was informed that an additional allocation of 
₹600 crore under the National Laboratories Scheme is essential to sustain and accelerate India’s 
indigenous R&D ecosystem and deliver deployable technologies in priority sectors. The detailed 
justification submitted by CSIR to the Committee is as below:- 
I.  Meeting National Strategic Commitments 

18 
 
 
CSIR is implementing national-level mission projects across health, energy, 
environment, aerospace, defence, and advanced manufacturing. These include precision 
medicine initiatives such as Phenome India, geo-hazard mitigation in the North-East 
and Himalayas, commercialization of Sustainable Aviation Fuel, critical minerals 
recovery, Green Hydrogen R&D, and indigenous API development for affordable 
healthcare. Mission-mode research is also being initiated in sunrise areas such as 
animal-free organoid models for biomedical R&D, White Hydrogen exploration, Next-
generation nuclear and solid-state battery technologies, Sub-surface geo-technical 
mapping in critical zones and EMI/EMC testing facilities as per CISPR and IS/IEC 
standards. These initiatives directly support national security, energy independence, 
healthcare resilience, climate commitments, and industrial competitiveness. Without 
enhanced funding, these strategic missions will face delays, impacting India’s 
technological self-reliance. 
 
II. Supporting Viksit Bharat-2047 and SDG Targets 
 
CSIR’s programmes contribute to inclusive growth and sustainability through initiatives 
such as: 
• Aroma, Floriculture and Seaweed Missions for rural livelihood enhancement 
• Smart Village initiatives and region-specific projects in the North-East  
• Waste-to-Wealth, Sustainable Packaging, Climate-Resilient Buildings, and Carbon 
Capture missions 
• Precision agriculture, genome-editing for crop improvement and SHRI ANNA 
nutrition initiatives 
 
These projects address Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) related to health, clean 
energy, industry innovation, climate action and poverty reduction, while empowering 
women, rural communities and MSMEs. 
 
III. Strengthening National Security and Strategic Capabilities 
 
CSIR is undertaking critical programmes such as Regional Transport Aircraft 
technologies, Deep-sea Autonomous Underwater Vehicles, Loitering Munitions, 
Advanced Materials missions, AI-enabled Defence Technologies, and Indigenous 
Laboratory Instrumentation. These strategic projects are essential for reducing import 
dependence and enhancing defence preparedness, and require sustained multi-lab 
collaboration and modern infrastructure. 
 
IV.  Bridging the Lab-to-Market Gap 
 
CSIR is executing vital and crucial research projects under its FIRST, NCP/FBR and 
FTT/FTC categories aimed at translating scientific research into commercial 
technologies. These projects are executed with TRL-linked milestones, defined outputs 
and outcomes, and measurable deliverables such as patents, deployable technologies, 
industry partnerships and societal impact. Additional funding will support: 
• Pilot plants for translational industries 
• Benchmark testing and certification facilities 

19 
 
• Scale-up of industrial enzymes, specialty chemicals and advanced materials 
• Indigenous manufacturing systems and battery-to-battery recycling technologies 
 
Such investments are crucial for industrial competitiveness, startup ecosystem growth 
and export-oriented innovation. 
 
V. Modernization of Ageing Infrastructure 
 
A significant portion of CSIR’s laboratory infrastructure is decades old. Modernization 
of high-end R&D facilities, instrumentation and testing centres is urgently required to 
maintain global competitiveness and support advanced research domains such as AI, 
quantum-ready materials, advanced batteries, hydrogen technologies and aerospace 
systems. 
 
VI. Scientific Social Responsibility 
 
Additional funding will also strengthen skill development and outreach programmes 
such as CSIR Jigyasa and capacity building for emerging interdisciplinary research. 
Investing in human resource skilling and scientific temperament inculcation will ensure 
sustained innovation capacity for the country. 
VII. Fiscal Prudence and Outcome-Oriented Planning 
The proposed additional ₹600 crore is modest compared to the scale of national 
missions and will catalyse multi-lab collaborative projects, leverage industry 
participation and generate significant economic and strategic returns. 
 
4.10 In response to a query raised by the Committee during its meeting on 8th September 2025, 
the Department stated that CSIR needs an additional ₹1500 crore to achieve its ambitions. In this 
context, the Committee observed that the Department's allocation for FY 2026-27 stands at 
₹6710.61 crore, which is only a marginal increase over the previous year. The Committee has 
subsequently sought an explanation for this allocation trend and requested details on the measures 
the Department intends to take to enhance its budgetary outlay. 
4.11 The Department attributed the reduction in budgetary allocation to unprecedented 
circumstances affecting national revenue. While this may impact the pace of certain R&D projects, 
CSIR will optimize internal resources and pursue collaborative funding with other Ministries to 
sustain priority research initiatives. Additionally, as directed by the Department of Expenditure, the 
National Laboratories Scheme—currently covering all CSIR R&D and establishment costs under 
"Other Central Expenditure"—is being recategorized as a Central Sector Scheme, excluding 
establishment expenditures, in the upcoming 16th Finance Commission Cycle. CSIR believes this 
restructuring will enable more focused and structured funding for its core R&D activities and any 
additional requirements under the new scheme will be submitted to the Ministry of Finance for 
consideration. 
4.12 The Committee acknowledges the critical role of CSIR in driving India’s indigenous 
R&D ecosystem and notes the comprehensive justification for an enhanced budgetary 

20 
 
allocation of ₹600 crore under the National Laboratories Scheme for the fiscal year 2026-27. 
After examining the submissions, the Committee observes that the requested funds are not 
merely for routine expansion but are directed toward high-priority national missions, 
strategic defence capabilities, and translational research aimed at bridging the lab-to-market 
gap. The Committee, therefore, recommends the following: 
1. Given the direct linkage of CSIR’s projects to national security (e.g., loitering 
munitions, AUVs), energy independence (Green Hydrogen, critical minerals), and 
healthcare resilience (indigenous API development), the Department should accord 
the highest priority to meeting this funding demand. Any delay or shortfall in 
allocation could impede India’s technological self-reliance and strategic 
preparedness. 
2. The Committee endorses the initiatives aligned with the Viksit Bharat vision and 
SDG targets, particularly those focused on rural livelihood enhancement (Aroma, 
Floriculture, Seaweed Missions), climate action, and waste-to-wealth generation. 
The Committee recommends that these societal missions be sustained with adequate 
funding to ensure inclusive growth and grassroot-level impact. 
3. The Committee expresses concern over the ageing infrastructure in CSIR 
laboratories. It strongly recommends that a portion of the additional funds be 
specifically earmarked for the modernization of high-end R&D facilities, pilot 
plants, and testing centres. This is essential to maintain global competitiveness in 
emerging fields such as AI, quantum materials, and advanced batteries. 
4. Recognizing the importance of bridging the lab-to-market gap, the Committee 
supports the funding for TRL-linked projects under the FIRST, NCP/FBR, and 
FTT/FTC categories. The recommended outlay should facilitate the establishment of 
pilot plants and scale-up facilities to boost industrial partnerships, support the 
startup ecosystem, and promote export-oriented innovation. 
4.13 The Committee also takes note of the recategorization of the National Laboratories 
Scheme as a Central Sector Scheme, with exclusion of establishment expenditures, in the 
upcoming 16th Finance Commission Cycle. While this restructuring is expected to enable 
more focused and structured funding for core R&D activities, the Committee recommends 
that CSIR should appropriately formulate and submit any additional requirements under the 
new scheme to the Ministry of Finance at the earliest for favourable consideration. The 
Committee also urges the Department of Expenditure to ensure that this transition does not 
disrupt ongoing research programmes and those adequate safeguards are put in place to 
maintain continuity of funding for critical national missions.

4.14 The Committee strongly recommends that DSIR and the Department of Expenditure 
should consider the request for an additional ₹600 crore allocation to CSIR favourably. The 
Committee believes that this enhanced outlay is a fiscally prudent investment that will 
catalyse multi-laboratory collaboration, leverage industry participation, and yield substantial 
economic and strategic returns for the nation. The Committee expects a firm commitment 
from the Government to ensure that these mission-mode projects are sustained without 
interruption and that CSIR is enabled to deliver on its mandate of building a self-reliant and

5.2 The Committee sought the Department's views on whether CSIR laboratories working in the 
domain of biological sciences—such as CCMB, Hyderabad; IGIB, Delhi; and CDRI, Lucknow—
should be placed under the administrative purview of the Department of Biotechnology (DBT) 
instead of CSIR, in order to achieve better synergy and more focused oversight in the biological 
research sector.  
5.3 The Department replied that the Biological Science laboratories of the Council of Scientific 
and Industrial Research (CSIR), such as CSIR–Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology 
(CCMB), Hyderabad; CSIR–Institute of Genomics and Integrative Biology (IGIB), Delhi; and 
CSIR–Central Drug Research Institute (CDRI), Lucknow, have been established as 
interdisciplinary institutions with mandates that are intrinsically aligned with CSIR’s national 
mission of scientific, translational and industrial research. CSIR–Central Drug Research Institute 
(CDRI), Lucknow, for example, has been established with the mandate of “discovery and 
development of therapeutics for nationally important diseases with global impact, understanding 
fundamental disease biology and training future drug researchers.” This mandate is aligned with 
CSIR’s vision of enhancing the quality of life of citizens through innovative science and 
technology, globally competitive R&D, sustainable solutions and capacity building to fulfill the 
objective of Atmanirbhar Bharat. In comparison, the vision of the Department of Biotechnology 
(DBT) is focused on advancing biotechnology research and capacity building within the life 
sciences domain. The vision, mission and mandate of CSIR biological laboratories extend beyond 
the specific ambit of DBT. Over the years, CSIR-CDRI has evolved into a unique national 
institution with integrated capabilities spanning the entire drug discovery and development value 
chain, from concept to clinical trials. Its multidisciplinary teams comprising expertise in life 
sciences, chemical sciences, medical sciences and pharmaceutical sciences jointly undertake 
biomedical and medicinal chemistry-driven drug discovery programmes. The institute’s product 
portfolio includes synthetic novel chemical entities, peptides, natural products, 
Phytopharmaceuticals, formulations, diagnostics and process technologies. As part of the CSIR 
ecosystem, these biological research laboratories benefit from seamless networking with other 
CSIR laboratories such as IIIM, IICB, IICT, NCL and IMTECH enabling end-to-end 
interdisciplinary and translational research. In the contemporary research landscape, biological 
challenges such as precision medicine, infectious diseases, antimicrobial resistance, gene and cell 
therapy, synthetic biology and AI-driven diagnostics inherently require convergence of biology 
with chemistry, physics, engineering sciences, materials science, computational modelling and data 
science. CSIR is uniquely structured to enable such convergence through its nationwide, mission-
oriented multidisciplinary laboratory network. Biological laboratories within CSIR function as part 
of a larger innovation ecosystem that facilitates seamless progression from fundamental discovery 
to translational research, industrial scale-up and technology deployment. While DBT plays a 
critical and complementary role in strengthening India’s biotechnology ecosystem, relocating 
CSIR’s biological laboratories under DBT would risk fragmenting the established cross-
disciplinary linkages that are central to CSIR’s translational and industrial R&D model. Several 

26 
 
national priorities, including affordable therapeutics, indigenous diagnostics, industrial 
biotechnology and bioengineering solutions, depend on close coupling between biology, chemistry 
and engineering pipelines, which is a defining strength of the CSIR framework. Further, CSIR 
biological laboratories actively collaborate with DBT and other scientific departments based on 
national priorities without requiring administrative restructuring. During the last three years, these 
biological laboratories have received extramural research funding from multiple Government of 
India agencies including DBT and thus, demonstrating effective inter-agency synergy through 
collaborative mechanisms. In fact, DBT has already led major programmes at some of these 
institutes, with substantial funding and guidance, including large initiatives like Genome India and 
InTGS. Transferring established CSIR laboratories to another administrative department would 
involve complex restructuring of human resource policies, financial and pension systems, 
procurement mechanisms, ongoing projects, intellectual property management and academic 
programmes under the Academy of Scientific and Innovative Research (AcSIR). Such large-scale 
institutional transfers may disrupt ongoing research, translational outputs and national mission 
programmes, and could adversely impact scientific productivity. In view of the above, the 
suggestion to place CSIR biological science laboratories under the administrative domain of the 
Department of Biotechnology may not be considered appropriate. Retaining laboratories such as 
CSIR-CCMB, CSIR-IGIB and CSIR-CDRI within the CSIR framework best serves scientific, 
strategic and national innovation objectives. Strengthening inter-agency collaboration among CSIR, 
DBT, ICMR and other scientific departments through joint programmes, mission-mode initiatives 
and coordinated funding mechanisms remains a more effective and efficient approach to achieving 
synergy than administrative reorganisation. DBT can continue its strategic funding without 
disrupting existing collaborations. 
5.4 The Committee recommends that CSIR and DBT should formalize their collaborative 
mechanisms through structured frameworks such as Memoranda of Understanding, joint 
steering committees and coordinated research calls to ensure that the nation derives 
maximum benefit from the combined expertise of both the Departments.  
5.5 On similar lines, the Committee sought the Department's views on whether CSIR-NEERI, 
Nagpur, should be placed under the administrative domain of Ministry of Environment, Forest and 
Climate Change (MoEFCC) to achieve better synergies, given that MoEFCC is one of the biggest 
clients of CSIR-NEERI. The Department replied that the Ministry of Environment, Forest and 
Climate Change (MoEFCC) primarily functions as a policy-making and regulatory authority, 
whereas CSIR–National Environmental Engineering Research Institute (CSIR-NEERI), Nagpur, is 
a national research and technology development institution mandated to undertake scientific 
assessments, develop environmental engineering solutions, and provide independent technical 
advice. Placing a research institution under a regulatory Ministry may give rise to perceived or 
actual conflicts of interest and could compromise the independence, objectivity, and credibility of 
scientific assessments. Maintaining an institutional separation between regulatory authorities and 
scientific research organisations is therefore essential to safeguard scientific neutrality and public 
confidence in evidence-based decision-making. CSIR fully recognises MoEFCC as one of its major 
stakeholders and beneficiaries of CSIR-NEERI scientific and technical outputs. However, CSIR is 
of the considered view that CSIR-NEERI should continue to function as an autonomous national 
R&D organization under the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), Ministry of 
Science & Technology. The present arrangement enables CSIR-NEERI to provide independent, 
objective and science-based technical support not only to MoEFCC, but also to State Governments, 
regulatory agencies, industry, the judiciary and other stakeholders, without any conflict of interest. 
This institutional positioning enhances the credibility and acceptance of CSIR-NEERI’s 
assessments in policy formulation, regulatory processes, judicial proceedings and international 
engagements. At the same time, CSIR-NEERI maintains close and effective collaboration with 
MoEFCC through sustained technical assistance, mission-mode programmes, expert committees 

27 
 
and policy support, thereby achieving the required synergies while preserving institutional 
autonomy. Being part of CSIR allows CSIR-NEERI to leverage interdisciplinary expertise across 
CSIR’s national laboratory network in areas such as materials, chemicals, energy, biotechnology, 
data science and earth sciences. Under CSIR’s thematic approach on Ecology, Environment, Earth 
& Ocean Sciences and Water, CSIR-NEERI functions as a key anchor laboratory, ensuring 
integrated and long-term research on air quality, climate change, waste management, water and 
wastewater, natural resources and environmental policy. Any administrative separation from CSIR 
could weaken these interdisciplinary linkages and fragment national environmental R&D efforts. 
CSIR-NEERI also benefits from CSIR’s autonomous research environment and its strong academic 
ecosystem through the Academy of Scientific and Innovative Research (AcSIR), supporting Ph.D. 
programmes in science and engineering and contributing to sustained talent development. 
International best practices similarly emphasize a clear functional distinction between regulatory 
bodies and independent scientific institutions. Accordingly, CSIR is of the view that the existing 
arrangement—where CSIR-NEERI functions under CSIR while providing comprehensive scientific 
and technical support to MoEFCC—offers an effective framework for achieving synergy, 
safeguarding scientific independence and advancing national objectives related to environmental 
protection, climate change mitigation and sustainable development. Strengthening institutional 
collaboration mechanisms is therefore considered preferable to altering administrative control. 
5.6 The Committee emphasizes the need for strengthening institutional collaboration 
mechanisms between CSIR-NEERI and MoEFCC. The Committee recommends that both 
organizations should formalize their collaborative framework through structured 
mechanisms such as joint research programmes, regular consultation meetings, and 
coordinated approaches to addressing national environmental challenges. The Committee 
recommends that MoEFCC should leverage CSIR-NEERI's scientific expertise as its primary 
technical arm for environmental assessments and policy support, while CSIR should ensure 
that CSIR-NEERI maintains and enhances its interdisciplinary research capabilities and 
continues to provide independent, credible and objective scientific inputs to all the 
stakeholders.  
5.7 During its study visit to CSIR-NEERI, Nagpur in December 2025, the Committee enquired 
whether the current sanctioned strength of the Institute is enough to cater to the ever-growing 
demand in the field of sustainable and environment friendly solutions and if not, what is the 
optimum strength that the Institute must have to cater to these demands and what plans does the 
Institute take its sanctioned strength to this optimum level. The Institute replied that the present 
sanctioned strength of CSIR-NEERI, while adequate for its earlier mandate, is not fully aligned 
with the scale, complexity, and diversity of responsibilities currently emerging requirement to the 
Institute. Over recent years, CSIR-NEERI’s role has expanded significantly from pollution control 
and compliance support to include Net-Zero transition planning, clean air and water missions, 
circular economy, climate adaptation, environmental health, and sustained international 
engagement under multilateral environmental agreements.  This expansion has coincided with 
rising demand from Government bodies, industry, and Ministries for technical support, pilot 
projects, and implementation guidance, as well as additional responsibilities arising from 
international obligations and regional capacity-building roles. At the same time, natural attrition 
due to retirements and existing vacancies has reduced the Institute’s effective manpower base, 
while newer interdisciplinary skill requirements remain under-represented in the current staffing 
profile. Accordingly, the current sanctioned strength, though efficiently utilized, does not fully 
match present or anticipated future requirements of a mission-oriented national environmental 
institution. Based on benchmarking with comparable international environmental research

5.16 The Committee also enquired about the role of the regional centres of the CSIR-NEERI and 
whether the Institute is planning to open more such centres in the future. The Committee also 
enquired whether the Institute can open such regional centres in different parts of the country to 
work on the local environmental issues of the region. The Institute replied that India’s 
environmental challenges are inherently diverse, region-specific, and context-dependent, shaped by 
variations in climate, geography, patterns of industrialisation and urbanisation, and local socio-
economic conditions. Recognising that centralised research alone cannot effectively address such 

31 
 
heterogeneity. CSIR-NEERI has established regional centres as decentralised extensions of its 
national expertise. These centres enable locally relevant, science-based solutions while remaining 
fully aligned with national priorities. The five regional centres and zonal laboratories of CSIR-
NEERI operate as field-level operational arms under a hub-and-spoke model, with the Nagpur 
Headquarters serving as the national hub. Located at Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai, and 
Hyderabad, these centres translate national research capability into region-specific action by 
identifying and addressing local environmental challenges such as industrial pollution hotspots, 
urban air and water quality issues, waste management constraints, and impacts arising from mining, 
agriculture, and infrastructure development. Each centre functions with a defined regional mandate 
aligned to local environmental priorities, enabling scientific interventions that are practical, 
implementable, and responsive to ground realities. While this decentralised structure has 
significantly enhanced outreach, responsiveness, and stakeholder engagement, the centres currently 
serve very large geographic areas and operate under constraints of manpower and infrastructure. 
Consequently, their existing number and capacity are not fully commensurate with the growing and 
increasingly differentiated environmental demands across regions. A core function of CSIR-
NEERI’s regional centres is to support State Governments and local authorities, including State 
Pollution Control Boards and Urban Local Bodies, through technical assistance for environmental 
monitoring and compliance, preparation and implementation of action plans such as clean air 
programmes, river rejuvenation initiatives, and waste management strategies, as well as targeted 
capacity-building and training. The centres also serve as platforms for field research, pilot projects, 
and demonstration activities, enabling on-site validation of technologies developed by CSIR-
NEERI and providing feedback to strengthen laboratory research. Their proximity to stakeholders 
facilitates faster deployment of solutions and timely response to environmental emergencies and 
regulatory needs, thereby strengthening sub-national environmental governance and enhancing the 
effectiveness of national programmes. In this context, CSIR-NEERI supports a calibrated, need-
based expansion of its regional presence, emphasising that expansion should be phased, 
strategically targeted, and adequately resourced to ensure effectiveness. Priority for expansion lies 
in ecologically sensitive regions, high industrial concentration zones, rapidly urbanising areas 
facing acute air, water, and waste challenges, and climate-vulnerable regions such as drought- and 
flood-prone areas. The proposed expansion of CSIR-NEERI’s regional centres will continue to 
follow a hub-and-spoke model, with the Nagpur Headquarters providing national coordination, 
advanced research, standards development, and international engagement, while regional centres 
focus on applied research, monitoring, pilot projects, and stakeholder interaction. Expansion will 
adopt a modular, mission-driven approach, beginning with focused units and scaling up based on 
demonstrated demand and outcomes, with centres co-located wherever feasible with State 
institutions, academic partners, or industrial clusters to optimise resources and foster collaboration. 
The Institute has emphasised that such expansion is contingent upon appropriate enabling support, 
including augmentation of sanctioned manpower strength, dedicated capital and operational 
funding, delegated administrative and financial powers at the regional level, alignment with 
national missions such as Net Zero, Clean Air, Water, and Circular Economy.

 The Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) conducts cutting-edge, 
multidisciplinary research across diverse domains—including health, energy, defence, aerospace, 
food technology, and sustainable materials—to address national priorities and societal needs. The 
true impact of this research, however, is realized through its robust technology transfer mechanism, 
which serves as the critical bridge connecting laboratory breakthroughs to the marketplace and the 
end consumer. CSIR has strategically shifted from traditional R&D to an "R&D Innovation" model, 
where research is increasingly guided by market demand, ensuring that technologies are developed 
with translation, validation, and scalability in mind. This is achieved through active collaboration 
with industrial partners, start-ups, and entrepreneurs, who license and scale up CSIR-developed 
technologies for commercial deployment. Recent examples include the transfer of a high-protein, 
low-glycemic index fortified rice to Tata Consumer Products, an indigenous coffee foam 
technology, and advanced defence gloves, demonstrating the range of innovations moving from lab 
to market. To facilitate this, CSIR has established dedicated technology transfer hubs, partnered 
with the National Research Development Corporation (NRDC) for commercialization, and created 
a dynamic online portal showcasing over 1,200 ready-to-implement technologies for industry 
uptake. This institutionalized focus on technology transfer ensures that CSIR's scientific excellence 
translates into tangible economic growth, industrial competitiveness, and improved quality of life 
for citizens, thereby fulfilling its mandate as the "Innovation Engine of India"

societal impact. 
 
6.10 The Committee further enquired that whether the Department has any plans to take equity 
stake in the companies to which it transfers its technology, in order to achieve better revenue for its 
hard work. The Department replied that CSIR is exploring the legitimate option of Section 8 startup 
model for CSIR labs to allow for equity stakes.  
 
6.11 The Committee observes that the average revenue per technology commercialized by 
NRDC varies significantly and is generally low in absolute terms. To address this, the 
Committee recommends that the Department formulate a comprehensive Standard 
Operating Procedure (SOP) to govern the process of transferring technologies to its industrial 
partners. The Committee recommends developing a more sophisticated and flexible licensing 
framework that moves beyond standard upfront fees and royalties, incorporating milestone-
based payments that structure deals with payments linked to the licensee achieving specific 
commercial benchmarks, such as successful pilot production, first commercial sale, or 
reaching a sales target. Furthermore, the framework should involve strategic decision-
making regarding exclusive versus non-exclusive licensing, determining when to offer 
exclusive licenses for higher fees to attract major industry players and when to employ non-
exclusive licenses to ensure the wider dissemination of socially important technologies. 
6.12 The Committee also recommends that the Department should explore the idea of 
establishing more verticals under CEL under different categories like healthcare, aerospace, 
energy, ecology, etc. These PSUs would work in close collaboration with CSIR laboratories, 
not only commercializing indigenous technologies but also contributing to their further 
development. The profits generated by these enterprises would flow back to the Government 
in the form of dividends. Additionally, by ensuring competitive pricing, this would ultimately 
serve the national interest and benefit the broader public, besides developing other businesses 
by CEL as mandated by the Department of Public Enterprises. 
6.13 The Committee further recommends that the Department should establish a dedicated 
and centralized "Technology Marketing & Commercialization Wing" with its separate 
budget to serve as a single-window interface for industry, functioning proactively by 
providing market intelligence to identify industry needs and map them to existing CSIR 
technologies. This wing could also be responsible for strategic branding and outreach, 

41 
 
developing a strong CSIR brand through targeted global marketing campaigns, technology 
showcases, and industry-specific roadshows, moving beyond a reliance on passive online 
portals. Additionally, it could feature dedicated deal facilitation, employing professionals with 
business development and negotiation expertise to structure and close technology transfer 
agreements more efficiently. 
6.14 The Committee observes that the Department is exploring the option of Section 8 
startup model for CSIR labs to allow for equity stakes. The Committee opines that the 
Department is thinking in the right direction. The Committee recommends for early setting 
up of the proposed Section 8 Company so as to facilitate monetization of CSIR technologies at 
higher valuations. The Committee also recommends moving from exploration to a structured, 
time-bound implementation of this equity-based model. For breakthrough technologies with 
high commercial potential, CSIR should consider taking a strategic equity stake in spin-off 
ventures or licensing partners instead of, or in addition to, upfront licensing fees and 
royalties. This would align CSIR's long-term interests with the company's success, potentially 
yielding significantly higher returns that can be reinvested into future research. A clear 
policy framework with guidelines on equity percentage, exit strategies, and conflict of interest 
must be developed to enable this.

7.5 The Committee enquired regarding the CSIR Scientists Recruitment & Assessment 
Promotion (CSRAP) Rules 2025 effective from 01.01.2026 and how these Rules are better than the 
old one and how will they ensure a time-bound, transparent & more efficient system of recruitment 
of scientists in CSIR. The Department informed the Committee that the CSIR Scientists 
Recruitment & Assessment Promotion (CSRAP) Rules, 2025 have been notified and came into 
effect from 01 January 2026, replacing the nearly two-and-a-half-decades-old CSRAP Rules, 2001. 
The revised Rules have been introduced with the objective of attracting, recruiting, and retaining 
high-quality scientific talent in CSIR, while ensuring a time-bound, transparent, and efficient 
system of recruitment and career progression. Salient features of CSRAP Rules, 2025 include: 
 The Recruitment and Assessment Board (RAB) has been designated as the centralized 
recruitment agency for CSIR. 
 End-to-end recruitment of Scientists at all levels shall be conducted centrally by RAB, 
replacing the earlier decentralized, laboratory-wise process. 
 Re-introduction of Scientist-B level, creating a stronger entry-level pipeline and 
structured career progression. 
 Recruitment to Scientist-B posts will be carried out through a two-stage process: 
 Written Examination with 70% weightage 
 Interview with 30% weightage 
 Based on performance in the written examination, 3 to 12 candidates per post will be 
shortlisted for interview by the Selection Committee. 
 Recruitment to Scientist-C, D, E, and F levels will follow a structured two-stage 
process: 
 Shortlisting by a Screening Committee 
 Final selection through interview by a Selection Committee 
 Promotion of Scientists up to Scientist-F shall continue under the Flexible 
Complementing Scheme (FCS), ensuring merit-based progression. 
 All assessments and promotions shall be prospective, with the effective date being the 
date on which the Scientist assumes charge of the promoted grade. 
 A maximum of three chances will be available to a Scientist for assessment interviews 
at a given level. 
 Scientists who do not qualify within the prescribed attempts will be governed by 
Modified Assured Career Progression (MACP) as per Government of India 
instructions. 
 
7.6 The Department further informed the Committee that the CSRAP Rules, 2025 represent a 
significant improvement over the earlier framework. Centralized recruitment by RAB—on the lines 
of established practices in organisations such as DRDO and ISRO—introduces greater 
professionalism, uniformity, and objectivity in the selection process across all CSIR laboratories 
and institutes. The reintroduction of Scientist-B and the provision that nearly half of the sanctioned 
scientific strength is recruited through an All-India competitive written examination ensure a broad, 
merit-based talent pool. The clearly defined 70:30 weightage between written examination and 
interview enhances transparency and reduces subjectivity in selections. Further, issuance of 
consolidated advertisements at defined intervals provides predictability and clarity to aspiring 
researchers regarding recruitment cycles and career prospects in CSIR. This structured, centralized, 
and rule-based approach strengthens confidence among candidates, improves timeliness in 
recruitment, and supports long-term human resource planning in CSIR. Overall, CSRAP Rules, 
2025 are designed to modernize scientific recruitment and assessment in CSIR, making it more 
transparent, efficient, predictable, and aligned with national best practices in R&D organisations.

acknowledging this as a timely and crucial step towards addressing the persistent vacancy 
crisis in CSIR. The Committee views this as a positive development that, if implemented

1.  INTRODUCTION 
1.1 The Department of Science & Technology (DST) is the nodal agency of the country  
for the promotion, coordination and strengthening of Science, Technology and Innovation 
(STI) in the country. It plays a central role in identifying critical gap areas across diverse 
S&T sectors and formulating appropriate policies, programmes and strategic interventions to 
address emerging societal, industrial and national developmental needs. The Department is 
also entrusted with promotin g frontier and emerging areas of science and technology in 
anticipation of future demands, technological disruptions and global advancements. 
1.2 In addition to its policy and planning functions, DST acts as a key interface linking 
the science and technolo gy ecosystem with various Ministries and Departments of the 
Government (both at the horizontal and vertical levels), as well as with academia, national 
laboratories, research and development institutions, and industry. Through this integrative 
approach, th e Department facilitates collaboration, convergence and knowledge exchange 
across stakeholders, thereby strengthening the overall innovation value chain in the country. 
1.3 With the overarching objective of enhancing national S&T capacity and capability, 
DST provides the largest share of extramural research and development support in India. This 
support is extended to scientists and researchers across institutions and disciplines through a 
competitive and merit -based mechanism. Earlier structured under thre e umbrella schemes  
namely (i) Science and Technology (S&T) Institutional and Human Capacity Building, (ii) 
Research and Development, and (iii) Innovation, Technology Development and Deployment , 
these programmes collectively aimed at reinforcing the country’s higher education system, 
scientific research base, industrial R&D ecosystem, and the broader Science, Technology and 
Innovation landscape. 
1.4 In order to enhance administrative efficiency and enable greater flexibility in the flow 
and utilizatio n of funds across programmes, these three umbrella schemes have been 
consolidated into a single unified scheme titled ‘Vigyan Dhara’, with the approval of the 
Union Cabinet. The restructuring is intended to promote optimal resource allocation, foster 
inter-programmatic synergies, and ensure responsive implementation aligned with national 
priorities. 
1.5 The Department continues to pursue sustained efforts toward strengthening and 
deepening the national STI ecosystem, with a view to positioning India as a gl obal forerunner 
in science and technology. Through its strategic initiatives and policy interventions, DST 
seeks to facilitate positive societal transformation, contribute to the creation of a safe, secure 
and inclusive society, and build resilience to eff ectively address future challenges and 
disruptions.

3.1 The Committee enquired about an overview of the major schemes/programmes of the

3.2 It was further submitted by  the Department that the establishment of the Anusandhan 
National Research Foundation (ANRF) and the operationalisation of the Research, 
Development and Innovation (RDI) Fund constitute a significant restructuring of India’s 
national research funding architecture. ANRF has been mandated to support mission -oriented 
and translational research through convergence across academia, industry and government, 
while the RDI Fund is designed to promote commercialisation, industry -led R&D, DeepTech 
validation and high  Technology Readiness Level (TRL) innovation. In this evolving 
ecosystem, the Department of Science and Technology (DST) is required to anchor the 
foundational tier of the research system. 
3.3 Together, the three institutions create a complementary, tiered  R&D architecture , 
which constitutes about 83.51% of the total BE 2026 -27 (₹28,049.32 crore) of the 
Department: 
 RDI Fund: High-TRL, market-ready innovation and commercialization 
 ANRF: Mission-driven translational research   
 Vigyan Dhara: Foundational science, human capital, research infrastructure, STI

4.  RESEARCH, DEVELOPMENT & INNOVATION (RDI) FUND 
4.1 The Department informed that the RDI Fund was established with a significant corpus 
of ₹1 lakh crore  to be deployed over a six -year period, following formal approval by the 
Union Cabinet on July 1, 2025. The Department of Science and Technology (DST) serves as 
the nodal ministry for this scheme, which is central to the national goal of raising R&D 
expenditure to 2% of GDP by 2030. By focusing on commercializing high -technology 
breakthroughs, the fund aims to align India’s innovation output with that of other leading 
global economies. 
4.2 The fund is specifically designed to support high -risk, high-reward projects in sunrise 
industries, including Green Hydrogen, Quantum Technologies, and Semiconductors. A 
critical technical objective of the RDI scheme is to support research at Technology Readiness 
Level (TRL) 4 and above, which involves taking prototypes de veloped in laboratories and 
scaling them into market -ready commercial products. To further this, a Deep Tech Fund of 
Funds is being established under the initiative to catalyze venture capital and private equity 
investment into next-generation startups. 
4.3 Unlike traditional schemes, the RDI Fund operates under a unique governance 
structure. DST has formulated and finalized comprehensive implementation guidelines and 
Special Financial Rules (SFRs) in close consultation with the Department of Economic 
Affairs (DEA) and the Department of Expenditure (DoE). These guidelines have also 
received the formal approval from the Executive Council of the Anusandhan National 
Research Foundation (ANRF), ensuring the fund operates within a cohesive national research 
framework. 
4.4 On being asked about the disbursal of funds, the Department submitted that the 
disbursement of funds is managed through a multi-tier system. The Technology Development 
Board (TDB) and the Biotechnology Industry Research Assistance Council (BIRAC)  were 
nominated as the initial Second Level Fund Managers (SLFMs) based on Cabinet approval. 
Both organizations have already initiated the operational rollout, with TDB launching its first 
call for project proposals on February 4, 2026, followed by BIRAC o n February 13, 2026. 
The department is also in the process of appointing additional SLFMs from the private and 
financial sectors to expand the fund's reach. 
4.5 While examining the financial performance of the fund under the scheme and its 
utilization, the Committee observed that while the initial BE for 2025 -26 was ₹20,000 crore, 
it was revised down to ₹3,000 crore (RE) as the guidelines and operational frameworks were 
being finalized. However, for the FY 2026-27, a full allocation of ₹20,000 crore  has again 
been made. The Department submitted that it expects the scheme to be in full disbursement 
mode during the coming year, focusing on accelerating private -sector-led R&D and fostering 
a robust deep-tech ecosystem. 
 

9 
4.6  The Committee acknowledges that the nomination of TDB and BIRAC as 
Second Level Fund Manag ers (SLFMs) is a positive start under the RDI Fund.  The 
Department could not utilize any amount out of the RE allocation of ₹3,000 crore in the 
current FY 2025-26 (as on 31.01.2026). The Committee recommends that in FY 2026-27, 
the Department must make an early start and expedite the selection and appointment of 
additional SLFMs from the private sector ; financial institutions ; and venture capital 
firms. Diversifying the fund management pool will enhance the scheme's reach across 
different industry segments and ensure that the evaluation process for projects is both 
technically rigorous and commercially viable.  
4.7 The Committee also recommends that the Department establish a quarterly 
disbursement and progress review mechanism. This will ensure that the massive corpus 
is utilized effectively throughout the year, preventing mid-year surrenders and ensuring 
that the momentum of industrial R&D is maintained and the funds allocated for the 
RDI are also utilized to the maximum. 
4.8 Given that the RDI Fund specifically targets Technology Readiness Levels (TRL) 
4 and above, the Committee recommends that the Department should define clear 
commercialization metrics for the projects it funds. The success of the RDI Fund should 
be measured not just by the amount of capital disbursed, but by the number of 
indigenous technologies that successfully transition from the laboratory to the 
commercial market. The Department should prioritize projects with a clear path  to 
production, especially in ‘Sunrise sectors’ like semiconductors and green energy.

5.1 The Department informed the Committee that t he Anusandhan  National Research 
Foundation (ANRF) was established to catalyze a robust research culture and bridge the gap 
between academia, industry, and the government. Its primary mandate is to uplift the Science 
and Technology (S&T) ecosystem across India’s vast ne twork of universities and colleges, 
particularly those with limited existing research infrastructure. By replacing the SERB, the 
ANRF aims to create a more integrated and agile funding mechanism that supports multi -

5.2 The department highlighted that a  cornerstone of the ANRF's institutional capacity -

already approved 21 positions across 20 States and one UT to embed eminent scientists in 
less-endowed institutions for strategic leadership and mentorship.

5.7 The Committee asked the Department about the reasons why the fund utilization 
remained at zero for last two consecutive years (2023 -24 and 2024 -25). The department 
replied that the FY 2023 -24 largely pertained to the legislative finalisation and preparator y 
phase preceding operationalisation of ANRF. As the statutory provisions came into force 
only in February 2024, no programmatic approvals or financial sanctions were undertaken 
during that year. In FY 2024 -25, the emphasis was on establishing the institut ional, 
administrative and financial architecture necessary for a newly constituted statutory body. 
The first meeting of the ANRF Governing Board was held in September 2024, wherein the 
Executive Council was authorised to develop and implement programmes al igned with the 
objectives of the ANRF Act, 2023. Given that FY 2024 –25 was substantially devoted to 
institutional structuring, scheme design, and stakeholder consultations, no fund disbursal took 
place during that financial year.

5.8  The Committee then enquired about the work done by the Department in the current 
FY 2025-26. The Department submitted that during FY 2025 -26, the Executive Council of 
ANRF has approved 12 new programs in identified strategic sectors, including emerging and 
high-impact technology domains. These programs are at various stages of implementation, 
including issuance of calls, and financial sanctioning. Further, more than 2,500 in stitutions 
were onboarded under the new TSA Hybrid financial model, with onboarding processes 
completed in May 2025. This has enabled streamlined fund flow mechanisms. 
5.9 The Committee notes the work initiated by the Department under ANRF. 
However, the Committee also observes that for the current FY 2025-26, the Department 
has been able to utilize only ₹1,191 crore  (as on 31.01.2026)  out of RE allocation of 
₹1,948 crore, which is merely 61.13% of the RE. The Committee is apprehensive 
whether the Department will be able to utilize the allocated amount during the current 
financial year. The Committee therefore recommends that the Department must make 
efforts to optimally utilize the funds made available to it during FY 2025 -26 in order to 
strengthen the research framework of the country. 
5.10 As regards the roadmap for the FY 2026-27, the Department submitted that the ANRF 
has been allocated a Budget Estimate (BE) of ₹2,000 crore  and plans to utilize this outlay to 
operationalize the remaining sectors of the MAHA missions, expand the PAIR networks, and 
strengthen the newly established Centres of Excellence in STI indicators and trans -
disciplinary research. A major focus will remain on mobilizing private sector contributions 
and aligning India's research missions with global grand challenges to maximize the impact 
of the national research corpus. 
5.11 The Committee appreciates the successful launch of the Partnership for 
Accelerated Innovation and Research (PAIR)  and its hub -and-spoke model. However, 
to truly democratize science, the Committee recommends that the Department set a 
target to expand the ‘Spoke’ network to include at least one state university or college 
from every aspirational district. This will ens ure that the mentor -mentee relationship 
transcends elite institutions and reaches the grass -roots level of the national education 
system. 
 
5.12 The Committee views the plan to list the ANRF on the Social Stock Exchange as 
a pioneering step for scientific funding. The Committee recommends that the 
Department should prioritize the finalization of the legal and financial frameworks 
required for this listing. This would allow the foundation to tap into global CSR funds 
and the Indian Diaspora’s contributions, creating a diversified and sustainable funding 
base that is less dependent on annual budgetary grants.

Committee conducted a comprehensive review of the 25 Technology Innovation Hubs (TIHs)

7.4 A significant evolution in the mission's structure is the transition of high -performing 
hubs into Technology Translational Research Parks (TTRPs). For instance, hubs at IISc 
Bangalore (ART PARK), IIT Kanpur (C3iHub), IIT Indore (DRISHTI CPS), and ISM 
Dhanbad (TEXMiN) are being upgraded to TTRPs to accelerate the translation of laboratory 
research into commercialized products and solutions. This shift aims to move from 
fundamental development to large-scale technological application and market deployment.  A 
major achievement under the mission is the launch of BharatGen, India's sovereign 
multimodal AI initiative led by a consortium at IIT Bombay, which focuses on developing 
foundational multilingual AI models for text and speech in 22 Indian languages. 
7.5 On being asked about the allocation for 2026-27 and the roadmap for its utilisation , 
the Department submitted that a Budget Estimate (BE) of ₹700 crore has been allocated for 
NM-ICPS. This fi gure is based on realistic requirements as the mission enters its core 
implementation phase. The Department plans to utilize these funds to further the 
establishment of TTRPs and scale up ongoing research and translation activities across the 
network of innovation hubs. Department is focusing on guiding the TIHs toward operational 
self-sustainability. The sustainability model for these hubs includes generating revenue 
through industry -sponsored R&D projects, technology licensing, consultancy services, and 
professional skill development activities. This transition toward performance -linked funding 
is a key pillar of the 2026 -27 strategy, ensuring that the mission's innovation ecosystem 
becomes less dependent on central assistance while remaining a primary en gine for India's 
deep-tech growth.  
7.6 The Committee observes that the financial trajectory of NM -ICPS reflects a 
strategic ‘right-sizing’ of funds based on implementation progress and TPE review.  The 
Committee also appreciates the significant milestone of BharatGen completing text 
services for all 22 official languages. The Committee recommends that  the Department 
should transition from Model Development to Ecosystem enabling. The Committee 
further recommends that the BharatGen may be made available to the Indian startups 
and government departments (e.g., Agriculture, Health, Justice) to build localized, 
multilingual applications on top of these sovereign foundational models. This will ensure 
that the public investment in AI translates into tangible citizen-centric services. 
7.7 The Committee commends the successful upgrading of four TIHs (IISc, IIT -K, 
ISM Dhanbad, and IIT Indore) into Technology Translational Research Parks 
(TTRPs). It is recommended that the Department should e stablish a transparent, merit-
based pathway for the remaining 21 TIHs. A performance -based evaluation based on 
Technology Readiness Levels (TRL) and private -sector investment should be used to 
identify the next cohort of 3  to 5 hubs for TTRP status. This t ransition is critical to 
shifting focus from academic research to industrial-scale application.

REPORT
I. the Chairman of the Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to
 submit the report on its behalf, present this 41st Report of the Committee. This report deals with the 'Mid-Term Appraisal' of the programmes
 and functioning of the Department of Science and Technology.
2. In the meeting of the Committee held on the 7th February, 1997, the Secretary and other officers of the Department of Science and
 Technology gave an overview of the various activities of the Department and the Committee sought clarifications on various aspects of the
 performance of the Department particularly in the fields of Basic Research and Allied-­areas and their financial aspects.
3. The Committee wishes to express its thanks to the Officers of the Department of Science and Technology for their cooperation and
 answering the queries raised by Members on various aspects on programmes initiated by the Department.
4. The Committee considered and adopted the draft report at its meeting held on the 5th March, 1997.
 
5. The Secretary, Department of Science and Technology, in his presentation before the Committee, gave an overview of the thrust areas in
 which the Department is engaged in pursuance of the national objective of making scientific and technological progress for attaining self-
reliance. Over the years, the Department and autonomous institutions under the Department of Science and Technology have been making
 consistent efforts in formulation of policy statements and guidelines on Science and Technology; promotion of new areas of scientific research;
 Co-ordination of inter-departmental Science and Technology efforts; Support basic and applied research in universities/labs/institutions;
 International Science and Technology co-operation; Support high quality research in autonomous bodies; Catalysing Science and Technology
 interaction in societal programmes, enterpreneurship development; Science popularisation, communication and Science and Technology
 Manage­ment Information system; Promotion of commercialisation of home grown technology; support to technology development
 programmes, technology information and assessment; providing scientific services in the areas of Surveying and Mapping through its
 autonomous organisations e.g. Survey of India (SOl) and National Atlas Thematic and Mapping Organisations (NATMO); Meteorology
 through India Meteorological Department and National Centre for Medium Range Weather Forecasting (NCMRWF) and Technology
 Development Board (TDB).
6. The Committee examined the performance of the Department during the current year and its major thrust areas identified in the Ninth
 Five Year Plan in the light of the presentation made by the Secretary, Department of Science and Technology.
7. The Committee feels that the expectations of people regarding timely returns on investments made in Science and Technology and their
 egalitarian distribution amongst various sections of the society have not met with desired success. Besides, Ministry should sincerely
 endeavour to achieve cost effective and quality oriented competitiveness in the industrial field. It is equally necessary to reduce the time lag in
 the transfer of technology from the laboratory to its commercial exploitation in the field. There is need for an urgent effort to that end.
 
7.1 The Committee observes that out of Rs. 242.55 crores of the Plan Budget, about Rs. 150 crores would be spent on basic research
 and on autonomous institutions. The rewards of research are not commensurate with the amounts being put in. The Committee feels there
 is urgent need to review the research projects keeping in view the national requirements and the likely returns from the research projects. '
In the case of Technology Board, the expenditure upto December, 1996, 'has been only Rs. 3 lakhs whereas expenditure of Rs. 4.62
 crores has been spent on international co­operation. Against the allocation of Rs. 34 crores as Plan expenditure for India Meteorological
 Department an amount of Rs. 5.53 crores has only been spent. The Committee is not satisfied with the low level of fund utilisation in
 respect of various programmes.
8. The Committee observes that the time lag between the clearance of the projects by the Programme Advisory Committee and release
 of funds needs to be reduced considerably. To that end, if necessary, a Technological Financial Board could be constituted to monitor the

 entire gamut of Research Projects including the release of funds and utility aspects.
9. The Secretary, while explaining the slow pace of the functioning of Technology Development Board (TDB) informed the
 Committee that the Board came into existence in the last week of September, 1996, and immediately after wards there were several
 meetings with the industry in which the Board spelt out the quantum and type of finances and help that could be rendered to the industry in
 ,carrying ;out new collaborations in various fields with them. The Board has 50 odd proposals and all of them are presently under
 evaluation through a rigorous procedure and until they are thoroughly examined and scrutinised, the finances would not be released.       
9.1 The Committee was not satisfied with the explanation regarding the delay in finalisation of the project under consideration of
 Technology Development Board and felt that the progress was far from satisfactory. The system needs to be improved upon to ensure that
 the programmes are designed in such a way that the Board can sanction the projects within the stipulated period.
10. The Secretary informed the Committee that in the field on international co­operation, there are three types of programmes v;z
.,
 Integrated long-term programme of co­operation in Science and Technology with India and Republic of Commonwealth of Independent
 States (CIS), programmes of co and operation with the developed countries and lastly technical co operation with the developing countries.
 Among the foremost areas in which the Government have co operation with the CIS countries are material technology, Bio-technology.
 energy-related issues and information technology. The Secretary further informed that they were facing some problems because of severe
 financial crunch existing in CIS countries whereas with developed countries they have equal partnership.
10.1 The Committee is of the view that the scientists 
of CIS countries today are migrating to developed countries. The Department
 should devise some programmes whereby their services could· be utilised productively. The  Committee recommends that the· Department
 should not only bear all the expenses of the scientists who give us technology and blue-print, but also should devise a compensation
 package for them.
11. The Secretary, informed about the functioning of the India Meteorological Department (IMD) and stressed that the Scientists of
 this Department were successful in making a long and definite forecast of seasonal rainfall i.e., Monsoons. for last nine years. Earlier IMD
 were giving forecast for the entire country. Since 1988 they have started concentrating even for smaller areas.
 
11.1 The Committee appreciates the efforts of India Meteorological Department in making reasonably accurate forecasts about the
 monsoons but at the same time is of the view that the Department can do much better and can improve its functioning so that our forecasts
 are fairly accurate. More so, in case of natural Calamities so, that ample and\timely relief operations can be provided to the. affected people.
 
12. The Committee is satisfied with the performance of the Department of Science and Technology in the case of societal programmes.
 Nevertheless, the Committee feels that much still remains to be achieved in this area. The Committee therefore observes that an integrate(l
 programme for the development of ' tribal people, particularly In the North-Eastern region of the country, needs to be drawn up on the lines
 of one Lunched in the Patalkot area of district Chindwara in Madhya. Pradesh recently.
