CHAPTER II 
ASSESSMENT OF THE DEMANDS FOR GRANTS OF THE MINISTRY OF EARTH 
SCIENCES 
 
ANALYSIS OF THE BUDGETARY TRENDS OF THE MINISTRY OF EARTH SCIENCES  
 
         The Committee notes that the Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES ) had projected an 
outlay of ₹4371.54 crore to the Ministry of Finance under Demand No. 24 for the financial 
year 2026–27. However, the Ministry of Finance approved an outlay of ₹3789.23 crore, which 
is about 86.67 % of the projected amount. The Committee is of the view that the pattern and 
extent of fund utilization during the current financial year significantly influence the 
allocation made in the subsequent year. A careful examination of the Ministry‟s expenditure 
pattern over the years indicates that i t has not been able to fully utilize the outlays sanctioned 
to it. For instance, the Ministry was allocated an outlay of ₹3658.08 crore at the BE stage in 
2025–26, which was subsequently revised downward to ₹3388.27 crore at the RE stage. 
Further, the Ministry has been able to incur an expenditure of only ₹2826.83 crore up to 31 st 
January, 2026. This relatively slow pace of expenditure appears to have contributed to the 
reduction in allocation made to the Ministry in BE 2026 –27 vis-à-vis the projected outlay. The 
Committee also observes that the gap between the outlay projected by MoES to the Ministry 
of Finance and the allocation approved has widened over the years. The outlay allocated to 
the Ministry in BE 2023–24 constituted 99.43% of the projected outla y. In BE 2024–25, the 
allocation was 107.90% of the projected outlay , while in BE 2025–26 it accounted for 97.69% 
of the projected outlay . However, the allocation for the forthcoming financial year represents 
only 86.67% of the projected outlay , indicating  a comparatively lower level of budgetary 
provision against the projected requirement.  In view of the above, the Committee urges the 
Ministry of Earth Sciences to take necessary measures to improve the rate of budget 
utilization and strive to achieve full utilization of the allocated funds in the coming financial 
year, so as to avoid any reduction in future budgetary allocations.                                                                                                                                 
(Para 2.7) 
 
ASSESSMENT OF THE PATTERN OF BUDGET UTILIZATION BY THE MINISTRY OF 
EARTH SCIENCES 
The Committee notes with concern  the persistent underutilization of budgetary 
allocations by the Ministry of Earth Sciences over the past few years. An analysis o f the 
pattern of expenditure indicates that the utilization of funds has ranged between 83% and 
93% in recent years , and the Ministry has not been able to utilize the full budgetary 
allocation in any of the recent years. The Committee is of the view that such a pattern reflects 
a slow pace of expenditure and limited capacity to absorb the funds allocated , particularly 
under the Capital Head.  The Committee further observes that the reduction in allocation at 
the Revised Estimates stage , as seen in 2025 –26, h as been attributed by the Ministry to 
procurement delays, implementation challenges, site finalization issues, and other technical or 
operational constraints . While acknowledging that certain scientific and technological 
projects may involve complex proced ures, the Committee is of the firm opinion that it is the 
responsibility of the Ministry to anticipate such challenges and establish effective mechanisms 
to overcome them in a timely manner . The Committee also notes that the capital allocation 
has shown a declining trend in recent years, partly due to lower utilisation and the completion 
of certain major capital procurements. In the Committee‟s view, the persistent shortfall in 

73 
 
utilisation has also contributed to a comparatively lower allocation in BE 2026 –27. The 
Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Ministry strengthen its planning, project 
management and financial monitoring mechanisms so as to ensure timely and efficient 
utilisation of allocated funds . The Ministry should institute periodic reviews of expenditure, 
particularly under capital-intensive projects, and take proactive steps to address procedural, 
technical and operational bottlenecks that delay implementation.                            ( Para 2.14)   
CHAPTER III 
ASSESSMENT OF THE SCHEMES OF THE MINISTRY 
PRITHVI VIGYAN (PRITHVI) 
 
The Committee recommends developing advanced indigenous technologies for desalination 
plants that run on non -renewable energy. Deployed in coastal areas and cities, these plants 
would augment fresh water supplies to help address existing shortages.                                    
(para 3.17)  
The Committee acknowledges the significant role played by the PRITHVI (Prithvi 
Vigyan) Scheme  in strengthening India‟s capabilities in Earth System S ciences through its 
integrated focus on atmosphere, oceans, cryosphere, geosciences and societal applications. 
The Committee notes that several Low-Temperature Thermal Desalination (LTTD) plants  
have been established in the Lakshadweep islands under the PRITHVI-OSMART initiative to 
address the critical issue of potable water availability for island communities. While the 
Committee recognizes the importance of these plants in ensuring sustainable drinking water 
supply, it also notes that the desalination pla nts currently operate using electricity generated 
through diesel generator sets, which power the island systems. Considering the environmental 
sensitivity of island ecosystems and the broader national commitment towards clean and 
renewable energy, the Comm ittee is of the view that reliance on diesel -based power sources 
should be progressively reduced. The Committee therefore recommends the Ministry to 
explore the feasibility of making these desalination plants eco -friendly by using sustainable 
power sources  such as solar energy, Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion (OTEC), or other 
suitable renewable energy technologies.              (Para 3.18)
  
The Committee also examined the proposal for establishing Maitri-II, a new research 
station in Antarctica to replace t he existing Maitri station, which was commissioned in 1989 
and has now exceeded its designed operational life. The Committee notes the Ministry‟s 
submission that the present station is facing structural deterioration and limitations in waste -
management and environmental compliance systems, making the establishment of a modern 
replacement station necessary to ensure safety, operational sustainability, and India‟s 
continued year -round scientific presence in Antarctica in accordance with evolving 
environmental norms under the Antarctic Treaty System. However, the Committee notes that 
the architectural and design consultant for the Maitri -II project has been selected through a 
global design competition and that the winning consortium comprises Ramboll Deutschlan d 
GmbH and bofArchitekten, Germany. In this regard, the Committee recalls that India‟s first 
Antarctic research station, Dakshin Gangotri, was constructed with the involvement of the 
Indian Army, demonstrating indigenous capability in undertaking complex o perations in 
extreme polar conditions. The Committee is therefore of the view that greater consideration 
could have been given to Indian firms with relevant engineering and infrastructure expertise 
in cold-weather construction technologies. Such an approac h could have contributed to cost 
savings while also providing impetus to the objectives of Make in India and promoting greater 
self-reliance in specialized polar infrastructure development. The Committee recommends 
that, in future projects of this nature, the Ministry explore ways to ensure greater 

74 
 
participation of Indian companies, either independently or through collaborations, so that 
domestic capabilities in polar infrastructure and extreme -environment engineering are 
further strengthened.                                                           (Para 3.19) 
 
DEEP OCEAN MISSION 
The Committee notes that the Deep Ocean Mission , launched in 2021, with an 
approved outlay of ₹4,077 crore , for a period of five years, is a flagship initiative aimed at 
strengthening India‟s capabilities in deep -sea exploration, resource assessment, marine 
biodiversity research and development of advanced ocean technologies. While the Committee 
acknowledges the efforts made by the Ministry and its institutions in progressing with certain 
components of the Mission, it observes with concern that the overall progress achieved so far 
does not appear commensurate with the objectives and timelines originally envisag ed. The 
Committee further notes that key components of the Mission, including the Samudrayaan 
programme and the development of an integrated deep -sea mining system for polymetallic 
nodules, are still incomplete. It is also observed that against the approve d project cost of 
₹4,077 crore, only about ₹1,445 crore has been utilised so far, which constitutes roughly 35 
per cent of the total project outlay. In the Committee‟s view, the pace of progress under 
certain critical verticals of the Mission needs to be s ignificantly accelerated to ensure that the 
intended outcomes are achieved within a reasonable timeframe. In this regard, the Committee 
recommends that the Ministry establish clearly defined and measurable milestones under 
each of the six verticals of the Deep Ocean Mission. The Committee further recommends that 
specific timelines be fixed for the achievement of these targets, along with a structured 
monitoring mechanism to periodically review progress and address implementation 
bottlenecks.                                                                                                (para 3.30) 
MISSION MAUSAM 
 
The Committee appreciates the efforts made by the Ministry under Mission Mausam, 
which aims to transform India into a “Weather-ready and Climate-smart” nation through the 
deployment of advanced observational systems, next -generation modelling, and improved 
weather forecasting and early warning mechanisms. The Committee notes the progress made 
in strengthening Doppler Weather Radar networks, operationa lizing advanced forecasting 
systems, developing AI -based weather interpretation tools, and establishing platforms for 
hyper-local weather information dissemination.  At the same time, the Committee expresses 
concern over the increasing incidence of extreme weather events, particularly cloudbursts, 
which in recent years have caused significant loss of life, damage to infrastructure, and 
disruption of livelihoods in several parts of the country, especially in mountainous and 
ecologically fragile regions. The C ommittee notes the Ministry‟s initiative to establish a state-
of-the-art cloud microphysics laboratory  at the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology 
(IITM), Pune, and to deploy specialised observing systems in cloudburst -prone regions such 
as the North-Eastern States, the Western Ghats, and the Western Himalayas. The Committee 
recommends that these research efforts should be strongly oriented towards developing 
reliable forecasting capabilities and an effective early warning system for cloudburst events so 
that timely alerts can be issued to vulnerable communities and disaster management 
authorities.                                                    (para 3.41)
  
           The Committee further notes that ocean –atmosphere interactions play a crucial role in 
influencing weather and climate patterns, including the formation and intensification of 
cyclones and extreme rainfall events. In this regard, the Committee takes note of the proposal 
under consideration for the development of floating radar systems mou nted on buoys  to 

75 
 
enhance meteorological observations over oceanic regions where land -based radar coverage is 
limited. The Committee believes that such systems could significantly improve monitoring of 
cloud formation and rainfall dynamics over the seas and  strengthen cyclone detection and 
tracking capabilities.  The Committee, therefore, recommends the Ministry to accord due 
priority to the development and deployment of floating radar observation systems and 
provide adequate financial and institutional suppo rt for this initiative under Mission 
Mausam.                                   (para 3.42) 
 
The Committee recommends that the Ministry should coordinate with bodies like 
Central Water Commission and Survey of India to develop scientific models for analyzing 
riverine water flow. This initiative would enable accurate flood forecasting, thereby 
mitigating damage, particularly in the nation's flood-prone regions.                         ( para 3.43)
  
CHAPTER IV  
ASSESSMENT OF THE FUNCTIONING OF THE INSTITUTIONS OF THE MINISTRY 
OF EARTH SCIENCES 
V ACANCIES 
The Committee observes that the Ministry of Earth Sciences is currently implementing 
three major national missions, namely Deep Ocean Mission, Prithvi Vigyan and Mission 
Mausam, which are of critical importance for advancing the country‟s capabilities in ocean 
exploration, weather and climate services,  and earth system science. The successful 
implementation of these missions depends significantly on the availability of adequate and 
skilled human resources across the Ministry and its affiliated institutions. However, a 
substantial number of vacancies exi st across different categories of posts in the Ministry and 
its institutions. The Committee has been informed that the Recruitment Rules for the entry -
level posts of the scientific cadre in the Ministry and its affiliated offices are under finalization 
in consultation with the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) . Further, the finalization 
of the sanctioned strength of the scientific cadre  is under consideration with the Department 
of Expenditure . The Ministry has also submitted that the Department of Per sonnel and 
Training (DoPT) is the cadre -controlling authority for administrative posts of the Ministry, 
except in the case of Multi-Tasking Staff (MTS) . The Committee is of the view that such a 
large number of vacancies, particularly in scientific and technical posts, could adversely affect 
the effective implementation of these critical national missions. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry pursue the matter vigorously with the concerned authorities, 
including UPSC, the Department of Expe nditure and DoPT, to expedite the finalization of 
recruitment rules, sanctioned strength and recruitment processes.                             (Para 4.4) 
INDIAN METEOROLOGICAL DEPARTMENT (IMD), NEW DELHI 
           The Committee notes that numerous advan ced technologies, including Artificial 
Intelligence, are being utilized globally to enhance the accuracy and affordability of weather 
forecasting. In this context, the Committee recommends that the Ministry should conduct a 
detailed outcome analysis of the  budgetary allocations made to the India Meteorological 
Department (IMD).                                                                                                         (Para 4.12)
  
         The Committee is of the opinion that accurate and timely weather prediction is critically 
important for a country like India , where a large segment of the population depends on 

76 
 
weather-reliant economic activities . The Committee has been informed that 48 Doppler 
Weather Radars (DWRs) are currently operational ac ross the country . However, the 
Committee observes that the existing network does not provide adequate coverage across 
several parts of the country , which may affect the accuracy and timeliness of short -range and 
nowcasting services, particularly for locali zed severe weather events. The Committee is of the 
view that DWRs are critical components of a modern weather observation system , as they 
provide high -resolution, real -time information on rainfall intensity, wind patterns, 
thunderstorms and severe weather systems. Expanding the DWR network across the country 
would significantly enhance forecasting capabilities, strengthen early warning systems, and 
support more effective disaster preparedness and response mechanisms. The Committee notes 
that under Mission M ausam, the Government has proposed the installation of an additional 
84 DWRs across the country to address the existing coverage gaps. The Committee further 
notes that the estimated expenditure for this expansion is approximately ₹942.57 crore . In 
view of the above, the Committee recommends that the Ministry may take necessary steps to 
ensure that the proposed additional Doppler Weather Radars are installed at the earliest  so 
that most parts of the country are adequately covered by the radar network. The Co mmittee 
further recommends that the required financial resources may be provided to IMD in a 
phased manner to facilitate timely implementation of the proposed expansion.   
(Para 4.13) 
         The Committee also notes that a large section of the public is unaware of the existence of 
Mausam app developed by IMD. Moreover, the user interface of the app is not very user 
friendly and pales in comparison to other popular apps in this domain. The Comm ittee 
therefore recommends that IMD  should take steps for populariz ation of the app. The 
Committee also recommends that IMD should improve the overall U ser Interface of the app 
to make it more appealing to the general public.                                                        (Para 4.14 ) 
INDIAN INSTITUTE OF TROPICAL METEOROLOGY (IITM), PUNE 
        The Committee recognizes the significant role played by the Indian Institute of Tropical 
Meteorology (IITM), Pune, as a premier national research institutio n engaged in advanced 
studies on the atmosphere, ocean and climate systems, particularly in improving weather and 
climate forecasts for the tropics and understanding the dynamics of the monsoon over India. 
The Committee notes the research undertaken by IIT M under Mission Mausam to examine 
the meteorological factors contributing to severe air pollution in Delhi during the winter 
months. In view of the continuing severity of air pollution in Delhi and the National Capital 
Region, the Committee is of the opini on that scientific research findings such as those 
generated by IITM are extremely valuable for informed policy -making and mitigation 
planning. The Committee therefore recommends that the research findings and analytical 
insights generated by IITM should b e shared regularly with relevant regulatory and policy -
making bodies , including the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), Delhi Pollution 
Control Committee (DPCC), and the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM), as 
well as other concerned agencies.                 (Para 4.18) 
 
NATIONAL CENTRE FOR MEDIUM RANGE WEATHER FORECASTING (NCMRWF), 
NOIDA 
            The Committee notes the important role played by the National Centre for Medium 
Range Weather Forecasting (NCMRWF), Noida , in developing and oper ating advanced 
numerical weather prediction models for short -range, medium -range, extended -range and 
seasonal forecasts, which are widely used by various user agencies including the India 

77 
 
Meteorological Department. The Committee appreciates the development  of the High-
Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) forecasting system , which is designed for short -range 
prediction of rapidly evolving weather systems, particularly in complex terrains such as the 
Himalayan region. Considering the increasing occurrence of extre me rainfall and cloudburst 
events in the Himalayan region and the serious damage caused by such incidents in recent 
years, the Committee is of the view that strengthening scientific capabilities for their 
prediction and early warning is of critical importa nce. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends the Ministry to provide sustained support to NCMRWF for further development 
and operationalization of high -resolution modelling systems such as HRRR, including 
enhanced assimilation of radar and satellite observati ons over mountainous regions. The 
Committee further recommends that efforts be made to integrate the outputs of these 
advanced models with early warning dissemination systems so that actionable and timely 
alerts can be provided to disaster management authorities and vulnerable communities.  
(Para 4.25) 
NATIONAL CENTRE FOR SEISMOLOGY (NCS), DELHI 
 The Committee notes that the National Centre for Seismology (NCS), Delhi , 
established in 2015, plays a critical role in monitoring seismic activity across the coun try, 
maintaining the National Seismological Network, conducting earthquake hazard assessments, 
and supporting research in seismology, earthquake precursor studies, and deep borehole 
investigations. However, the Committee is constrained to note that even af ter nearly a decade 
of its establishment, the NCS does not have any sanctioned posts of its own and continues to 
function with personnel drawn on a loan basis from the Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES) 
and the India Meteorological Department (IMD). The Com mittee finds it difficu lt to 
understand why a specializ ed national institution entrusted with such crucial responsibilities 
is still operating without a dedicated cadre of scientific, technical, and administrative staff.  
While noting the Ministry‟s submiss ion that proposals for the creation of dedicated posts for 
NCS have been submitted under the PRITHVI scheme, the Committee strongly recommends 
that the matter be pursued on priority and that the approval process be expedited.                                      
(Para 4.29) 
INDIAN NATIONAL CENTRE FOR OCEAN INFORMATION SYSTEM (INCOIS), 
HYDERABAD 
           The Committee recognizes the critical role played by the Indian National Centre for 
Ocean Information Services (INCOIS)  in providing ocean information and advisory services 
that support fisheries, maritime operations, coastal management and disaster preparedness. 
The Committee is of the view that a robust and comprehensive ocean observation network is 
essential for improving the accuracy and reliability of ocean forecasts, early warning systems 
and long -term marine research.  The Committee notes that there remain long -standing 
observational gaps in near  shore wave measurements along several parts of the Indian 
coastline. In this regard, the Wave Monitoring Along Near shore (WAMAN)  project has 
played an important role in generating real -time coastal wave observations that support 
operational wave forecasting, early warning services, maritime safety and scientific research. 
However, the Committee observes that the present WAMAN network covers only selected 
segments of the coastline. The Committee therefore recommends that the network of wave 
buoys under WAMAN be progressively expanded to cover the entire Indian coastline so that a 
more comprehensive and reliable near shore observation system can be established.                                                                        
(Para 4.38) 

78 
 
        The Committee also notes that coastal regions in the country remain relatively u nder-
observed, with limited availability of physico -chemical, biological and fisheries -related data. 
The absence of observations for several parameters constrains the accuracy of ocean 
information and advisory services and limits the effectiveness of forec asting systems. In this 
context, the Committee emphasizes the importance of establishing regional shore stations 
equipped with appropriate laboratory and monitoring facilities to support long -term coastal 
observations, data analysis, model validation and c apacity building. The Committee is of the 
view that strengthening coastal observation infrastructure through an expanded WAMAN 
network and the establishment of shore stations will significantly improve ocean forecasting 
capabilities and generate valuable l ong-term datasets. The Committee therefore recommends 
that the Ministry provide adequate financial support to INCOIS for strengthening the 
WAMAN network and for establishing the proposed regional shore stations in a time -bound 
manner.                                     (Para 4.39) 
CENTRE FOR MARINE LIVING RESOURCES AND ECOLOGY (CMLRE), KOCHI 
        The Committee notes that the Fishery and Oceanographic Research Vessel  (FORV) 
Sagar Sampada, which serves as the backbone of the Marine Living Resources programme 
implemented by the Centre for Marine Living Resources and Ecology (CMLRE), was 
commissioned in 1984 and has been in service for more than four decades. The Committee is 
concerned that the ageing of the vessel has resulted in several operational limitations and that, 
in its current condition, the vessel may remain operational for deep-sea surveys for only about 
seven more years. In view of these limitations and considering the growing requirements of 
deep-sea research under programmes such as the D eep Ocean Mission and the PRITHVI 
Scheme, the Committee strongly feels that the country requires a modern and advanced 
Fishery and Oceanographic Research Vessel capable of supporting expanded scientific 
observations in deep and distant waters. Given that F ORV Sagar Sampada is already nearing 
the end of its operational life, the Committee recommends that the Ministry expedite the 
necessary procedural formalities and take time -bound steps for the acquisition and 
construction of the new vessel. The Committee i s of the view that the new Fishery and 
Oceanographic Research Vessel should be built and commissioned at the earliest, preferably 
within the next two to three years, so that India‟s marine research programmes are not 
adversely affected due to the declining operational capability of the existing vessel.                                                                                              
(Para 4.44) 
NATIONAL CENTRE FOR POLAR AND OCEAN RESEARCH (NCPOR), GOA 
        The Committee takes note of India‟s growing engagement in the Arctic through scientific 
expeditions, international collaborations, and the operation of the Himadri research station in 
Svalbard. The Committee observes that polar research has acquired increasing significance in 
recent years due to its direct relevance to global climate systems, ocean circulation, sea -level 
rise and their impact on weather patterns, including the Indian monsoon. The absence of a 
dedicated ice-class Polar Research Vessel has be en a major constraint in expanding India‟s 
polar research activities, particularly in the wider Arctic Ocean. The Committee notes with 
satisfaction that in -principle approval has already been accorded by the Department of 
Expenditure for the acquisition of a Polar Research Vessel with ice-breaking capabilities at an 
estimated cost of ₹2,329.40 crore. In view of the strategic and scientific importance of this 
project, the Committee recommends that the Ministry expedite the remaining procedural 
formalities an d ensure that adequate financial resources are made available so that the 
project progresses in a time -bound manner. The Committee further recommends that, 
wherever feasible, Indian shipbuilding firms should be actively involved in the construction of 

79 
 
the Polar Research Vessel. Such an approach would not only strengthen domestic 
shipbuilding capabilities but also contribute to the objectives of promoting indigenous 
manufacturing and technological self-reliance in specialized marine infrastructure.                                                                                                                          
(Para 4.50) 
NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF OCEAN TECHNOLOGY (NIOT), CHENNAI 
         The Committee notes that the National Institute of Ocean Technology (NIOT) has 
transferred around 40 technologies between 2020 –26, generating a total revenue of ₹1.64 
crore. The Committee expresses concern that these technologies are being transferred at 
relatively low prices compared to their commercial potential. It is o bserved that private 
partners often earn significant profits from these technologies, while the originating public 
institutes receive only a marginal share of the value created. The Committee understands that 
there is no robust mechanism to verify whether the benefits of these low -cost technology 
transfers reach the intended target users, and that the fees for renewal of licenses after expiry 
remain undefined. In view of this, the Committee recommends that the Ministry of Earth 
Sciences should adopt a more competitive, market-aligned pricing framework for technology 
transfer. Licensing fees should reflect the true commercial value, uniqueness, and societal 
impact of publicly funded technologies. The Committee further recommends the 
establishment of clear pro cedures and norms for technology valuation and licensing, with the 
National Research Development Corporation (NRDC) and the technology developer jointly 
determining fees. To ensure transparency, accountability, and proper utilization of publicly 
funded technologies, all technology transfer agreements should be subjected to periodic third -
party audits, and the outcomes of such audits should govern future licensing and renewal 
terms.                                      (Para 4.58)

REPORT
I, the Chairman of the Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and Forests, having been authorised by the
 Committee to submit the report on its behalf present this 42nd Report of the Committee. The report is based on the 'Mid-Term
 Appraisal' of the Programmes and Functioning of the Department of Space, undertaken by the Committee.
2. In the meeting of the Committee held on the 16th January, 1997, the Secretary and other officials of the Department of
 Space gave an overview of the activities of the Department and the Committee sought clarifications on the various !aspects on the
 performance and functioning of the Department during the year 1996-97 particularly in the fields of Research and Development,
 application of Satellite Technology for Rural Uplift and allied areas and its financial aspects.
3. The Committee wishes to express its thanks to the officers of the Department of Space for their co-operation and answering
 the queries raised by Members on various aspects of the programmes and initiatives taken by the Department.
4. The Committee considered and adopted the draft report at its meeting held on the 5th March, 1997.
5. The Secretary, Department of Space in his presentation before the Committee, gave a graphic account of the performances
 and achievements of the Department of Space during the year 1996-97 and an overview of the thrust areas in which the
 Department is presently engaged in pursuance of the national objectives of attaining the goal of total self-reliant use of space
 technology for National Development, which has not only revolutionised the present but promises to shape our future. Since the
 modest beginning in 1972 the Department of Space and the autonomous institutions functioning under the Department have been
 making consistent efforts in formulation of policy statements on guidelines on Space programmes which are carried out through
 the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO), the National Remote Sensing Agency (NRSA), the Physical Research
 Laboratory (PRL), the National Mesosphere-Stratosphere-Troposphere Radar Facility (NMRF) and other agencies. Programmes
 taken by the Department are: exploration and promotion of new avenues for application of space technology; co-ordination of
 inter-departmental space programmes and subsequent application efforts including research and development efforts; support
 R&D programmes in Universities/Laboratories/Institutions; support application oriented advanced research in autonomous
 bodies; international co-operation in sharing space technology; increasing role of space technology in academia and industry;
 catalysing space programmes for social development through satellite communication, rural uplift, tribal development, monitoring
 of rescue and warning system in cyclone prone areas, etc.; commercialization of space technology and .services offered in
 international market; providing satellite services in the areas of surveying and mapping, locating natural resources, etc.; and
 support to meteorological users, especially in weather forecasting.
6. The Committee considered the performance of the Department in various fields during the current year and its major
 thrust areas identified for the 9th five year plan in light of the presentation made by the Secretary, Department of Space.

7. With the state-of-the-art technology for remote sensing satellite data applications, drought monitoring and assessment,
 disaster management, wasteland management, water resources management, ocean/marine resource management, mineral
 prospecting, forests resources surveying and management, etc. have become scientifically possible. Thus IRS has been the
 integrated mission for sustainable development. Therefore, it is necessary that the multi-purpose activities of the Department
 should reflect the aspirations of the people. The Committee feels that the space programmes should be more and more benefit
 oriented and the Department should earnestly help to percolate the benefits of space technology to different sections of the
 society.
8. The Committee observes that remote sensing is catching up as a major source of activity for national development which
 was, by the large, until recently a Government activity. The Department of Agriculture, Environment and Forests,
 Oceanography, Science and Technology and Other Departments have been using it for .their individual requirements. There is a
 large magnitude of value addition to the remote sensing data, which can be used in marketable form in several disciplines, both
 Government and Non-Government. Therefore, more and more private entrepreneurs are to be associated in the process of remote
 sensing data utilization programme.
 
9. The Secretary informed the Committee that the development of Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV) for
 launching INSAT class satellites which was to take place during the 8th plan, got procrastinated due to a delay in the transfer of
 cryogenic engine technology from Russia. However, with the mechanical mug up from Russia and successful firing of the upper
 stage engine of GSL V, the first test flight of GSL V is targeted for launching in 1997-98 i.e., during the 9th plan period.
10. The Committee is of the view that because of the non-availability of the cryogenic engine technology tile Indian space
 programme has got delayed. Therefore, the Department of Space should take initiative to develop indigenous technology
 required for launching of GSL V.
11. The Secretary explained the question of "brain-drain" in ISRO. In the wake of the economic reforms introduced in 1991-
92 and the subsequent increase in the activities of and remuneration for personnel in the private sector, there has been a flight of
 talent in technical fields towards more remunerative sectors. The Committee was informed that in the period between 1990-94
 about 85 people left ISRO every year. During 1995-96 the figure was 135. Roughly 42% of these people who left ISRO, had the
 computer technology area as their field of specialisation, and 27% of them had electronics and teleco!l1munication as their field
 for specialisation. Particularly the exodus of computer scientists, especially software experts, from various centres of ISRO have
 become fairly significant over the last couple of years. The problem was more pronounced among junior scientists.
12. The Committee finds that occasions did arise when scheduled critical work slowed down owing to 
8 number of young
 scientists/engineers leaving ISRO en-block. The Committee recommends that the problems must be addressed urgently to
 prevent the flight of talent. Government should provide pay perks and amenities that help to arrest the trend.
13. The Secretary also apprised the Committee of the progress made in regard to GRAMSAT Satellite Network Project. The
 concept of GRAMSAT is to promote awareness among the village population through various programmes being devised by the
 local rural development agency. It is a system which is being tested at Jhabua, M.P., aimed at the problems of the local
 population, which is predominantly tribal. The present problems in Jhabua ,concern literacy, agricultural practices, health,
 hygiene and the role of women in panchayat raj. The GRAMSAT project is also targeted to cover atleast 25-30 districts, during
 the 9th Five year plan. The project aims to produce population relevant development programmes.
14. The Committee feels that the GRAMS AT project needs to be made economically viable because the area, it covers is
 mainly inhabited by people having low per capita income. The GRAMSAT project should also draw up a time schedule to cover
 the villages in India for rural development on time bound basis.  
15. The Secretary explained about INSAT- II’s disaster warning system and the role it played during the recent Andhra Pradesh
 cyclone. The INSAT-II is capable of analysing the cyclonic formation as it gradually approaches the coastal area. At present there are
 250 receivers located at various places on the coastal side for the purpose of detecting the cyclone.
16. The Committee recommends that in order to avoid disasters in the coastal region, the INSAT-II Satellite Disaster Warning
 System should be augmented and designed to cover the whole of coastal region in order to avoid further human casualties, loss of
 livestock etc.
17. The Secretary explained that IRS data were being used for various socio-economic development programmes, including
 hydrology, underground water exploration with greater than 92% accuracy and for mapping surface water bodies for optimal
 implementation of irrigation schemes, improving agricultural production, wasteland development, urban plan­ning, environmental
 monitoring, identification of appropriate location for establishing industries, etc.
18. The Committee is strongly of the view that there is need to exploit remote sensing technological capabilities commercially,
 specially In Asia-Pacific and West Asian Region where most of the world's undernourished and underdeveloped population live. The
 Government should explore the possibility of Asian countries using our space technology for the progress of their space programmes
 including launching of their own satellites.
19. The Secretary also informed the Committee that the actual allocation for space programmes for the Eighth plan period was Rs.
 3,160 crores. It is Rs. 11,000 crores for the Ninth plan period, which is between Rs. 7,000 to 7,500 crores at the 1991-92 prices. The
 Department of Space, therefore, needed and enhanced outlay for its space programmes.
20. The Committee is satisfied with the progress made by the Department of Space in respect of the Space related programmes. The
 Committee reiterates its
 view that the space programmes should not be allowed to stagnate or suffer. Adequate advance planning in this
 field is necessary and the Department of Space should go shea4lln right earnest to Plan its vision beyond the year 2000. To achieve that
 end necessary goals. should be fixed and requirements of technology should be identified and designed so that the programme does not

REPORT
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Department of Biotechnology on the recommendations contained
 in the Thirty-Fourth Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology, Environment
 and Forests on the Demands for Grants (1996-97) of the Department of Biotechnology which was presented to the Rajya Sabha on 27th
 August, 1996. There are 14 recommendations contained in the Thirty-Fourth Report of the Committee. Action Taken notes on the
 Recommendations of the Committee, were' received from the Department on
21st January, 1997.                                                                                             
On scrutiny of the Action Taken Report as received from the Department of Biotechnology, the Committee finds that 11
 recommendations have been fully implemented. The Committee is not satisfied with the action take n by the Ministry in regard to its
 recommendation Nos. 17 & 21 and in case of one reply, the Department has been asked to take expeditious action.
The Committee's recommendation, action taken thereon and comments of the Committee on the action taken by the Department of
 Biotechnology are given in the succeeding paragraphs:-
RECOMMENDATIONS:
The Committee was appraised that Biotechnology based programmes have also been initiated for upliftment of rural women and
 for providing opportunities to women scientists and steps have been taken for development of appropriate technologies and their
 transfer and, demonstrations for providing income and employment generation in rural areas. The technologies developed by DBT
 which are ready for transfer for the benefit of women include Biofertilizers, Biopesticides, Sericulture, Plant tissue culture,
 Vermicomposting, Spirulina production, Mushroom cultivation, Medicinal and aromatic plants and Aquaculture, poultry and livestock.
(para 17)
Action Taken by the Department
The Department has further initiated action to augment the programmes for upliftment of Rural women and for providing
 opportunities to women scientists during the 9th plan period. The issue has been discussed in detail by the Working Group for the
 formulation of 9th plan. A separate budget head for special programmes for women has been proposed in the plan document. The
 technologies developed for the Plant tissue culture especially for a number of forest trees, horticulture and plantation crops would
 directly benefit the women further in terms of employment opportunities and income generation. Demonstration trials at the farmers'
 field are already been conducted in which the participation of women is further encouraged. Similarly, there involvement of rural
 women 
in the production and use or biopesticides, vermicomposting, mushrooms, spirulina, aquaculture, poultry and livestock and
 sericulture products.
1
 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               "            I
COMMENTS
The Committee is not satisfied with the Ministry's  reply as no detail of the programmes have been given. Nor has it been indicated
 as to where these programmes are being conducted or are proposed to be conducted and the number of women who have benefited
 from the programmes. It is also not clear how the women entrepreneurs market their products and solve their problems in this regard.
 The Committee would like to have a comprehensive status note on the subject.
RECOMMENDATION
The Committee recommends that efforts should be made to open at least one centre during the year 1996-97 in each state/union
 territory. The DBT should make out a case for allocation of more funds under major head 3425 and sub-head 119.13 and efforts 
be
 made for transfer of technology for both BGA and Rhizobium.
(Para 21)
Action Taken by the Department
The technology development and demonstration programme in Biofertilizers was started in the year 1990 which was subsequently
 converted' into Mission Mode Programme. Technologies for the production of Rhizobial and algal Biofertilizers are in the process of
 transfer for commercial production. Steps have been taken to locate the production centres all over the country and first two centres
 have been established in the state of Madhya Pradesh. The centres located in Jammu &  Kashmir, Punjab, Delhi, West Bengal, Uttar
 Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra where technology development programme is in progress are also producing Biofertilizers for
 demonstration and awareness building programme. In addition, these centres are selling the produce at very nominal rate  to the farmers
 of the state and adjoining areas.
COMMENTS
The Committee is not satisfied with the slow pace of the progress in the transfer of technology for commercial production of
 Rhizobial and Algal biofertilizers. The Department should clearly indicate the time schedule by which the production centres would be
 established and commercial production start.
RECOMMENDATION

The Augmentation of Bioinformatic Centre has further been discussed by the Scientific Advisory Committee of the Department. A
 bas\: paper in under preparation for converting bioinformatic centre into a society and for Biotechnology Information Forecasting and
 harnessing.
Action Taken by the Department
In view of Bioinfonnatic impact on the high tech area research areas the Committee feels it necessary to strengthen the
 Bioinformatics in a big way. The facilities available for the purpose be augmented to provide Silicon Graphic based high performance
 computing environment for molecular visualisation to researchers in modern biology/biotechnology. Efforts may also be initiated to
 form a Biotechnology/Information Forecasting Commission for better access to the scientists in the country.
(para 24)
 
 
COMMENTS:
While the Committee notes the reply, it would like to impress upon the Department the need for expeditions action.
RECOMMENDATION:
The Committee satisfied with the efforts made by the DBT for initiatives taken to promote research and development programmes,
 demonstration activities, technology transfer, patenting of inventions and conservation of natural resources, especially genetic diversity
 using biotechnology tools. The Committee notes that with the involvement of the state level organisations initiatives have been taken to
 promote this field in the States of Haryana, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh and Orissa. A beginning should therefore be made to involve all
 States and Union Territories and direct linkage be established with the socio­economic ministries and departments and with other
 organisations involved in scientific work and joint proposal be mooted. The Committee recommends that DBT should identify the rural
 areas in each State/Union Territory for the purpose. The Panchayats should be involved to make the projects result oriented.
(Para-25)
Action taken by the Department
The Department has already initiated a programme for the demonstration of biotechnologies like Biofertilizers, Biopesticides,
 Sericulture, Aquaculture, Mushroom Cultivation, Spirulina Production, Vermicomposting, Cultivation of Medicinal and Aromatic
 Plants etc. in the rural areas for the upliftment of SCIST population and weaker sections. Various projects under this programme are
 being implemented with the help of Science/Medical/Agricultural/Colleges/Agricultural UniversitieS/1ITslVoluntary
 Organisations/NGOs with the direct involvement of target population. These projects are at different stares of implementation and
 hence its impact can be assessed only after the completion of the projects, approximately by 
1999-2000. Under this programme an
 Expert Committee has been constituted for generation of new projects, identification of new technologies and the implementing
 agencies and to ensure successful implementation of the projects with regular monitoring. The Deptt. has prepared a 10 year profile
 starting from the financial year 1997-98. Under this programme it has been proposed to undertake the following activities, in addition to
 the already identified ones, in different parts of the country: (i) Biological software for substainable agriculture covering biofertilizers,
 bio-control agents, vermicomposting, organic manure, micro nutrient improvement etc. (ii) Bio-resource survey with the involvement
 of local people specifically in the conservation of biological resources which are of economic importance to the nation. (iii) Training
 for the use of agro-technology packages for biomass production as an economic activity. (iv) Establishment of biotechnology
 demonstration, application and training centres for target population in different regions of the country where there is a larger
 concentration of the target population. At least 
10 such centres would be established in West Bengal, Orissa. North­ Eastern Hills,
 Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh in the Agriculture Universities/Krishi Vigyan Kendras/existing NFOs who
 are involved in such type of programmes. The large scale demonstration trials of Tissue Culture raised plants are being conducted at
 various locations in different states. The plantlets are raised by two Tissue Culture Pilot Plant facilities set up by Deptt. of
 Biotechnology. The State Forest Deptt./AgenciesIVoluntary Organisations are conducting these trials. The Ministry of Environment
 and  Forest has been associated and provides assistance to the State Forest Departments. The field trials of tissue culture raised
 plantation crops are being conducted in collaboration with Spices Board, Coffee Board and related user Agencies/Ministries. The
 Deptt. has also supported hardening facilities in different agroclimatic regions in collaboration with various State S&T councils who
 coordinate the field level activities in the States of West Bengal, Madhya Pradesh and Arunachal Pradesh. Efforts are being made
 through the assistance of Biotech Consortium India Ltd. (BCIL) to transfer Biopesticides technology to the Industries. So far 5
 industries have shown interest in the product.
COMMENTS:
The Committee notes the reply.
RECOMMENDATION:
The Committee observes that topics of interest need to be identified for production of video-films. This would provide publicity to
 subjects being dealt with by DBT especially for the upliftment of rural population, SC/ST, women and other weaker sections of the
 society. These video films should be distributed to the States for dissemination of information for benefit of rural areas.
(Para 26)
Action taken by the Department
Under the Programme titled "Biotechnology based programme for SCIST population and weaker sections" efforts will be made for

 the production of video films on the successful technology demonstration models. A video film on production, benefit and use of
 biofertilizers has already been produced and being shown in various farmers melas. The large scale distribution of video films in the
 State has already been started for dissemination of information for the benefit of rural areas. The Deptt. has initiated action on the

 well as gaining basic knowledge in the area of biofertilizer, biopesticides, embryo transfer technology Two films on Tissue Culture

COMMENTS:
The Committee would like to have a note on the feedback received as a result of video films shown on production benefits. The
 Committee would also like to have a status note on the distribution of video films and the feed back, if any received on their showing.
RECOMMENDATION:
 
The Committee expresses its concern over the delay in the establishment of the CDFD centre at Hyderabad and steps should be
 taken to make the establishment operative during the current year itself.
(Para 28)
Action taken by the Department
The Deptt. has taken steps to provide initial funds for the project. A Society has already been registered and the Centre has been
 made operational from the premises of Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology, Hyderabad. Two meetings of the Society have been
 held; the Scientific Advisory Committee has also met once.
 
 
COMMENTS:
The Committee notes the reply.
RECOMMENDATION:
The Committee notes with. satisfaction the work done by the Institute in the development of detection kits eveloped by the Institute
 and its Leprosy Vaccine Trials. The Committee is of the view that the Institute should focus more on product oriented research taking
 leads form the basic research results supported by the Department, rather than duplicating its efforts on the basic research. NIl should
 direct its research towards more products in a realistic manner so that results are used for industrial exploitation of indigenous
 technology. The results of research should also enjoy the benefit of National and International patent protection. The Committee hopes
 that the allocation of Rs. 9.00 crores for the purpose would be fully utilised.
(Para 31)
Action taken by the Department
The NIl has focussed the research efforts both in basic and product oriented areas. There is no duplication of research efforts. Five
 technologies have been transferred to industry for commercialisation during the 8th Plan period, which are diagnostic kits; PCR based
 probes for sexing of empryos which is now a customised service. The Institute has applied for 29 International Patents for 6 products
 and 11 National Patents for 11 products out of which for 3 products the International Patents have been granted during the 8th plan
 period. Very recently the Immunodiagnostic kit for Silkworm has been perfected. The Institute would fully utilise the allocated funds.
COMMENTS:
The Committee notes the reply.
RECOMMENDATION:
The Budget Estimates for 1996-97 provide a sum of Rs. 5.00 crores for NCCS. The Committee appreciates the results of successful
 cultivation of skin cultures and their transplantation in burn and vitiligo cases. Further efforts in standardisation of such techniques will
 help Medical Institutions and practitioners. At the same time it should be ensured that the Centre maintains its service facilities as per
 its mandate and takes up R&D projects according to the needs of the society. The Committee recommends that New Laboratory-cum-
Residential Complex of NCCS should be completed at the earliest and made functional during the year.
(Para 33)
Action taken by the Department
The Centre for Cell Science alongwith its R&D activities is continuing the service facilities with a supply of Cell Cultures to user
 scientists. During 1995-96, 698 cultures comprising 232 different cell lines were supplied to 108 Research Institutes located in 59
 different cities. The supply of cultures is increasing exponentially over the years. The Centre has started functioning from its new
 premises which has been completed and would be inaugrated by June, 1997. The Laboratories and Animal House Buildings have been
 completed and are fully functional.

RECOMMENDATION:
The Committee recommends that new facilities namely X-ray crystallography and 600 MHz FTNMR being created to take
 up structural biology studies specially from the view point- to drug designing and targeting should be expedited.
(Para 37)
Action taken by the Department
The 600 MHz FTNMR facility set up at Tata Institute of Fundamenta1 Research Institute, Mumbai is functional; the X-
crystallography facility set up at Bhabha Atomic Research Centre, Mumbai has initiated the work instructural biology. A major
 project on X-ray crystallography for structural biology studies in association from Bose Institute and I1CB, Calcutta has been
 sanctioned at Saha Institute of Nuclear Physics, Calcutta. This facility has also started work on drug designing and drug
 targeting.
COMMENTS:
The Committee notes the reply.
RECOMMENDATION:
According to the "Background Note" the sanctioned staff strength of DBT as on 01.03.1996 is 251. The note is however
 silent on the vacancies as on date. The Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation made in its 21st report regarding the
 appointments and adequate promotion avenues for the scientists. The Committee further recommends that a total Cadre
 Review including the scientists' feeder cadre be taken up at the earliest and an independent Cadre Controlling Cell be set up.
 The Committee observes that DBT should have its own Recruitment Rules, for Scientists and Support Staff.
(Para 38)
Action taken by the Department
The Department has 44 vacant posts as on date out of these five positions fall in group 'A' and none in group 'B'
 (Gazetted). Efforts are being made to fill up these posts. As regards promotional avenues of Scientists are concerned, they are
 covered under the Flexible Compementing Scheme, according to which they are eligible for promotion after every five years
 of completion of satisfactory service upto the post of Advisor in the scale of Rs. 5900­7300. Nineteen Scientific Officers have
 got promotion after January, 1995 and position of promotion is up-to-date as on date. The recruitment rules for all the
 scientific posts have since been notified and some amendments to bring these rules at par with the Recruitment rules of
 Department of Science and Technology are under active consideration in consultation with Department of Personnel and
 Training and Union Public Service Commission. The Department itself is the Cadre Controlling Authority in respect of
 Scientific posts and is following the norms laid down in the Recruitment Rules which were notified in April, 1989. The non-
scientific posts are covered under the Central Staffing Scheme/Central Sectt./Central Sectt. Clerical Service for which the
 Cadre Controlling authority is Department of Personnel and Training.
COMMENTS:
The Committee notes the reply.

The Committee observes that the DBT should draw up a comprehensive plan of action for projects in hilly areas especially
 in Uttranchal and other backward and tribal areas of Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and North Eastern region. Therefore, it should
 approach Planning Commission with its requirements for additional funds.
(Para 40)

The Oeptt. has already identified the tribal areas of North Eastern States as well as that of Bihar, Orissa, Madhya Pradesh
 and Kerala for the identification of Genetic disorders! health interventions. The North Eastern States have been identified for
 the implementation of Biotechnology based programmes for the benefit of tribals in the areas like demonstration of large
 cardamom, medicinal and aromatic plants and other proven technologies.

The Committee notes the reply.

The Committee in its twenty first Report expressed its satisfaction over the fact that BIBCOL had started trial runs for the
 production of vaccine from bulk. An investment of Rs. 4.52 crores and Rs. 1.10 crores was made in the year 1993-94 and
 1994-95 in BIBCOL and an amount of Rs. 3 crores has been earmarked for investment purposes for the year 1996-97.
 Attention of the Committee has been drawn to an annexure to be Report of Auditor for the year ended 31.03.94 which
 indicates that the fixed assets of BIBCOL have neither been physically verified by the management at reasonable intervals nor

REPORT
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Department of Electronics on the recommendations contained
 in the Thirty-Second Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology, Environment
 and Forests on the Demands for Grants (1996-97) of the Department of Electronics which was presented to the Rajya Sabha on 27th
 August, 1996. There are 9 recommendations contained' in the Thirty-Second Report of the Committee. Action Taken notes on the
 recommendations of the' Committee', were received from the Department on 3rd February, 1997. 
On scrutiny of' the Action, Taken Report as 'received from the Department of Electronics, the Committee finds that 3
 recommendations have been fully implemented. The Committee is not satisfied ·with the action taken by the Ministry in regard to its
 recommendation' No.2 and in case of reply to recommendation No.3, the Department has been asked to develop certain models based
 on the latest changes. In regard to recommendation No.

The Committee's' recommendation, action taken thereon and comments of the Committee on the action taken by the Department
 of Electronics are given in the succeeding paragraphs:-
RECOMMENDATIONS:
1. The Committee observes that the overall budgetary allocation of Rs. 132.50 crores for 1996-97 has sharply declined in
 comparison to the budgetary allocation of Rs. 147 crores in 1995-96. There have been reductions in the budgetary allocation of the
 National Centre for Software Technology, System Engineering and Consultancy Programme, Electronics Material Development
 Programme, Electronics Industry Development Programme, Japanese Language Training Programme, Power Sector Electronics
 Programme, Industrial Electronics Promotion Programme, Software Export Promotion Programme, National Radar Council,
 Electronics for Rural Se,ctor a Health Care Transportation Systems Programme, Industrial Robotics and Integrated Automation,
 Energy conservation through Industrial Electronics, Capital Goods Development Programme, Technology Missions and Centre for
 Liquid Crystal Research,
Action taken by the Department
Reduction in budgetary support goes to suggest reduction in the overall activities of the DOE.
Reply: The proposed funds for the programmes for the year 1996-97 were more than th'ose for the year 1995-96. The
 Department of Electronics projected requirement of funds for the year 1996-97 submitted to Planning Commission was Rs. 293.90
 crores compared to 1995-96 budgetary allocation of Rs. 147 crores. However, Planning Commission could allocate only Rs. 132.50
 crores to DOE for 1996-97 due to resource crunch.
1.1 The National Centre for Software Technology (NeST) is a Society generating

2
income through consultancy, R&D projects and training programmes conducted by it. Over the years, it has increasingly become
 self-supporting. Their R&D requirements have been clubbed with the budget provision for IDC.
The R&D budget for (i) System Engineering and Consultancy Programme, (ii) Power Sector Electronics Programme, (iii)
 Industrial Electronics and Promotion Programme, (iv) National Radar Council (v) Electronics for Health Care, (vi) Industrial
 Robotics and Integrated Automation, (vii) Energy Conservation through Industrial Electronics, (viii) Capital Goods Development
 Programme, (ix) Electronics Material Development Programme and (x) Technology Missions have been clubbed with the Budget
 for TDC for better focus and optimum utilisation of funds. It may be noted that IDC budget which in 1995-96 was only Rs. 1.75
 crores had been increased to Rs. 24.17 crores in 1996-97 by clubbing the funds requirements of the above Programmes.
1.2 The Electronics industry development project is a project for man power development supported by World Bank and
 Swiss Development Cooperation. The project started in June 1991 and is coming to' an end in March 1997. Most of the
 expenditure for various activities has been incurred till 1995-96. The residual work to be completed in 1996-97 has lower
 financial requirements than in 1995-96.
1.3 The Budget provision for the Japanese language training has been curtailed keeping in view that the industry who are the
 ultimate beneficiary of this programme, should also financially contribute towards this programme.
1.4 Thus, the reduction in budgetory support in 1996-97 is not because of lack of programmes but because of lack of funds
 allocated by Planning Commission.
COMMENTS:
The Committee notes the position.
RECOMMENDATIONS:
2. While the overall staff strength is set to register a decline in 1997 as compared to 1996, it is significant to note that the
 posts in higher scales of Rs. 450~5700 and above are on the increase. The decline in the number of posts is mainly confined to
 the Pay Scale of Rs. 3700-5000 and below. This reflects the state of depression which has its bearing on the generation of
 employment.
Action taken by the Department
The Department of Electronics was set up in 1970. At the time of its inception, more posts in the lower level were filled than
 the higher one's. The Department is following the Flexible Complementing Scheme (FCS) in respect of its S&T personnel.
 Under the FCS Scheme, the promotion of S&T personnel is person oriented i.e. at the time of promotion, the lower post is

 automatically abolished and the higher post is created.' Hence, gradually the posts in the higher scales have been increasing and
 the lower grades are declining. Moreover, the Government has imposed 10% cut in the staff strength. An exercise to this effect
 was also carried out in this Department and a target of 9.61 % has been achieved by I" abolishing various posts. This is also one of
 the reasons for variations in the number of posts.
COMMENTS:
The Committee is not satisfied with the reply. The Committee feels that the number of higher posts should he in proportion to
 certain number of lower posts. If a sufficient number of lower posts cannot be justified there should be a corresponding reduction
 in the number of higher posts. The Department of Electronics should give a note on the subject.

RECOMMENDATIONS:
3. The Committee strongly feels that the DOE has failed to orient itself to the changing needs of the country and development. The
 Department appears to have deviated from its directed policy and therefore it needs introspection for a suitable direction in the context
 of National development.
Action taken by the Department
The Department of Electronics has not deviated from its directed policy. With Iiberalisation of economy, DOE is placing more
 emphasis on its promotional role. As financial allocations have been drastically reduced against requirements and further because of
 the directive that no new programmes are to be supported in the last year of the 8th Plan, all the development programmes could not
 be addressed fully. However, the 9th Plan proposes several new initiatives for accelerated development of electronics.
COMMENTS
As a result of developments in science, changes take place in the field of electronics at a faster pace. Department of Electronics
 should keep itself abreast with all the developments, possess the knowledge, equipment and wherewithal to assess the utility and
 potential of such changes and be in a position to recommend what is best suited in the context of national requirements. If required it
 should be in the position to develop certain models based on the latest changes without effecting substantial changes in its production
 base and recommend the same to the industry.
RECOMMENDA TIONS:
4. The Committee observes that an amount of Rs. 10.40 crores could not be utilised due to non-materialisation of DANIDA project.
 The Committee observes that the project was not planned properly taking all the contingencies into account. This also reflects on the
 inability of the Department to utilise foreign assistance.
Action taken by the Department
The terms & conditions of DANIDA project were not acceptable to DOE both technically and financially. Firstly, the DANIDA
 project was a mixed credit/loan and not a grant-in ­-aid. Secondly, DANIDA insisted procurement of equipment impart training only
 from Denmark, wherein 60% of loan amount would have flown back to Denmark. Thirdly, the entire project management activity was
 to be handled by Danish contractor and not by STQC. Hence, DOE decided to drop the project on its own, as these terms and
 conditions were found to be not suitable.
Regarding proper utilisation of foreign assistance, it is pertinent to mention that STQC has successfully implemented the Indo-
German project for 15 years from 1980 to 1995. Even currently, another Indo-German project viz. Society for Electronics Test
 Engineering. (SETE) is being successfully implemented. This shows that STQClDOE is able to utilise foreign assistance effectively,
 provided the terms and Conditions are favourable to the Indian Government.
COMMENTS:
The Committee feels that Department of Electronics should have, before accepting the project, seen through the terms and
 conditions carefully. It should have declined the offer ab initio if it did not suit us instead of first accepting and then dithering on the
 same. In future, greater care should be taken in accepting the foreign projects and national interest should be uppermost in our 'minds.
RECOMMENDA TIONS:
5 (a): There has been significant increase in the operational expanses (Plan as well as Non-Plan) of Electronics Regional Test
 Laboratories. The actual expenditure was Rs. 3.12 crores (Plan) and Rs. 1.17 crores (Non-Plan) in 1994-95. It went up to Rs. 3.26
 crores (Plan) and Rs. 1.40 crores (Non-Plan) and remained at that level in the revised estimates for 1995-96. The budget estimates
 for 1996-97 provide Rs. 3.75 crores (Plan) and Rs. 1.40 crores (Non-Plan). The Committee feels there is need to check the Non-
Plan expenditure. Same is the case in respect of operational expenses of Electronics and Test and Development centres.
(b): The Committee feels that there is need to make such laboratories and test centres self supporting. They should provide test
 facilities on commercial basis instead of depending on budgetary support.
Action taken by the Department
(a): The reasons for increase in the operational expenditure (Plan as well as Non-Plan) of Electronics Regional Test Laboratories

 salaries and increase in travel allowance of employees, electricity, telephone bills, etc. because of enhancement in tariff.

ACQUISITION ON AN' ICEBREAKERIMULTIPURPOSE OCEANOGRAPHIC RESEARCH VESSEL
The Department related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and Forests
 in its 35th Report on Demands for Grants 1996-97 of the Department of Ocean Development has recommended that
 the Department should work out the economics of all the alternatives to acquire, including the purchase of a new vessel
 and plan its strategy accordingly, and further that the Committee should be apprised of economics of all the proposals.
The specifications of an Icebreaker-cum-Multipurpose vessel was drawn up by an Expert Group constituted by the
 Department and was circulated in the international market in 1994. However, no offer was received which conform'
 precisely to our specifications. In the meantime, in view of the then political scenario in Russia, an Expert Group
 visited Russia for a market survey. The Expert Group had a meeting with the Chief Expert of the Russian Federal

 modifications for other oceanographic research was pursued. However, Russia could not offer such a second hand
 vessel meeting our requirements.
Following the recommendations of the Parliamentary Committee, yet another attempt was made to explore the
 availability of any suitable second hand vessel.
The results of our enquiry are as follows:
1.    There is a vessel under construction in Germany and will cost around 76 million DM or in other words around
 Rs. 150 crores. The requirements of any modifications for our work has not been explored.
(b) Two old vessels, namely, (1) CARIBOO and (2) LIVONIA are available. The CARIBOO would cost around
 US $s 8 million (around Rs. 30 crores); whereas LIVONIA may cost 20 million US $s (around Rs. 70 crores);
(c) The offers. of these second hand vessels received do not indicate the helipad specifications and modifications
 may include helipad construction also. Further, as per the present Antarctic requirements, the vessel should be
 capable of accommodating around 65 persons in each Expedition. These vessels do not meet our requirements.
2. Against the above background, the broad economics are as follows:-
(a) Considering the lowest offer of a second hand vessel of around Rs. 30 crores only, even without any
 modification requirements, would mean an additional annual maintenance charges of atleast Rs. 10 crores per
 annum, based on the experience of ORV Sagar Kanya.
(b) . The Antarctic Expeditions leave in December and return to India towards the end of March. If it has to be
 used for oceanographic survey, the same has to be carried out between April and October. During this period,
 the period of monsoons also overlap.
(c) Even assuming that some oceanographic work is possible, the ship will have to be mobilised after proper dry
 docking etc. and made· ready for the Antarctic Expedition. It is likely that about one month of ship time will
 be lost in the process and additional expenditure incurred. In other words, in practical terns, the vessel would
 be utilised only for Antarctic expeditions.

Present Arrangement for Antarctic Expeditions:-
The Department has entered into a three year charter covering upto 1997-1998 season. The total charter cost per annum is around
 Rs. 9 crores approximately.
The chartering of a vessel providing their own officers and crew. The Department's budget is limited and the present budget does
 not allow for purchase of new vessel costing around Rs. 150 crores or more. In fact the present budget does not also allow even
 investments of the order of Rs. 30 crores besides additional operational and maintenance costs.     
On the other hand chartering of a vessel on an average of around Rs. 10 crores per annum would meet our Antarctic requirements
 and does not cost any additional investment on employment, maintenance, operational costs, spares, dry docking, etc. Acquisition of a
 second hand vessel and modifications cannot make it all purpose and will have limited functions only. In the event the future Antarctic
 programme involves going to Rose Sea or other difficult areas of Antarctica, it would be necessary to deploy an Icebreaker rather than
 Ice Class vessels, such as CARIBOO 
or LIVONIA.
Taking the overall considerations, as desired by Secretary DOD, a joint meeting of JS, JS & FA and Adviser was convened to
 examine this issue. The meeting arrives at the following conclusions:

(b)    (b) the option of a purchase of second hand vessel and further modifications will not prove to be more cost effective than the
 present arrangement for chartering the vessel for the Antarctic Expedition;
(c) The Department already has ORV Sagar Kanya and FORV Sagar Sampada. In addition, it has recently commissioned a CRV
 Sagar Paschmi. Another CRV is expected to be commissioned very soon.
